molla — Rust + WGPU Physics Engine

Introduction

molla is a pure-Rust, wgpu-accelerated physics engine. It is a from-scratch reimplementation of the algorithms that ship in NVIDIA Newton and NVIDIA Warp, expressed in idiomatic Rust with WGSL kernels so that the same binary runs on Vulkan, Metal, DirectX 12, and (one day) WebGPU. There is no CUDA in the build graph, no external runtime in the hot loop, and no vendor lock-in: a laptop with an AMD APU, an Intel Arc card, an Apple M-series chip, or an NVIDIA discrete GPU are all first-class targets.

This book is the long-form companion to the source. It covers what the engine looks like, what the code is doing, and — just as importantly — what is not in scope and why. If you only have five minutes, the short version is below; if you have an afternoon, jump straight to the Architecture overview or to the Scene catalog for ~100 self-contained Bevy demos that exercise every solver and kernel.

What molla is, in one paragraph

A modular Cargo workspace with a top-level molla facade library, reusable functionality crates under crates/, and the molla_viewer Bevy application under bin/. The public facade keeps use molla::prelude::* stable while implementation ownership is split by function: core IDs/errors, math, storage, compute runtime, kernels, simulation data, geometry, solvers, FEM, sensors, actuators, autograd, and optimizers each live in their own crate. The viewer depends on the facade and is the showroom; it is not a reusable library crate.

Design ethos

molla is opinionated. The choices that shaped the codebase are:

  1. GPU-first, but always CPU-checkable. Every kernel has a CPU implementation that produces the same output (modulo float-op ordering). The two paths run side-by-side in #[ignore]-gated parity tests. The CPU path is not a fallback — it is the oracle.
  2. Mixed precision by design. Host-side state is f64. GPU kernels are f32 because WGSL has no f64. Conversions happen exactly once, at the Buffer<T> boundary in storage. No code in the math layer ever sees a precision-mixing site.
  3. Data layout mirrors Newton. Model (immutable), State (positions / velocities / forces), Control (joint targets, wrenches), Contacts (collision output) are the four pillars. The shape is good, downstream adapters depend on it, and copying it makes Newton’s test fixtures usable verbatim as oracles.
  4. One reference algorithm per regime, then expand. Semi-implicit Euler for unconstrained rigid, Featherstone ABA for articulated, XPBD for constrained / particles / cloth, VBD for soft bodies, MPM for granular and snow, and a full FEM stack (heat / elasticity / Stokes / Navier-Stokes / Maxwell). Each was bootstrapped, tested, and benched before the next one was started.
  5. Switchable CPU↔GPU at all times. The Engine exposes a Backend::Cpu | Backend::Gpu toggle. Solvers, sensors, actuators, sparse linear algebra, FEM steppers, and the viewer all honor it. You can flip the toggle at runtime in the viewer’s UI and watch the wall-clock change without rebuilding.

Newton / Warp lineage

molla’s references are the read-only xtra/newton/ and xtra/warp/ trees, both Apache-2.0. We read them — we do not port them line for line. Algorithms are reimplemented clean-room from the documented behaviour and test fixtures; invariants are ported into Rust tests rather than executed through an external runtime.

When the same primitive exists in Warp (raycast, FFT, marching cubes, sparse-grid, tile primitives, gaussian splats, autograd tape), molla ships the same primitive with the same name where it makes Rust ergonomics work. ~30 scenes in the viewer are direct ports of warp/examples/*.py so behaviour can be eyeballed against the upstream renderer.

Why Rust + wgpu?

The original brief — “GPU physics that runs on something other than NVIDIA” — has only one good answer in 2026: WebGPU as the lingua franca. wgpu is the mature Rust implementation of that spec. Choosing it gets us Vulkan (Linux desktop + Steam Deck), Metal (Apple laptops + iPad), DirectX 12 (Windows), and WebGPU (browser) from a single backend with no platform-specific code in the engine. The cost is the WGSL feature set: no f64, no atomic<f32>, no subgroup intrinsics in the stable spec, no cooperative_matrix. The engine is designed around those constraints — atomic-CAS loops on u32 reinterpreted as f32, host-resident f64 state, persistent device buffers — and it pays back the constraint in portability.

Rust as the host language gives us deterministic memory layout via bytemuck, lifetime-safe buffer ownership through the Buffer<T> abstraction, and the same glam types on host (DVec3 / DMat3 / DQuat) and (via codegen) the device side. The codebase has zero unsafe blocks outside of Pod/Zeroable derives.

Scope: everything below Stage 51

The roadmap is split into numbered stages, each a self-contained deliverable with tests + benches + a viewer scene (see Stage history). At the time of writing, stages 0 through 51 are complete:

  • 0–6: scaffolding, math, storage, GPU runtime, semi-implicit Euler, XPBD rigid + capsule + cylinder + GJK + EPA + BVH + trimesh.
  • 7–13: joint types (revolute / prismatic / fixed / free / ball / D6 / distance / CABLE), equality constraints (CONNECT / weld / joint mimic), articulation (Featherstone ABA + CRBA + RNEA), specialty shapes (cone, convex hull, heightfield, SDF).
  • 14–19: GPU sensors (raycast / camera / IMU / contact / frame transform), GPU IK, GPU narrow-phase, multi-DOF Featherstone, GPU broadphase (LBVH).
  • 20–24: VBD soft bodies (cloth / cable / tets / jelly), mesh utilities (decimate / SDF bake / marching cubes), differentiable Featherstone, raycast adjoint, MPM (explicit + semi-implicit + implicit Bingham + 27-stencil), sparse-grid (NanoVDB-equivalent).
  • 25–35: hardening, joint-mimic equality, neural LSTM controllers, soft self-collision, soft VT contact GPU, cloth-collar self-collision, fast-impact CCD.
  • 36–46: FEM framework v1 (P1 nodal scalar), elasticity (linear
    • St.-Venant-Kirchhoff), Stokes (Taylor-Hood + Uzawa-CG), adjoint FEM, GPU FEM, P2 elements, APIC FEM-MPM hybrid, Navier-Stokes (IMEX), DG (P0 / P1 / P2 + Barth-Jespersen
    • HLL/HLLC/Roe SWE flux), magnetostatics (H(curl) Nedelec), eddy currents (time-harmonic Maxwell + AMG + AMS), Gaussian splat renderer (forward + reverse + SH band 3), AMR, distortion energy.
  • 47–51: nonconforming cross-mesh L² projection, surface-only cross-mesh quadrature, penalty + Signorini hard contact, Coulomb friction, active-set update loop.

Each stage has a test, a bench (where applicable), and a viewer scene. The stage system is for historical / changelog purposes only — you don’t need to know which stage shipped which kernel to use the engine. The prelude re-exports the most common types and you write use molla::prelude::* and go.

Explicit out-of-scope

These were considered and deliberately rejected, mostly because they are either NVIDIA-only or non-portable:

  • Style3D cloth. Newton’s production cloth solver — multi-year effort, not needed for molla’s audience (robotics + games + VFX research).
  • Kamino PADMM. Out of scope for the current native solver set.
  • TensorCore tile matmul / cooperative_matrix. wgpu does not expose the extension portably across the four backends. molla’s tile-matmul kernel is a plain WGSL implementation.
  • CUDA Graphs. wgpu has no capture / replay API. The molla equivalent is persistent device buffers + single-encoder dispatch batching (see Stage 24d.2 for the MPM case study).
  • Multi-GPU peer access. wgpu is single-device. The Engine type owns one wgpu::Device and one wgpu::Queue.
  • General LCP / NLP solver. Position-based constraints (XPBD) and reduced-coordinate articulation (Featherstone) cover the workhorse cases.
  • Own renderer. Visualization piggybacks on Bevy (in the viewer crate) and the Gaussian-splat differentiable renderer for the diff-render scenes. The engine has zero renderer dependencies.

Audience

This book is written for:

  • Rust users who want a physics engine that doesn’t drag a CUDA toolchain into their build.
  • Robotics researchers who want differentiable trajectories on the laptop they already own.
  • Graphics + simulation engineers who want a clean reference reimplementation of Newton / Warp’s algorithms with readable, test-covered Rust.
  • Anyone porting Newton/Warp algorithms — the data model is intentionally familiar and the test fixtures are reused.

What this book is not: an introduction to physics simulation in general. We assume you know what a quaternion is, what XPBD does in broad strokes, and why a semi-implicit Euler is different from RK4. Newton’s docs and the seminal papers each chapter links to are the right starting points for the underlying numerics.

How this book is organized

  • Foundations — what’s in crates/molla, how the workspace is laid out, what each Cargo feature gates, and the design rules every contributor needs to follow.
  • Math & Numerics — the host f64 math layer, the BSR sparse algebra, iterative solvers, optimizers, graph coloring, radix sort.
  • Compute & GPU — the wgpu runtime, the Buffer<T> / Storage abstraction, the kernel infrastructure, the tile-compute primitives, the persistent-buffer pattern.
  • Geometry & Collision — shape primitives, hull builder, BVH, spatial hash, broad-phase, narrow-phase (GJK / EPA / MPR), hydroelastic, sparse grids.
  • Simulation Core — Model / State / Control / Contacts, ModelBuilder, joints, articulation, CRBA / RNEA / Jacobian, IK.
  • Solvers — semi-implicit, XPBD, VBD, Featherstone, and MPM.
  • Finite-Element Method — the FEM v1 framework and everything built on top (P2, DG, Stokes, Navier-Stokes, APIC, adjoint, AMR, magnetostatics, eddy currents, multigrid, nonconforming meshes, Signorini contact, Coulomb friction).
  • Sensors — raycaster, tiled camera, IMU, contact, frame transform.
  • Actuators & Control — composable pipeline, PD / PID, neural controllers (MLP + LSTM), DC motor clamping, Hill-type muscle.
  • Differentiable Physics — tape-based autograd, Featherstone reverse adjoint, XPBD / VBD / MPM / FEM / raycast / splat adjoints.
  • Viewer — the Bevy adapter, the scene catalog.
  • Testing & Performance — strategy, parity tests, FD gradient checks, criterion benches, GPU port status matrix.
  • Roadmap — chronological stage history, open follow-ups, the out-of-scope list.

Start where you need. The Scene catalog is the most fun way in if you just want to see what the engine does. The Architecture overview is the right place if you’re embedding the engine in something else and want to know what each layer is doing.

Architecture overview

molla is structured as a stack of layers, each of which depends only on the ones below it. The same engine binary can run wholly on the CPU, wholly on the GPU, or on a mix of both, and the layering makes that toggle a single line of code instead of an architectural surgery.

The layered design

                ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
                │  adapters    molla_viewer (Bevy ECS)    │
                ├─────────────────────────────────────────┤
                │  solvers     SemiImplicit · XPBD ·      │
                │              Featherstone · VBD · MPM · │
                │              FEM steppers               │
                ├─────────────────────────────────────────┤
                │  sim         Model · State · Control ·  │
                │              Contacts · ModelBuilder    │
                ├─────────────────────────────────────────┤
                │  geometry · sensors · actuators · fem · │
                │  autograd · optim                       │
                ├─────────────────────────────────────────┤
                │  compute     Engine · Backend selector  │
                │  kernels     58 WGSL kernels + Rust     │
                │              dispatchers + CPU oracles  │
                ├─────────────────────────────────────────┤
                │  storage     Buffer<T> · BufferUsage    │
                ├─────────────────────────────────────────┤
                │  math        f64 host (DVec3 / DMat3 /  │
                │              DQuat / Transform / BSR)   │
                ├─────────────────────────────────────────┤
                │  core        BodyId / JointId / Errors  │
                └─────────────────────────────────────────┘

Read it bottom-up — each layer is built from the ones below it.

core — IDs and errors

core defines the typed handles (BodyId, JointId, ParticleId, ShapeId, WorldId) and the engine-wide Error enum (thiserror-derived; no anyhow inside the engine crate). Everything else uses these.

math — host arithmetic

math is the host-side f64 math layer. It wraps glam::DVec3 / DMat3 / DQuat (renamed Vec3 / Mat3 / Quat for terseness), exposes Transform, SpatialVector / SpatialInertia for Featherstone spatial algebra, the BSR sparse matrix + iterative solvers (CG, BiCGStab, GMRES, PCG), the small-matrix decompositions (SVD3, polar, QR3, symmetric eig3), and the graph-coloring utilities.

storage — the buffer abstraction

storage::Buffer<T> is the single chokepoint where host f64 becomes device f32. Every piece of long-lived data in Model, State, Control is a Buffer. A buffer holds either a host Vec (CPU mode) or a wgpu::Buffer (GPU mode), tracked by BufferUsage. Conversions happen once on upload / download — math code never sees mixed precision.

compute — the wgpu runtime

compute::Engine owns the wgpu::Device + Queue and exposes the Backend enum: Backend::Cpu skips device dispatch entirely; Backend::Gpu uses the real adapter. The engine is constructed once (via pollster for the sync API) and threaded into every solver / sensor that needs a device.

kernels and functionality-owned GPU dispatchers

GPU dispatchers are split by ownership instead of by CPU/GPU:

  1. Shared dispatch wrappers and WGSL sources live in crates/molla-kernels/.
  2. Functionality-specific dispatchers live next to their owner crate; for example GJK/EPA/MPR, LBVH, and mesh-BVH raycast live in crates/molla-geometry/, FEM GPU kernels live in crates/molla-fem/, and tiled/radix primitives live in crates/molla-compute-primitives/.
  3. crates/molla/src/kernels/ is now a compatibility surface for molla::kernels::*, not the source of ownership.

Each dispatcher still follows the same pattern: a WGSL source file, a Rust type that owns the wgpu::ComputePipeline and bind-group layouts, and CPU/oracle coverage in the owning crate’s tests where applicable.

geometry, sensors, actuators, fem, autograd, optim

These sit at the same horizontal level. They consume kernels + math + storage and expose pluggable building blocks. The FEM stack alone is ~30 kernels deep and is documented as its own chapter family.

sim — the data model

sim::Model is the immutable simulation description. [sim::State] is the time-varying positions / velocities / forces. [sim::Control] is the user input (joint targets, applied wrenches). [sim::Contacts] is the collision-pipeline output that solvers consume each step. [sim::ModelBuilder] is the fluent authoring API used by procedural scene/test builders.

solvers — the step functions

Each solver implements the [Solver] trait: given &Model, &State, &Control, &Contacts, dt, write the next State. Solver kinds in prelude:

  • SemiImplicitSolver — unconstrained Euler, the baseline (Stage 1).
  • XpbdSolver — position-based constraints, particles + rigid + cloth.
  • FeatherstoneSolver — reduced-coordinate articulated rigid (ABA).
  • VbdSolver — Vertex Block Descent for cloth + cable + tets + jelly. There is no FEM solver in this list — FEM steppers live in fem and are wired into specific scenes via state structs.

Adapters

The Bevy adapter is the molla_viewer crate. The engine roadmap is physics-only: no importer/exporter, MJCF/USD/URDF/Gmsh path, or external FFI solver wrapper is part of the supported architecture.

The CPU↔GPU rule

This is the architecture’s most load-bearing convention:

Every solver, sensor, actuator, FEM stepper, and primitive kernel can step on either CPU or GPU, and the choice is a runtime Backend toggle — not a compile-time feature.

Concretely:

  • The gpu Cargo feature gates the availability of the GPU path (it pulls in wgpu + pollster). With gpu off, the CPU paths still compile and run.
  • With gpu on, every XxxSolver::new_cpu() / new_gpu(&engine) pair gives the user a runtime choice.
  • Parity tests live with the crate that owns the functionality (crates/molla-solvers/tests/*_gpu.rs, crates/molla-kernels/tests/*_gpu.rs, etc.) unless they are facade/product compatibility coverage in crates/molla/tests/. They take the same input, run both backends, and assert that the trajectories agree to within the documented tolerance (1e-4 for f32-narrowing, 1e-3 for adjoint-vs-FD checks).

The viewer’s UI has a [CPU] / [GPU] radio button — flipping it rebuilds the active solver from scratch and continues simulating. No restart, no recompile.

See design_rules.md for the full convention list, including why we picked BSR B=1 everywhere, why we use the atomic-CAS pattern over atomic<f32>, and why we don’t depend on cooperative_matrix.

What lives where

crates/molla-core — core handles and errors

Extracted foundation crate. It owns stable IDs (BodyId, JointId, ShapeId, ParticleId, WorldId), the public Error / Result types, MAXVAL, and Axis. The facade re-exports it as molla::core so existing paths keep working.

crates/molla-math — host math and numerics

Extracted foundation crate for Real, Vec3, Quat, Mat3, Transform, spatial algebra, dense/sparse CPU numerics, iterative solvers, and robust losses. The facade re-exports it as molla::math.

crates/molla-storage — buffer abstraction

Extracted foundation crate for Buffer<T>, BufferElement, and BufferUsage. It owns the host/device conversion boundary and is re-exported as molla::storage.

crates/molla-compute — runtime only

Extracted foundation crate for runtime selection and wgpu device/queue ownership (Engine, Backend, AdapterInfo). Higher-level MPM and tile functionality has moved out: MPM drivers live in molla-solvers, tiled compute primitives live in molla-compute-primitives, and the 2-D Stam stable-fluid solver lives in molla-fem because its GPU projection reuses FEM FFT-Poisson.

crates/molla-compute-primitives — tiled compute primitives

Functional crate for reusable tiled compute code. It owns tiled matmul, block-Cholesky, convolution/filtering, stream compaction, and MC-GP helpers plus their WGSL files. The facade keeps molla::compute::tile_* compatibility paths.

crates/molla-sim — raw simulation data model

Extracted functional crate for Model, State, Control, Contacts, ModelBuilder, shape descriptors, raw TriMesh, and raw soft-surface model descriptors. The facade re-exports it as molla::sim.

Raw soft-surface descriptors live here; FEM boundary-facet extraction lives in molla-fem, and the old molla::geometry::soft_surface::* facade path re-exports both sides for compatibility.

crates/molla-optim — host optimizers

Extracted functional crate for host-side Adam and SGD optimizer state. The facade re-exports it as molla::optim.

crates/molla-actuators — actuator models

Functional crate for actuator code. It owns the host Hill-type muscle model and the GPU-first PD/PID, neural MLP/LSTM, delay, clamping, and actuator-pipeline orchestrators. molla::actuators::* remains a facade compatibility path while the dispatch wrappers and WGSL files live under molla-kernels.

crates/molla-kernels — extracted GPU dispatch slices

Started kernel crate. It currently owns dense3, robust-loss, optimizer Adam/SGD, scan, Dahl friction, contact reduction, GPU hydroelastic anchor reduction, sensor dispatch wrappers, actuator/clamping/muscle dispatch wrappers, and rigid-body solver dispatch wrappers for integrate-bodies, CRBA, RNEA, Jacobian, XPBD, Featherstone, VBD/soft-contact, implicit-MPM, FFT, sparse-grid, Gaussian splat raytrace, and Featherstone adjoint, plus their WGSL files. Radix sort lives in molla-compute-primitives; geometry GJK/EPA/MPR, mesh-BVH raycast, and LBVH live in molla-geometry, with compatibility re-exports from molla-kernels. The facade keeps molla::kernels::* compatibility through thin re-export modules only; implementation ownership lives in the kernel, geometry, compute-primitive, or functionality crate.

crates/molla-sensors — sensor helpers

Functional crate for sensor code. It owns the GPU-first raycast, tiled camera, IMU, contact aggregation, and frame-transform orchestrators, plus the CPU finite-difference raycast adjoint/oracle. molla::sensors::* remains a facade compatibility path.

crates/molla-geometry — geometry primitives

Started functional crate for geometry/collision code. It currently owns Aabb, SpatialHashGrid, MeshBvh, tet AABB helpers, convex support functions, convex hull authoring, world-frame shape-transform/AABB helpers, QEM mesh decimation, dense mesh SDF baking, sparse volume/SDF storage, marching cubes, brute-force/SAP/BVH broad phase, CPU narrow-phase dispatch, GJK/EPA/MPR convex queries, Gaussian splat math, hydroelastic contact, soft BVH/VT CCD, and the CPU contact-reduction primitive plus warm-start/matching extras; the broader collision pipeline remains in the facade until the kernel and domain dependencies are untangled.

crates/molla-solvers — solver and dynamics helpers

Started functional crate for solver code. It currently owns CPU-only CRBA mass-matrix assembly, recursive Newton-Euler inverse dynamics, geometric Jacobian helpers, inverse kinematics, VBD soft-contact helpers, the shared Solver trait, the CPU/GPU semi-implicit rigid-body solver, CPU/GPU XPBD, CPU/GPU VBD, CPU/GPU Featherstone, the implicit MPM CPU driver, and the explicit GPU MpmSimulation driver. Featherstone’s tape helper API is gated behind molla-solvers/autograd; the public facade enables that feature to preserve the compatibility API without making standalone solver users depend on autograd unconditionally.

crates/molla-autograd — CPU tape and adjoints

Started functional crate for autograd code. It currently owns the engine-agnostic CPU tape, differentiable arm helper, Featherstone adjoint data/trace helpers, XPBD distance-constraint adjoint helpers, and the differentiable CPU MPM forward/adjoint pair. The facade still exposes molla::compute::mpm_cpu_diff::* as a compatibility re-export.

crates/molla-fem — finite-element methods

Extracted functional crate for FEM code. It compiles the FEM module tree independently: mesh/function spaces, quadrature, assembly, CPU/GPU solvers, DG/AMR/APIC coupling, Stokes/NS paths, magnetostatics, eddy currents, Signorini, nonconforming contact, and FEM-specific GPU kernels. The facade molla::fem::* module is a compatibility re-export of molla-fem; generic GPU BSR sparse algebra lives in molla-kernels and is also preserved through the old molla::math facade path.

crates/molla — the facade and remaining engine

This is the part you would embed in your application. Zero dependencies on Bevy, ROS, or any rendering / IO format. ~50k lines of Rust + ~30k lines of WGSL.

compute~3kwgpu runtime + MPM + tile primitives
math~3khost math + BSR + iterative solvers + dense3
autograd~2ktape + Featherstone reverse + raycast adjoint
actuators~1.5kPD / PID / DC / neural / muscle / delay
sensors~1.5kraycast / camera / IMU / contact / frame xform
storage~0.5kBuffer<T>

bin/molla_viewer — the showroom

A Bevy 0.18 + bevy_egui + bevy_frost + bevy_glacial application that loads any of ~100 scenes and renders them in real time. It is kept under bin/ because it is a runnable app, not a reusable library crate. It is deliberately a single file (src/main.rs, ~24k lines) so the “add a scene” workflow is one PR that touches one file.

Why bevy_frost + bevy_glacial:

  • bevy_frost is an egui-themed glass UI kit. It provides the right-rail control pane and the per-scene sliders.
  • bevy_glacial is an orbit camera + grid + gizmos plugin. It saves the viewer from reimplementing scene-camera logic from scratch.

Both are pulled from bresilla/* repos because they are not yet on crates.io. They are pure Bevy plugins — there is no molla code in either.

xtra/ — read-only reference

The directory is excluded from the Cargo workspace (exclude = ["xtra"]) so cargo build never compiles it. The trees are:

  • xtra/newton/ — the NVIDIA Newton tree. It is a read-only algorithm reference and is not part of the Rust build graph. Apache-2.0.
  • xtra/warp/ — the NVIDIA Warp tree. warp/examples/*.py are the reference renderings for the ~30 Warp* scenes in the viewer. Apache-2.0.

You can ignore xtra/ entirely unless you are porting a new algorithm — at which point you’ll want both trees open in your editor (see the [reference_warp_newton.md] note in user memory).

Modularization rule

molla is being split by functionality, not by CPU/GPU backend. Each functional crate owns both its CPU oracle and its GPU implementation wherever a GPU path is feasible. crates/molla stays as the public facade and bin/molla_viewer stays as a runnable viewer only.

Crate boundaries

molla is being modularized by functionality. The current workspace has the foundation crates molla-core, molla-math, molla-storage, runtime-only molla-compute, tiled compute primitive crate molla-compute-primitives, data-model crate molla-sim, host optimizer crate molla-optim, the first molla-actuators slice, the first molla-kernels slices, the first molla-sensors slice, the first molla-geometry slice, the first molla-solvers slice, the first molla-autograd slice, the first molla-fem slice, and the wheeled-vehicle crate molla-vehicle extracted; molla remains the public facade plus remaining engine modules; bin/molla_viewer is the binary-only Bevy application.

            │   molla_viewer     │   Bevy 0.18 application
            │  bin/molla_viewer  │

                      │ depends on
                      ▼
            ┌────────────────────┐
            │       molla        │   public facade + engine modules
            └─────────┬──────────┘
                      │ re-exports
                      ▼

The rules

  1. Library crates know nothing about Bevy, ROS, JSON, YAML, or external asset formats. The main molla facade/engine only knows about simulation data, solvers, kernels, and physics modules it owns.
  2. bin/molla_viewer is allowed to depend on Bevy + bevy_egui + bevy_frost + bevy_glacial + mimalloc. That is the full surface; the viewer binary package is the only place those dependencies live.
  3. No importer/exporter or external solver-wrapper crates. Procedural model construction is the supported surface; physics modules own physics data and kernels only.
  4. Optional native dependencies are behind Cargo features. See features.md. The features gate compilation of whole modules so a clean cargo build on a stock Rust toolchain succeeds without SuiteSparse / LAPACKE installed.
  5. There is no Python in the build graph. The xtra/ trees are read-only references and are not workspace members.

Modularization direction

The accepted direction is functional crate boundaries, not CPU-vs-GPU splits. crates/ is for reusable libraries, bin/ is for runnable applications, and crates/molla remains the public facade that preserves molla::prelude::*.

The exclude = ["xtra"] line is what stops cargo build from ever descending into the Newton / Warp reference trees. They are read-only references kept side-by-side in the repository for convenience.

Dependency rules for outside users

If you depend on molla from another crate:

  • Default features include gpu — your build will pull wgpu
    • pollster. Use default-features = false to skip those if you only want the CPU paths.
  • russell is off by default and reserves the direct-solver surface for optional sparse-linear-algebra experiments. The current implementation stays pure Rust in the nix dev shell.
  • The prelude is stable. Anything outside prelude may move between minor releases until 0.1.0.

The crate is on 0.0.1 at present; no SemVer guarantees yet. The PLAN’s quality bar is that every shipped feature has a trajectory or unit test, an example, a bench, and CPU/GPU parity — that is the unofficial release criterion.

Feature flags

molla keeps feature flags small and physics-focused. Importers, external solver wrappers, MJCF/USD/URDF pipelines, and FFI bindings are intentionally not feature flags in this roadmap.

Engine-crate features (molla)

gpu — the wgpu backend (default-on)

Pulls in wgpu 27 and pollster, enabling GPU dispatchers and GPU solver constructors. CPU paths still compile and remain the correctness oracle.

russell — direct solver shim

Enables fem::DirectSolver / fem::solve_steady_state_direct. The current implementation is pure Rust; no SuiteSparse/LAPACKE dependency is required.

Viewer-crate features (molla_viewer)

profile

Forwards bevy/trace_tracy for Tracy instrumentation.

log_diag

Prints Bevy/molla diagnostics once per second without Tracy.

Matrix

FeatureCrateDefaultPullsGates
gpumollayeswgpu, pollsterGPU kernels, GPU solvers/sensors
russellmollano—FEM direct solve shim
profilemolla_viewernobevy/trace_tracyTracy spans
log_diagmolla_viewerno—text diagnostics

There is no MuJoCo/MJCF/URDF/USD/Gmsh feature in the physics-only plan.

Build & test commands

The Makefile at the repository root is the canonical entry point for building, testing, and running. GPU-touching targets go through the RUN_WITH wrapper (default nixVulkan) so the wgpu Vulkan loader is reachable from the nix devShell; outside the devShell, override it with RUN_WITH= (empty) to run plain cargo.

Quick reference

TargetWhat it does
make build / bcargo build -p molla_viewer (the viewer pulls in every crate)
make compile / ccargo clean then build
make run / rnixVulkan cargo run -p molla_viewer
make test / tcargo test -p molla_viewer (viewer suite; skips #[ignore] GPU)
make test-gpuOne GPU test lane: P=<crate> T=<test-file> A=<extra args>
make test-allcargo test --workspace --all-targets
make checkcargo check -p molla_viewer
make check-allcargo check --workspace --all-targets
make hardenThe full gate: whitespace check, fmt --check, no-default-features build+test, clippy --all-features -D warnings, all-feature tests
make benchnixVulkan cargo bench
make docsBuild the mdBook into docs/
make cleancargo clean

There is no make fmt target — run cargo fmt --all directly (or rely on make harden, which checks formatting).

Useful variables: RUN_WITH= (drop the nixVulkan wrapper), RUN_WITH=nixGL (OpenGL instead of Vulkan), APP_PKG=<pkg> (build/run/test a different package), BACKEND=x11 (display backend; .envrc auto-detects).

The two cargo modes

molla has two effective build modes, gated by Cargo features.

Default mode — gpu on

nixVulkan cargo build --workspace --all-targets
nixVulkan cargo test  --workspace

Compiles everything. The #[ignore]-gated GPU parity tests don’t run; the CPU paths + CPU oracle tests do. This is the everyday lane.

Headless / CI mode — gpu off

cargo build --workspace --no-default-features
cargo test  --workspace --no-default-features

Skips wgpu entirely. Every _gpu test compiles out (they’re #[cfg(feature = "gpu")]-gated). Useful when you don’t have a wgpu adapter (cloud CI runners, docker images without GPU passthrough).

Running GPU parity tests

GPU tests are gated behind #[ignore] because they need a real wgpu::Adapter. They all run through one generic Makefile lane — pick the package with P=, the integration-test file with T=, optional extra test-binary args with A=, and RELEASE=1 for the perf-gated lanes:

make test-gpu                                        # default: molla-solvers cpu_gpu_parity
make test-gpu P=molla-solvers T=xpbd_gpu_parity      # XPBD rigid parity
make test-gpu P=molla-solvers T=vbd_cloth_gpu        # VBD cloth suite
make test-gpu P=molla-solvers T=joint_muscle_gpu     # Hill muscle parity
make test-gpu P=molla-fem     T=fem_transient_gpu    # GPU FEM heat stepper
make test-gpu P=molla-fem     T=fem_wave_gpu         # GPU FEM Newmark wave
make test-gpu P=molla-geometry T=gjk_gpu A=--nocapture
make test-gpu P=molla-kernels T=tire_fem_gpu A=tire_fem_cpu_vs_gpu_rolling_contact_hub_x_parity
make test-gpu P=molla-fem T=fem_ns_gpu RELEASE=1 A='--skip gpu_ns_perf'

Each invocation expands to nixVulkan cargo test -p $(P) --features gpu --test $(T) -- --ignored $(A), so any lane can also be run by hand. To discover the available lanes, list the GPU test files:

ls crates/*/tests | grep gpu

Benches

Benches use criterion and live with their owning functionality crates. make bench runs the whole inventory; to run a specific bench:

nixVulkan cargo bench -p molla-solvers --bench bench_xpbd_pile_gpu --features gpu

The bench inventory is in each owning crate’s Cargo.toml under its [[bench]] sections. For example solver/XPBD/VBD/MPM benches are in crates/molla-solvers, geometry benches in crates/molla-geometry, kernel benches in crates/molla-kernels, sensor benches in crates/molla-sensors, math benches in crates/molla-math, and facade step benches in crates/molla.

Paired CPU-vs-GPU benches (suffix _cpu_vs_gpu) print side-by-side reports in one criterion group so you can eyeball the wall-clock ratio at matched problem sizes.

Running the viewer

make run

For an optimised build, run cargo directly:

nixVulkan cargo run -p molla_viewer --release

The viewer recognises hotkeys for the marquee scenes — see viewer/overview.md.

Common gotchas

  • wgpu init fails with “no adapter found” — you forgot the nixVulkan wrapper (RUN_WITH was overridden to empty). Or you’re in --no-default-features mode (which is fine, but then GPU tests don’t apply).
  • cargo test --features gpu run directly hangs or panics — GPU tests must go through make test-gpu (or a manual nixVulkan prefix) so a real adapter is reachable.
  • Long initial build — first compile pulls ~400 Mb of dependencies (Bevy, wgpu, egui, glam, criterion, …). Subsequent incremental builds are fast.

Design rules

The conventions below are load-bearing. Every contributor — human or AI — has to respect them; reviewers reject PRs that violate them without an explicit deviation note. These are not style guidelines — they are architectural invariants the rest of the engine assumes.

1. Physics must be switchable CPU↔GPU at all times

Every solver, sensor, actuator, FEM stepper, and primitive kernel can step on either CPU or GPU, and the choice is a runtime Backend toggle — not a compile-time feature.

Concrete consequences:

  • Every kernel ships with both a Rust CPU reference implementation and a WGSL device implementation. They produce the same output modulo float-op ordering nondeterminism.
  • Every solver exposes new_cpu() and new_gpu(&engine) constructors. The viewer can swap backends at runtime by dropping the old solver and constructing the new one.
  • Every kernel has a tests/<name>_gpu.rs parity test that runs both backends on identical inputs and asserts trajectory agreement within a documented tolerance (typically 1e-4 for f32-narrowing).
  • The CPU path is the oracle, not the fallback. When a GPU parity test fails, the CPU path is the source of truth — you debug by reading the CPU code, not the WGSL.

This rule predates the gpu Cargo feature flag. The Cargo feature gates availability (it pulls in wgpu). The CPU↔GPU rule is about runtime selection within a build that has the feature on.

See user memory note: “GPU-first rule” — implement physics in WGSL first, copy from Newton / Warp, never start with a Rust host loop. CPU is the oracle, not the starting point.

2. BSR B = 1 everywhere

molla’s sparse matrix type is math::BsrMatrix — block-sparse-row with a runtime block dimension B. Every actual user of the type sets B = 1, which recovers a plain CSR matrix.

Why we ship a parameterised type and then only ever use B = 1:

  • The data layout (row_offsets + col_idx + values) is the same as CSR, so all the iterative solvers (cg, bicgstab, gmres, pcg) work bit-identical on either.
  • The room to grow to B > 1 exists. FEM elasticity has natural 3×3 block structure; if the per-iter BSR matvec becomes the bottleneck we can lift B without rewriting the solver layer.
  • WGSL’s lack of dynamic-size shared memory and pointer-into-storage restrictions make a templated B more painful on the GPU than on the CPU. Keeping B = 1 lets the GPU mirror (BsrGpu) be a trivial three-buffer (row_offsets, col_idx, values) layout with one matvec shader.

The rule is not “BSR with B > 1 is forbidden”. The rule is “don’t introduce B > 1 without a measured win that justifies the GPU complexity”. As of Stage 51 no such win has been measured, so every sparse matrix in the engine is effectively CSR.

3. Persistent buffers, single-encoder dispatch

The naive way to drive a GPU compute kernel is:

loop {
    create_buffer();
    create_bind_group();
    create_command_encoder();
    dispatch();
    submit();
    readback();
}

This was the Stage 24d v1 MPM pattern and it ran at 20 Hz on 10k particles. The Stage 24d v2 dispatcher hoisted the per-iter uniform buffer + bind group + readback staging into MpmSimulation::new_with_device(), then introduced a step_n API that encodes N substeps into a single wgpu::CommandEncoder and submits once. Measured speedup: 6.9× (20 Hz → 75 Hz).

The convention going forward:

  • Allocate persistent buffers at solver construction time. Not per-step.
  • Cache bind groups + pipeline handles once. Look up by buffer identity, not by re-creating per step.
  • Batch substeps into one encoder + one submit. Use step_n / step_n_with patterns; the user-facing step is a back-compat wrapper around step_n(_, _, 1).
  • Read back exactly once per visible frame. Per-substep readback is the most common perf bug; the GPU is happy to crunch 100 substeps in 13 ms, but the wgpu submit + readback overhead per call dominates if you call it 100 times.

The MPM dispatcher (compute::MpmSimulation::step_n) and the FEM GPU-resident CG (fem::CgStepperGpu) are the worked examples.

4. Atomic-CAS pattern for f32 reductions

WGSL has atomic<u32> and atomic<i32>. It does not have atomic<f32>. Floating-point reductions need a workaround.

The molla convention is a compare-and-swap loop:

// Conceptually: *target += addend;
fn atomic_add_f32(target: ptr<storage, atomic<u32>, read_write>, addend: f32) {
    loop {
        let old_bits = atomicLoad(target);
        let old_f = bitcast<f32>(old_bits);
        let new_f = old_f + addend;
        let new_bits = bitcast<u32>(new_f);
        let res = atomicCompareExchangeWeak(target, old_bits, new_bits);
        if (res.exchanged) { break; }
    }
}

Naga (the WGSL→SPIR-V translator wgpu uses) rejects pointer-to-storage as a function argument from one storage binding to another. The consequence: every atomic-add target lives in its own bound buffer and you ship one helper per target (e.g. atomic_add_mass and atomic_add_mom for the MPM grid). You can’t have a generic atomic_add_f32 helper that takes a pointer to any storage buffer.

This is annoying. It is also unavoidable until WGSL adds either atomic<f32> or generic pointers — neither is on the spec roadmap.

Where the pattern shows up:

  • MPM grid (shaders/mpm.wgsl) — mass + momentum scatter from particles to grid.
  • FEM assembly (shaders/fem_assembly.wgsl) — element-matrix scatter into the global CSR.
  • 3DGS backward (shaders/splat_raytrace_backward.wgsl) — 5 per-splat gradient channels.
  • Sparse grid mass + position scatter.

5. No cooperative_matrix, no subgroup intrinsics

wgpu has experimental subgroup_* operations behind a feature flag; the WGSL spec does not stabilise them. NVIDIA’s VK_KHR_cooperative_matrix extension is not exposed portably through wgpu either. molla therefore commits to:

  • No subgroup_* calls in shipped WGSL. If a shader needs a reduction it spells the reduction out (workgroup shared memory
    • barrier + log₂N tree).
  • No cooperative_matrix tile matmul. The molla compute::tile_matmul kernel is a plain WGSL implementation (var<workgroup> tile loads + per-thread inner products). It is not competitive with cuBLAS or Metal Performance Shaders at large M / N / K, and that’s a deliberate trade for portability.

When a workload genuinely needs TensorCore-class throughput, the right answer in molla is don’t use molla — call cuBLAS or Metal Performance Shaders from the host side and pass the result back as a Buffer. The engine doesn’t pretend to be a generic matrix library.

6. Host f64, device f32, conversions at the buffer boundary

The math layer is f64 end-to-end (math::Real = f64). The WGSL device side is f32 end-to-end (WGSL has no f64). The conversion happens exactly once, when a Buffer<T> is uploaded or downloaded:

  • Buffer::host() -> &[T_host] — f64 view.
  • Buffer::upload(&device, &queue) — narrows to f32, writes to wgpu::Buffer.
  • Buffer::download_from_device(&device, &queue) — widens back to f64.

The conversion is bytemuck-cast through a packed f32 representation in the wgpu buffer; the f64 host vector is the source of truth between substeps.

Solvers never mix the two precisions in the same arithmetic operation. If a solver needs intermediate device-side state, that state lives in a separate Buffer and never crosses back to the host until the substep is done.

7. Errors are typed, no anyhow in the engine

molla::core::Error is a thiserror-derived enum. Library code never uses anyhow::Result — that’s reserved for the viewer and applications. The reason is the standard library-hygiene one: applications want to add context; libraries want to be exhaustively matchable.

The few places anyhow shows up — like the former usd_molla crate that briefly existed — were application-level code, not engine.

8. No unsafe outside Pod-compatible data

The engine has zero unsafe blocks outside of:

  • bytemuck::Pod / Zeroable derives.

Workspace lint unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn = "deny" enforces that any new unsafe is flagged and reviewed.

9. Tests are #[ignore]’d when they need a wgpu adapter

The default cargo test lane should pass on a CPU-only CI runner. Tests that require a real wgpu::Adapter are marked #[ignore] so they only run when the developer explicitly opts in via the make test-*-gpu Makefile targets or cargo test -- --ignored.

The exception is crates/molla/tests/cpu_smoke.rs — pure-CPU smoke tests that run in the default lane.

10. Reference Newton + Warp

Per the user memory note: when implementing a new physics primitive, consult both xtra/warp (compute primitives) and xtra/newton (algorithms). molla copies Newton’s structure expressed via Warp-style spatial operations in Rust + WGSL. The two trees together are the reference; consulting only one is the common mistake.

Vectors, matrices, transforms

crates/molla/src/math/mod.rs is the type-aliases hub for the host side. Everything physics-facing on the CPU runs in f64; the matching f32 mirrors live in crates/molla/src/math/gpu.rs and are produced at the buffer boundary by BufferElement::to_gpu.

The Real scalar and glam aliases

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
/// Host-side scalar. The crate is `f64` everywhere on the host —
/// see the precision policy in `PLAN.md` §7.
pub type Real = f64;

pub type Vec3 = glam::DVec3;
pub type Quat = glam::DQuat;
pub type Mat3 = glam::DMat3;

pub const GRAVITY: Real = 9.806_65;
}

molla never owns its own Vec3/Mat3/Quat types — every algebraic primitive is a glam::D* alias. The crate gets glam’s vectorised SIMD paths, swizzles, and From/Into for free, and the cost is a single re-export wall in math/mod.rs. Storage layout is glam’s: Mat3 holds three columns left-to-right (m.col(0), m.col(1), m.col(2)); a Quat is (x, y, z, w). Both invariants leak into the WGSL mirrors, so do not change them without coordinating with GpuMat3.

Transform — rigid pose

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[repr(C)]
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, PartialEq)]
pub struct Transform {
    pub position: Vec3,
    pub rotation: Quat,
}
}

crates/molla/src/math/transform.rs defines a rigid transform as (position, rotation) — first apply rotation to the body-local frame, then translate by position. The layout matches Warp’s wp.transform byte-for-byte, so a Transform (host f64, padded to 32 bytes through GpuTransform) round-trips cleanly into WGSL.

The key entry points:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Transform {
    pub const IDENTITY: Self;
    pub const fn new(position: Vec3, rotation: Quat) -> Self;
    pub const fn from_translation(t: Vec3) -> Self;
    pub const fn from_rotation(r: Quat) -> Self;
    pub fn compose(&self, other: &Self) -> Self;
    pub fn inverse(&self) -> Self;
    pub fn transform_point(&self, p: Vec3) -> Vec3;
    pub fn transform_vector(&self, v: Vec3) -> Vec3;
    pub fn inverse_transform_point(&self, p: Vec3) -> Vec3;
    pub fn rotation_matrix(&self) -> Mat3;
    pub fn renormalize(&mut self);
    pub fn to_gpu(&self) -> GpuTransform;
}
}

compose(self, other) reads as “first apply other, then self” — the convention that lets you write world = parent_world.compose(&child_local) without juggling sides. After composition we always normalize() the quaternion; quaternion drift is the dominant numerical hygiene problem in long-running articulated integration, and one normalise per compose is cheap. Integrators that step quaternions explicitly should additionally call [Transform::renormalize] every step (see solvers::semi_implicit).

Transform::IDENTITY is const so it can be used as a default field value without Default blanket trickery — every model-builder field that holds an unset pose initialises to IDENTITY.

Glam vs hand-rolled — why not a custom Mat3?

molla’s predecessor stacks (Newton / Warp) carry their own wp.transform/wp.spatial_* types. Rust has glam, glam has been the de-facto game-engine pick for half a decade, and glam::DMat3 already inlines into the same SIMD that a custom type would synthesise. The single concession is that glam stores columns, which means anything that reads “row-major” in a textbook or a Warp shader needs translating: m.row(i) returns a Vec3 of that row, and mset(&mut m, i, j, v) (in dense3.rs) sets row i column j.

Cross-references:

  • Spatial algebra builds 6-component types (SpatialVector, SpatialInertia, SpatialMatrix6) on top of the 3-component aliases here.
  • Small-matrix decompositions ships SVD/QR/eig for the 3×3 case used in IK regularisation and per-vertex polar decomposition.
  • Storage abstractions shows the host→f32 conversion path that bridges these types to WGSL.

Spatial algebra

crates/molla/src/math/spatial.rs ships molla’s 6-component spatial algebra primitives — the workhorses of Featherstone’s articulated-body algorithms (ABA, CRBA, RNEA). All types use the [linear; angular] ordering, matching Warp’s wp.spatial_vector (spatial_top = linear). Mixing conventions across modules is a silent-correctness hazard, so the layout is documented at every boundary and repr(C) is enforced so the GPU mirrors line up.

SpatialVector — twists and wrenches

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[repr(C)]
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, Default, PartialEq)]
pub struct SpatialVector {
    pub linear: Vec3,
    pub angular: Vec3,
}
}

The same struct represents motion vectors (twists: linear + angular velocity) and force vectors (wrenches: force + torque) — context distinguishes them, not type. SpatialVector::ZERO, ::new(linear, angular), ::linear(v), ::angular(w) cover construction; +, -, scalar *, and Neg are implemented componentwise.

SpatialInertia — rigid-body inertia

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[repr(C)]
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, PartialEq)]
pub struct SpatialInertia {
    pub mass: Real,      // kg
    pub com: Vec3,       // body-frame COM, m
    pub inertia: Mat3,   // at COM, body frame, kg·m²
}
}

This is the compact form used when the inertia is still attached to a single body — sphere/cuboid constructors are provided, plus inv_mass() / inv_inertia() that return 0 and Mat3::ZERO when mass == 0 (the static / kinematic sentinel).

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
SpatialInertia::sphere(mass, radius);
SpatialInertia::cuboid(mass, full_extents);  // (sx, sy, sz)
}

SpatialInertia::ZERO is the const “no body” placeholder.

SpatialMatrix6 — articulated inertia

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, PartialEq)]
pub struct SpatialMatrix6 {
    pub m: [[Real; 6]; 6],  // row-major
}
}

Featherstone’s ABA accumulates child contributions through the backward pass, and the simple (mass, com, inertia) representation isn’t closed under that update — the articulated inertia outgrows it. SpatialMatrix6 carries the full 6×6 in row-major layout (matches Warp’s wp.spatial_matrix).

Methods:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
SpatialMatrix6::ZERO;
SpatialMatrix6::identity();
fn scale(self, s: Real) -> Self;
fn add(&self, o: &Self) -> Self;
fn sub(&self, o: &Self) -> Self;
fn mul_sv(&self, v: SpatialVector) -> SpatialVector;
fn outer(u: SpatialVector, v: SpatialVector) -> Self;
fn from_body(mass: Real, com: Vec3, inertia_world: Mat3) -> Self;
}

mul_sv(v) is M · v with v = [linear; angular] laid out as [v0..v2, v3..v5]. outer(u, v) is u · vᵀ, used in ABA’s rank-1 update

I^A := I^A − (I^A · S) · (I^A · S)ᵀ / (Sᵀ · I^A · S)

from_body(mass, com, inertia_world) builds the spatial inertia of a rigid body about an arbitrary reference point, per Featherstone (2008) eq. (2.63):

        [ m·I₃                     m·skew(c)         ]
I_s =   [ m·skew(c)ᵀ   I_C − m·skew(c)·skew(c)       ]

with [v; w] ordering. The skew matrix skew(c) is built inline (skew3 private helper); since skew is antisymmetric the bottom-left block ends up -m·skew(c) rather than the transpose, and the code exploits that.

Spatial cross products

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn spatial_cross(a: SpatialVector, b: SpatialVector) -> SpatialVector;
pub fn spatial_cross_dual(a: SpatialVector, b: SpatialVector) -> SpatialVector;
}

Two operators, matching Newton’s spatial_cross / spatial_cross_dual WGSL builtins (xtra/warp/_src/builtins.py):

  • spatial_cross(a, b) — motion-vector cross product:

    linear  = w_a × v_b + v_a × w_b
angular = w_a × w_b

    Drives the Coriolis terms in ABA’s forward sweep.

  • spatial_cross_dual(a, b) — force-vector cross product (the dual operator):

    linear  = w_a × v_b
angular = w_a × w_b + v_a × v_b

    Drives the Coriolis bias in ABA’s wrench accumulation.

spatial_jacobian_column — single-DoF Jacobian columns

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub enum JacobianKind { Revolute, Prismatic }

pub fn spatial_jacobian_column(
    kind: JacobianKind,
    joint_axis_world: Vec3,
    joint_origin_world: Vec3,
    body_point_world: Vec3,
) -> SpatialVector;
}

Builds one column of the spatial Jacobian for a single-DoF joint’s effect on a downstream body’s reference point. All inputs are in the world frame — callers (CRBA, IK, sensor frame transforms) are responsible for transforming joint axes / origins to world before calling.

Revolute joints produce (axis × (body_point − joint_origin), axis); prismatic joints produce (axis, 0). Multi-DoF joints (Ball, D6, Distance, CABLE) decompose into multiple single-DoF columns by sweeping through their axes and calling this helper per axis.

The function mirrors Newton’s spatial_jacobian builtin (xtra/warp/_src/builtins.py:2261) and is the host fallback for the GPU Jacobian kernel — both paths must produce identical column vectors for parity tests to pass.

Cross-references:

  • Articulation (Featherstone ABA) and CRBA / RNEA / Jacobian consume these primitives directly.
  • Vectors, matrices, transforms covers the underlying Vec3/Mat3/Quat aliases.

Small-matrix decompositions

crates/molla/src/math/dense3.rs ships specialised decompositions for 3×3 dense matrices — SVD, QR, symmetric eigendecomposition, and polar decomposition — plus the reverse-mode adjoint of SVD with Tikhonov regularisation for degenerate singular values. These are the small-matrix counterparts of dense_solve; the 3×3 case dominates because it shows up once per particle, per vertex, or per body in inner loops.

Callers:

  • IK regularisation (Stage 16) — when (JᵀJ + λI) Cholesky fails or the condition number is huge, fall back to an SVD-based damped pseudoinverse.
  • Per-vertex polar decomposition for VBD soft-body co-rotational energy (Stage 20).
  • Per-particle inertia eigendecomposition for MPM plasticity (Stage 24d).

The matching WGSL kernel lives in crates/molla-kernels/shaders/dense3_svd.wgsl and is dispatched by crate::kernels::Dense3Kernel.

Algorithm choices — Jacobi vs Householder vs Givens

All three forward decompositions deliberately avoid Householder reflections even though textbooks prefer them at scale: Householder needs conditional vector compaction, which is painful in WGSL with no warp-shuffle and only workgroupBarrier() for synchronisation. Jacobi and Givens are loop-free and branch-light, so the host code and the WGSL kernel share their structure.

  • SVD via one-sided Jacobi. svd3 rotates column pairs of the working matrix by Givens rotations chosen to zero the off-diagonal entries of MᵀM. After convergence, the columns of M are orthogonal; their norms are the singular values, normalised columns form U, and the accumulated rotations form V. Reference: Demmel & Veselić “Jacobi’s Method is More Accurate than QR” (1992), Golub & Van Loan 3rd ed. §8.6.3.
  • QR via three Givens rotations. Zero the (1,0), (2,0), (2,1) sub-diagonal entries in turn. Each Givens is its own transpose, so R = G₃·G₂·G₁·M and Q = G₁ᵀ·G₂ᵀ·G₃ᵀ.
  • Symmetric eigendecomposition via cyclic Jacobi. Same rotation recipe as SVD but applied to a symmetric input directly. Reads the upper triangle and assumes the lower mirrors it.

Both Jacobi-style sweeps share two private constants:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
const JACOBI_EPS: Real = 1.0e-14;
const JACOBI_MAX_SWEEPS: usize = 32;
}

JACOBI_MAX_SWEEPS = 32 is a hard cap. Well-conditioned 3×3 inputs converge in 4-6 sweeps; the cap guards against pathologies (matrices with duplicate eigenvalues that cause Jacobi to spin on the rotation choice). The cap is the same on the host and in the WGSL kernel so parity tests don’t see drift from differing iteration counts.

Public API

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn svd3(m: Mat3) -> (Mat3, Vec3, Mat3);
pub fn qr3(m: Mat3) -> (Mat3, Mat3);
pub fn eig3_sym(m: Mat3) -> (Vec3, Mat3);
pub fn polar_decompose_3(m: Mat3) -> (Mat3, Mat3);
pub fn cond2_3(m: Mat3) -> Real;
}
  • svd3(m) returns (U, σ, V) with M = U · diag(σ) · Vᵀ. Singular values are non-negative but not sorted — sort externally if needed. If the constructed U ended up as a reflection (det(U) < 0), the routine flips the smallest-σ column’s sign in both U and V so the factorisation still holds with non-negative σ.
  • qr3(m) returns (Q, R) with Q orthogonal and R upper-triangular. The strict lower triangle of R is explicitly zeroed at the end so callers can rely on R[i,j] == 0 for i > j.
  • eig3_sym(m) returns (λ, V) such that A = V · diag(λ) · Vᵀ. Asymmetric input gives garbage — symmetrise at the call site. Eigenvalues are not sorted.
  • polar_decompose_3(m) returns (R, S) with R orthogonal and S symmetric positive semi-definite. Implemented as a thin SVD wrapper: R = U · Vᵀ, S = V · diag(σ) · Vᵀ. If det(M) < 0, R ends up improper (det(R) = -1); VBD-style co-rotational energy normally wants a proper rotation, so callers that need one post-process the result.
  • cond2_3(m) returns the 2-norm condition number σ_max / σ_min, or Real::INFINITY when σ_min == 0. IK uses this as the Cholesky-vs-SVD switch.

adj_svd3 — reverse-mode adjoint of SVD

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn adj_svd3(
    _a: Mat3,
    u: Mat3,
    sigma: Vec3,
    v: Mat3,
    adj_u: Mat3,
    adj_sigma: Vec3,
    adj_v: Mat3,
) -> Mat3;
}

The forward decomposition is A = U · diag(σ) · Vᵀ. Given the forward outputs (U, σ, V) and the upstream gradients (adj_U, adj_σ, adj_V) of some downstream scalar loss J, this returns adj_A = ∂J/∂A. Three contributions get summed:

  1. Direct σ term. U · diag(adj_σ) · Vᵀ.
  2. U-rotation term. Ω_U = Uᵀ · adj_U − adj_Uᵀ · U (twice the skew part of Uᵀ · adj_U); u_term = U · ((F ⊙ Ω_U) · Σ) · Vᵀ.
  3. V-rotation term. Symmetric to (2), with Ω_V and Σ · (F ⊙ Ω_V).

The literal arithmetic mirrors xtra/warp/warp/native/svd.h::adj_svd3 (Apache-2.0); references for the math are McAdams et al. “Computing the Singular Value Decomposition of 3×3 Matrices” (2011) for the forward, Townsend “Differentiating the Singular Value Decomposition” (2016) for the adjoint.

Degenerate σ — Tikhonov regularisation

The adjoint divisor F_ij = 1 / (σⱼ² − σᵢ²) is undefined when two singular values coincide. molla uses

F_ij = (σⱼ² − σᵢ²) / max((σⱼ² − σᵢ²)², ε²)

with ε = ADJ_SVD_EPS = 1.0e-12. The result is bounded by 1/ε for all inputs and is exactly 1/(σⱼ² − σᵢ²) away from the degeneracy. At exact degeneracy the regularised F_ij → 0, which is the mathematically correct limit — the rotational gauge between equal-σ columns is genuinely ambiguous, and projecting the gradient onto the symmetric part is what the limit gives you. The implementation lives in the private helper safe_inv_sq_diff:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn safe_inv_sq_diff(a: Real, b: Real, eps: Real) -> Real {
    let d = b * b - a * a;
    d / (d * d + eps * eps)
}
}

adj_polar(f, r, s, adj_r, adj_s) is the polar-decomposition adjoint, expressed through SVD — it recovers (U, σ, V) from F, propagates adj_R = U·Vᵀ and adj_S = V·Σ·Vᵀ back to (adj_U, adj_σ, adj_V), then hands off to adj_svd3. The (r, s) arguments are unused in the math (they’re recoverable from F) but kept in the signature for parity with the autograd convention.

Larger systems — dense_solve

For n × n problems beyond 3×3 — typically the IK normal equations (JᵀJ + λI) · dq = Jᵀ · e with dof up to ~30 — see crates/molla/src/math/dense_solve.rs:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn dense_chol(a: &mut [Real], n: usize) -> Result<()>;
pub fn forward_sub(l: &[Real], b: &[Real], n: usize) -> Result<Vec<Real>>;
pub fn back_sub(l: &[Real], y: &[Real], n: usize) -> Result<Vec<Real>>;
pub fn dense_chol_solve(a: &mut [Real], b: &[Real], n: usize) -> Result<Vec<Real>>;
pub fn dense_eig_sym(a: &[Real], n: usize) -> Result<(Vec<Real>, Vec<Real>)>;
pub fn dense_psd_pinv_solve(a: &[Real], b: &[Real], n: usize) -> Result<Vec<Real>>;
}

Row-major flat storage; an n × n matrix is a Vec<Real> of length n * n. dense_chol errors when the input isn’t SPD (negative pivot); dense_psd_pinv_solve is the IK fallback path that crate::solvers::ik uses when Cholesky reports a breakdown on near-singular (JᵀJ + λI). The fallback builds the full symmetric eigendecomposition, clamps tiny eigenvalues at max(eigval) · 1e-12, and forms

x = Σᵢ (vᵢ · vᵢᵀ · b) / max(λᵢ, λ_floor)

which is equivalent to the SVD-based pseudoinverse for SPD matrices. The clamp keeps the solution finite when J becomes rank-deficient (joint-limit lock-up, singular configurations).

Sparse linear algebra

molla’s sparse stack is built on a block-sparse-row (BSR) matrix. With block size B = 1 it degenerates to plain CSR, which is the configuration almost every consumer actually wants — FEM assemblies, implicit-MPM grid systems, SpGEMM products, BSR-GPU mirrors. Keeping the single BsrMatrix type for both cases avoids the maintenance overhead of carrying parallel CSR and BSR codebases.

Three layers stack on top of each other:

  1. CPU BSR matrix — crates/molla/src/math/sparse.rs. Construction from triplets, matvec, axpy, transpose, basic SpGEMM, plus three iterative solvers (CG, BiCGSTAB, restartable GMRES) implemented against a [LinearOperator] trait so callers can plug in a closure or a custom matrix-free operator. See BsrMatrix (CPU).
  2. GPU BSR mirror — crates/molla/src/math/sparse_gpu.rs. Three storage buffers (row_offsets, col_indices, values) holding the CSR layout with f32 values; a single BsrAlgebraKernel owns the compiled pipelines for matvec, axpy, transpose, SpGEMM, and SpGEMM’s on-device symbolic phase. See BsrGpu (GPU).
  3. Closure-driven iterative solvers — crates/molla/src/math/iterative.rs. A second copy of CG, PCG, and BiCGSTAB with a matrix-free API (F: Fn(&[Real]) -> Vec<Real>), plus a built-in Jacobi preconditioner. See Iterative solvers.

When CSR vs blocked

The crate defaults to B = 1 / CSR. The few places B > 1 still make sense are:

  • Featherstone CRBA outputs a dof × dof mass matrix where every entry is a dense B × B joint block. The current code path materialises it as a dense Vec<Real> and uses dense_chol; if we ever needed a banded BSR layout this is where it would land.
  • Hypothetical multi-component rigid-body Jacobians (J ∈ R^(6 × dof) in blocks of 6×1). Not used today — the spatial-Jacobian path materialises columns directly into a flat Vec.

All FEM, MPM, and GPU code uses B = 1. BsrGpu::upload errors on B != 1 to make the constraint explicit:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
if m.b != 1 {
    return Err(Error::Build(format!(
        "BsrGpu::upload: only B = 1 supported in v1, got B = {}",
        m.b
    )));
}
}

Design tradeoffs

The BSR format keeps two invariants that the GPU side relies on:

  1. Column indices within a row are sorted ascending. Constructors (from_pattern, from_triplets, from_scalar_triplets) sort the pattern up front. SpGEMM relies on this — its numeric kernel binary-searches c_col_indices[lo..hi] to find the output slot for a contribution.
  2. Repeated (row, col) triplets accumulate into one slot. from_scalar_triplets and from_triplets both coalesce duplicates; FEM assembly is the dominant consumer and relies on it heavily.

The format does not support pattern unions natively. axpy on the GPU is documented as “same pattern, unchecked” — pattern-changing operations route through SpGEMM or rebuild on the host. See BsrGpu (GPU) for the gory details.

Iterative solvers — closure-driven vs trait-driven

molla ships two near-duplicate sets of CG/BiCGSTAB:

  • The trait-driven path (crates/molla/src/math/sparse.rs::{cg, bicgstab, gmres}) takes a &dyn LinearOperator plus &mut x and writes in place. This is what the FEM solvers, MPM implicit pass, and any code that already has a custom LinearOperator impl call.
  • The closure-driven path (crates/molla/src/math/iterative.rs::{cg_solve, pcg_solve, bicgstab_solve}) takes F: Fn(&[Real]) -> Vec<Real> and returns a fresh CgResult struct. Ad-hoc consumers and tests use this.

Both paths converge to the same iterates given the same matrix; the choice is API ergonomics, not numerics. Style3D, Stam-fluid, and the parameter-ID experiments use the closure-driven version because they build their A·x callable inline from a few flat host buffers.

  • BsrMatrix (CPU) — full CPU API.
  • BsrGpu (GPU) — GPU mirror + kernels.
  • SpGEMM design — full-GPU symbolic phase (Stage 39F).
  • Iterative solvers — closure-driven CG/PCG/BiCGSTAB.

BsrMatrix (CPU)

crates/molla/src/math/sparse.rs defines the host-side block-sparse-row matrix and its iterative solvers.

Layout

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
pub struct BsrMatrix {
    pub b: usize,             // block dimension; B = 1 ⇒ CSR
    pub block_rows: usize,
    pub block_cols: usize,
    pub row_offsets: Vec<usize>,  // length block_rows + 1
    pub col_idx: Vec<usize>,      // length = total nonzero blocks
    pub values: Vec<Real>,        // b² · nnz_blocks values, row-major per block
}
}

The conceptual size is (block_rows · B) × (block_cols · B). Within each block the values are stored row-major. Across blocks within a row the col_idx is sorted ascending; constructors enforce this.

Construction

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl BsrMatrix {
    pub fn from_pattern(
        b: usize,
        block_rows: usize,
        block_cols: usize,
        pattern: Vec<(usize, usize)>,
    ) -> Result<Self>;

    pub fn from_triplets(
        b: usize,
        block_rows: usize,
        block_cols: usize,
        triplets: &[(usize, usize, Vec<Real>)],
    ) -> Result<Self>;

    pub fn from_scalar_triplets(
        nrows: usize,
        ncols: usize,
        triplets: &[(usize, usize, Real)],
    ) -> Result<Self>;
}
}

from_pattern allocates a zero-valued matrix with the given block positions; the pattern is sorted+deduped internally. from_triplets takes a list of (block_row, block_col, B² values) and accumulates duplicates into a single slot. from_scalar_triplets is the fast path for B = 1 matrices — takes flat (row, col, value) and avoids the per-triplet Vec<Real> allocation that dominated FEM assembly time on 16³+ meshes.

A contract test pins the equivalence between the two triplet builders so callers can rely on byte-identical CSR layout regardless of which path they use:

from_scalar_triplets must produce byte-identical CSR (row_offsets, col_idx, values) to from_triplets with vec![val] wrappers. Locks the equivalence the FEM assembly path now relies on.

Empty rows produce equal consecutive row_offsets[]; this is exercised by the from_scalar_triplets_handles_empty_rows_and_interior_cols test in the source.

Algebra

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl BsrMatrix {
    pub fn nrows(&self) -> usize;          // block_rows * b
    pub fn ncols(&self) -> usize;          // block_cols * b
    pub fn diagonal(&self) -> Vec<Real>;   // B = 1 only
    pub fn mv(&self, x: &[Real], y: &mut [Real]) -> Result<()>;
    pub fn get_diag(&self) -> Vec<Real>;   // BSR-aware diagonal
    pub fn scale(&mut self, s: Real);
}
}

mv is the matvec y = A · x. get_diag returns the per-row-block diagonal as a flat (block_rows · b) vector — collects the diagonal of each diagonal block. diagonal is a B = 1-only convenience that returns scalars; it’s the cheaper path for the Jacobi preconditioner when you know the matrix is CSR.

LinearOperator trait + ClosureOp

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub trait LinearOperator {
    fn rows(&self) -> usize;
    fn cols(&self) -> usize;
    fn mv(&self, x: &[Real], y: &mut [Real]) -> Result<()>;
}

pub struct ClosureOp<F>
where F: Fn(&[Real], &mut [Real]) -> Result<()> {
    pub rows: usize,
    pub cols: usize,
    pub f: F,
}
}

BsrMatrix implements LinearOperator. ClosureOp is the adapter that lets a closure stand in for a matrix — handy when the operator is formed implicitly ((J · Jᵀ + λI) · x for IK normal equations, the implicit-MPM grid solve, FEM Schur complements).

Iterative solvers

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug)]
pub struct IterConfig {
    pub max_iter: usize,
    pub tol: Real,
    pub restart: usize,  // GMRES only
}

#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug)]
pub struct IterStats {
    pub iters: usize,
    pub residual: Real,
    pub converged: bool,
}

pub fn cg(
    op: &dyn LinearOperator,
    b: &[Real],
    x: &mut [Real],
    m_inv_diag: Option<&[Real]>,
    cfg: &IterConfig,
) -> Result<IterStats>;

pub fn bicgstab(
    op: &dyn LinearOperator,
    b: &[Real],
    x: &mut [Real],
    m_inv_diag: Option<&[Real]>,
    cfg: &IterConfig,
) -> Result<IterStats>;

pub fn gmres(
    op: &dyn LinearOperator,
    b: &[Real],
    x: &mut [Real],
    m_inv_diag: Option<&[Real]>,
    cfg: &IterConfig,
) -> Result<IterStats>;
}

All three solvers write into x in place — pass an initial guess if you have one (warm-start from a previous solve, for example). The m_inv_diag argument is the Jacobi preconditioner: pass None for unpreconditioned, or Some(&inv_diag) where inv_diag[i] == 1.0 / diag(A)[i] (zero diagonals become zero — pass-through). The trait-driven path is what the FEM solvers, MPM implicit pass, and multigrid V-cycles call.

GMRES restarts at cfg.restart iterations (default 30); the implementation uses Givens rotations to maintain the Hessenberg factorisation in-place and falls back to upper-triangular back-sub at restart time.

A perf gate enforces that 1000×1000 tridiagonal CG converges in under 100 ms in release mode — see the cg_meets_dod_1000x1000_in_under_100ms test.
