BsrGpu (GPU)

crates/molla/src/math/sparse_gpu.rs is the on-device mirror of BsrMatrix. It carries the three CSR buffers and gates compute through a single BsrAlgebraKernel that owns all the compiled pipelines.

The module is gated behind #![cfg(feature = "gpu")]. The host counterpart works without the gpu feature; everything in this page disappears in CPU-only builds.

BsrGpu — the buffer triple

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct BsrGpu {
    pub row_offsets: Arc<wgpu::Buffer>,
    pub col_indices: Arc<wgpu::Buffer>,
    pub values: Arc<wgpu::Buffer>,
    pub nrows: u32,
    pub ncols: u32,
    pub nnz: u32,
}
}

row_offsets and col_indices are u32 buffers; values is f32. Shape metadata stays on the host so dispatchers can size workgroup grids without round-tripping. Arc<wgpu::Buffer> lets the same buffers be borrowed across multiple bind groups (the SpGEMM path binds the same row_offsets into both its symbolic and its numeric pipelines).

Precision boundary

The CSR layout values are f32 on the device, f64 on the host (matches BsrMatrix). Upload converts f64 → f32, readback the reverse:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let values_f32: Vec<f32> = m.values.iter().map(|&v| v as f32).collect();
}

This is the same tradeoff fem::gpu_data documents — WGSL has no f64, and a Vulkan-only path would fork the codebase.

Upload / readback

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl BsrGpu {
    pub fn upload(
        device: &wgpu::Device,
        queue: &wgpu::Queue,
        m: &BsrMatrix,
    ) -> Result<Self>;

    pub fn read_back(
        &self,
        device: &wgpu::Device,
        queue: &wgpu::Queue,
    ) -> Result<BsrMatrix>;
}
}

upload rejects B != 1 and validates the CSR shape invariants (row_offsets[last] == values.len() == col_idx.len(), row_offsets.len() == block_rows + 1). Without those checks an inconsistent host matrix would silently produce out-of-bounds reads inside the WGSL kernels. read_back rebuilds a host BsrMatrix and promotes f32 → Real, slicing each buffer down to its logical length (wgpu may pad allocations up to 16 bytes).

BsrAlgebraKernel — pipeline owner

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct BsrAlgebraKernel { /* … */ }

impl BsrAlgebraKernel {
    pub fn new(device: Arc<wgpu::Device>, queue: Arc<wgpu::Queue>) -> Self;

    pub fn matvec(
        &self,
        a: &BsrGpu,
        x_buf: &wgpu::Buffer,
        y_buf: &wgpu::Buffer,
        alpha: f32,
        beta: f32,
    ) -> Result<()>;

    pub fn axpy_same_pattern_unchecked(
        &self,
        a: &BsrGpu,
        b: &mut BsrGpu,
        alpha: f32,
        beta: f32,
    ) -> Result<()>;

    pub fn transpose(&self, a: &BsrGpu) -> Result<BsrGpu>;
    pub fn spgemm(&self, a: &BsrGpu, b: &BsrGpu) -> Result<BsrGpu>;
}
}

Build once per device, reuse across many dispatches. The constructor compiles four WGSL modules (bsr_mv_gpu.wgsl, bsr_axpy.wgsl, bsr_transpose.wgsl, bsr_spgemm.wgsl) plus a fifth (bsr_spgemm_symbolic.wgsl) for the GPU-symbolic SpGEMM path, and stamps out the bind-group layouts up front.

matvec — generalised SpMV

matvec(a, x_buf, y_buf, alpha, beta) computes y = α · A · x + β · y. Buffers must already be allocated as STORAGE | COPY_SRC | COPY_DST. With β = 0 the previous contents of y_buf are read but masked out — so a freshly-allocated y_buf is fine, you don’t have to zero it.

The dispatch grid is (min(nrows, 65535), ceil(nrows / 65535), 1) — 2D so that very tall matrices stay under the per-axis dispatch limit.

Prepared matvec — Stage 41 v5

The FEM CG inner loop dispatches the same matvec thousands of times per solve. To avoid per-call uniform allocation and bind-group creation, the kernel exposes a “prepared” path:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct PreparedMatvec { /* uniform_buf, bg_io, bg_u, dim_x, dim_y */ }

impl BsrAlgebraKernel {
    pub fn prepare_matvec(
        &self,
        a: &BsrGpu,
        x_buf: &wgpu::Buffer,
        y_buf: &wgpu::Buffer,
        alpha: f32,
        beta: f32,
    ) -> Result<PreparedMatvec>;

    pub fn matvec_into_pass(
        &self,
        pass: &mut wgpu::ComputePass<'_>,
        prepared: &PreparedMatvec,
    );
}
}

prepare_matvec caches the uniform buffer and bind groups for a fixed (A, x, y, α, β). matvec_into_pass records one extra dispatch into an existing compute pass — no extra encoder / submit. This is what lets the FEM solver fold its CG batch into a single compute pass.

axpy_same_pattern_unchecked — sparse axpy with a safety contract

B = α · A + β · B. Documented contract: caller asserts that A and B share identical row_offsets AND col_indices — only values differ. The function verifies only the cheap scalar shape (nnz, nrows, ncols); a true pattern check would need reading row_offsets + col_indices back to the host (two mappable readbacks), which makes the call unusable inside any per-iter solver loop. Mismatched patterns produce numerical garbage silently — build the pattern once at upload time and keep it across all axpy calls. The pattern-union case is intentionally not in v1.

transpose(a) -> BsrGpu

Host computes the transposed pattern (counts per column, prefix-sum, scatter map) and uploads three small u32 buffers; GPU runs a single bsr_transpose_scatter dispatch that scatters values into their transposed slots. The host-symbolic step is fast enough that moving it on-device hasn’t shown up in a profile, but the same bitmap-count approach used for SpGEMM (next page) would work.

spgemm(a, b) -> BsrGpu

Dispatcher that picks between host-symbolic + GPU-numeric and the full-GPU symbolic variant based on max(A.nrows, B.ncols):

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub const SPGEMM_GPU_SYMBOLIC_CUTOVER: u32 = 64;
}

For matrices smaller than 64 the host-symbolic v1 path wins (kernel launch overhead dominates); for larger problems the GPU symbolic path takes over. See SpGEMM design for the full explanation of why bitmaps beat hashtables on FEM-shaped inputs.

Parity testing

Every kernel here has an oracle: run the matching BsrMatrix op on the host and compare with BsrGpu::read_back. The parity tests in crates/molla-kernels/tests/bsr_gpu_parity.rs cover matvec, axpy, transpose, and SpGEMM at multiple sizes — the contract is bit-identical CSR structure plus an f32-tolerance comparison on values.

SpGEMM design

Sparse-matrix-times-sparse-matrix is the most structurally awkward kernel in the BSR algebra suite. The output’s pattern is itself the result of a computation, so a single-pass scheme can’t pre-allocate the right layout. molla ships two paths and picks at dispatch time; this page explains both.

The entry point is BsrAlgebraKernel::spgemm(a, b) in crates/molla/src/math/sparse_gpu.rs. The cutover threshold:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
/// Below this matrix dimension (in scalar B = 1 units) `spgemm`
/// falls back to the host-symbolic v1 path.
pub const SPGEMM_GPU_SYMBOLIC_CUTOVER: u32 = 64;
}

For max(A.nrows, B.ncols) < 64 the host-symbolic path wins on kernel-launch overhead; for larger problems the full-GPU path takes over. Empirically the cross-over sits between 32 and 64 on every GPU the project has tested.

Path 1 — host-symbolic + GPU-numeric (Stage 38a)

The Stage 38a baseline. Host reads back both patterns, walks them in the obvious nested-loop fashion to build C’s row_offsets and col_idx, plus a per-output-slot contribution list ((slot_a, slot_b) pairs that sum into the slot). GPU then runs a single numeric kernel that, for each output slot, iterates the contribution list and accumulates a_value · b_value into the slot.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn spgemm_host_symbolic(&self, a: &BsrGpu, b: &BsrGpu) -> Result<BsrGpu>;
}

Pros:

  • Single numeric kernel, no atomics, easy to reason about.
  • Trivially correct — the host walk is the same code you’d write for a CPU SpGEMM.

Cons:

  • Two pattern readbacks per call (each ~20-100 µs of submit-and-wait latency).
  • O(C-nnz) host memory for the contribution-pair flat array.
  • Doesn’t scale past ~64 since the host walk is single-threaded.

Path 2 — full-GPU SpGEMM with bitmap symbolic (Stage 39F)

The production path for everything ≥ 64. Four dispatches, all on-device:

  1. Symbolic count. One workgroup per A-row. Walks A[row, :], for each nonzero (row, k) walks B[k, :], and atomicOrs the B-col indices into a per-row dense bitmap of width ceil(B.ncols / 32) u32s. After the row is processed, the workgroup popcounts the bitmap to produce count[row] — the number of unique columns that will appear in C[row, :].

  2. Scan. Exclusive scan of count[] produces c_row_offsets[]. Uses ScanKernel — the same Stage 38e scan dispatcher that’s reused across the project.

  3. Symbolic write. Walks each row’s saved bitmap and emits the set bit positions in ascending order to c_col_indices[]. The “set-bits ascending” order is what gives the output the sorted-column-indices invariant that BsrMatrix relies on, for free.

  4. Numeric. One workgroup per A-row. For each (a_slot, b_slot) pair, binary-searches c_col_indices[c_row_offsets[row]..] to find the output slot and CAS-adds a · b into c_values. The CAS-add idiom is documented in Kernel infrastructure — WGSL has no atomic<f32>, so float atomics are spelled with bitcast + atomicCompareExchangeWeak.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn spgemm_gpu_symbolic(&self, a: &BsrGpu, b: &BsrGpu) -> Result<BsrGpu>;
}

The four pipelines (symbolic_count, symbolic_write, numeric_atomic_add, plus the older bsr_spgemm_numeric for the host-symbolic path) are all compiled and cached up front by BsrAlgebraKernel::new.

Why dense bitmaps and not a parallel hashtable?

Warp’s bsr_mm uses a workgroup-local hashtable with global overflow. For the FEM/Schur problems that motivate Stage 39F the hashtable overflow path always fires:

  • FEM mass / stiffness matrices are roughly 7-banded (each vertex touches ~7 neighbours through the element graph).
  • A 7-banded × 7-banded SpGEMM produces ~49 unique columns per C-row.
  • The 16-bucket workgroup hashtable in the Warp design holds at most a quarter of the working set, so the overflow path takes over and the workgroup-local cache buys nothing.

Dense bitmaps are the cleaner answer for this shape:

  • Storage. nrows · ceil(ncols / 32) · 4 bytes — ≈ 2 MB at 4096². Comfortable for any FEM mesh that fits in device memory.
  • Insertion. O(1) atomicOr per insert; natural dedup falls out of bit-set semantics.
  • Output order. Walking set bits in ascending order produces sorted col_indices for free; no separate sort dispatch needed.

The downside — wasted bits in sparse rows — is irrelevant at typical FEM densities. For dramatically larger ncols (millions) the bitmap storage would dominate and a sparse hashtable would win; that case doesn’t exist in molla’s current workload, but the dispatcher is structured so a third path could slot in below SPGEMM_GPU_SYMBOLIC_CUTOVER without churning the public API.

Atomics for the numeric phase

Multiple (a_slot, b_slot) pairs can contribute to the same output slot — even within a single A-row when both inputs have repeated column ranges that line up. Each contribution does the standard atomicCompareExchangeWeak float-add:

fn atomic_add_csr(slot: u32, value: f32) {
    if (value == 0.0) { return; }
    var old_bits = atomicLoad(&csr_values[slot]);
    loop {
        let old_f = bitcast<f32>(old_bits);
        let new_bits = bitcast<u32>(old_f + value);
        let r = atomicCompareExchangeWeak(&csr_values[slot], old_bits, new_bits);
        if (r.exchanged) { return; }
        old_bits = r.old_value;
    }
}

(From crates/molla-fem/shaders/fem_assembly.wgsl; the SpGEMM kernel uses the same pattern.)

Cross-references

  • BsrGpu (GPU) — the dispatcher entry point.
  • Scan & 64-bit radix sort — the scan that turns count[] into c_row_offsets[].
  • Kernel infrastructure — the float-atomic CAS-add idiom.

Iterative solvers

crates/molla/src/math/iterative.rs ships closure-driven Krylov-subspace solvers — CG, Preconditioned CG, and BiCGSTAB. They complement the trait-driven solvers in BsrMatrix (cg, bicgstab, gmres) with a cleaner API that returns a fresh result struct and takes F: Fn(&[Real]) -> Vec<Real> instead of &dyn LinearOperator. Both paths converge to the same iterates given the same matrix; the choice is API ergonomics.

Conventions

  • All three solvers are f64.
  • op(v) represents A · v; self-adjoint for cg_solve / pcg_solve, no symmetry constraint for bicgstab_solve.
  • tol is the relative tolerance against ‖b‖: convergence when ‖b − A·x‖ ≤ tol · max(‖b‖, ε).
  • All three return after max_iters if they fail to converge — the caller inspects CgResult::residual and decides whether to relax tol, swap preconditioner, or fall back to a direct solve.

CgResult

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[derive(Clone, Debug)]
pub struct CgResult {
    pub x: Vec<Real>,
    pub iters: usize,
    pub residual: Real,  // relative
}

impl CgResult {
    pub fn converged(&self, tol: Real) -> bool;
}
}

CG and PCG

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn cg_solve<F>(op: F, b: &[Real], x0: &[Real], tol: Real, max_iters: usize) -> CgResult
where F: Fn(&[Real]) -> Vec<Real>;

pub fn pcg_solve<F, P>(
    op: F,
    precond: P,
    b: &[Real],
    x0: &[Real],
    tol: Real,
    max_iters: usize,
) -> CgResult
where F: Fn(&[Real]) -> Vec<Real>,
      P: Fn(&[Real]) -> Vec<Real>;
}

Plain CG with the standard scalar recurrence (α = rr / pAp, β = rr' / rr). PCG adds one extra step per iteration: z = M⁻¹·r, and the recurrence runs on rz = ⟨r, z⟩ instead of rr. M must be SPD for the convergence guarantee to hold.

Edge cases:

  • Zero RHS ⇒ zero solution, exit immediately.
  • Degenerate search direction (|pAp| < 1e-30) ⇒ exit gracefully with whatever residual we have. Don’t fault.
  • Initial guess already converged ⇒ exit with iters = 0.

Jacobi preconditioner

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[derive(Clone, Debug)]
pub struct JacobiPreconditioner { /* inv_diag: Vec<Real> */ }

impl JacobiPreconditioner {
    pub fn new(diag: &[Real]) -> Self;
    pub fn apply(&self, r: &[Real]) -> Vec<Real>;
    pub fn inv_diag(&self) -> &[Real];
}
}

Cheapest possible preconditioner — one division per row per matvec. M⁻¹ = diag(1 / aᵢᵢ). Zero diagonals become zero (pass-through); substituting 1 would scale non-zero RHS in a null-space row, which is the wrong behaviour. Effective when the diagonal already dominates (mass matrices, implicit-MPM grid systems, finite-difference Laplacians with non-uniform coefficients) and harmless on well-conditioned systems. For SPD matrices, JacobiPreconditioner is itself SPD, preserving the symmetry guarantee that PCG requires.

Typical wiring:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use molla::math::iterative::{pcg_solve, JacobiPreconditioner};

let m = JacobiPreconditioner::new(&diag);
let result = pcg_solve(
    |x| matvec(x),
    |r| m.apply(r),
    &b,
    &x0,
    1e-8,
    200,
);
}

When to pick which

  • cg_solve (unpreconditioned) — small systems where you trust the conditioning, or as the baseline when benchmarking PCG. Test fixtures and the 1D Laplacian smoke tests run unpreconditioned.
  • pcg_solve with JacobiPreconditioner — the default for any diagonally-dominant SPD system. Implicit-MPM grid solves, Stam-fluid pressure Poisson, FEM mass-matrix smoothers, parameter-ID normal equations — all use this.
  • bicgstab_solve — non-symmetric A. The PDE-with-advection cases (Navier-Stokes, magnetostatics with anisotropic media). See the BiCGSTAB note below for the stability caveats.

BiCGSTAB — stability caveats

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn bicgstab_solve<F>(
    op: F,
    b: &[Real],
    x0: &[Real],
    tol: Real,
    max_iters: usize,
) -> CgResult
where F: Fn(&[Real]) -> Vec<Real>;
}

BiCGSTAB stagnates when one of the orthogonality scalars (ρ, ω) collapses near zero — inherent to the algorithm, not a bug. molla guards with two heuristics drawn from Saad’s Iterative Methods for Sparse Linear Systems §7.4:

  1. Restart on |ρ| or |ω| collapse. When either scalar falls below 1e-30, re-seed the shadow residual from the current true residual and restart the recurrence (r̂ = r, ρ = α = ω = 1, p = v = 0). One fresh matvec, almost always recovers convergence on systems where plain BiCGSTAB would stall.

  2. Bail on tt → 0. When ‖t‖² < 1e-30 — the preconditioned s lies in the kernel of A — accept the half-step x ← x + α·p and exit. Textbook safe-exit.

Even with these guards, BiCGSTAB remains less robust than GMRES for pathological non-symmetric systems. Fall back to crate::math::sparse::gmres if you hit a system where BiCGSTAB can’t converge — GMRES has stronger convergence guarantees at the cost of more memory (it stores restart basis vectors).

GPU port

There’s no closure-driven GPU mirror. WGPU has no native sparse BLAS, and the WGSL kernel for “user closure” would need to be hand-written per consumer; instead each on-device solver wires its own BsrAlgebraKernel matvec into a custom CG loop. Stage 27.1 in PLAN.md tracks the deferred port.

Optimizers

crates/molla/src/optim/ ships the two canonical first-order optimizers — Adam and SGD with momentum / Nesterov / weight decay — both as plain Rust state structs that consume f64 slices. Differentiable physics, parameter ID, and policy-learning code paths in molla all need gradient descent on a flat parameter vector, and these are the shared primitives that everyone depends on.

The shape mirrors Warp’s wp.optim.{Adam, SGD} (xtra/warp/warp/_src/optim/{adam,sgd}.py). On the GPU side, the fused-update kernels live in crates/molla-kernels/shaders/optim_{adam,sgd}.wgsl and are dispatched by crate::kernels::{optim_adam, optim_sgd}.

CPU + GPU precision

Host paths run on f64 (the engine’s Real); GPU kernels run on f32 because WGSL has no f64. The Rust dispatch wrappers in crate::kernels convert host f64 slices to f32 storage at upload time.

Adam

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug)]
pub struct AdamConfig {
    pub lr: Real,
    pub beta1: Real,
    pub beta2: Real,
    pub eps: Real,
    pub weight_decay: Real,  // 0.0 disables (AdamW-style when nonzero)
}

#[derive(Clone, Debug)]
pub struct AdamState {
    pub m: Vec<Real>,    // first-moment EMA
    pub v: Vec<Real>,    // second-moment EMA
    pub step: u32,       // 1-based count of updates applied
}

impl AdamState {
    pub fn new(n_params: usize) -> Self;
    pub fn reset(&mut self);
    pub fn step(&mut self, params: &mut [Real], grads: &[Real], cfg: &AdamConfig);
}
}

AdamConfig::default() is the canonical Kingma & Ba choice (lr = 1e-3, β₁ = 0.9, β₂ = 0.999, ε = 1e-8, no weight decay).

The update is the standard formula with the bias-correction divisor clamped to Real::EPSILON (guards against β₁ = 1 / β₂ = 1 degeneracies). Optional decoupled weight decay (AdamW, Loshchilov & Hutter 2019) is applied after the moment-correction step using the pre-update θ:

m_t = β₁·m_{t-1} + (1−β₁)·g_t
v_t = β₂·v_{t-1} + (1−β₂)·g_t²
m̂_t = m_t / (1 − β₁^t)
v̂_t = v_t / (1 − β₂^t)
θ_t = θ_{t-1} − lr · m̂_t / (√v̂_t + ε)
θ_t -= lr · wd · θ_{t-1}       # if wd != 0

When weight_decay == 0.0 the path is bit-identical to plain Adam.

Log-space Adam for positive parameters

For positive-only parameters (Young’s modulus, density, mass, viscosity) that may span orders of magnitude, Adam’s scale-invariance breaks down: a fixed lr either oscillates wildly when the parameter is small or stalls when it’s large. The pattern used across the parameter-ID tests in crates/molla-fem/tests/fem_diff_optim.rs is to optimise in log-space:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// Optimize ξ = ln(E) so the Adam step size is scale-invariant.
// Chain rule: dJ/dξ = dJ/dE · E.
let mut xi = e_init.ln();
let mut adam = AdamState::new(1);
let cfg = AdamConfig { lr: 0.05, ..AdamConfig::default() };

for _ in 0..200 {
    let e: Real = xi.exp();
    // ... forward + adjoint → dj_de ...
    let mut grad = vec![dj_de * e];          // chain rule
    let mut xi_vec = vec![xi];
    adam.step(&mut xi_vec, &grad, &cfg);
    xi = xi_vec[0];
}
let e_recovered = xi.exp();
}

The · E factor is the chain rule for ξ = ln(E) ⇒ dJ/dξ = dJ/dE · E. Adam then runs on ξ where a lr of 0.05 is a 5% multiplicative step on E regardless of the current magnitude. This is the recipe behind every FEM-elastic parameter-ID experiment in the test suite.

SGD

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug)]
pub struct SgdConfig {
    pub lr: Real,
    pub momentum: Real,      // 0.0 disables
    pub dampening: Real,
    pub weight_decay: Real,
    pub nesterov: bool,
}

#[derive(Clone, Debug)]
pub struct SgdState {
    pub buf: Vec<Real>,      // momentum buffer
    pub step: u32,
}

impl SgdState {
    pub fn new(n_params: usize) -> Self;
    pub fn reset(&mut self);
    pub fn step(&mut self, params: &mut [Real], grads: &[Real], cfg: &SgdConfig);
}
}

The semantics match molla’s GPU sgd_step_kernel:

g̃   = g + wd · θ
b_t = μ·b_{t-1} + (1−damp)·g̃    if t > 0
    = g̃                          if t == 0
g_eff = g̃ + μ·b_t                if Nesterov
      = b_t                       otherwise
θ_t = θ_{t-1} − lr · g_eff

The first-step special case (b_0 = g₀ rather than μ·0 + (1−damp)·g₀) is what SgdState::step peeks at — the step counter distinguishes it from subsequent steps.

SgdConfig::default() is plain SGD with lr = 1e-3, no momentum.

Fused-update GPU kernels

The shaders/optim_adam.wgsl kernel runs one thread per parameter and does the full Adam update in registers:

m[i] = β₁·m[i] + (1−β₁)·g[i]
v[i] = β₂·v[i] + (1−β₂)·g[i]²
m̂   = m[i] / (1 − β₁^t)
v̂   = v[i] / (1 − β₂^t)
θ[i] -= lr · m̂ / (√v̂ + ε)
θ[i] -= lr · wd · θ_pre    // if wd != 0          (decoupled, AdamW)

theta, m, v are mutated in place; grad is read-only. All buffers are f32. Workgroup size 256 — matches fem_vector_ops.wgsl sizing for warp-aligned vector ops on NVIDIA / Intel / AMD desktop adapters. The optim_sgd.wgsl kernel follows the same shape.

The crate::kernels::optim_{adam,sgd} Rust dispatch wrappers handle the f64 → f32 conversion, pipeline + bind-group setup, and the single dispatch per call. Stage 38c parity tests pin CPU and GPU within f32 tolerance after many steps; finite-difference gradient checks (crates/molla-kernels/tests/optim_gpu_parity.rs) catch shader regressions early.

Cross-references

  • Tape-based autograd feeds gradients into these optimizers in the differentiable-physics test suite.
  • FEM adjoint is the main producer of per-parameter gradients in parameter-ID experiments.

Graph coloring

crates/molla-math/src/coloring.rs (Stage 38d) centralises the constraint-graph colouring step used by VBD and XPBD. Before this module, each parallel-constraint solver carried its own copy of the same recipe; now there’s a single source of truth.

Why coloring matters for parallel constraint projection

VBD’s per-vertex Gauss-Seidel iteration and XPBD’s distance-constraint projection are both constraint-batch parallel: within a single batch, no two constraints write to the same vertex, so the GPU can dispatch one thread per constraint without a write-hazard. Across batches, you need a barrier — vertex updates from batch k must be visible to batch k+1.

The colouring step partitions a constraint set into the minimum number of batches that satisfy that invariant. It runs once per scene at build time, never per frame, so the GPU never sees the raw graph.

Public API

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn greedy_color(adjacency: &[Vec<u32>]) -> Vec<u32>;
pub fn mcs_color(adjacency: &[Vec<u32>]) -> Vec<u32>;
pub fn color_constraints(constraint_verts: &[Vec<u32>]) -> Vec<u32>;
pub fn group_by_color(colors: &[u32]) -> Vec<Vec<usize>>;
}

The algorithms mirror the reference implementation in xtra/warp/warp/native/coloring.cpp (Gaia / Anka Chen, Apache-2.0).

greedy_color

Degree-ordered greedy colouring (Fratarcangeli & Pellacini 2015). Sort vertices by descending degree; for each vertex in that order, assign the smallest colour unused by its already-coloured neighbours. Cheap (O(V log V + E)) and usually within 1-2 colours of optimal on constraint graphs.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let edges = vec![vec![0u32, 1], vec![1, 2], vec![2, 3]];
let colors = color_constraints(&edges);
// constraint 0 and 1 share vertex 1 ⇒ different colours
// constraint 1 and 2 share vertex 2 ⇒ different colours
assert_ne!(colors[0], colors[1]);
assert_ne!(colors[1], colors[2]);
}

mcs_color

Maximum Cardinality Search ordering (Pereira & Palsberg 2005) followed by the same smallest-unused-colour assignment as greedy_color. The MCS step builds an ordering where, at each step, the next vertex is the unordered one with the most already-ordered neighbours.

On chordal graphs MCS produces an optimal colouring; on general graphs it typically beats degree-ordered greedy by 1-2 colours. For the structured grid-cloth constraint graphs molla tests against, MCS hits the theoretical optimum (4 colours for a rectangular grid).

The implementation uses a bucket-based priority queue (McsBuckets) to keep all operations amortised O(1). Time complexity is O(V + E).

color_constraints — the line-graph helper

The real workhorse. constraint_verts[c] lists the vertices touched by constraint c. The function builds the conflict graph (one node per constraint; two constraints adjacent iff they share at least one vertex) and returns a per-constraint colour via mcs_color.

Naively this is O(C²). The implementation bucket-groups constraints by vertex and only adds pairwise edges within each bucket, giving O(Σ_v deg(v)²) — much cheaper on the sparse constraint graphs that real meshes produce.

group_by_color — partition into batches

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let groups: Vec<Vec<usize>> = group_by_color(&colors);
// groups[c] is the sorted list of constraint indices assigned colour c.
}

The outer vec has length max(colors) + 1. Callers dispatch one GPU pass per colour over its index list, with a barrier between passes.

End-to-end wiring

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use molla::math::{color_constraints, group_by_color};

// 1. Build the constraint set.
let constraint_verts: Vec<Vec<u32>> = build_edges_from_mesh(&mesh);

// 2. Colour once at scene-build time.
let colors = color_constraints(&constraint_verts);
let batches = group_by_color(&colors);

// 3. Each frame, dispatch one pass per colour batch.
for batch in &batches {
    dispatch_constraint_pass(batch, /* shared state */);
    // barrier between batches handled by wgpu's pass boundary
}
}

A typical 4×4 grid cloth produces 24 constraints (12 horizontal + 12 vertical) and an MCS colouring uses 4 colours; the color_constraints_distance_constraint_graph test verifies the upper-bound contract (n_colors ≤ 6) and asserts no adjacent constraints share a colour. Theory says 4 suffices; greedy occasionally blows up to 5-6 on degenerate orderings, which is why the test only asserts the upper bound.

Limitations + design notes

  • Both algorithms run on the CPU. Colouring is a one-shot preprocessing step; the GPU never sees the raw graph. Pushing it on-device is technically possible (parallel speculative colouring á la Çatalyürek et al.) but not motivated yet.
  • No edge weights. The line graph is unweighted — every constraint costs one slot in its colour batch. Constraint-cost balancing (longer constraints take more flops) isn’t modelled; in practice the variance across constraints in a single batch is small enough that thread-block stragglers don’t matter.
  • Deterministic. Both algorithms tie-break by lowest index for full reproducibility. Same input → same colour assignment across runs.

Cross-references

  • XPBD is the main consumer for distance constraints.
  • VBD consumes the same machinery for vertex-block descent on soft-body energy.

Scan & 64-bit radix sort

molla’s GPU pipelines lean on two device-wide primitives:

  • ScanKernel (crates/molla-kernels/src/scan.rs) — exclusive or inclusive u32 prefix scan. Three passes, scales to ≈ 16 M elements.
  • RadixSortKernel64 (crates/molla-compute-primitives/src/radix_sort.rs) — 8 passes of 8-bit radix on (u64 key, u32 value) pairs. Plus segmented sort via segment-tag prefix.

Both are designed for reuse: build once per device, dispatch many times. Most callers don’t construct them directly — they’re owned by higher-level kernels (BsrAlgebraKernel, LbvhKernel, broad-phase spatial-hash builder, …) and exposed only through that surface.

ScanKernel — 3-pass device-wide scan

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct ScanKernel { /* … */ }

impl ScanKernel {
    pub fn new(device: Arc<wgpu::Device>, queue: Arc<wgpu::Queue>) -> Self;

    pub fn exclusive_scan_u32(
        &self,
        input: &wgpu::Buffer,
        output: &wgpu::Buffer,
        n: u32,
    ) -> Result<()>;

    pub fn inclusive_scan_u32(
        &self,
        input: &wgpu::Buffer,
        output: &wgpu::Buffer,
        n: u32,
    ) -> Result<()>;

    pub fn total_sum_u32(&self, input: &wgpu::Buffer, n: u32) -> Result<u64>;
}
}

Stage 38e — replaces the single-workgroup Hillis-Steele scan that tile_stream_compaction.wgsl shipped, for the cases that need n ≫ workgroup_size (sparse-grid insert, hash-grid buckets, contact pair compaction, SpGEMM).

Algorithm — scan-then-fixup

Two-level Blelloch / Harris pattern, matching Warp’s scan.cu and NVIDIA’s 2007 GPU Gems chapter:

Pass 1 (scan_local)
  Per-workgroup exclusive Hillis-Steele scan over WG_SIZE = 256
  elements. Each workgroup writes its inclusive total into
  group_sums[wg_id].

Pass 2 (scan_groups)
  Single-workgroup exclusive scan over group_sums. Internally
  tiled so a single dispatch covers up to WG_SIZE² = 65 536
  groups → 16 M elements before a hierarchical fallback is
  needed.

Pass 3 (scan_fixup)
  Each workgroup adds group_sums[wg_id] to all its elements;
  inclusive variant also adds input[i] to convert exclusive →
  inclusive.

The single-WG pass-2 tile is what bounds the maximum input size:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
const WG_SIZE: u32 = 256;
const MAX_GROUPS: u32 = WG_SIZE * WG_SIZE;   // 65 536 groups → 16 M elements
}

The 256 KiB group_sums scratch buffer is allocated up front at ScanKernel::new so dispatch never has to grow it. The uniform buffer is similarly preallocated and just written each call.

Concurrency contract

Internal group_sums + uniforms buffers are shared across calls on a single instance. Issuing a second scan before the first’s GPU submission has drained will race on those buffers — pass-1 of the second scan may read stale group_sums. For pipelined usage (multiple scans in flight) construct one ScanKernel per logical stream, or device.poll(...) between calls. Single-threaded “submit, poll, submit” usage is safe and what every current consumer does.

total_sum_u32 — small extra readback

Convenience wrapper: runs an inclusive scan into a scratch buffer and reads back the last u32 as a host u64. Adds one mapped-readback worth of latency, so use sparingly — the typical pattern is “scan to get offsets, then exclusively read the last element of an already-existing scan output” rather than calling this.

RadixSortKernel64 — 8-pass 64-bit sort

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct RadixSortKernel64 { /* … */ }

impl RadixSortKernel64 {
    pub const MAX_SEGMENTS: u32 = 1u32 << 16;  // 65 536

    pub fn new(
        device: Arc<wgpu::Device>,
        queue: Arc<wgpu::Queue>,
        initial_capacity: usize,
    ) -> Result<Self>;

    pub fn sort_pairs_u64(
        &mut self,
        keys_lo: &wgpu::Buffer,
        keys_hi: &wgpu::Buffer,
        values: &wgpu::Buffer,
        n: u32,
    ) -> Result<()>;

    pub fn segmented_sort_pairs_u64(
        &mut self,
        keys_lo: &wgpu::Buffer,
        keys_hi: &wgpu::Buffer,
        values: &wgpu::Buffer,
        segment_offsets: &wgpu::Buffer,
        n_segments: u32,
        n_total: u32,
    ) -> Result<()>;
}
}

8 passes of 8-bit radix. The 64-bit key is stored as two parallel u32 buffers (keys_lo, keys_hi); each pass dispatches three shader entry points (count_block_bins, scan_global_bins, scatter) and ping-pongs between the caller’s buffers and a private scratch pair. After 8 passes the final sorted result lands back in the caller’s buffers.

Stability

The scatter kernel processes each block’s elements in input-index order from a single thread, so the i-th occurrence of digit d in block b always lands at block_bins[d, b] + i. Across blocks the global scan visits (digit, block) in row-major order so earlier blocks always get lower output offsets. Stability is load-bearing for LBVH construction: ties on Morton codes need to break deterministically so the WGSL delta function in lbvh.wgsl sees the same ordering the build pass expects.

Why radix and not bitonic / merge

Discussed in the WGSL header shaders/radix_sort.wgsl. TL;DR:

  • 4/8-pass 8-bit radix is the textbook GPU LBVH choice — Karras 2012, OptiX, Embree, NVIDIA Warp / cuBQL all do this.
  • Bitonic sort is O(n log² n) and loses past n ≈ 10k.
  • Merge sort hits memory bandwidth before radix does.

Radix wins because the work per pass is O(n) with very high arithmetic intensity in the count + scatter steps, and 64-bit keys only need 8 passes.

Segmented sort via segment-tag prefix

Segmented sort is the awkward one — pre-existing GPU radix kernels typically don’t ship it. molla’s approach is a prefix-tag trick:

1. Host-XOR each key's keys_hi top 16 bits with (segment_id << 16).
2. Run a single 64-bit global sort. The tag dominates, so segments
   stay contiguous AND sort within each segment.
3. Mask out the tag bits.

The cost is that keys must not use the top 16 bits of keys_hi when using segmented sort. With n_segments ≤ 65 536 (the assertion in MAX_SEGMENTS) this is safe by construction. The plain sort_pairs_u64 has no such restriction.

The tag step needs a single readback of segment_offsets and one mapped read+write of keys_hi — both happen host-side. The actual sort is then a single 8-pass dispatch.

Validation guard

Before tagging, the code validates segment_offsets:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
if offsets_host[seg + 1] < offsets_host[seg] {
    return Err(/* non-monotonic */);
}
if offsets_host[n_segments] != n_total {
    return Err(/* coverage mismatch */);
}
}

Hoisted ahead of the host slicing so malformed offsets produce a real error instead of panicking deep inside a &mut hi_host[start..end].

Perf

Both kernels were tuned to be one-shot fast on modern desktop GPUs. On an RTX 4070, the perf gate in radix_sort_perf.rs keeps a 1 M-key 64-bit sort under ~5 ms; scan does 16 M elements in ~3 ms. Numbers shift by ±50% between vendors but the asymptotic shape is consistent because both kernels are bandwidth-bound at large n.

Cross-references

  • SpGEMM design consumes the scan for the symbolic phase’s count → c_row_offsets step.
  • BVH uses the radix sort for Morton-code ordering of leaves before the LBVH build.
  • Sparse grids (NanoVDB-equivalent) uses scan for bucket prefix-sums during insert.

GPU runtime

crates/molla/src/compute/engine.rs owns the wgpu runtime. One Engine per process holds the Device + Queue references that every kernel dispatcher borrows.

Backend enum

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)]
pub enum Backend {
    /// Pure CPU — no `wgpu` resources allocated. Useful for tests
    /// and for CPU-fallback paths every solver must provide.
    Cpu,
    /// Pick whatever GPU backend wgpu finds best on this host.
    AutoGpu,
    /// Force a specific wgpu backend (Vulkan, Metal, Dx12, …).
    Gpu(wgpu::Backends),
}
}

Cpu is not a fake adapter — there are no wgpu resources at all. Every solver and sensor that supports a CPU path checks Engine::device() and falls back to the host implementation when None. This is what makes the test suite runnable on CI machines without GPUs.

Engine

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct Engine { /* … */ }

impl Engine {
    pub fn new_cpu() -> Self;
    pub fn new_gpu() -> Result<Self>;
    pub fn new(backend: Backend) -> Result<Self>;

    pub fn backend(&self) -> Backend;
    pub fn adapter_info(&self) -> Option<&AdapterInfo>;
    pub fn device(&self) -> Option<&Arc<wgpu::Device>>;
    pub fn queue(&self) -> Option<&Arc<wgpu::Queue>>;
}
}

new_cpu allocates nothing. new_gpu (= new(Backend::AutoGpu)) walks the wgpu::Instance, picks the highest-performance adapter, and requests a device with that adapter’s native limits. new(backend) is the general constructor; Backend::Gpu(wgpu::Backends::VULKAN) forces a specific API.

device() / queue() return None on CPU backends. Callers that require GPU should bail loudly:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let device = engine.device()
    .ok_or_else(|| Error::Gpu("GPU backend required".into()))?;
}

Adapter selection — the limits decision

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let (device, queue) = pollster::block_on(adapter.request_device(&wgpu::DeviceDescriptor {
    label: Some("molla::compute::Engine"),
    required_features: wgpu::Features::empty(),
    required_limits: adapter.limits(),
    experimental_features: wgpu::ExperimentalFeatures::default(),
    memory_hints: wgpu::MemoryHints::Performance,
    trace: wgpu::Trace::Off,
}))
.map_err(|e| Error::Gpu(format!("device request failed: {e}")))?;
}

The key choice is required_limits: adapter.limits() — molla requests whatever this adapter natively supports, not wgpu::Limits::downlevel_defaults(). The reason is documented inline:

downlevel_defaults caps storage buffers at 4 per stage, which we exceed in the rigid-body integrator (7 model + 5 state + 1 control = 13). Modern desktop GPUs typically allow 16+, mobile / web much less; if we ever target the browser we’ll need to consolidate buffers.

The downside is that molla won’t run on WebGPU today. The Stage 41 rigid-body kernel and the FEM elasticity stack both bind more than the WebGPU minimum; targeting browsers means consolidating into fewer, fatter storage buffers.

AdapterInfo

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[derive(Clone, Debug)]
pub struct AdapterInfo {
    pub vendor: u32,         // PCI id when reported
    pub name: String,        // device name
    pub backend: String,     // "Vulkan", "Metal", "Dx12", "Gl", "BrowserWebGpu"
    pub is_software: bool,   // true for software rasterisers (e.g. llvmpipe)
    pub driver: String,
}
}

Surfaces in --version output of molla_viewer and as a sanity check at startup. Software adapters (llvmpipe, SwiftShader) are allowed — they run but at a fraction of native speed; they exist mainly so the GPU paths can be exercised on CI without real hardware.

Feature gating

The gpu Cargo feature gates everything in this module. With --no-default-features:

  • Engine::new becomes Engine::new_cpu-only.
  • wgpu doesn’t link.
  • BsrGpu, BsrAlgebraKernel, ScanKernel, RadixSortKernel*, every Tile*Kernel, and all crate::kernels::* GPU dispatchers disappear.
  • The CPU paths (host BsrMatrix, all *_cpu reference functions, the iterative solvers in crate::math::iterative, host Featherstone, etc.) all still compile.

Default features include gpu. CI tests both with and without the feature to keep CPU-only configurations honest.

Cross-references

  • Storage abstractions — Buffer<T> is the upload / download primitive that bridges host vectors to the Device exposed here.
  • Kernel infrastructure — the dispatcher pattern every kernel module uses.
  • Persistent-buffer pattern — when to keep GPU buffers resident across many dispatches.

Storage abstractions

crates/molla/src/storage/ defines Buffer<T> — a homogeneous array that mirrors itself across host and device memory. Both halves are functional under the gpu feature; without it only the host half exists, so all tests against the math + sim layer can drive the host-only path directly.

The host is f64, the device is f32. The conversion happens exactly once at the buffer boundary through the BufferElement trait, which keeps every physics module from sprinkling as f32 / as f64 everywhere.

BufferElement — the host↔gpu bridge trait

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub trait BufferElement: Copy + 'static {
    type Gpu: bytemuck::Pod + bytemuck::Zeroable + Copy;
    fn to_gpu(&self) -> Self::Gpu;
    fn from_gpu(gpu: &Self::Gpu) -> Self;
}
}

Implementations cover every math type that ever lives in a buffer:

Host typeGpu mirrorSize (bytes)
Real (f64)f324
Vec3 (DVec3)[f32; 4] (vec3 padded)16
Mat3 (DMat3)GpuMat348
TransformGpuTransform32
Quat (DQuat)[f32; 4]16
SpatialVectorGpuSpatialVector32
u32u324
i32i324

The Gpu mirrors live in crates/molla/src/math/gpu.rs. GpuMat3 stores three vec4-padded columns to match WGSL’s mat3x3<f32> column alignment of 16. GpuTransform and GpuSpatialVector each hold two padded vec3s. The gpu_struct_sizes_match_wgsl_expectations test pins those sizes:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
assert_eq!(core::mem::size_of::<GpuTransform>(), 32);
assert_eq!(core::mem::size_of::<GpuSpatialVector>(), 32);
assert_eq!(core::mem::size_of::<GpuMat3>(), 48);
}

BufferUsage

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)]
pub enum BufferUsage {
    Storage,            // read-only on device (e.g. Model data)
    StorageReadWrite,   // read-write on device (e.g. State arrays)
    Uniform,            // small constants
}
}

Picked at allocation time to set the correct wgpu::BufferUsages bit mask. Storage and StorageReadWrite differ only conceptually — both translate to STORAGE | COPY_SRC | COPY_DST; the read-only-ness is enforced by the binding type in the bind-group layout, not by the buffer.

Buffer<T>

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct Buffer<T: BufferElement> {
    host: Vec<T>,
    usage: BufferUsage,
    state: SyncState,
    #[cfg(feature = "gpu")]
    device: Option<wgpu::Buffer>,
}
}

Construction:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl<T: BufferElement> Buffer<T> {
    pub fn from_vec(host: Vec<T>, usage: BufferUsage) -> Self;
    pub fn zeros(len: usize, usage: BufferUsage) -> Self where T: Default;
    pub fn from_slice(slice: &[T], usage: BufferUsage) -> Self;
}
}

from_vec is the most efficient — moves the existing Vec<T> in. zeros is convenient when you just need allocated state. None of these allocate a GPU buffer; that’s deferred.

Sync-state machine

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
enum SyncState {
    HostOnly,      // no GPU yet allocated
    InSync,        // host and device hold equal data
    HostDirty,     // host was mutated since last upload
    DeviceDirty,   // device was mutated since last download
}
}

The state machine lets the buffer track which side is authoritative without round-tripping. host() errors when the state is DeviceDirty — the caller has to download() first. host_mut() similarly errors and additionally marks the new state HostDirty. A kernel that writes the buffer in place is expected to call mark_device_dirty() afterwards.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn host(&self) -> Result<&[T]>;
pub fn host_mut(&mut self) -> Result<&mut [T]>;
pub fn mark_device_dirty(&mut self);  // gpu only
}

The pattern protects against a class of stale-read bugs that would otherwise be invisible until the next CPU/GPU parity test failed.

GPU half

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[cfg(feature = "gpu")] impl<T: BufferElement> Buffer<T> {
    pub fn ensure_device(&mut self, device: &wgpu::Device) -> Result<()>;
    pub fn upload(&mut self, queue: &wgpu::Queue) -> Result<()>;
    pub fn download(&mut self, device: &wgpu::Device, queue: &wgpu::Queue) -> Result<()>;
    pub fn device_buffer(&self) -> Option<&wgpu::Buffer>;
}
}
  • ensure_device lazily allocates the wgpu::Buffer sized for host.len() * size_of::<T::Gpu>(). No-op if already allocated. Empty buffers stay un-allocated (wgpu requires non-zero size).
  • upload converts f64 → f32 per element via BufferElement::to_gpu and writes through Queue::write_buffer. Marks state InSync.
  • download issues a staging-buffer round-trip with MAP_READ, pollster::block_ons the map fence, then converts f32 → f64 back into the host vec. Marks state InSync.

download blocks the calling thread. It’s the simplest possible implementation — there’s no async API in molla today; persistent-buffer paths avoid download entirely (see Persistent-buffer pattern).

Why f64 host / f32 device

Long-running articulated integration accumulates drift at the f32 epsilon scale within ~10⁴ steps. Featherstone, RNEA, and CRBA all need f64 to stay stable across the kinds of multi-second time windows that physics-for-robotics demands. f32 on the GPU is the WGSL ground truth — there is no f64 in WGSL today (a small subset of GPUs expose it through Vulkan extensions, but that’s a forked codebase).

The boundary is exactly the BufferElement::{to_gpu, from_gpu} pair. No other code in molla converts between the two. This constraint is what makes the CPU paths the precision-of-record for every solver — the GPU paths converge to within f32 tolerance after conversion-aware comparison.

Test coverage

The buffer module ships a small test set in crates/molla/src/storage/buffer.rs that pins the round-trip behaviour without needing a GPU. End-to-end GPU tests run against specific kernel pipelines (fem_gpu_parity, sparse_gpu_parity, mpm_gpu_parity) and exercise the upload/download path indirectly.

Cross-references

  • Vectors, matrices, transforms — the host types that show up in BufferElement impls.
  • GPU runtime — the Engine that hands out Device / Queue references.
  • Persistent-buffer pattern — when Buffer<T> isn’t the right abstraction (resident solver state, repeated dispatches).

Kernel infrastructure

Every WGSL kernel in molla follows the same dispatcher pattern. This page documents the shape — how pipelines are built, how bind groups are laid out, and the float-atomic CAS-add idiom that WGSL’s missing atomic<f32> forces.

Dispatcher pattern

A typical kernel module exposes one type that owns the compiled pipelines and bind-group layouts. Build it once per device, dispatch it many times. The canonical shape:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct FooKernel {
    device: Arc<wgpu::Device>,
    queue:  Arc<wgpu::Queue>,

    pipeline: wgpu::ComputePipeline,
    layout_io: wgpu::BindGroupLayout,
    layout_uniforms: wgpu::BindGroupLayout,
}

impl FooKernel {
    pub fn new(device: Arc<wgpu::Device>, queue: Arc<wgpu::Queue>) -> Self {
        let shader = device.create_shader_module(wgpu::ShaderModuleDescriptor {
            label: Some("molla::foo"),
            source: wgpu::ShaderSource::Wgsl(include_str!("../../shaders/foo.wgsl").into()),
        });
        let layout_io = device.create_bind_group_layout(/* … */);
        let layout_uniforms = device.create_bind_group_layout(/* … */);
        let pipeline_layout = device.create_pipeline_layout(&wgpu::PipelineLayoutDescriptor {
            label: Some("molla::foo layout"),
            bind_group_layouts: &[&layout_io, &layout_uniforms],
            push_constant_ranges: &[],
        });
        let pipeline = device.create_compute_pipeline(&wgpu::ComputePipelineDescriptor {
            label: Some("molla::foo pipeline"),
            layout: Some(&pipeline_layout),
            module: &shader,
            entry_point: Some("foo_main"),
            compilation_options: wgpu::PipelineCompilationOptions::default(),
            cache: None,
        });
        Self { device, queue, pipeline, layout_io, layout_uniforms }
    }

    pub fn dispatch(&self, /* args */) -> Result<()> {
        let bg_io = self.device.create_bind_group(/* … */);
        let bg_u  = self.device.create_bind_group(/* … */);
        let mut encoder = self.device.create_command_encoder(/* … */);
        {
            let mut pass = encoder.begin_compute_pass(/* … */);
            pass.set_pipeline(&self.pipeline);
            pass.set_bind_group(0, &bg_io, &[]);
            pass.set_bind_group(1, &bg_u, &[]);
            pass.dispatch_workgroups(groups_x, groups_y, groups_z);
        }
        self.queue.submit(std::iter::once(encoder.finish()));
        Ok(())
    }
}
}

ScanKernel, RadixSortKernel{,64}, BsrAlgebraKernel, Dense3Kernel, TileMatmulKernel, TileConvolutionKernel, all the fem_* and mpm_* dispatchers — they all wear this skin.

Bind-group conventions

Every kernel splits resources into two groups:

  • Group 0 — IO. Storage buffers (read-only inputs, read-write outputs). Read-only inputs are bound at slot indices 0..k, read-write outputs at slots k..n. Convention varies per kernel but is consistent within a kernel.
  • Group 1 — Uniforms. A single struct of compile-time-known layout, padded to 16-byte alignment, holding shape parameters (dimensions, scalar coefficients, step counters). The uniform struct is #[repr(C)] and derives bytemuck::Pod + Zeroable.
#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[repr(C)]
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, bytemuck::Pod, bytemuck::Zeroable)]
struct Uniforms {
    n: u32,
    inclusive: u32,
    num_groups: u32,
    _pad: u32,        // 16-byte align
}
}

Padding fields are explicit. WGSL’s uniform layout rules require vec3-aligned-to-16; the host-side #[repr(C)] struct must match or bytemuck::bytes_of will write the wrong layout into the uniform buffer.

Read-only vs read-write bind entries

The helper functions ro_storage(binding) and rw_storage(binding) appear across every kernel module and abbreviate the layout entries:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn ro_storage(binding: u32) -> wgpu::BindGroupLayoutEntry {
    wgpu::BindGroupLayoutEntry {
        binding,
        visibility: wgpu::ShaderStages::COMPUTE,
        ty: wgpu::BindingType::Buffer {
            ty: wgpu::BufferBindingType::Storage { read_only: true },
            has_dynamic_offset: false,
            min_binding_size: None,
        },
        count: None,
    }
}
}

rw_storage is identical except read_only: false. The WGSL side matches with var<storage, read> or var<storage, read_write>.

Workgroup size — the 256 convention

Most molla kernels use @workgroup_size(256). The pick matches Warp’s default and is the sweet spot for AMD/NVIDIA/Intel desktop adapters — big enough for warp-level reductions to amortise, small enough to keep occupancy reasonable on small inputs.

const WG_SIZE: u32 = 256u;

@compute @workgroup_size(WG_SIZE)
fn kernel_main(@builtin(global_invocation_id) gid: vec3<u32>) {
    let i = gid.x;
    if (i >= u.n) { return; }   // bounds check; let the tail bail out
    // …
}

The trailing bounds check is mandatory because dispatch grids are sized to the nearest workgroup multiple. Skipping the check produces out-of-bounds reads on the last workgroup.

Float atomics — CAS-add idiom

WGSL has no atomic<f32>. Float reductions that need to commute across thread groups (FEM assembly, MPM P2G, SpGEMM numeric) bit-cast through atomic<u32> and atomicCompareExchangeWeak until the swap succeeds:

fn atomic_add_csr(slot: u32, value: f32) {
    if (value == 0.0) { return; }
    var old_bits = atomicLoad(&csr_values[slot]);
    loop {
        let old_f = bitcast<f32>(old_bits);
        let new_bits = bitcast<u32>(old_f + value);
        let r = atomicCompareExchangeWeak(&csr_values[slot], old_bits, new_bits);
        if (r.exchanged) {
            return;
        }
        old_bits = r.old_value;
    }
}

The host-side buffer is declared array<atomic<u32>> in the WGSL binding; the bytemuck/f32 slice on the host is the same memory viewed without the atomic wrapper. The pattern shows up in:

  • shaders/fem_assembly.wgsl (FEM CSR scatter)
  • shaders/fem_elasticity_assemble.wgsl
  • shaders/fem_ns_advect.wgsl (advection scatter)
  • shaders/fem_stokes_assemble.wgsl
  • shaders/bsr_spgemm_symbolic.wgsl (SpGEMM numeric)
  • shaders/apic_locate_tet.wgsl (APIC P2G locate-and-add)
  • shaders/splat_raytrace_sh_backward.wgsl (Gaussian splat adjoint)

The if (value == 0.0) return; early-exit matters: contributors with zero-valued blocks (off-pattern slots) shouldn’t busy-wait on the CAS loop.

Workgroup-scoped reductions

For per-workgroup reductions (scan, sort, prefix sum) the standard pattern is a var<workgroup> shared array, an explicit workgroupBarrier() between read and write phases, and the Hillis-Steele or Blelloch ping-pong:

var<workgroup> tile_a: array<u32, 256>;
var<workgroup> tile_b: array<u32, 256>;

tile_a[lane] = v;
workgroupBarrier();

var step: u32 = 1u;
loop {
    if (step >= WG_SIZE) { break; }
    // … read tile_a, write tile_b, swap …
    workgroupBarrier();
    step = step * 2u;
}

See shaders/scan.wgsl for a complete example.

Why Arc<wgpu::Device> everywhere

Kernel dispatchers hold Arc<wgpu::Device> and Arc<wgpu::Queue> because the wgpu types are Clone (cheap reference counting under the hood) but Rust’s borrow checker doesn’t propagate that across struct fields. Arc makes the kernels self-contained and lets one Engine hand its device out to a dozen kernel dispatchers without lifetime juggling. The cost is one atomic increment at construction time — negligible compared to the pipeline compile.
