Tile compute primitives

Stage 37.8 bundled together a small suite of reusable compute primitives — workgroup-tiled GEMM, separable convolution, named filters, block-Cholesky factorisation, stream compaction, and a Monte-Carlo gradient estimator. They live in crates/molla/src/compute/tile_*.rs and share two conventions:

  • A CPU reference function (*_cpu) that’s the precision oracle and the no-feature fallback.
  • A GPU dispatcher (Tile*Kernel) gated behind the gpu feature.

This page covers each tile primitive at a glance; deep details live in the source modules and the WGSL shader headers.

tile_matmul — workgroup-tiled GEMM

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn matmul_cpu(
    a: &[f32], b: &[f32], c: &mut [f32],
    m: usize, n: usize, k: usize,
) -> Result<()>;

#[cfg(feature = "gpu")]
pub struct TileMatmulKernel { /* … */ }
}

Row-major C = A · B with A: m × k, B: k × n, C: m × n. The WGSL kernel uses 16×16 workgroup tiles loaded into workgroup memory once per tile and reused across k-axis traversals — the classic shared-memory matmul. The host wrapper TileMatmulKernel::dispatch_blocking allocates buffers, uploads A and B, dispatches, reads C back.

Shape (M, K, N) → grid (ceil(N/16), ceil(M/16), 1). The implementation is a textbook starting point, not optimised for any specific aspect ratio.

tile_convolution — separable 2D convolution

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, PartialEq)]
pub struct Kernel5 {
    pub coeffs: [f32; 5],
}

impl Kernel5 {
    pub const fn box5() -> Self;
    pub const fn gaussian5() -> Self;    // (1, 4, 6, 4, 1) / 16
    pub const fn identity() -> Self;     // δ-function
    pub const fn laplacian1d() -> Self;  // (0, 1, -2, 1, 0)
}

pub fn convolve_separable_cpu(
    input: &[f32], output: &mut [f32],
    width: usize, height: usize,
    kernel: &Kernel5,
) -> Result<()>;
}

Two-pass separable 5-tap convolution with clamp-to-edge boundary. The GPU side wires two pipelines (conv_horiz, conv_vert) and chains them through a scratch buffer. Used by viewer post-processing, preview filters, and the Stage 37.x wave-equation experiments.

tile_filtering — named filter wrappers

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn box_filter_cpu(input, output, width, height) -> Result<()>;
pub fn gaussian_filter_cpu(input, output, width, height) -> Result<()>;
pub fn laplacian_filter_cpu(input, output, width, height) -> Result<()>;
pub fn identity_filter_cpu(input, output, width, height) -> Result<()>;

// GPU variants take a TileConvolutionKernel + device + queue.
}

Thin wrappers over convolve_separable_cpu with named filter coefficients (box, Gaussian, Laplacian, identity). The math is identical — convolution is convolution — but exposing the named filters as their own API keeps call-sites readable. Identity is the smoke-test path: it should return the input unchanged.

tile_block_cholesky — single-workgroup SPD factorisation

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn cholesky_cpu(a: &mut [f32], n: usize) -> Result<()>;
pub fn cholesky_cpu_lenient(a: &mut [f32], n: usize) -> Result<()>;
pub fn frobenius_recon_error(orig: &[f32], factor: &[f32], n: usize) -> f32;

#[cfg(feature = "gpu")]
pub struct TileBlockCholeskyKernel { /* … */ }
}

In-place row-major Cholesky. On exit the lower triangle of a holds L with L · Lᵀ = A; the strict upper triangle is zeroed. cholesky_cpu returns Error::Internal if any pivot is < 1e-30 (non-SPD); cholesky_cpu_lenient clamps negative pivots to zero and proceeds — only use it when you genuinely want the clamped pseudo-factor (incomplete-Cholesky preconditioning of nearly-SPD systems).

The GPU path is a single-workgroup factor with 64 threads, capped at N ≤ 1024. For larger N it returns garbage (no protection in the shader; the host wrapper rejects explicitly). Multi-workgroup tiling is a v2 — the current consumers are all small-N FEM Schur complements where a single workgroup suffices.

tile_stream_compaction — gather-via-scan

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub const MAX_N: usize = 1024;

pub fn compact_cpu(input: &[f32], mask: &[bool]) -> Result<Vec<f32>>;
pub fn mask_to_u32(mask: &[bool]) -> Vec<u32>;

#[cfg(feature = "gpu")]
pub struct TileStreamCompactionKernel { /* … */ }
}

Single-workgroup Hillis-Steele scan + scatter. Walks input/mask, emits a dense vector of every entry where mask[i] == true. The GPU path is capped at n ≤ MAX_N = 1024 so a single workgroup covers the input; multi-workgroup decoupled-look-back is a v2.

For the cases that need n ≫ 1024, use the ScanKernel directly — it ships the production-grade scan path.

tile_mcgp — SPSA gradient estimator

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug)]
pub struct McgpConfig {
    pub n_samples: usize,
    pub epsilon: Real,
    pub seed: u64,
}

pub fn mcgp_estimate<F>(f: &F, params: &[Real], config: &McgpConfig) -> Vec<Real>
where F: Fn(&[Real]) -> Real;

pub fn finite_diff_central<F>(f: &F, params: &[Real], h: Real) -> Vec<Real>
where F: Fn(&[Real]) -> Real;
}

Stochastic gradient estimator for losses that aren’t tape-recordable (or where building the tape is too expensive). Given a black-box f: &[Real] -> Real and a parameter vector, runs n_samples perturbations of the form params ± ε · noise[k] (Rademacher ±1 noise) and accumulates the per-component gradient estimate:

g_i ≈ (1/N) · Σₖ (f(p + ε·dₖ) − f(p − ε·dₖ)) / (2 ε) · dₖ,i

This is the SPSA recipe of Spall (1992) — one of the cheapest stochastic gradient approximations and a useful complement to molla’s tape autograd (crate::autograd::tape) when the loss isn’t tape-recordable.

The estimate is noisy by design. An n_samples = 64 estimator on a smooth quadratic typically lands within ~5 % of the true gradient. Tighten the tolerance by raising n_samples (variance ∝ 1/N) or by using a Richardson-style averaged perturbation pattern (a v2 nice-to-have).

The internal RNG is a tiny xorshift64 keyed off the config seed, so two runs with the same seed produce the same gradient — important for reproducible parameter-ID experiments.

finite_diff_central is the deterministic O(2n) reference used as the oracle in tests; exposed publicly for callers who want a gold-standard FD check alongside the noisy SPSA estimate.

Cross-references

  • Kernel infrastructure — the dispatcher pattern every Tile*Kernel follows.
  • Scan & 64-bit radix sort — for stream compaction beyond the 1024 cap.
  • Tape-based autograd — the deterministic alternative to SPSA when the loss is tape-recordable.

Persistent-buffer pattern

Buffer<T> from Storage abstractions is the right tool when a host array is the source of truth and the device copy just mirrors it. For long-lived solver state — buffers that the GPU mutates across thousands of dispatches without the host ever needing to look — the upload/download semantics of Buffer<T> are the wrong abstraction. Use persistent GPU buffers instead.

When to use persistent buffers

The pattern: upload once, dispatch many. The buffer’s contents are authoritative on the device for the lifetime of the solver. The host side keeps the wgpu::Buffer handle (typically in an Arc<wgpu::Buffer> field of the kernel/solver struct) and never copies back unless the caller asks for a snapshot.

Three current users:

1. MPM resident state

The MPM grid (velocities, masses, force accumulators) is the largest buffer in the project and gets read+write every substep. Copying it host↔device per frame would cost more than the actual physics.

crate::compute::mpm and crate::compute::implicit_mpm allocate the grid buffers at scene-build time, zero them on the device, and the host never sees them again until the caller asks for a snapshot via an explicit MpmState::snapshot_* method. The state lives entirely on the device for the duration of n_substeps.

2. FEM CG bind-group caching

The CG inner loop dispatches the same (A, x, y) matvec thousands of times per solve. The “prepared matvec” path in BsrAlgebraKernel (Stage 41 v5) caches the uniform buffer + IO bind group up front so the inner loop becomes a single dispatch_workgroups with zero per-iter allocation:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct PreparedMatvec {
    uniform_buf: wgpu::Buffer,
    bg_io: wgpu::BindGroup,
    bg_u: wgpu::BindGroup,
    dim_x: u32,
    dim_y: u32,
}

impl BsrAlgebraKernel {
    pub fn prepare_matvec(&self, a, x_buf, y_buf, alpha, beta) -> Result<PreparedMatvec>;
    pub fn matvec_into_pass(&self, pass: &mut wgpu::ComputePass<'_>, prepared: &PreparedMatvec);
}
}

prepare_matvec is called once per CG solve; matvec_into_pass is called every CG iteration into a long-lived compute pass. The whole CG batch ends up as one encoder submission, which is what unlocks the latency reductions the FEM perf gates measure.

See BsrGpu for the prepared-matvec API in detail.

3. GPU FEM steppers

The FEM solvers (fem::solvers, fem::elasticity_gpu, fem::stokes_ns, fem::magneto) keep their assembled mass + stiffness matrices, vector workspaces, and boundary-condition encodings on the device for the lifetime of the simulation. Reassembly per step is done in-place — there’s an axpy_same_pattern_unchecked rebuild path that lets viscoelastic mass matrices update without rebuilding the sparsity pattern.

The host side keeps a MeshGpu / FemMatricesGpu struct of Arc<wgpu::Buffer> handles. CPU never reads back unless a test explicitly asks (parity tests, post-mortem diagnostics).

The pattern in code

The typical solver struct shape:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct FemElasticityGpu {
    device: Arc<wgpu::Device>,
    queue:  Arc<wgpu::Queue>,

    // Persistent solver state — written by kernels, never round-tripped.
    k_matrix: BsrGpu,            // stiffness matrix
    m_matrix: BsrGpu,            // mass matrix
    u: Arc<wgpu::Buffer>,        // displacements
    v: Arc<wgpu::Buffer>,        // velocities
    f_ext: Arc<wgpu::Buffer>,    // external forces

    // Pipeline owners — built once per device.
    algebra: BsrAlgebraKernel,
    scan: ScanKernel,
    // …
}

impl FemElasticityGpu {
    pub fn new(/* … */) -> Self { /* allocate + upload once */ }

    pub fn step(&mut self, dt: f64) -> Result<()> {
        // 100% on-device — no upload, no download.
    }

    pub fn snapshot_displacements(&self) -> Result<Vec<f64>> {
        // Explicit readback — only call from test or diagnostic code.
    }
}
}

Compare with Buffer<T>’s sync-state machine: persistent buffers don’t need one because there’s no ambiguous “which side is fresh?” question — the device is always fresh, and the host only reads through a named snapshot method.

When NOT to use persistent buffers

  • Hot reload of host-side data. When the caller mutates a Model field and expects it to take effect next step, Buffer<T> with host_mut + upload is the right primitive. Persistent buffers force the caller to call a rebuild method explicitly.
  • One-shot kernels. TileMatmulKernel::dispatch_blocking allocates fresh buffers per call. Caching them across calls would save ~50 µs of allocation but add ownership complexity. Don’t bother unless a profile says you should.
  • Tests. Test code reads results back to compare against a CPU oracle. Buffer<T>’s download is exactly that — the persistent pattern means tests need to call snapshot methods that themselves exist only for tests, which couples test infrastructure into production paths.

Lifetime + concurrency

Arc<wgpu::Buffer> is the standard handle. wgpu’s runtime reference-counts GPU resources internally, so dropping the Arc releases the buffer once all outstanding command-encoder references resolve. The same buffer can be bound into multiple bind groups simultaneously — wgpu’s tracker prevents read-write hazards across passes.

Two solvers sharing a buffer (e.g. an FEM displacement field consumed by both the elasticity stepper and a rendering pipeline) just hand each other Arc<wgpu::Buffer> clones. No additional synchronisation is needed inside a single command encoder — wgpu inserts the barriers.

Cross-references

  • GPU runtime — Engine::device() / Engine::queue() is what the persistent buffers get wired against.
  • Storage abstractions — the round-tripping Buffer<T> for the cases where you do want the host as the source of truth.
  • BsrGpu — the prepared-matvec implementation that’s the canonical example of the pattern.

Shape primitives

The collision pipeline is parameterised over a single enum (ShapeGeometry in crates/molla/src/sim/builder.rs:17) covering every primitive molla knows how to collide. Each variant ships a closed-form support function (crates/molla/src/geometry/support.rs) so GJK (GJK), EPA (EPA), and MPR (MPR) can drive every convex shape uniformly.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub enum ShapeGeometry {
    Sphere      { radius: Real },
    Plane       { normal: Vec3 },
    Box         { half_extents: Vec3 },
    Capsule     { half_height: Real, radius: Real },
    Cylinder    { half_height: Real, radius: Real },
    Cone        { half_height: Real, radius: Real },
    Ellipsoid   { half_axes: Vec3 },
    Triangle    { v0: Vec3, v1: Vec3, v2: Vec3 },
    TriMesh     { mesh_id: u32 },
    ConvexHull  { hull_id: u32 },
    Heightfield { field_id: u32 },
    Sdf         { sdf_id: u32 },
}
}

Capsule / Cylinder / Cone are oriented along the shape-local +Y axis. The body’s Transform rotates them into world frame.

Support functions

Every convex variant has an analytic support(direction) -> point map declared in crates/molla/src/geometry/support.rs. The signatures (slightly abridged):

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn support(geom: ShapeGeometry, xf: &Transform, dir_world: Vec3) -> Vec3;
pub fn support_with_hulls(geom: ShapeGeometry, xf: &Transform, dir_world: Vec3, hulls: &[Vec<Vec3>]) -> Vec3;

pub fn support_sphere     (radius: Real, dir: Vec3) -> Vec3;
pub fn support_box        (half: Vec3,   dir: Vec3) -> Vec3;
pub fn support_capsule    (half_height: Real, radius: Real, dir: Vec3) -> Vec3;
pub fn support_cylinder   (half_height: Real, radius: Real, dir: Vec3) -> Vec3;
pub fn support_cone       (half_height: Real, radius: Real, dir: Vec3) -> Vec3;
pub fn support_ellipsoid  (half_axes: Vec3,   dir: Vec3) -> Vec3;
pub fn support_convex_hull(vertices: &[Vec3], dir: Vec3) -> Vec3;
pub fn support_triangle   (v0: Vec3, v1: Vec3, v2: Vec3, dir: Vec3) -> Vec3;
pub fn support_minkowski  (
    geom_a: ShapeGeometry, xf_a: &Transform,
    geom_b: ShapeGeometry, xf_b: &Transform,
    dir_world: Vec3,
) -> Vec3;
}

The public support rotates dir_world into shape-local space via xf.rotation.conjugate(), evaluates the analytic map, and rotates the result back. Degenerate (zero-length) directions short-circuit to the shape origin (crates/molla/src/geometry/support.rs:29-34).

Per-shape formulas

  • Sphere — r · normalize(dir). Trivial.
  • Box — pick the corner whose component signs match dir: Vec3::new(±h.x, ±h.y, ±h.z) with the sign of each component copied from dir.
  • Capsule — end-cap centre selected by sign(dir.y), plus a sphere support of the cap radius along dir. Three lines of code (support.rs:93-97).
  • Cylinder — ±half_height along Y plus the radial edge radius · dir.xz / |dir.xz|. The degenerate dir = ±Y case picks +X as a stable fallback so GJK doesn’t NaN.
  • Cone — compares apex_dot = half_height·dir.y against base_edge·dir. Whichever is larger wins; the apex is at (0, +half_height, 0), the base disc at y = -half_height. Note the standard graphics convention (apex up) — some CAD tools use apex-down.
  • Ellipsoid — closed form (a²·dx, b²·dy, c²·dz) / |(a·dx, b·dy, c·dz)|. Reduces to a sphere when all three semi-axes match (support.rs:144-158). Mirrors Newton’s geometry/ellipsoid.py.
  • ConvexHull — linear scan argmax_v v·dir over the hull’s vertices. O(N) per query; adequate for hulls up to ~50 verts (Stage 21 hull builder caps at that). For larger hulls a DOP / hill-climb with edge graph would be needed but the CPU pipeline does not currently use one.
  • Triangle — argmax of three vertex dot products. Used by the per-triangle narrow-phase dispatch when a TriMesh leaf is emitted.

Plane, TriMesh, Heightfield, and Sdf return Vec3::ZERO from support — these shapes are routed through dedicated narrow- phase paths because their support map is unbounded (plane) or discontinuous (heightfield).

Distance / closest-point operations

pair_contact in narrow_phase.rs ships closed-form distance & contact routines for the cheap pairs:

  • Sphere–sphere — sphere_sphere (narrow_phase.rs:392). One subtract + length check + normal divide.
  • Sphere–plane — project the centre onto the plane normal, subtract the radius.
  • Sphere–box — clamp the sphere centre to the box’s local AABB (Mat3 rotate-into-local), recover the world contact point.
  • Sphere–capsule — closest_point_on_segment against the capsule’s spine, then a sphere-sphere reduction.
  • Capsule–capsule — closest_segment_segment for the two spines (narrow_phase.rs:1113) followed by a sphere-sphere reduction on the cap radii.
  • Capsule–plane — two end-caps tested independently, up to two manifold points.
  • Box–plane — eight corners against the plane half-space; keep the four deepest (box_plane, narrow_phase.rs:522).
  • Box–box — full SAT with 15 separating axes (3 + 3 face normals plus 9 edge-edge cross products), face / edge / face-edge manifold extraction (box_box_sat, narrow_phase.rs:594).
  • Ellipsoid–sphere / Ellipsoid–plane — closest-point on ellipsoid via the first-octant Newton iteration in closest_point_on_ellipsoid (narrow_phase.rs:1196).

Everything else (cylinder–box, capsule–box, cone–*, hull–*, ellipsoid–{box, capsule, cylinder, ellipsoid}, triangle–*) routes through gjk_epa_pair_with_hulls (narrow_phase.rs:1385). Plane fallbacks (cylinder_plane_fallback, cone_plane_fallback, hull_plane_fallback) exist because plane is a half-space and GJK isn’t well-defined against it.

Triangle meshes, heightfields, SDFs

TriMesh / Heightfield / Sdf are first-priority in the dispatch (narrow_phase.rs:314-331). They have to come before the generic GJK arm because their support maps are not well-defined — the routing would otherwise feed a broken support into GJK.

  • TriMesh → trimesh_pair walks the mesh BVH (BVH) and dispatches per-triangle narrow-phase against the other shape.
  • Heightfield → expands the AABB into the height grid, generates the touching triangles on the fly, and dispatches as for TriMesh.
  • Sdf → ball-marches against the SDF gradient (analytic SDFs only; SdfGrid voxelised fields go through the hydroelastic path).

Convex hull builder

crates/molla/src/geometry/hull.rs implements an incremental 3D QuickHull suitable for asset-load workloads. The output feeds directly into ShapeGeometry::ConvexHull { hull_id } via ModelBuilder::add_hull. CPU-only — per the GPU-first carve-out, hull construction is tooling and runs once, not per substep.

Public API

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct ConvexHullMesh {
    pub vertices: Vec<Vec3>,
    pub faces:    Vec<[u32; 3]>,
}

impl ConvexHullMesh {
    pub fn is_empty(&self) -> bool;
    pub fn edges(&self) -> Vec<(u32, u32)>;
}

pub fn convex_hull(points: &[Vec3]) -> ConvexHullMesh;
}

ConvexHullMesh::edges materialises the unique undirected edge list (u < v) used by the viewer’s hull-overlay wireframe. The vertex list alone is what ModelBuilder::add_hull consumes — the face data is for visualisation and topology-aware callers.

Algorithm

Classic incremental QuickHull, as outlined in the module header at hull.rs:1-23:

  1. Seed tetrahedron. Pick four extreme points (per-axis min/max plus the farthest point from the resulting triangle) and check their signed volume is non-degenerate.
  2. Partition. Bucket every remaining point by the face it sits “outside” of. A point is outside face f iff f.normal · (p - f.anchor) > eps.
  3. Iterate. Repeatedly:
    • Pick the face with the largest outside set.
    • Find the farthest outside point p_far.
    • Walk the BFS / DFS frontier of faces p_far can see (its horizon) and delete them.
    • Stitch the silhouette edges to p_far as a fan of new triangles.
    • Re-partition the deleted faces’ outside sets against the new fan.
  4. Done. When every face’s outside set is empty, the surviving faces are the hull.

The result is a triangulated manifold: each edge is shared by exactly two faces; ConvexHullMesh::edges relies on this and would return duplicates on a non-manifold output.

Robustness

Numerical robustness uses an ε scaled to the input diameter (hull.rs:99-107). Without this, hulls of geometry expressed in mm behave differently from the same geometry in metres — fixed-ε tolerances either reject valid coplanar candidates or accept near-coplanar noise.

Degenerate inputs are handled defensively:

  • < 4 points — return the unique input vertices verbatim. The caller decides what to do (typically: bail out, this isn’t a hull).
  • Colinear / coplanar inputs — fall back to a 2D hull projected on the dominant plane (we find the projection axis by picking the smallest eigen-direction of the centred covariance — equivalent to Newton’s geometry/hull.py fallback). If even that fails (all points within eps of each other), return the unique points and no faces.
  • Coplanar at the tetra-seed step — bail back to the 2D fallback rather than emit a zero-volume tetra (which would feed GJK a flat Minkowski difference).

These guards mean convex_hull(points).is_empty() == true is a reliable “input was degenerate” signal. Procedural callers that need to detect this check faces.is_empty() after the call.

Cost / vertex caps

QuickHull is O(N · log N) on average and O(N²) worst-case (adversarial inputs that hit every face). Practical cost on a 10k- point mesh-collision cloud: a few ms on one core, which is fine for asset-load. For runtime hull rebuilds (point clouds streamed at 60 Hz) the implementation would need an incremental update path that molla doesn’t ship.

The ShapeGeometry::ConvexHull consumer uses a linear-scan support function (support_convex_hull in support.rs:165-176) — the cost is O(V) per support query. For hulls up to ~50 vertices that’s cheaper than a DOP / hill-climb-with-edge-graph; past that the linear scan dominates. The hull builder doesn’t cap output vertices itself, but downstream callers commonly run the result through mesh decimation to get a low-V hull for narrow- phase use.

BVH

Three distinct BVHs ship with molla, each tailored to a different workload:

TypeSourceScopeRefit?
Bvhgeometry/bvh.rsshape AABBs (broad phase)rebuild
MeshBvhgeometry/mesh_bvh.rsper-mesh triangle AABBsstatic
TetBvhgeometry/tet_bvh.rsper-tet AABBs (deformable)CPU BVH + flat GPU AABBs
GPU LBVHmolla-geometry/src/lbvh.rs + molla-geometry/shaders/lbvh.wgslshape AABBs (broad phase)radix-rebuild

Broad-phase Bvh

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct BvhNode {
    pub aabb:   Aabb,
    pub child0: i32, // > 0 internal, == shape_index when leaf
    pub child1: i32, // -1 sentinel for leaves
}

pub struct Bvh {
    pub nodes:        Vec<BvhNode>,
    pub root:         i32,
    pub infinite_idx: Vec<u32>, // half-space planes
}
}

Bvh::build(&model, &state, margin) rebuilds the tree from scratch each step. Top-down construction: compute per-shape AABBs via shape_world_aabb, partition planes out (their AABB is infinite), then recursively split the finite shapes on the longest centroid axis with a median pivot (bvh.rs:113-141).

Bvh::pairs(&model, out) traverses the tree and writes overlap pairs to out. The algorithm uses the classic descend-larger-node strategy (bvh.rs:249-261): when both children are internal, the one with the larger AABB descends first so the smaller AABB is tested against more of the tree (better pruning).

Half-space planes are excluded from the tree and paired against every finite shape that survives the filters (bvh.rs:262-307). That’s because their AABB is infinite — putting them in the tree poisons the cull. The cost is O(P × F) where P is the plane count (typically 1).

The CPU path uses median split (mid = indices.len() / 2, bvh.rs:141). SAH-based splitting would prune harder but the median split is sub-millisecond on 1024 shapes and parity-tested against brute force on both 100- and 1k-shape grid scenes (bvh.rs:335-371).

Per-mesh MeshBvh

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct BvhNode {
    pub aabb_min:   Vec3,
    pub aabb_max:   Vec3,
    pub prim_start: u32, // first tri index in triangle_order
    pub tri_count:  u32,
    pub left:       u32,
    pub right:      u32,
    pub is_leaf:    u32,
}

pub struct MeshBvh {
    pub nodes:          Vec<BvhNode>,
    pub triangle_order: Vec<u32>, // bvh-leaf-ordered tri perm
}

impl MeshBvh {
    pub fn build(vertices: &[Vec3], indices: &[[u32; 3]], max_leaf_size: usize) -> Self;
    pub fn triangles_overlapping_aabb(&self, min: Vec3, max: Vec3, out: &mut Vec<u32>);
    pub fn ray_cast(&self, origin: Vec3, dir: Vec3, max_t: Real) -> Option<RayHit>;
}
}

Built once at model finalisation (or after any set_mesh_vertices call) and stored on the TriMesh entry. The default max_leaf_size = 4 is Embree’s recommendation — small enough that leaf scans pull in only a couple of cache lines, big enough that the tree stays shallow.

The flat-Vec layout matches what a GPU upload wants: each node fits in 8 × f32 (32 bytes), and the triangle-order permutation gives contiguous triangle ranges per leaf for vectorised narrow-phase. The WGSL counterpart (crates/molla-geometry/shaders/mesh_bvh_raycast.wgsl) consumes the same node layout.

Tet BVH (Stage 20.4)

tet_bvh.rs is the lighter-weight cousin used for soft-body tet-vs-tet paths and source-side nonconforming-contact lookup. Per Stage 20.4’s risk carve-out, the GPU-facing implementation still keeps a flat AABB list for deformable-mesh uploads, while Stage 47 v5 adds a CPU median-split TetBvh over the same AABBs for point-location prefiltering.

  • Tet meshes deform every substep — a true BVH would require per-substep refit, and a per-vertex GPU traversal of a per-substep BVH is the central technical risk Stage 20.4 flags.
  • The demo workload is two ~150-tet jelly cubes (≈ 22 500 per-vertex × per-tet checks per substep). At that scale a GPU brute-force AABB test against the flat array dispatches in microseconds; the win from a real GPU tree wouldn’t justify the refit cost.
  • CPU-side nonconforming projection has a different profile: many quadrature points query a static source mesh during matrix assembly. There, TetBvh::point_candidates avoids a brute-force source-tet scan while leaving the exact barycentric containment test unchanged.
#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[repr(C, align(16))]
pub struct TetAabb {
    pub min_x: f32, pub min_y: f32, pub min_z: f32,
    pub tet_id: u32,
    pub max_x: f32, pub max_y: f32, pub max_z: f32,
    pub _pad:  f32,
}

pub fn recompute_tet_aabbs(
    tet_indices: &[u32], vertices: &[Vec3],
    margin: Real, out: &mut [TetAabb],
);
pub fn tet_meshes_aabb_overlap(aabbs_a: &[TetAabb], aabbs_b: &[TetAabb]) -> bool;
pub fn tet_mesh_root_aabb(aabbs: &[TetAabb]) -> Option<(Vec3, Vec3)>;
pub fn tet_closest_face(p: Vec3, v0: Vec3, v1: Vec3, v2: Vec3, v3: Vec3) -> Option<(Real, Vec3)>;

pub struct TetBvh { /* nodes + tet_order */ }

    pub fn build(aabbs: &[TetAabb], max_leaf_size: usize) -> Self;
    pub fn point_candidates(&self, aabbs: &[TetAabb], p: Vec3, out: &mut Vec<u32>);
}
}

The struct is intentionally [f32; 8] (not Real) for a clean vec4 + vec4 GPU upload (32 bytes). tet_closest_face is the CPU oracle for the GPU per-vertex tet-penalty kernel: it walks the tet’s four faces, returns the maximum signed distance (positive outside, negative inside), and the achieving face’s outward normal.

The Stage 20.5 follow-up (proper GPU tree + GPU refit) is queued behind the rigid-vs-rigid LBVH that’s already in production.

GPU LBVH

crates/molla-geometry/src/lbvh.rs + crates/molla-geometry/shaders/lbvh.wgsl implement the standard Karras parallel LBVH:

  1. Morton-code AABB centroids via the existing 64-bit radix sort.
  2. Hierarchy build — Karras 2012 binary-radix-tree construction. Every internal node is assigned to one workgroup.
  3. AABB refit — per-leaf parent walk with atomicMin / atomicMax on shared bounding boxes.
  4. Pair-finder — top-down traversal in a workgroup; emits pairs into a global counter.

The host dispatcher (LbvhBroadPhase) is opt-in via CollisionPipeline::enable_gpu_broad_phase and replaces the CPU SAP/BVH pair generator. The downstream pipeline (narrow phase, GPU prefilter, full GPU narrow phase) is unchanged — the output is the same Vec<ShapePair> format. refit_only = true reuses last frame’s tree topology and skips the radix-sort step; appropriate for cloth / soft-body scenes where shape topology is fixed.

collect_shape_aabbs is the helper that walks the model + state and packs AABBs into the GPU-friendly vec4 + vec4 layout the WGSL traversal expects.

Spatial hash

crates/molla/src/geometry/spatial_hash.rs exposes a CPU-side, host-friendly version of the same fixed-bucket spatial hash that the cloth particle self-collision kernel (shaders/xpbd_particles.wgsl) embeds for GPU parallelism. The two agree on cell coordinates byte-for-byte: the hash function and the cell_of floor-floor-floor are picked so cross-checks between CPU oracle and GPU result are trivial.

API

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct SpatialHashGrid { /* ... */ }

impl SpatialHashGrid {
    pub fn new(cell_size: Real) -> Self;
    pub fn clear(&mut self);
    pub fn cell_size(&self) -> Real;
    pub fn len(&self) -> usize;
    pub fn is_empty(&self) -> bool;

    pub fn insert(&mut self, id: u32, point: Vec3);
    pub fn insert_aabb(&mut self, id: u32, min: Vec3, max: Vec3);

    pub fn query_aabb<'a>(&'a self, min: Vec3, max: Vec3)
        -> impl Iterator<Item = u32> + 'a;
    pub fn query_neighbours<'a>(&'a self, point: Vec3)
        -> impl Iterator<Item = u32> + 'a;

    pub fn cell_of(&self, p: Vec3) -> (i32, i32, i32);
}
}

The grid is unordered and non-deduplicating: inserting the same id twice puts it in the bucket twice. query_aabb therefore yields duplicates if a caller inserted via insert_aabb for an id spanning multiple cells. The caller dedupes if it matters.

Storage

Cells live in a HashMap<(i32, i32, i32), Vec<u32>>. This is intentional — unbounded coord ranges (negative coordinates, arbitrarily large worlds, sparse particle distributions) all work without a pre-sized table. The reference Vec is fine for cloth- grade scenes (≤ ~50 entries per bucket). Profiling on dense particle clouds (>500 entries per bucket) would motivate a small-vec / inline-storage upgrade — molla doesn’t ship one yet.

SpatialHashGrid::clear() drops every inserted entry but keeps the cell-map capacity for reuse — which is what every per-frame rebuild wants.

Particle self-collision

The cell size convention follows the GPU kernel: cell_size = 2 × max_radius so the 3×3×3 stencil around a particle covers every potentially-overlapping neighbour. query_neighbours(p) is the direct hook for that:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
for j in grid.query_neighbours(particle.position) {
    if j == i { continue; }
    if (particle.position - others[j as usize].position).length() < 2.0 * radius {
        // emit contact
    }
}
}

The bucket structure means each query touches at most 27 cell look-ups regardless of particle density — the cost is bounded by the local particle count, not by the global count. That’s the property the GPU kernel exploits to keep self-collision a constant-time-per-particle workload.

CPU/GPU agreement

The hash function matches WGSL exactly. cell_of is floor(p * inv_cell) — and the floor here uses Rust f64::floor which, on every IEEE-754 platform, agrees with WGSL’s floor() for finite inputs. Floor(-0.5) == -1 in both Rust and WGSL, so a particle at x = -0.5 lands in cell -1 on both sides; that’s explicitly tested in spatial_hash.rs:193-197.

The query_aabb parity test (spatial_hash.rs:217-268) generates 500 random points and ten random AABB queries, verifies the grid results are a superset of brute-force (it has to be a superset because the bucket-query touches every cell intersecting the AABB, not every cell containing a point inside the AABB), and that every brute-force hit appears in the grid result. The “grid yields a superset, never a subset” invariant is what callers rely on when the grid is used as a broad-phase pre-filter.

Where it’s used

  • The cloth XPBD particle self-collision pass embeds a fixed-bucket version directly inside the kernel.
  • Mesh-authoring tools that walk neighbours (e.g. detecting duplicate vertices during convex-hull construction) use the CPU grid directly.
  • Custom narrow-phase variants and oracle tests that need a “fast nearby-particle” iterator without lifting the GPU binding.

For ordered, deterministic-iteration AABB queries, prefer the BVH. The spatial hash is the right tool when the query set is fundamentally point-shaped (particle systems, point clouds) and the caller is OK with unspecified iteration order.

Broad phase

The broad phase generates candidate ShapePair { a, b } records that the narrow phase will probe for actual contact. molla ships three CPU broad phases plus a GPU one. All four produce the same pair set (modulo order) — they’re benchmarked head-to-head and parity-tested against brute force in crates/molla/src/geometry/bvh.rs:332-371.

AlgorithmSourceDefaultWhen to prefer
Brute forcegeometry/broad_phase.rs::brute_force_pairstests onlyparity checks, < 20 shapes
Sweep-and-Prune (SAP)geometry/broad_phase.rs::BroadPhase::sap_pairsyesup to a few hundred shapes
Top-down BVHgeometry/bvh.rs::Bvh::pairsopt-in> few hundred shapes
GPU LBVHmolla_geometry::LbvhBroadPhaseopt-in (gpu feature)> 1 k shapes

Pair filtering

Every broad phase routes its candidate pairs through pair_passes_filters (broad_phase.rs:19-52) before emitting them:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn pair_passes_filters(
    model: &Model,
    shape_body: &[i32],
    body_world: &[i32],
    i: usize,
    j: usize,
) -> bool;
}

The filter applies five rules in order:

  1. Static pair — two shapes both attached to no body (or anchored statics) cannot collide.
  2. Self-collision — two shapes on the same body are skipped.
  3. World partitioning — shapes in different worlds (multi-env parallel rollouts) are skipped.
  4. Collision-group bitmask — groups[i] & groups[j] == 0 skips. The default group is 0xffff_ffff (every bit on) which means “collide with everything”.
  5. Explicit exclusions — model.shape_collision_filter_pairs is a sorted Vec<(u32, u32)> of (lo, hi) pairs to skip; binary-searched per pair.

Every algorithm calls the filter at the leaf level so the pair list is canonical (a < b, deduplicated) before the narrow phase sees it.

Brute force

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn brute_force_pairs(
    model:  &Model,
    state:  &State,
    margin: Real,
    out:    &mut Vec<ShapePair>,
);
}

O(N²) AABB-overlap check over every pair. Two uses: a parity oracle for the SAP / BVH implementations, and a fallback for tiny scenes where the SAP setup cost wouldn’t amortize.

Sweep-and-Prune

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct BroadPhase { /* SAP scratch state */ }

impl BroadPhase {
    pub fn new() -> Self;
    pub fn sap_pairs(
        &mut self,
        model:  &Model,
        state:  &State,
        margin: Real,
        out:    &mut Vec<ShapePair>,
    );
}
}

Default for CollisionPipeline (pipeline.rs). Algorithm:

  1. AABB cache. Compute world-space AABBs for every shape via shape_world_aabb, expanded by margin.
  2. Partition. Planes (infinite AABB) bucketed separately from finite shapes — they get paired against every non-static finite shape regardless of axis.
  3. Axis pick. best_sweep_axis picks the axis with the largest centroid-coordinate variance — minimises sweep collisions on average (broad_phase.rs:224-241).
  4. Sort. Sort finite-shape indices by AABB-min on that axis.
  5. Sweep. For each shape i, scan forward until shape j’s min exceeds shape i’s max — at which point every later shape also can’t overlap. For shapes inside the active set, check full 3D AABB intersection.

The SAP scratch (aabbs, finite_idx, infinite_idx) is kept on the BroadPhase struct so it persists across frames — no per-step allocation.

Top-down BVH

Bvh — Bvh::build constructs the tree from scratch every step (top-down median-split), then Bvh::pairs traverses it with the descend-larger-node heuristic to emit overlap pairs. Wins over SAP once shape count gets large enough that the sweep’s near-linear scan starts to hurt (a few hundred shapes is the crossover on a modern CPU).

GPU LBVH

crates/molla-geometry/src/lbvh.rs ships a Karras-2012 LBVH (“Maximizing parallelism in the construction of BVHs, octrees, and k-d trees”) with a parallel pair-finder. Enable via:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pipeline.enable_gpu_broad_phase(&engine, /* refit_only: */ false);
}

When refit_only = true, the kernel reuses the previous frame’s tree topology and only re-runs AABB refit + the pair-finder. Appropriate for cloth / soft-body scenes where shape topology is fixed across frames — saves the radix-sort step.

The output flows into CollisionPipeline::pair_buf exactly like SAP would. The rest of the pipeline (GPU prefilter, full GPU narrow phase, CPU fallback) is unchanged. LbvhPairs is the host-side result struct with the pair list + a count buffer.

collect_shape_aabbs is the helper that walks the model + state and packs shape AABBs into the GPU’s vec4 + vec4 layout. Half- space planes are excluded (infinite AABB poisons the build) and paired against the finite shapes in a separate host-side scan, mirroring the CPU BVH’s behaviour.

Cross-cutting: margin

Every broad phase takes a margin: Real parameter that gets added to each AABB before the overlap test. The narrow phase consumes the same value and uses it as the contact-generation threshold — a shape pair with a non-zero margin will register a contact at penetration depth -margin (still positive separation but inside the “about to touch” zone). This is what hooks the continuous collision detection in vt_ccd into the broad phase — the CCD pre-pass inflates AABBs by the swept-volume extent so the narrow-phase sees fast-moving pairs as candidates.

Narrow phase

The narrow phase consumes the broad-phase pair list and produces real contacts. Entry point is pair_contact in crates/molla/src/geometry/narrow_phase.rs:48:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn pair_contact(
    model:               &Model,
    state:               &State,
    pair:                ShapePair,
    default_friction:    Real,
    default_restitution: Real,
    out:                 &mut Vec<ContactManifold>,
);

pub struct ContactManifold {
    pub a_shape:             u32,
    pub b_shape:             u32,
    pub point:               Vec3,
    pub normal:              Vec3, // unit, points A → B
    pub depth:               Real, // ≥ 0 on output
    pub friction:            Real,
    pub rolling_friction:    Real,
    pub torsional_friction:  Real,
    pub restitution:         Real,
}

pub const MAX_MANIFOLD_POINTS: usize = 4;
}

The contact normal points from a toward b. Solvers correct b += depth * normal and a -= depth * normal. depth > 0 is the overlap; values arrive non-negative.

Per-pair material rule

pair_material (narrow_phase.rs:382) combines per-shape friction / restitution / rolling / torsional values via max, matching Newton’s pair rule. The shape arrays are guaranteed finite at this point — the builder substitutes the NaN “use default” sentinels with the configured defaults at finalize time. Pairs that exceed the array (which would indicate an upstream bug) fall back to the caller-supplied default_*.

Dispatch table

pair_contact is one giant match on (geom_a, geom_b). The order matters: special primitives (Plane, TriMesh, Heightfield, Sdf) are dispatched before the generic GJK + EPA arm because GJK is not well-defined against unbounded / discontinuous supports.

Fast paths (closed-form)

  • Sphere–Sphere → sphere_sphere
  • Sphere–Plane → sphere_plane (with flip_manifold reverse)
  • Sphere–Box → sphere_box
  • Box–Plane → box_plane (up to 4 manifold points — keep four deepest corners)
  • Box–Box → box_box_sat (15-axis SAT with face/edge/face-edge manifold extraction, narrow_phase.rs:594)
  • Sphere–Capsule → sphere_capsule
  • Capsule–Plane → capsule_plane (up to 2 manifold points, one per cap)
  • Capsule–Capsule → capsule_capsule via closest_segment_segment
  • Sphere–Ellipsoid → ellipsoid_sphere
  • Plane–Ellipsoid → ellipsoid_plane

Each routine has a “reversed” sibling that calls into the canonical form then maps the output via flip_manifold so the a/b order on the input pair is preserved on the output.

Plane fallbacks

  • Cylinder–Plane → cylinder_plane_fallback
  • Cone–Plane → cone_plane_fallback
  • ConvexHull–Plane → hull_plane_fallback

These exist because plane is a half-space — GJK can’t terminate against it (the support function is unbounded). The fallback walks the convex shape’s “lowest” support points along the plane normal directly.

Mesh / heightfield / SDF (priority-routed)

(TriMesh, _) / (_, TriMesh) → trimesh_pair. The mesh-side BVH is walked: query the mesh BVH with the other shape’s world AABB, recover the triangle list, dispatch per-triangle narrow phase.

(Heightfield, _) / (_, Heightfield) → heightfield_pair. Expands the AABB into the grid coordinate system, generates touching triangles on the fly (two per quad cell), routes through the same triangle-based GJK+EPA path as TriMesh.

(Sdf, _) / (_, Sdf) → sdf_pair. Ball-marches against the analytic SDF gradient. (Voxelised SDF grids go through the hydroelastic path instead, since they’re the “soft body has a pressure field” use case.)

GJK + EPA

Everything else (capsule-box, cylinder-cylinder, ellipsoid-box, triangle-*, cone-*, hull-*) routes through gjk_epa_pair_with_hulls (narrow_phase.rs:1385). GJK either returns “disjoint” (no contact) or hands its 4-vertex simplex to EPA for the penetration-depth pass. The hulls parameter resolves ShapeGeometry::ConvexHull { hull_id } support queries against the model’s hull table.

NarrowPhaseBackend (Stage 28.1 v2)

The backend is selectable at runtime via CollisionPipeline::set_narrow_phase_backend:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub enum NarrowPhaseBackend {
    Gjk,    // (default) CPU GJK + EPA via pair_contact
    MprCpu, // CPU MPR portal refinement (geometry/mpr.rs)
    MprGpu, // GPU MPR batch dispatch (kernels/mpr.rs)
}
}
  • Gjk — the default. Best general-purpose choice; no GPU dependency, exhaustive shape-type support.
  • MprCpu — prefer when EPA’s polytope expansion stalls (deep penetration scenes — cloth reset states, MPM coupling). MPR returns depth + normal in one algorithm.
  • MprGpu — batches all eligible convex pairs through one dispatch on the MprKernel. Wins on pair counts ≥ 256 where the per-dispatch overhead amortizes.

Pairs the chosen backend cannot resolve (Plane, TriMesh, Heightfield, SDF, Triangle on either side, or GPU FALLBACK status) fall through to the CPU GJK + EPA path transparently — callers always get a complete manifold set.

When the full GPU narrow phase is enabled (CollisionPipeline::enable_gpu_full_narrow_phase), it takes precedence over the MPR backend choice. Both run on the GPU but only one at a time — they’re alternative implementations of the same convex-pair contract.

Output contract

pair_contact pushes 0..N ContactManifold entries onto out, where N ≤ MAX_MANIFOLD_POINTS = 4. Box–box and box–plane can produce 4; cylinder–plane / capsule–plane up to 2; everything else 0 or 1. The material fields (friction, rolling_friction, torsional_friction, restitution) are stamped on every emitted manifold by the post-loop at narrow_phase.rs:368-374 — the geometry routines themselves don’t touch them.

GJK

Gilbert–Johnson–Keerthi finds whether two convex shapes overlap. On overlap it yields the 4-vertex Minkowski-difference simplex that EPA needs for the penetration-depth pass. On disjoint inputs it additionally returns the closest points on each shape and the distance between them.

References:

  • Ericson, Real-Time Collision Detection (2005), §9.5.
  • van den Bergen, A Fast and Robust GJK Implementation (1999).

CPU implementation: crates/molla/src/geometry/gjk.rs. GPU boolean-overlap port: crates/molla-geometry/shaders/gjk.wgsl (Stage 15).

Public API

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct GjkDistance {
    pub point_a:  Vec3,
    pub point_b:  Vec3,
    pub distance: Real,
}

pub enum GjkResult {
    Disjoint(GjkDistance),
    Overlap(GjkSimplex),
}

pub struct GjkSimplex {
    pub points: Vec<SupportPoint>,
}

pub struct SupportPoint {
    pub w: Vec3, // support_A(d) − support_B(−d)  (Minkowski-diff)
    pub a: Vec3, // support_A(d)                 (world)
    pub b: Vec3, // support_B(−d)                (world)
}

pub fn gjk(
    geom_a: ShapeGeometry, xf_a: &Transform,
    geom_b: ShapeGeometry, xf_b: &Transform,
) -> GjkResult;

pub fn gjk_with_hulls(
    geom_a: ShapeGeometry, xf_a: &Transform,
    geom_b: ShapeGeometry, xf_b: &Transform,
    hulls:  &[Vec<Vec3>],
) -> GjkResult;
}

SupportPoint keeps the per-shape support points alongside the Minkowski-difference vertex. That lets the disjoint-case path recover world-space closest points on the originals via the simplex’s barycentric weights without re-running the support map.

Algorithm

GJK walks a simplex (up to 4 vertices) through Minkowski-difference space, searching toward the origin. Each iteration:

  1. Compute v = closest point on the current simplex to the origin in Minkowski space.
  2. Search direction is -v. Take a new support point along that direction in the Minkowski difference.
  3. Termination check: if the new support is no closer to the origin than v already is, the simplex has converged → return Disjoint.
  4. Otherwise add the new point and reduce the simplex to the smallest sub-feature (vertex / edge / triangle / tetrahedron) containing the origin’s projection.
  5. If the tetrahedron contains the origin → return Overlap.

The termination criterion (Ericson §9.5) is

v·v - v·w ≤ ε · v·v        where w is the new support point.

i.e. the new support cannot push the closest point closer to the origin than the current v.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// gjk.rs:111-128 (excerpt)
let v_dot_v = v.length_squared();
let new_pt  = compute_support(geom_a, xf_a, geom_b, xf_b, hulls, -v);
let v_dot_w = v.dot(new_pt.w);
if v_dot_v - v_dot_w <= 1e-10 * v_dot_v {
    let (pa, pb, dist) = closest_on_simplex_with_points(&simplex);
    return GjkResult::Disjoint(GjkDistance { point_a: pa, point_b: pb, distance: dist });
}
}

Simplex update

do_simplex routes by current simplex size:

  • 2 vertices (line). do_simplex_line (gjk.rs:204-219): classify origin against the edge — if “behind” the newer vertex, drop the older one; otherwise keep both and search perpendicular via the triple product (ab × ao) × ab.
  • 3 vertices (triangle). do_simplex_triangle (gjk.rs:221-255): test the origin against each edge plane; either drop a vertex and recurse, or pick the half-space above/below the triangle and search the face normal.
  • 4 vertices (tetrahedron). do_simplex_tetra (gjk.rs:257-293): test against the three faces incident to the newest vertex (ABC / ACD / ADB); drop the opposite vertex if any is on the origin’s side, otherwise the tetra contains the origin → ContainsOrigin.

The simplex always keeps the newest support point at the back of the Vec and uses index conventions [a] / [b, a] / [c, b, a] / [d, c, b, a] (newest last) so the routines can address by position without tracking which vertex is which.

Closest-point recovery

When GJK terminates Disjoint with 1, 2, or 3 simplex vertices, closest_on_simplex_with_points projects the origin onto the simplex sub-feature, recovers barycentric weights, and combines the per-shape a/b support points by the same weights:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// gjk.rs:350-373 (excerpt)
fn closest_on_simplex_with_points(s: &[SupportPoint]) -> (Vec3, Vec3, Real) {
    match s.len() {
        1 => (s[0].a, s[0].b, s[0].w.length()),
        2 => {
            let t  = project_t_onto_segment(s[0].w, s[1].w);
            let pa = s[0].a + (s[1].a - s[0].a) * t;
            let pb = s[0].b + (s[1].b - s[0].b) * t;
            (pa, pb, ((s[0].w + (s[1].w - s[0].w) * t).length()))
        }
        3 => /* barycentric on triangle */,
        4 => /* should be Overlap; fall back to closest face */,
    }
}
}

This is what makes GJK useful for non-contact queries (distance-to-shape pickers, swept tests, IK reachability): the “disjoint” branch is genuinely informative, not just a no-overlap flag.

Iteration cap

MAX_ITERS = 64 (gjk.rs:90). On adversarially-shaped inputs (numerically near-tangent surfaces) the no-progress termination fails to trigger and GJK can spin. The cap means it bails out and treats the situation as “touching” — handing off whatever closest points the current simplex produces. Empirically the cap is hit only on synthetic stress tests; production scenes converge in ≤ 8 iterations.

GPU port (Stage 15)

shaders/gjk.wgsl runs the boolean overlap variant — one thread per shape pair from the broad phase. The per-pair output is a u32 flag (0 = disjoint, 1 = overlap). When the host has bound a real simplex output buffer the kernel additionally writes the 4-vertex Minkowski-difference simplex into gjk_simplex[i] (12 × vec4<f32> per pair: 4 vertices × 3 vec3 each for w, a, b) for EPA to bootstrap from.

The kernel inlines support functions for Sphere / Box / Capsule / Cylinder / Cone / Ellipsoid. ConvexHull and TriMesh stay on CPU — they would need additional storage for hull vertex tables and per-mesh BVH traversal that’s not worth the per-pair-kernel complexity at current pair counts. Plane is also CPU-handled because GJK doesn’t terminate against half-spaces.

This kernel feeds the GPU prefilter — its job is to rapidly cull non-overlapping pairs and pass only the overlapping ones to the full GPU EPA pass.

EPA

The Expanding Polytope Algorithm picks up where GJK leaves off — given a 4-vertex Minkowski-difference simplex that contains the origin, EPA grows the simplex face-by-face until the face nearest the origin is on the polytope boundary. The distance from origin to that face is the penetration depth; the face normal is the contact normal.

Reference: van den Bergen, Proximity Queries and Penetration Depth Computation on 3D Game Objects (2001).

CPU implementation: crates/molla/src/geometry/epa.rs. GPU port (Stage 15): crates/molla-geometry/shaders/epa.wgsl.

Public API

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct EpaContact {
    pub point_a: Vec3,
    pub point_b: Vec3,
    pub normal:  Vec3, // unit, points from A into B
    pub depth:   Real, // ≥ 0
}

pub fn epa(
    geom_a: ShapeGeometry, xf_a: &Transform,
    geom_b: ShapeGeometry, xf_b: &Transform,
    simplex: &GjkSimplex,
) -> Option<EpaContact>;

pub fn epa_with_hulls(
    geom_a: ShapeGeometry, xf_a: &Transform,
    geom_b: ShapeGeometry, xf_b: &Transform,
    simplex: &GjkSimplex,
    hulls:   &[Vec<Vec3>],
) -> Option<EpaContact>;
}

Option is the safety hatch — EPA returns None only when the initial polytope build degenerates beyond recovery (every cardinal fallback face has zero distance to origin, indicating both shapes collapse to a point in Minkowski space). Production scenes never hit this; tests use the Option to assert no NaNs leak through.

Algorithm

  1. Initial polytope. Pad the GJK simplex (which may be 1, 2, 3, or 4 vertices) into a 4-vertex tetrahedron strictly containing the origin. If the simplex pad fails or produces a tetra with the origin on a face, build_initial_faces_or_fallback (epa.rs:181-220) falls back to four cardinal-axis support points.
  2. Find nearest face. Walk the polytope’s faces; pick the one whose plane is closest to the origin along its outward normal.
  3. Expand. Take a new support point along that face’s normal. If the new support sits within TOL = 1e-6 of the face plane, the face is on the polytope boundary → converged. Return the contact derived from this face.
  4. Otherwise expand the polytope:
    • Find every face whose outward normal can “see” the new vertex (the visible faces).
    • Collect the silhouette (edges that appear in exactly one visible face) as directed edges.
    • Delete the visible faces.
    • Stitch a fan of new triangles from each silhouette edge to the new vertex.
  5. Loop until convergence or MAX_ITERS = 64.

The silhouette computation uses the standard “cancel directed edges” trick (epa.rs:124-141):

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let mut directed: Vec<(usize, usize)> = Vec::new();
for &fi in &visible_faces {
    let f = &faces[fi];
    for k in 0..3 {
        let a = f.indices[k];
        let b = f.indices[(k + 1) % 3];
        // If the reverse edge (b → a) was just inserted, cancel
        // it — that means two adjacent visible faces shared this
        // edge, so it's not on the silhouette.
        if let Some(p) = directed.iter().position(|&(x, y)| x == b && y == a) {
            directed.remove(p);
        } else {
            directed.push((a, b));
        }
    }
}
}

Each surviving directed edge (a, b) becomes a new triangle (a, b, new_idx) whose outward winding follows from the original face’s CCW orientation.

Contact extraction

The converged face has three vertex indices into vertices (carrying the per-shape a/b support points). Project the origin onto the face plane and recover barycentric weights (u, v, w); mix the per-shape support points by the same weights to get point_a / point_b on the original shapes. The contact normal is the face’s outward normal; the depth is the plane distance from the origin.

This is the same pattern as GJK’s disjoint-case closest-point recovery — preserving the per-shape support data in SupportPoint::a / SupportPoint::b is what makes it possible.

Fallback / degenerate inputs

EPA needs a non-degenerate tetra to start. The simplex coming in may be just a vertex (radially-symmetric shapes whose Minkowski difference passes through the origin) or coplanar (a flat plate normal to the Minkowski-axis collapses both supports to the same point). build_initial_faces_or_fallback does two things:

  1. Try padding the simplex with cardinal-axis support points until it’s a non-degenerate tetra strictly containing the origin.
  2. If that fails (e.g. two co-linear sphere centres → simplex on the X axis), discard the simplex and build a fresh 4-vertex tetra from ±X, ±Y, ±Z support points.

Either path then triggers a “reject if origin lies on a face” check; on rejection the routine retries with a different vertex ordering or returns None.

The iteration cap (MAX_ITERS = 64) prevents infinite expansion on numerically pathological inputs — EPA emits the current best face if it can’t converge. This is rare; MprCpu / MprGpu backends in the narrow phase are the recommended escape hatch when EPA stalls in deep-penetration regimes.

GPU port (Stage 15)

shaders/epa.wgsl runs one thread per pair (matching GJK’s layout). Per-thread fixed-size arrays cap the polytope at MAX_VERTICES = 32 and MAX_FACES = 64 — enough for ~95% of realistic contacts. Pairs that overflow or fail to converge emit status = STATUS_FALLBACK = 2; the host’s collision pipeline then re-runs them through CPU EPA.

The output stride is 16 f32 per pair, identical to the MPR output so callers can share decode helpers:

[0..3]   normal.xyz, depth
[4..7]   point_a.xyz, _
[8..11]  point_b.xyz, _
[12..15] status_bits_as_f32, _, _, _

This format (depth in slot [3], status in slot [12]) lets the host detect FALLBACK by reading just one of the 16 floats.

MPR (Minkowski Portal Refinement)

MPR is an alternative narrow-phase to GJK + EPA. Like GJK it operates on the Minkowski difference A − B, but instead of building a simplex around the origin and then expanding it (the EPA step), it constructs a portal — a triangle on the boundary of the Minkowski difference whose extension hits the origin — and refines it until the portal face is tight against the origin.

Two practical wins over GJK + EPA:

  1. One algorithm, both answers. GJK only resolves yes/no overlap; EPA computes depth + normal as a separate pass. MPR returns depth + normal in a single algorithm.
  2. Robust on deep penetration. EPA’s polytope expansion can diverge when the GJK simplex is highly distorted (50% interpenetration, concentric cylinders, MPM reset states). MPR’s portal refinement is a single smooth descent and tends to converge where EPA stalls.

References:

  • Snethen (2007), the original MPR paper.
  • Newhouse, Game Programming Gems 7 (2008) ch. 2.5, “XenoCollide: Complex Collision Made Simple”.

Stage 28 ships the CPU implementation at crates/molla/src/geometry/mpr.rs; Stage 28.1 adds the WGSL port in crates/molla-geometry/shaders/mpr.wgsl.

Public API

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct Manifold {
    pub point_a: Vec3,
    pub point_b: Vec3,
    pub normal:  Vec3, // unit, points A → B
    pub depth:   Real,
}

pub trait SupportFn {
    fn support(&self, dir: Vec3) -> Vec3;
}

pub struct ShapeSupport<'a> {
    geom:  ShapeGeometry,
    xf:    &'a Transform,
    hulls: &'a [Vec<Vec3>],
}

impl<'a> ShapeSupport<'a> {
    pub fn new(geom: ShapeGeometry, xf: &'a Transform) -> Self;
    pub fn with_hulls(geom: ShapeGeometry, xf: &'a Transform, hulls: &'a [Vec<Vec3>]) -> Self;
}

pub fn mpr_collide<A: SupportFn + ?Sized, B: SupportFn + ?Sized>(
    a:         &A,
    b:         &B,
    tolerance: Real,
    max_iters: u32,
) -> Option<Manifold>;
}

The SupportFn trait abstracts over analytic primitives, hulls, and closures — the algorithm only ever queries a shape through it. The output mirrors EpaContact so callers can swap GJK

  • EPA ↔ MPR freely.

Portal-loop algorithm

The portal loop has five phases (mpr.rs:150-257):

Phase 1 — Interior point v0. Compute a point that’s guaranteed inside the Minkowski difference. Strategy: average opposing supports per shape to get each shape’s centroid estimate (always interior to a convex shape), then return the difference. Using six cardinal-axis directions (±X, ±Y, ±Z, mpr.rs:119-137) avoids the degenerate case where +X / −X supports of a flat plate collapse to the same point.

Phase 2 — First portal vertex v1. Take a support along the ray from v0 toward the origin, i.e. along -v0. If v1 · (-v0) ≤ 0, the origin is outside the supporting half-space → no overlap; return None.

Phase 3 — Second portal vertex v2. Search direction is perpendicular to the segment (v0, v1) and in the half-plane containing the origin: v0 × v1. Take a support along that direction; reject if it’s not past the origin half-plane.

Phase 4 — Third portal vertex v3 (the “origin-encloses” loop). Form a candidate face from (v0, v1, v2) with normal pointing away from v0 (toward the boundary). Take a support v3 past that face. Test whether the ray from v0 to the origin pierces the triangle (v1, v2, v3):

  • If the origin is “outside” edge (v1, v3) of the v0–v1–v3 plane, replace v2 with v3 and retry.
  • If the origin is outside edge (v2, v3) of the v0–v2–v3 plane, replace v1 with v3 and retry.
  • Otherwise the triangle (v1, v2, v3) brackets the origin-direction ray → proceed to refinement.

The test uses sign comparisons on v0.w.cross(v3.w).dot(v_i.w), which is proportional to the signed volume of the tetrahedron (origin, v0, v3, v_i).

Phase 5 — Portal refinement. Each iteration:

n        = (v2 - v1) × (v3 - v1)             // portal-face normal
if n · (v1 - v0) < 0: n = -n                  // outward orient
face_dist = v1 · n̂                            // origin-to-plane distance
v4        = support(n̂)                        // sample past the portal
new_dist  = v4 · n̂

if new_dist - face_dist < tolerance:          // ← termination
    return extract_contact(v1, v2, v3, n̂)

If termination doesn’t fire, replace whichever of v1 / v2 / v3 keeps the new sub-tetrahedron (v0, v1, v2, v3) bracketing the ray v0 → origin. The replacement test is the standard Snethen 2007 §3.3 / Newhouse 2008 §2.5 criterion — compare signs of (v4 × v0) · v_i (proportional to the signed volume of the tetra (origin, v0, v4, v_i)):

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// mpr.rs:323-344
let cross_v4_v0 = v4.w.cross(v0.w);
let d1 = v1.w.dot(cross_v4_v0);
let d2 = v2.w.dot(cross_v4_v0);
let d3 = v3.w.dot(cross_v4_v0);
if d1 >= 0.0 {
    if d2 >= 0.0 { v3 = v4; } else { v2 = v4; }
} else {
    if d3 >= 0.0 { v1 = v4; } else { v3 = v4; }
}
}

The convergence criterion (new_dist - face_dist < tolerance) is the right one for the MPR loop: it says “the next support point is not significantly further past the portal face than the portal face is from the origin”, i.e. the polytope can’t expand meaningfully in that direction any more. Newton uses 1e-6; values down to 1e-9 improve accuracy at the cost of a couple extra iters.

When MPR beats GJK/EPA

  • Cylinder-cylinder, capsule-capsule. The Minkowski difference of two cylinders along arbitrary axes has many near-flat regions that EPA’s polytope expansion picks up coplanar faces from, stalling convergence. MPR’s smooth portal descent handles them cleanly.
  • Deep penetration. When the GJK simplex contains the origin with one vertex much further than the others, EPA’s first polytope is highly distorted. MPR doesn’t need the GJK simplex at all — its interior point comes from a centroid estimate.
  • Reset states / large penetration jumps. Cloth that snaps to a new rest pose, MPM particles re-seeded inside a rigid body — scenarios where the previous frame’s contact info is invalid.

Manifold extraction

After convergence, extract_contact (mpr.rs:354-374) projects the origin onto the portal plane, computes barycentric coordinates of that projection on triangle (v1, v2, v3), and mixes the per-shape support points by the same weights to recover point_a / point_b on the original shapes.

The normal is the converged outward portal-face normal (which is the contact normal A → B in world coordinates because the Minkowski difference is A − B). On degenerate portals (zero-area triangle), the routine falls back to the last valid normal seen during the loop.

GPU port (Stage 28.1)

shaders/mpr.wgsl runs one thread per pair matching the GJK / EPA kernels — the portal loop is purely scalar per pair (3 vertices + 1 interior point + one new sample per iteration), so workgroup-level parallelism wouldn’t help. Output stride is 16 f32 per pair, identical to EPA so the host can share decode helpers:

[0..3]   normal.xyz, depth
[4..7]   point_a.xyz, _
[8..11]  point_b.xyz, _
[12..15] status_bits_as_f32, _, _, _

Termination criterion matches CPU verbatim (new_dist - face_dist < tolerance). If the iteration cap is hit the kernel emits the current portal with the last valid normal as STATUS_OK, not FALLBACK — callers can inspect the depth and decide whether to accept (the v1 GPU result agrees with CPU to ~6 decimal digits even on hard cases). Pairs that genuinely can’t proceed (degenerate Minkowski difference) emit STATUS_FALLBACK and the host re-runs them on the CPU GJK + EPA path.

Enable with CollisionPipeline::set_narrow_phase_backend(NarrowPhaseBackend::MprGpu) plus enable_mpr_gpu_backend(&engine, capacity, tolerance). The backend is at runtime parity with the CPU MPR backend; the GPU wins on pair counts ≥ ~256 where the per-dispatch overhead amortises.

Contact reduction

A box-on-box face contact can emit 4–8 candidate points from SAT, a triangle-mesh patch can emit dozens, hydroelastic integration hundreds. The solver doesn’t want them all — redundant contacts on the same patch are wasted work and the system never quite reaches a stable rest. Contact reduction coalesces many narrow-phase contacts on the same shape pair into a small canonical manifold (typically 4 points).

Two implementations cohabit:

  • crates/molla/src/geometry/contact_extras.rs — the voxel-bin pruner. Per-frame, in the live Contacts buffer.
  • crates/molla/src/geometry/contact_reduction.rs — the slice-API reducer + temporal warm-start. Generic max-N-per-pair primitive.

GPU port at crates/molla-kernels/shaders/contact_reduction.wgsl (Stage 28.1).

Voxel-AABB pruning (contact_extras)

The per-frame helper used inside the pipeline:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn contact_id(
    a_shape: u32, b_shape: u32, point: Vec3, voxel_size: Real,
) -> u64;

pub fn reduce_contacts(contacts: &mut Contacts, voxel_size: Real);

pub fn build_contact_id_table(
    a_idx: &[u32], b_idx: &[u32], point: &[Vec3],
    voxel_size: Real, out: &mut Vec<u64>,
);

pub fn match_contacts(
    prev_ids: &[u64], next: &[Contact], voxel_size: Real,
) -> Vec<i32>;
}

contact_id hashes (min(a, b), max(a, b), voxel(point)) into a u64. Two contacts on the same shape pair separated by less than voxel_size hash to the same id — they’re treated as “the same persistent contact” for warm-starting. Picking the voxel size trades match-rate (larger ⇒ more warm-starts survive) against patch resolution (larger ⇒ legitimately-different contacts get collapsed).

reduce_contacts bins contacts by (a_shape, b_shape, voxel(point)) and keeps only the deepest contact per voxel. This stops a 4-corner box-plane stack from emitting 4 contacts that overlap into the solver — they collapse to one per voxel cell.

match_contacts is the temporal-coherence hook: given the previous frame’s contact-ID list and the current frame’s contacts, return an array prev_idx of length next.len() where prev_idx[i] is the index of the matching previous contact (or -1 if no match). Friction’s Lagrange-multiplier warm-start keys off this.

Slice-API reducer

Standalone primitive that callers can use outside the live Contacts buffer (oracle tests, MPR fixtures, custom narrow phases):

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct Contact {
    pub a_shape: u32,
    pub b_shape: u32,
    pub id:      u64, // opaque; preserved on output
    pub point:   Vec3,
    pub normal:  Vec3,
    pub depth:   Real,
}

pub fn reduce_contacts(contacts: &[Contact], max_per_pair: usize) -> Vec<Contact>;
pub fn reduce_with_history(
    prev: &[Contact], current: &[Contact],
    max_per_pair: usize, match_radius: Real,
) -> Vec<Contact>;
}

“Deepest + farthest spread” policy

The algorithm (contact_reduction.rs:84-195, matching Newton’s solvers/contact/contact_reduction_global.py):

  1. Group contacts by (a_shape, b_shape).
  2. For each group, always keep the deepest contact (first slot).
  3. Greedily add the contact whose minimum distance to any already-kept point is maximal — i.e. expand the convex hull of the kept set as fast as possible.
  4. Stop when the group hits max_per_pair or runs out of candidates.

This produces a well-conditioned manifold: 4 corners of a face, not 4 points clustered at one corner. For a box-on-box face contact that gives the solver exactly the 4 corner contacts it needs to capture the patch geometry, no more.

Tie-break rules (contact_reduction.rs:159-184):

  • Spread first (with eps = 1e-12).
  • On a spread tie, prefer deeper.
  • On both a tie, prefer lower input index.

Output order is deterministic for a given input — deepest first, then greedy spread order.

Warm-start matching

reduce_with_history runs the reducer on current, then walks each reduced contact and attaches the closest unclaimed previous contact within match_radius:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// contact_reduction.rs:238-262
for cur in reduced.iter_mut() {
    let key = (cur.a_shape, cur.b_shape);
    if let Some(prev_indices) = prev_by_pair.get(&key) {
        let mut best: Option<usize> = None;
        let mut best_d2 = match_radius * match_radius;
        for &pi in prev_indices {
            if claimed[pi] { continue; }
            let d2 = (prev[pi].point - cur.point).length_squared();
            if d2 <= best_d2 { best_d2 = d2; best = Some(pi); }
        }
        if let Some(pi) = best { cur.id = prev[pi].id; claimed[pi] = true; }
    }
}
}

The claimed array enforces a one-to-one match so two current contacts don’t both inherit the same id. Rule of thumb for match_radius: 2 × contact_margin for rigid-body face contacts, ~1 mm for cloth, ~2× expected motion for ragdolls / hands.

Graph-coloring partitioning

crates/molla-math/src/coloring.rs provides the constraint-graph coloring utility used by both the contact reducer (when the solver wants conflict-free parallel batches) and the XPBD distance-constraint pass:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn greedy_color(adjacency: &[Vec<u32>]) -> Vec<u32>;
pub fn mcs_color(adjacency: &[Vec<u32>]) -> Vec<u32>; // chordal-optimal
pub fn color_constraints(constraint_verts: &[Vec<u32>]) -> Vec<u32>;
pub fn group_by_color(colors: &[u32]) -> Vec<Vec<usize>>;
}

color_constraints builds the line graph (constraints are edges in the original graph; the line graph makes constraints sharing a vertex adjacent) and returns a per-constraint color via MCS (Pereira & Vidigal 2014). On chordal graphs MCS is optimal; on general graphs it’s near-greedy. group_by_color slices into parallel-safe batches: every constraint within a color is guaranteed to act on disjoint vertex sets, so the solver can dispatch them concurrently without atomics.

The contact reducer doesn’t currently route through this — the reducer’s per-pair groups are independent by construction (one shape pair → one group, no cross-pair vertex sharing). The coloring path becomes relevant when reducer output goes into the XPBD substep, which needs conflict-free batches for its Jacobi-style parallel projection.

GPU reduction kernel

shaders/contact_reduction.wgsl ports the per-group greedy algorithm verbatim. The host packs up to MAX_PER_GROUP = 64 contacts per shape pair into a dense slab; one workgroup per group runs the scalar reduction (only thread 0 of each workgroup does work — the per-group n is too small for workgroup-level parallelism to pay):

@compute @workgroup_size(64)
fn contact_reduce(
    @builtin(workgroup_id) wg: vec3<u32>,
    @builtin(local_invocation_id) lid: vec3<u32>,
) {
    let g = wg.x;
    if (g >= u.group_count) { return; }
    if (lid.x != 0u) { return; }      // scalar per group
    reduce_one_group(g);
}

The “greedy farthest-point” inner loop is byte-for-byte the same as CPU — same tie-break with eps = 1e-6 (slightly looser than the CPU’s 1e-12 to accommodate f32 precision; the CPU/GPU parity test verifies the deepest contact survives in both paths). Per-group output cap is MAX_OUT_PER_GROUP = 4. Output layout mirrors input: a same-shaped slab plus a per-group count buffer so the host can know how many of the 4 slots are valid.

The kernel sits behind the ContactReductionKernel host dispatcher (crates/molla-kernels/src/contact_reduction.rs); see pack_groups_host and unpack_output_host for the slab-packing / unpacking helpers exposed for tests.

Sparse grids (NanoVDB-equivalent)

A 1024³ dense SDF needs 1024³ × 4 B = 4 GiB even though the non-empty (narrow-band) voxels typically cover well under 1% of the volume. crates/molla/src/geometry/sparse_grid.rs implements a clean-room WGSL-friendly port of NanoVDB’s three-level Root → Internal → Leaf topology (Museth 2013, “VDB: High-Resolution Sparse Volumes with Dynamic Topology”; the “NanoVDB” name comes from NVIDIA’s CUDA-side single-allocation refactor). molla maintains its own layout — portable wgpu, no CUDA dependency.

Topology

Root      ─ HashMap<[i32; 3], u32>     → child internal idx
Internal  ─ 32 × 32 × 32 u32 children + 1024-u32 activity bitmask
Leaf      ─ 8  × 8  × 8  f32 values   + 16-u32   activity bitmask

Voxel coord (x, y, z) decomposes as (root_key, internal_idx, leaf_idx) via fixed bit shifts:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub const LEAF_DIM:        i32   = 8;   // 8³ = 512 voxels / leaf
pub const LEAF_SHIFT:      i32   = 3;   // 2³ = 8 voxels per leaf axis
pub const LEAF_MASK_U32S:  usize = 16;  // 8³ / 32 bits

pub const INTERNAL_DIM:        i32   = 32;   // 32³ = 32768 children
pub const INTERNAL_SHIFT:      i32   = 8;    // LEAF_SHIFT + 5
pub const INTERNAL_MASK_U32S:  usize = 1024; // 32³ / 32 bits
}
leaf_local(x, y, z)     = (x & 7,        y & 7,        z & 7)
internal_local(x, y, z) = ((x >> 3) & 31, (y >> 3) & 31, (z >> 3) & 31)
root_key(x, y, z)       = ( x >> 8,       y >> 8,       z >> 8     )

Each internal node spans 2⁸ = 256 voxels per axis. A 1024³ volume fits in (1024 / 256) = 4 root keys per axis = 64 root entries — well within the linear-search budget of the WGSL traversal. NanoVDB ships with three internal levels for arbitrary world sizes; molla collapses the upper levels into one root because v1 targets 1024³–4096³ assets where the root never gets large.

Why this layout

  • Leaf 8³ matches NanoVDB’s tile size. A leaf is a contiguous 512 × 4 = 2048 bytes — easy to fit in shared memory if we ever go workgroup-per-leaf.
  • Internal 32³ keeps the child-pointer array cache-friendly (32 × 32 × 32 × 4 = 128 KiB per internal node). Wider would waste storage; narrower would mean more internal nodes.
  • Root as a hash map keeps the top of the tree mutable on the CPU without a fixed pre-allocation. The GPU sees the root as a flat (key, child_idx) array — Stage 24e.1 adds an open-addressing hash table for O(1) GPU lookup; Stage 24e shipped a linear-scan fallback.

Mask bit layout

Both the leaf and internal masks use the standard “one bit per slot, packed into u32 words” convention:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// Leaf::set (sparse_grid.rs:126-130)
let idx = leaf_local(x, y, z);                // 0..=511
self.values[idx] = value;
self.mask[idx >> 5] |= 1u32 << (idx & 31);    // word `idx/32`, bit `idx%32`

// Leaf::get (sparse_grid.rs:133-138)
if (self.mask[idx >> 5] >> (idx & 31)) & 1 == 1 {
    Some(self.values[idx])
} else {
    None
}
}

idx >> 5 is the u32 word index; idx & 31 is the bit within that word. Same pattern for the internal mask, where idx is the flattened (ix, iy, iz) triple (ix + 32 * iy + 32 * 32 * iz).

Leaf::active_count / InternalNode::active_count are sums of u32::count_ones() over the mask — the population count (popcount) tells you how many voxels are active without walking the values.

Public CPU API

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct Leaf {
    pub values: Box<[f32; 512]>,
    pub mask:   [u32; LEAF_MASK_U32S],
}

pub struct InternalNode {
    pub children: Box<[u32; 32 * 32 * 32]>, // u32::MAX = no child
    pub mask:     Box<[u32; INTERNAL_MASK_U32S]>,
}

pub struct SparseGrid {
    pub root:       HashMap<[i32; 3], u32>,
    pub internals:  Vec<InternalNode>,
    pub leaves:     Vec<Leaf>,
    pub background: f32,
}

impl SparseGrid {
    pub fn new(background: f32) -> Self;
    pub fn insert(&mut self, x: i32, y: i32, z: i32, value: f32);
    pub fn lookup(&self, x: i32, y: i32, z: i32) -> f32;
    pub fn for_each_active_leaf<F: FnMut(u32, [i32; 3])>(&self, f: F);

    pub fn leaf_count(&self) -> usize;
    pub fn internal_count(&self) -> usize;
    pub fn root_count(&self) -> usize;
    pub fn active_voxel_count(&self) -> u64;
    pub fn storage_bytes(&self) -> usize;
}
}

SparseGrid::insert (Stage 24e.1 — mutable) allocates internal / leaf nodes lazily and only on first touch (sparse_grid.rs:211-236). The two-step allocation (alloc internal if missing, then alloc leaf if missing) keeps the cost proportional to the new topology, not the existing structure. Stage 24e.2 adds delete for runtime stripping (not yet wired up here — the topology is monotonic in v1 plus mutable insert).

for_each_active_leaf is the “do work per active region” hook; on the GPU side the equivalent is one workgroup per active leaf.

GPU upload — SparseGridGpu

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct SparseGridGpu {
    pub root_entries:        Vec<i32>, // [key.x, key.y, key.z, internal_idx]…
    pub root_table:          Vec<i32>, // open-addressing hash table (Stage 24e.1)
    pub root_table_capacity: u32,
    pub internal_children:   Vec<u32>, // 32³ u32 per internal
    pub internal_masks:      Vec<u32>, // 1024 u32 per internal
    pub leaf_values:         Vec<f32>, // 512  f32 per leaf
    pub leaf_masks:          Vec<u32>, // 16   u32 per leaf
    pub background:          f32,
}

impl SparseGridGpu {
    pub fn from_grid(grid: &SparseGrid) -> Self;
}
}

Everything is flat u32/f32 so the buffers pack into wgpu::Buffer without f64↔f32 conversion shenanigans. from_grid sorts the root by key so the layout is byte-deterministic across runs (HashMap iteration order isn’t deterministic).

Stage 24e.1 — root_hash3 GPU lookup

The Stage 24e linear scan over root_entries is fine for ≤ 64 entries but scales poorly as a 4096³ asset pushes past 1024 roots. Stage 24e.1 adds an open-addressing hash table sized to load factor 0.7 (power-of-two capacity for cheap slot & mask wrap-around). The hash function is the same in Rust and WGSL:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn root_hash3(key: [i32; 3]) -> u32 {
    let mut h: u32 = 0x9E37_79B9;          // golden-ratio seed
    for &k in &key {
        let mut k = k as u32;
        k = k.wrapping_mul(0xCC9E_2D51);
        k = k.rotate_left(15);
        k = k.wrapping_mul(0x1B87_3593);
        h ^= k;
        h = h.rotate_left(13);
        h = h.wrapping_mul(5).wrapping_add(0xE654_6B64);
    }
    // Murmur3 finalizer.
    h ^= h >> 16;
    h = h.wrapping_mul(0x85EB_CA6B);
    h ^= h >> 13;
    h = h.wrapping_mul(0xC2B2_AE35);
    h ^= h >> 16;
    h
}
}

WGSL u32 wraps modulo 2^32 exactly like Rust’s wrapping_*, so the two implementations agree byte-for-byte. The choice of MurmurHash3 finalizer + golden-ratio seed is dictated by the expected workload — sequential coordinates dominate when SDF narrow-band voxels are baked in scan order, and the bit-mixing above spreads them evenly across the table. The (avg_probes, max_probes) stats helper (sparse_grid.rs:435-480) lets tests verify the load factor / probe-length contract without instrumenting the GPU.

root_table_capacity == 0 selects the linear-scan fallback for back-compat with the Stage 24e v1 traversal.

SparseSdf — narrow-band SDF wrapper

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct SparseSdf {
    pub grid:      SparseGrid,
    pub origin:    Vec3,    // world position of voxel (0, 0, 0)
    pub cell_size: Real,
    pub nx: u32, pub ny: u32, pub nz: u32, // logical voxel extent
}

impl SparseSdf {
    pub fn sample(&self, p: Vec3) -> Real;
    pub fn normal(&self, p: Vec3) -> Vec3;
    pub fn logical_voxel_count(&self) -> u64;
}

pub fn bake_mesh_to_sparse_sdf(
    mesh: &TriMesh, resolution: u32, padding: Real, narrow_band: u32,
) -> SparseSdf;

pub fn sparse_sdf_from_dense(
    dense: &crate::geometry::sdf_bake::SdfGrid, narrow_band: u32,
) -> SparseSdf;
}

Thin wrapper mirroring the dense SdfGrid API. Trilinear sample returns the stored value if the surrounding 8 voxels are all active, otherwise the background. normal uses central differences. logical_voxel_count is the dense-equivalent voxel count — used by the storage-cost audit (a 1024³ logical SDF can be much sparser than its dense equivalent; ratio of storage_bytes to logical_voxel_count * 4 is the compression factor).

bake_mesh_to_sparse_sdf walks the mesh BVH, computes signed distances on the narrow-band voxels only, and skips the rest. The narrow-band width is the inflation in voxels around the surface where samples are kept — typical value 3-4 for collision queries (close enough to capture the surface, far enough not to miss). sparse_sdf_from_dense is the trivial down-conversion: walk the dense grid, keep cells whose |sdf| < narrow_band * cell_size.

Marching cubes & SDF baking

A pair of asset-load tools that round-trip between meshes and sampled signed-distance fields:

  • crates/molla/src/geometry/sdf_bake.rs — bake_mesh_to_sdf voxelises a TriMesh into a regular 3D grid of signed distances.
