  • crates/molla/src/geometry/marching_cubes.rs — marching_cubes extracts a triangle mesh from a sampled SDF (the reverse direction).

bake → marching_cubes round-trips a mesh through a SDF; the fidelity is bounded by voxel resolution.

These types support both hydroelastic contact (the soft body’s pressure field is E · max(0, -sdf)) and the sparse grid NanoVDB-equivalent (which stores only the narrow band of the dense SDF).

SdfGrid

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct SdfGrid {
    pub nx: u32,
    pub ny: u32,
    pub nz: u32,
    pub origin:    Vec3, // world corner of voxel (0, 0, 0)
    pub cell_size: Real, // uniform voxel side length
    pub data:      Vec<Real>, // length nx · ny · nz, row-major (x fastest)
}

impl SdfGrid {
    pub fn len(&self) -> usize;
    pub fn is_empty(&self) -> bool;
    pub fn at(&self, x: u32, y: u32, z: u32) -> Real;
    pub fn voxel_pos(&self, x: u32, y: u32, z: u32) -> Vec3;
}
}

Layout: data[x + y * nx + z * nx * ny] (X fastest, then Y, then Z) — standard row-major to match (i, j, k) → linear in WGSL loops. Sample positions are origin + (x, y, z) * cell_size.

bake_mesh_to_sdf always emits a cubic grid (nx == ny == nz) but the type stores the three axes independently to leave room for non-uniform fields later (Stage 22.2 has those slated for the heightfield → SDF path).

at(x, y, z) returns +∞ for out-of-range coordinates so callers that walk a 3×3×3 stencil don’t have to special-case the boundary.

Sample functions

hydroelastic.rs ships two helpers that consumers reach for:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn sample_sdf_trilinear(grid: &SdfGrid, p: Vec3) -> Real;
pub fn sample_sdf_gradient (grid: &SdfGrid, p: Vec3) -> Vec3;
}

sample_sdf_trilinear does the standard 8-corner trilinear blend: floor the local coordinate, fetch the 8 surrounding voxels, blend xyz first then z. Returns +∞ (treated as “deep outside”) when the query is out-of-bounds — same convention as SdfGrid::at.

sample_sdf_gradient uses central differences over the 6 neighbour stencil:

grad.x = (sdf(x+1, y, z) - sdf(x-1, y, z)) / (2 * cell_size)
grad.y = (sdf(x, y+1, z) - sdf(x, y-1, z)) / (2 * cell_size)
grad.z = (sdf(x, y, z+1) - sdf(x, y, z-1)) / (2 * cell_size)

This gives the outward normal of the surface — +∇sdf because the SDF increases outward.

Baking — bake_mesh_to_sdf

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn bake_mesh_to_sdf(
    mesh:       &TriMesh,
    resolution: usize,
    padding:    Real,
) -> SdfGrid;
}

Algorithm (sdf_bake.rs:14-34):

  1. Compute the mesh’s AABB, expand by padding (world-space metres), divide into a resolution × resolution × resolution voxel grid.
  2. Unsigned distance pass. For each grid sample, find the closest point on every triangle via closest_point_on_triangle; keep the minimum unsigned distance.
  3. Sign pass. Determine sign via parity of an axis-aligned ray intersection count: odd → inside (negative), even → outside (positive). Robust enough for closed manifold meshes (the only kind supported); open meshes return ±d arbitrarily near the boundary.

Performance: O(resolution³ × triangle_count). Fine for asset-load workloads — 32³ × 1k tris ≈ 33M ops, ms-range. Stage 21.1 parallelises the closest-distance pass with rayon: voxels are independent so fan-out is embarrassingly parallel and the resulting data array is byte-deterministic across runs (each voxel’s min reduction sees the same triangles in the same order within its task). The sign pass remains sequential because it threads parity state along +X across cells in a row.

closest_point_on_triangle

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn closest_point_on_triangle(
    p: Vec3, a: Vec3, b: Vec3, c: Vec3,
) -> (Real, Vec3);
}

Returns (unsigned_distance, closest_point). The standard 7-region classification (Eberly 2000): for each of the 7 Voronoi regions of the triangle (3 vertices, 3 edges, 1 face), test whether p projects into that region, and if so return the closest point in the region.

Used by:

  • bake_mesh_to_sdf (the unsigned-distance pass).
  • bake_mesh_to_sparse_sdf in sparse_grid.rs (narrow-band SDF baking — only voxels within narrow_band * cell_size are computed).
  • narrow_phase.rs::trimesh_pair indirectly, for the per-triangle contact test against the other shape.

The routine works in f64 end-to-end (no precision loss from a mid-routine downcast); GPU ports of the same algorithm in shaders/raycast.wgsl use f32 for memory efficiency but produce parity-equivalent results within the tolerance of single-precision arithmetic.

Marching cubes

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn marching_cubes(sdf: &SdfGrid, iso: Real) -> TriMesh;
}

Standard Lorensen-Cline 256-case lookup. The two hard-coded tables (EDGE_TABLE, TRI_TABLE) are the canonical Newman/Lorensen ones — see Paul Bourke’s “Polygonising a Scalar Field” or Ken Museth’s openvdb mesh-extractor. iso = 0 reproduces the underlying surface for an SDF baked via bake_mesh_to_sdf.

Per cell:

  1. Compute the 8 corner SDF values and form an 8-bit cube index cube_index = Σᵢ (sdf_i < iso ? 1 << i : 0).
  2. EDGE_TABLE[cube_index] tells which of the 12 cube edges have a sign change; interpolate the iso-surface crossing on each such edge via interp(iso, p_a, p_b, sdf_a, sdf_b) (linear interpolation of t = (iso - sdf_a) / (sdf_b - sdf_a)).
  3. TRI_TABLE[cube_index] lists which of those edge vertices form triangles (up to 5 triangles per cell, 15 indices terminated by -1).
  4. Emit the triangles with fresh vertex indices.

The output is unwelded — each triangle gets fresh vertices for its 3 corners even when shared with an adjacent cell. Welding is left to a separate TriMesh::weld_duplicates pass; the unwelded output keeps marching cubes itself dead-simple (no hash for shared edges) at the cost of ~6× the vertex count.

Cells with EDGE_TABLE[cube_index] == 0 (entirely inside or entirely outside the iso-surface) short-circuit immediately (marching_cubes.rs:57). Grids with nx, ny, or nz < 2 return an empty mesh — there are no cells to iterate.

Mesh decimation

crates/molla/src/geometry/decimate.rs implements Garland-Heckbert Quadric Error Metric (QEM) edge-collapse decimation. Stage-21 deliverable per PLAN.md §21 — produces LOD chains for collision vs render meshes (e.g. render mesh keeps 100k tris, collider drops to 5k).

Public API

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn decimate(mesh: &TriMesh, target_tri_count: usize) -> TriMesh;
pub fn decimate_lod_chain(mesh: &TriMesh, factors: &[f64]) -> Vec<TriMesh>;
}

decimate reduces mesh to approximately target_tri_count triangles. Returns a new mesh; the input is unchanged. If target_tri_count >= mesh.indices.len() the mesh is returned verbatim (with a fresh BVH). If target_tri_count == 0 the mesh is reduced as far as the topology guards allow — that could be more than 0 tris if every remaining collapse would cause a flip.

decimate_lod_chain produces multiple LOD levels in one pass, sharing the QEM priority queue across levels. Each entry of factors is a fraction in (0, 1] of the input triangle count (e.g. [0.5, 0.25, 0.1] produces three meshes at 50%, 25%, 10% of the original). Output meshes are returned in the same order as factors. Cheaper than calling decimate N times because the QEM state (vertex quadrics + topology) is collapsed in-place and snapshots are taken at each target — so you pay one decimation’s worth of work for the deepest factor and snapshot the intermediate levels for free.

Algorithm

Garland-Heckbert “Surface Simplification Using Quadric Error Metrics” (SIGGRAPH ’97). Each vertex carries the sum of the squared-distance quadrics of its incident faces. A quadric Q ∈ ℝ⁴ˣ⁴ represents the sum of squared distances from a point to a set of planes; collapsing edge (u, v) replaces both endpoints with a single new vertex whose position minimises the combined quadric Q_u + Q_v. The error of any candidate collapse is vᵀ Q v for the chosen position.

The collapser repeatedly pops the lowest-error edge from a priority queue:

  1. Initial quadrics. For each face f with plane n · x = d (unit normal n, offset d), build the 4 × 4 outer-product quadric Q_f = [n; d] · [n; d]ᵀ. Sum into each incident vertex.
  2. Edge queue. For every edge (u, v), compute the combined quadric Q_uv = Q_u + Q_v, find the position p* that minimises pᵀ Q_uv p (solve the 3×3 linear system from Q_uv’s top-left 3×3 block, fall back to the midpoint when the system is singular), and push (error, u, v, p*) onto a min-heap.
  3. Collapse loop. Pop the lowest-error edge:
    • Run topology guards (see below). Skip if any guard fails.
    • Replace u and v with a new vertex at p*. Update incident face indices.
    • Sum quadrics: Q_new = Q_u + Q_v.
    • Re-evaluate every edge incident to new; push fresh entries onto the heap.
  4. Stale-entry skip. Each vertex carries a version counter bumped on every collapse. Heap entries store the version they were inserted at; popped entries whose recorded version doesn’t match the current vertex version are stale and discarded.

The version counter is what makes the heap incremental. The Stage 21 v1 implementation rebuilt the whole heap on every collapse — Stage 21.1 made the inner heap incremental with rayon-parallel cost evaluation on the initial seed pass. Combined effect: ~100× faster on a 50k-tri mesh.

Topology guards

Two guards filter out collapses that would corrupt the mesh:

  • Normal-flip check. Skip collapses that flip any incident face’s normal — i.e. for every face still using u or v, verify the post-collapse face normal points the same direction as the pre-collapse normal. Prevents self-intersection through the surface.
  • Non-manifold check. Skip collapses whose merged 1-ring would create a non-manifold edge (two faces sharing more than 2 vertices). Standard “link condition” from Dey, Edelsbrunner & Guha 1998 — the link of edge (u, v) (the boundary of the union of star(u) ∪ star(v)) must equal link(u) ∩ link(v).

Both guards fire conservatively — if the topology near the edge is ambiguous (degenerate triangles, dangling edges), the collapse is refused. The result is that on broken inputs decimation stops short of the target rather than producing garbage.

Boundary preservation is a known Garland-Heckbert simplification: molla doesn’t add the boundary-preservation quadrics, so open meshes drift at the boundary as decimation proceeds. Closed manifolds (the common case for collision authoring) decimate cleanly.

Edge-collapse strategy details

decimate.rs::DecimateState owns:

  • vertex_quadrics: Vec<Mat4> — sum of incident face quadrics.
  • vertex_versions: Vec<u32> — bumped on every collapse to invalidate stale heap entries.
  • vertex_alive: Vec<bool> — false after a vertex is removed.
  • face_indices: Vec<[u32; 3]> — per-face vertex indices (with sentinel u32::MAX for collapsed faces; compacted before output).
  • heap: BinaryHeap<HeapEntry> — min-heap on cost (Rust’s BinaryHeap is a max-heap, so cost is stored as Reverse(cost)).
  • vertex_incident_faces: Vec<HashSet<u32>> — adjacency cache rebuilt on collapse.

collapse_one() is the work unit: pop, validate (version check, guards), compute the new vertex position via the quadric minimiser or midpoint fallback, update adjacency, bump versions, re-seed incident edges. Each call performs O(deg(new_vertex)) heap pushes where deg is the vertex valence — typically 6 for a closed manifold, so the per-collapse cost is small.

into_trimesh() is the final pass: walk the alive vertices and faces, compact indices, return a new TriMesh. The output BVH is rebuilt from the compacted geometry — collision queries against the decimated mesh are immediately ready.

Performance

QEM decimation is O(N log N) in practice (heap operations dominate, each costing O(log N)). On a 50k-tri input reduced to 1k, the implementation completes in ~50 ms on one core (Stage 21.1 measurement). decimate_lod_chain with three factors (0.5 / 0.25 / 0.1) on the same input costs ~52 ms — the marginal cost of snapshotting intermediate levels is a few percent.

Best paired with the convex hull builder for collision authoring: hull the input cloud first, then decimate the hull mesh to keep the vertex count in the ~50 range where support_convex_hull’s linear-scan support function performs well.

Gaussian splats

crates/molla-geometry/src/gaussian_splat.rs defines the 3D Gaussian splat primitives that feed the differentiable raytrace renderer and the forward / backward WGSL kernels in crates/molla-kernels/shaders/splat_raytrace*.wgsl.

Stage 44 evolved through four revisions, each adding shading fidelity while keeping the core geometry pipeline byte-identical:

RevTypeAddsCoefficients
v1GaussianSplat3dforward-only diffuse RGB3
v2(same type)reverse-mode adjoint via SplatParam—
v3GaussianSplatSh3dspherical-harmonic colour, bands 0..=29 × 3 = 27
v4GaussianSplatShBand3dadds band 3 (Kerbl 2023)16 × 3 = 48
v4GaussianSplatShDiffuseView3ddiffuse / view-dependent split1 + 15

All four share the same geometric kernel (anisotropic 3D Gaussian density along a ray) — they differ only in how per-splat colour is parameterised.

v1 — GaussianSplat3d (diffuse RGB)

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct GaussianSplat3d {
    pub position: Vec3,    // world-space mean μ
    pub scale:    Vec3,    // per-axis stddev (must be > 0)
    pub rotation: Quat,    // covariance is R · diag(s²) · Rᵀ
    pub color:    [Real; 4], // diffuse RGB + reserved alpha
    pub opacity:  Real,    // bare opacity ∈ [0, 1]
}

impl GaussianSplat3d {
    pub fn new(
        position: Vec3, scale: Vec3, rotation: Quat,
        color_rgb: Vec3, opacity: Real,
    ) -> Self;
    pub fn color_rgb(&self) -> Vec3;
}
}

Ray-Gaussian density integral

A 3D Gaussian splat is an anisotropic Gaussian with mean μ, rotation R, scale s, opacity o. For a ray (p, d), the forward path transforms the ray into the splat’s canonical (unit-isotropic) frame:

o_local = R⁻¹ · (p - μ) / s          (component-wise division)
d_local = R⁻¹ · d        / s

The maximum density along the canonical ray is reached at the point of closest approach to the origin:

ρ_max = exp( -½ · |d_local × o_local|² / |d_local|² )

(because the squared distance from origin to the line o_local + t · d_local is |d × o|² / |d|²). The per-splat α is α = min(1, ρ_max · o). This is the standard analytic approximation used in Newton’s warp_raytrace/gaussians.py::canonical_ray_max_kernel_response and most 3DGS renderers — it captures the dominant integrand of the line-integral over the Gaussian density without resorting to a numerical erf evaluation.

The hit distance along the world ray for sorting purposes is the projection of (μ - p) onto d — i.e. the parametric t where the ray reaches the splat centre’s projection. This is the camera-distance sort matching Newton’s default.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn map_ray_to_canonical(
    splat: &GaussianSplat3d, ray_origin: Vec3, ray_dir: Vec3,
) -> (Vec3, Vec3); // (o_local, d_local) — d not normalised

pub fn canonical_ray_max_response(o_local: Vec3, d_local: Vec3) -> Real;

pub fn gaussian_response(
    ray_origin: Vec3, ray_dir: Vec3, splat: &GaussianSplat3d,
) -> Real;

pub fn splat_camera_distance(
    ray_origin: Vec3, ray_dir: Vec3, splat: &GaussianSplat3d,
) -> Real;
}

map_ray_to_canonical is careful with quaternion conventions (gaussian_splat.rs:140-164): it uses the BAC-CAB expansion v + 2 q_w (q_v × v) + 2 (q_v × (q_v × v)) rather than glam’s canonical q v q* formula. For unit q the two agree, but the FD adjoint oracle perturbs q off the unit sphere; the WGSL quat_rotate uses BAC-CAB, so the CPU forward must match exactly or the FD gradient check fails.

Depth sort + α-composite

The forward composite (composite_forward_cpu):

C_out = Σᵢ Cᵢ · αᵢ · ∏_{j<i}(1 - αⱼ),    T_out = ∏ᵢ (1 - αᵢ)

Front-to-back α-compositing. The host sorts splats by splat_camera_distance, skips splats with t ≤ 0 or t > max_distance, and clamps tiny α below min_alpha for performance. Termination short-circuits when transmittance drops below 1e-4 — invisible splats further down the ray don’t contribute.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn composite_forward_cpu(
    ray_origin: Vec3, ray_dir: Vec3, splats: &[GaussianSplat3d],
    max_distance: Real, min_alpha: Real,
) -> (Vec3, Real); // (rgb, transmittance)

pub fn composite_rgb_cpu(
    ray_origin: Vec3, ray_dir: Vec3, splats: &[GaussianSplat3d],
    max_distance: Real, min_alpha: Real,
) -> Vec3;
}

v2 — Reverse-mode adjoint (SplatParam)

SplatParam (gaussian_splat.rs:287-333) lists every per-splat learnable parameter as an enum variant — Position, Scale, Rotation, Color, Opacity. The reverse-mode backward kernel (shaders/splat_raytrace_backward.wgsl) writes gradients into the same enum-indexed slots; fd_grad_one_splat is the CPU finite-difference oracle used by the parity test:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn fd_grad_one_splat(
    ray_origin: Vec3, ray_dir: Vec3, splats: &[GaussianSplat3d],
    splat_index: usize, param: SplatParam,
    max_distance: Real, min_alpha: Real, h: Real,
) -> Vec3;
}

The FD step h is the standard symmetric ± h perturbation; on the unit quaternion this is the off-sphere perturbation the BAC-CAB discussion above hinges on.

v3 — Spherical harmonics, bands 0..=2

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub const SH_BAND_2_COUNT: usize = 9; // bands 0, 1, 2

pub const SH_C0: Real = 0.28209479177387814;    // 1 / (2 √π)
pub const SH_C1: Real = 0.4886025119029199;    // √(3 / 4π)
pub const SH_C2A: Real = 1.0925484305920792;   //  ½ √(15/π)
pub const SH_C2B: Real = -1.0925484305920792;
pub const SH_C2C: Real = 0.31539156525252005;  //  ¼ √(5/π)
pub const SH_C2D: Real = -1.0925484305920792;
pub const SH_C2E: Real = 0.5462742152960396;   //  ¼ √(15/π)

pub struct GaussianSplatSh3d {
    pub position: Vec3, pub scale: Vec3, pub rotation: Quat,
    pub sh:       [Vec3; SH_BAND_2_COUNT], // 9 coefficient triples
    pub opacity:  Real,
}

impl GaussianSplatSh3d {
    pub fn diffuse(position: Vec3, scale: Vec3, rotation: Quat, rgb: Vec3, opacity: Real) -> Self;
    pub fn from_sh (position: Vec3, scale: Vec3, rotation: Quat, sh:  [Vec3; 9], opacity: Real) -> Self;
    pub fn eval_color(&self, dir: Vec3) -> Vec3;
}

pub fn eval_sh(coeffs: &[Vec3; SH_BAND_2_COUNT], dir: Vec3) -> Vec3;
pub fn sh_basis(dir: Vec3) -> [Real; SH_BAND_2_COUNT];
}

diffuse(rgb) sets sh[0] = rgb / SH_C0 so eval_sh returns rgb for any view direction — the v1 back-compat sanity check.

sh_basis(dir) evaluates the 9 basis functions at the normalised direction. Order is band-major: [Y_00, Y_{1-1}, Y_{10}, Y_{11}, Y_{2-2}, Y_{2-1}, Y_{20}, Y_{21}, Y_{22}]. The bands 1 / 2 entries match the standard Sloan-2008 convention (the same one used by Kerbl 2023 “3D Gaussian Splatting” and the gaussian-splatting reference renderer).

v4 — Band 3 + diffuse/view split

Band 3 adds 7 more harmonics for finer angular detail:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub const SH_BAND_3_COUNT:   usize = 16; // bands 0..=3
pub const SH_VIEW_DEP_COUNT: usize = 15; // band 1 + 2 + 3 (no diffuse)

pub struct GaussianSplatShBand3d {
    pub position: Vec3, pub scale: Vec3, pub rotation: Quat,
    pub sh:       [Vec3; SH_BAND_3_COUNT],
    pub opacity:  Real,
}

pub struct GaussianSplatShDiffuseView3d {
    pub position: Vec3, pub scale: Vec3, pub rotation: Quat,
    pub diffuse:  Vec3,                       // band-0 contribution
    pub sh_view:  [Vec3; SH_VIEW_DEP_COUNT],  // bands 1..=3
    pub opacity:  Real,
}
}

GaussianSplatShDiffuseView3d separates the band-0 (“diffuse”) coefficient from the higher bands so callers can train the direction-independent component independently from the view-dependent ones — Kerbl 2023 finds this gives faster convergence and avoids the diffuse term getting absorbed into spurious specular highlights.

Sibling WGSL kernels: splat_raytrace_sh.wgsl / splat_raytrace_sh_backward.wgsl (band 0..=2), splat_raytrace_sh_band3.wgsl / splat_raytrace_sh_band3_backward.wgsl (band 0..=3), and splat_raytrace_sh_diffuse_view.wgsl for Stage 44 v5 diffuse/view forward. The diffuse/view GPU path is exposed as molla_kernels::SplatRaytraceKernel::dispatch_sh_diffuse_view; it binds splat_diffuse separately from the flat splat_sh_view buffer (splat_count * 15 Vec3s) and evaluates diffuse + Σ sh_view[k] · Y[k+1](ray_dir) per pixel on the GPU. That avoids CPU-baking the split parameterisation into full 16-slot band-3 SH buffers during iterative differentiable-splat workflows. All variants share the same α-composite inner loop — the only differences are the SH coefficient count and the view-direction evaluation formula.

CPU oracle coverage

The CPU functions (composite_*, eval_sh*, fd_grad_*_one_splat) exist primarily as oracles for the GPU forward + backward kernels. The parity tests (tests/splat_raytrace_*.rs) check that:

  • GPU forward agrees with CPU forward to within 1e-5 for diffuse splats and 1e-4 for SH splats (single-precision f32 causes the slightly looser SH bound).
  • GPU diffuse/view forward agrees with composite_sh_diffuse_view_rgb_cpu in the ignored diffuse_view_gpu_forward_matches_cpu adapter test.
  • GPU backward agrees with CPU finite-difference gradient to within 1e-3 on random splat configurations.

Production rendering goes through the GPU kernels — the CPU paths are not intended for production-size scene rendering (a 10k-splat scene through composite_forward_cpu is seconds, not milliseconds).

Soft contact pipeline

Stage 33 ships cross-mesh soft-vs-soft vertex-triangle (VT) and edge-edge (EE) contact for cloth and tet meshes, plus continuous collision detection (CCD) for tunnelling-prevention at large substeps. The pipeline composes:

SoftSurface  ──▶  SoftBvh  ──▶  VT / EE contact gather
   ▲                              │
   └── ClothMeshId / TetMeshId    └── soft_ccd::vt_ccd → root-finder

Raw registry descriptors live under crates/molla/src/sim/soft_surface.rs because they are model data. Geometry re-exports those descriptors for compatibility and owns the derived acceleration/contact pieces in crates/molla/src/geometry/: soft_surface.rs (boundary_facets), soft_bvh.rs, and soft_ccd.rs.

SoftSurface registry

Cloth tris and tet boundary tris are unified under a single “soft surface” so the downstream contact gather can treat them interchangeably:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub enum SoftSurfaceKind {
    TetMesh, // boundary triangulation of a volumetric tet mesh
    Cloth,   // tessellation tris (already in Model.tri_indices)
}

pub struct ClothMeshId(pub u32);

pub const INVALID_VERT: u32 = u32::MAX;

pub struct SoftSurface {
    pub kind:                SoftSurfaceKind,
    pub vertex_offset:       u32,                  // index into Model.particle_q
    pub vertex_count:        u32,
    pub tri_offset:          u32,                  // index into Model.soft_surface_tris
    pub tri_count:           u32,
    pub edge_offset:         u32,                  // Stage 33.1 — EE contact
    pub edge_count:          u32,
    pub tet_mesh_id:         Option<TetMeshId>,
    pub cloth_mesh_id:       Option<ClothMeshId>,
    pub self_collision:      bool,                 // Stage 33.3
    pub friction:            Real,                 // Stage 33.5
    pub restitution:         Real,                 // Stage 33.5
}

pub fn compute_tet_surface_triangles(tets: &[[u32; 4]]) -> Vec<[u32; 3]>;
pub fn compute_surface_edges(tris: &[[u32; 3]]) -> Vec<[u32; 2]>;
pub fn boundary_facets(mesh: &FemMesh) -> Vec<[u32; 3]>;
}

compute_tet_surface_triangles extracts the boundary triangulation of a tet mesh via the standard “tris that belong to exactly one tet” pass — group by sorted vertex triple, keep tris with count 1. The original CCW winding (from outside the tet) is preserved so downstream normal queries get the outward direction.

A key invariant: the resulting tri list is sorted by sorted-key (sim/soft_surface.rs). HashMap iteration order isn’t stable across runs; without the sort, the per-tri global IDs that downstream code (LBVH, soft-VT contact gather, friction warm-start LUT keyed on (vertex_global_id, tri_global_id)) computes would shuffle frame to frame — breaking warm-starts and parity tests.

compute_surface_edges returns the unique undirected edges as [min, max] pairs. Used by Stage 33.1’s EE contact gather.

SoftBvh — cross-mesh BVH

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct SoftBvh {
    pub tri_aabbs:      Vec<Aabb>,
    pub tri_to_surface: Vec<u32>, // global tri idx → SoftSurface idx
    // internal nodes hidden
}

impl SoftBvh {
    pub fn build(model: &Model, state: &State) -> Self;
    pub fn refit(&mut self, model: &Model, state: &State);
    pub fn query_aabb(&self, min: Vec3, max: Vec3, out: &mut Vec<u32>);
}
}

The BVH spans every soft-surface triangle across every cloth and tet mesh — one tree for the whole soft-body world. The contact gather walks per-vertex queries through this BVH; the per-tri global IDs index back into Model.soft_surface_tris and the surface ownership in tri_to_surface lets the gather filter out same-surface pairs (Stage 33’s cross-mesh-only default) or allow them (Stage 33.3 self-collision, gated by SoftSurface::self_collision).

Refit-only update is cheap (AABB-only, no topology change). The full rebuild only re-pays itself when the soft mesh count changes — which it doesn’t, mid-rollout.

GPU port (Stage 33.2) is the existing crate::kernels::lbvh dispatcher reusing the AABB array prepared here. The CPU oracle remains live for the per-vertex contact gather logic.

VT + EE contact

The contact gather pass walks per-vertex queries through the SoftBvh:

  1. AABB query — expand the vertex’s swept AABB by the contact margin, recover the candidate triangle list.
  2. Per-tri test — for each candidate, classify the closest point on the triangle (3 vertices, 3 edges, 1 face — the standard 7-region split from closest_point_on_triangle in sdf.md). Emit a VT contact when the projected distance falls below the margin.
  3. Same-surface filter — for non-self-collision surfaces, skip pairs where tri_to_surface[tri_idx] matches the vertex’s owning surface. For self-collision surfaces, also skip triangles topologically incident to the vertex (looked up via Model.soft_vertex_incident_tris) to avoid trivial “I touch myself” emissions.

Stage 33.1 EE contact reuses the same BVH plus the per-surface edge lists from compute_surface_edges. Edge-edge contact is emitted when the segment-segment closest-points pair falls below the margin AND the projections are in the interior of both edges (Bridson’s classic test).

VT-CCD root finding (Stage 33.4)

Per-substep VT contact misses fast tunnelling — a vertex moving fast enough to skip past a triangle between consecutive positions doesn’t trigger the discrete test. Stage 33.4 adds the continuous variant:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn vt_ccd(
    v_at_t0:   Vec3,
    v_at_t1:   Vec3,
    tri_at_t0: [Vec3; 3],
    tri_at_t1: [Vec3; 3],
) -> Option<Real>; // earliest t ∈ [0, 1] of valid contact, or None

pub fn vt_ccd_normal(
    v0: Vec3, v1: Vec3,
    tri0: [Vec3; 3], tri1: [Vec3; 3],
    t: Real,
) -> Vec3; // outward triangle normal at TOI t
}

Math

Given a vertex and a triangle that each move linearly between t = 0 and t = 1, we want the earliest t* ∈ [0, 1] at which the vertex passes through the triangle plane AND the projection lies inside the triangle. The Bridson (2003) formulation expresses the signed distance from vertex to triangle plane as

f(t) = ((B(t) - A(t)) × (C(t) - A(t))) · (V(t) - A(t))

which is a cubic in t (each of (B-A), (C-A), (V-A) is linear in t; the cross product is quadratic; the dot is cubic). Roots of f(t) = 0 are the coplanar instants; we filter each root by whether the barycentric projection sits inside the triangle.

Root-finder strategy

Two stages (soft_ccd.rs:101-167):

  1. Sign-change sweep. Sample f(t) at 20 equally-spaced sub-intervals across [0, 1]. Each sign change pins down at least one root in that sub-interval; bisect to refine.
  2. Bisection. Standard binary halving for up to 60 iterations (2⁻⁶⁰ ≈ 8.7e-19, far below the ROOT_EPS = 1e-7 tolerance). Exits early when |f(t)| < ROOT_EPS or the interval shrinks below ROOT_EPS.
#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// soft_ccd.rs:129-166 (excerpt)
const N: usize = 20;
let mut prev_f = f(0.0);
for k in 1..=N {
    let t = k as Real / N as Real;
    let curr_f = f(t);
    if (prev_f >= 0.0) != (curr_f >= 0.0) {
        if let Some(t_root) = bisect(&f, prev_t, prev_f, t, curr_f) {
            if let Some(t_hit) = check_root(t_root, ...) {
                return Some(t_hit);  // earliest valid root wins
            }
        }
    }
    prev_t = t;
    prev_f = curr_f;
}
}

The inside-triangle filter (check_root) computes barycentric coords at the candidate t and rejects projections that fall outside the triangle (with a small slack BARY_SLACK = 1e-4 to admit grazing edge contacts).

Termination + slack

ROOT_EPS = 1e-7 is the practical convergence threshold (tighter just burns iterations — the snap-back in the integrator uses TOI - eps with a 1e-4 eps anyway).

BARY_SLACK = 1e-4 is generous enough to admit legitimate grazing-edge contacts but tight enough to reject projections that sit well outside the triangle. This is the dominant source of “missed” CCD contacts; setting it tighter rejects valid edge cases and setting it looser pulls in spurious near-misses.

v1 ships VT-CCD only; EE-CCD (the 4D quartic case) is deferred to Stage 33.4.1.

Friction + restitution (Stage 33.2.1 / 33.5)

Per-surface friction and restitution coefficients live on SoftSurface::friction and SoftSurface::restitution. Pair-rules:

  • Friction combines via geometric mean: μ = sqrt(μ_a · μ_b). Zero on either side disables tangential resistance for the contact.
  • Restitution combines via min(e_a, e_b) — molla’s pessimistic rule; one inelastic surface dominates.

Defaults per kind: Cloth { friction = 0.4, restitution = 0.0 }, TetMesh { friction = 0.4, restitution = 0.1 }. Settable via the SoftSurface getters/setters at builder time.

Cross-mesh path

The end-to-end cross-mesh contact path (cloth-vs-cloth, cloth-vs-tet, tet-vs-tet) hands off through:

  1. SoftBvh::refit updates the per-tri AABBs from state.particle_q.
  2. Per-vertex broad-phase query produces a candidate tri list.
  3. Per-tri VT test produces a discrete-time contact OR
  4. vt_ccd produces a continuous-time-of-impact (TOI) when the discrete test misses but the swept AABB indicates a crossing.
  5. Emitted contacts feed XPBD / VBD penalty terms with friction + restitution per the rules above.

Per-substep refit + per-vertex tree traversal makes the dominant cost O(N_vertices × log(N_tris)). For two ~150-tet jelly cubes the per-step cost is well under 0.5 ms on CPU; GPU port (Stage 33.2) brings it under 50 µs.

Hydroelastic contact

Point contacts (one normal + one tangent at a single point) work fine for sphere-on-sphere or capsule-on-plane collisions, but they’re noisy for patch contacts — a cloth resting on a sphere, two boxes stacked face-to-face, a finger pressed against a soft ball. The contact “point” jitters between patch vertices each frame; the solver damps it out but the system never quite reaches rest.

Drake’s hydroelastic contact model (Elandt, Drumwright, Sherman & Kuchenbecker 2019) replaces the point contact with a distributed pressure field over the intersection volume of the two bodies. molla ships a soft-on-rigid implementation at Stage 22.1 (crates/molla/src/geometry/hydroelastic.rs), with a GPU port (Stage 41 v2 sub-4) in shaders/hydroelastic.wgsl. The Stage 39D polish adds wrench-preserving reduction (reduce_with_anchor) and bucket aggregation (aggregate_by_bucket).

Model

The soft body carries a SdfGrid representing its hydroelastic pressure field. The pressure inside the body is a linear function of penetration depth into the body:

p(x) = E · max(0, -sdf(x))           [units: Pa = N/m²]

E is the hydroelastic modulus (Drake’s “elastic modulus”). The contact force is the integral of pressure over the intersection surface — for soft-on-rigid that’s the rigid body’s surface, discretised as a quadrature point cloud with per-point area weights.

v1 scope (Stage 22.1)

  • Soft-on-rigid only. Soft body has an SDF pressure field; rigid body is sampled at discrete surface points.
  • Soft-on-soft is deferred. Both volumes overlap → genuinely 3D intersection. Requires either marching cubes on min(p_a - p_b, 0) for the iso-surface, or a tetrahedralised volume integration. Neither is in v1.
  • Linear hydroelastic — pressure is E · max(0, -sdf).
  • Per-sample friction — each contact carries a Dahl-friction contact id for persistent bristle state across substeps.
#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct HydroelasticConfig {
    pub hydroelastic_modulus: Real, // E (Pa); 1e4..1e7 for rubber, 1e9+ for plastic
    pub max_pressure:         Real, // safety cap on per-sample pressure
    pub friction_coefficient: Real, // Coulomb μ (0.4 default)
    pub culling_distance:     Real, // skip samples this far outside the SDF
}

pub enum HydroelasticPolicy {
    SoftOnRigid,    // v1 scope
    SoftOnSoft,     // not implemented in v1
}

pub struct SurfaceSample {
    pub position: Vec3, // rigid-body local frame
    pub normal:   Vec3, // outward-facing surface normal, local frame
    pub area:     Real, // quadrature weight (m²)
}

pub struct HydroelasticContact {
    pub point:      Vec3, // world contact point
    pub normal:     Vec3, // world outward (out of soft, into rigid)
    pub pressure:   Real, // Pa
    pub area:       Real, // m²
    pub contact_id: u32,  // for friction warm-start
}

pub struct HydroelasticManifold {
    pub contacts:           Vec<HydroelasticContact>,
    pub total_normal_force: Real,
    pub net_force:          Vec3,
}
}

compute_hydroelastic_contact

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn compute_hydroelastic_contact(
    soft_sdf:      &SdfGrid,
    rigid_samples: &[SurfaceSample],
    soft_pose:     Transform,
    rigid_pose:    Transform,
    cfg:           &HydroelasticConfig,
) -> HydroelasticManifold;
}

Algorithm (hydroelastic.rs:211-262):

  1. For each rigid surface sample, transform its local position into world via rigid_pose, then into the soft body’s local frame via soft_pose.inverse().
  2. Trilinearly sample the soft body’s SDF at that point.
  3. If sdf < 0 (inside the soft body), compute pressure = E · (-sdf), clamped to max_pressure.
  4. The contact normal points OUT of the soft body — that’s +∇sdf (SDF increases outward), computed via central differences in sample_sdf_gradient. Transform back to world.
  5. Assign a stable contact id (typically (rigid_shape_id, sample_index) packed into a u32) and emit a HydroelasticContact.

Output total_normal_force is the quadrature approximation to the surface integral of pressure · area. The empty manifold case (no penetration) trivially yields total_normal_force = 0, net_force = ZERO.

Surface sampling helpers

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn sample_sphere_surface(r: Real, count: usize) -> Vec<SurfaceSample>;

pub fn sample_plane_patch(
    extent_x: Real, extent_z: Real,
    nx: usize,    nz: usize,
    plane_y: Real, normal: Vec3,
) -> Vec<SurfaceSample>;
}

sample_sphere_surface uses Fibonacci-spiral sampling — count samples on a unit sphere scaled to radius r, each carrying its spherical-area weight. sample_plane_patch produces a uniform nx × nz grid of samples on a finite plane patch.

PatchSample — signed force_magnitude contract

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct PatchSample {
    pub point:          Vec3, // world contact point
    pub normal:         Vec3, // unit, world frame (soft → rigid)
    pub force_magnitude: Real, // SIGNED; see below
}

impl PatchSample {
    pub fn force(&self) -> Vec3 { self.normal * self.force_magnitude }
}

pub fn manifold_to_samples(manifold: &HydroelasticManifold) -> Vec<PatchSample>;
}

Sign convention: for raw samples emitted by hydroelastic integration force_magnitude ≥ 0. After reduce_with_anchor the centroid and anchor samples can each carry a negative force_magnitude when the moment-balance split coefficient α leaves [0, 1] — the centroid pulls one way and the anchor pulls the other, summing to the total normal force. Callers projecting onto a friction cone or capping by magnitude should treat this field as signed and use force_magnitude.abs() when they need the actual magnitude.

Stage 39D — anchor reduction

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct AnchorReducedContact {
    pub centroid: PatchSample, // spatial centroid of the patch
    pub anchor:   PatchSample, // center of pressure
}

impl AnchorReducedContact {
    pub fn net_force(&self) -> Vec3;
    pub fn net_moment(&self) -> Vec3;
}

pub fn reduce_with_anchor(samples: &[PatchSample]) -> Option<AnchorReducedContact>;
}

Reduces a distributed pressure patch to exactly two contacts that together reproduce both the net force AND the net moment about any reference point. Half the contact count of the input (one per region rather than dozens of quadrature samples), without losing the wrench.

Math

Let F_total = Σ fᵢ · n̂ᵢ and M_total = Σ rᵢ × (fᵢ · n̂ᵢ). Both contact forces are along n̂ = F_total / |F_total|. Write:

F_c = α     · n̂ · |F_total|        at r_centroid
F_a = (1-α) · n̂ · |F_total|        at r_cp

with α ∈ ℝ (not necessarily in [0, 1] — the anchor can pull the opposite way to balance the moment). The two reference points:

  • r_centroid = (1/N) Σ rᵢ — spatial centroid (equal weights).
  • r_cp = (Σ fᵢ rᵢ) / Σ fᵢ — center of pressure (force-weighted).

The moment equation r_centroid × F_c + r_cp × F_a = M_total projects onto the plane perpendicular to n̂ and yields a 2D linear system in (|F_c|, |F_a|). The closed-form solution (hydroelastic.rs:610-624):

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let dr          = r_centroid - r_cp;
let dr_cross_n  = dr.cross(force_dir);
let denom       = dr_cross_n.length_squared() * total_force_mag;
let alpha = if denom > 1.0e-20 {
    let target_m = m_total - r_cp.cross(force_dir) * total_force_mag;
    target_m.dot(dr_cross_n) / denom
} else {
    1.0 // degenerate: r_centroid == r_cp, anchor carries nothing
};
}

Verification: tests/hydroelastic_polish.rs::anchor_contact_reproduces_moment checks the pair reproduces the original patch’s wrench to within 1%.

Stage 39D — bucket aggregation

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub enum StiffnessReduction {
    Parallel,    // k_agg = Σ k_i
    Series,      // k_agg = 1 / Σ (1/k_i)
}

pub struct AggregateStiffnessConfig {
    pub voxel_size:           Real, // position-bin edge length
    pub normal_bin_angle:     Real, // angular bin width (rad)
    pub stiffness_reduction:  StiffnessReduction,
}

pub struct AggregatedContact {
    pub point:               Vec3,
    pub normal:              Vec3,
    pub force_magnitude:     Real,
    pub aggregate_stiffness: Real,
    pub sample_count:        u32,
}

pub struct StiffnessSample<'a> {
    pub patch:     &'a PatchSample,
    pub stiffness: Real,
}

pub fn aggregate_by_bucket(
    samples: &[StiffnessSample<'_>],
    cfg:     &AggregateStiffnessConfig,
) -> Vec<AggregatedContact>;
}

The molla equivalent of Newton’s hashtable+voxel+normal-bin reducer in contact_reduction_hydroelastic.py. Coarse bucketing collapses many quadrature samples into one canonical contact per (position_voxel, normal_bin) cell.

Bucket key

Position voxel: positions are translated by the patch centroid before voxelising (hydroelastic.rs:778-782). Without this, a patch positioned at (5, 0, 5) would split into different buckets from one at the origin, and a patch straddling x = 0 would split across floor(-ε) = -1 and floor(+ε) = 0 even when the patch is much smaller than the voxel. Translation + round-based binning (not floor) sidesteps both issues.

Normal bin: snap each axis component of the unit normal to a direction-cosine grid with step sin(angle). round, not floor, again — round is symmetric around zero so a patch with n ≈ +Y and small ±x/z wobble collapses cleanly into bin (0, ±1, 0) without straddling a grid edge near each axis. Singularity-free at every axis-aligned direction (where equirectangular grids would pole-out).

Stiffness reduction

The two cases correspond to spring topologies:

  • Series — contacts mounted in line (same line of action, stacked depth-wise). Compliance c = Σ cᵢ = Σ 1/kᵢ, so k_agg = 1 / Σ (1/kᵢ). Used when collapsing duplicate contacts that touch the same rigid-body point through different paths.
  • Parallel — contacts mounted side-by-side (independent patches sharing the load). k_agg = Σ kᵢ. Used when summing distinct contact area inside the same bucket — each sample contributes independent surface area; total resistance is the sum.

Newton’s policy: parallel inside a bucket, series across buckets when collapsing to a single anchor pair.

GPU port

shaders/hydroelastic.wgsl mirrors compute_hydroelastic_contact line-for-line: one thread per surface sample, transforms world → soft-local, trilerps the SDF, computes pressure + central- difference normal, writes the per-sample (normal, point, force) to three output buffers:

contact_normal[i]       — world-frame outward normal (zero if no contact)
contact_point[i]        — world-frame contact point
contact_normal_force[i] — pressure · sample area (N) (zero if no contact)

The downstream Dahl-friction kernel ([crate::kernels::DahlFrictionKernel]) consumes these directly, keyed on a host-provided contact_id for persistent bristle state across substeps. The host wires the friction-coefficient buffer and the bristle-state buffer separately — the hydroelastic kernel itself only handles the pressure-field path.

The kernel uses an SOA layout (separate sample_local_pos, sample_local_normal, sample_area arrays) to keep the SDF read the dominant memory cost: each sample reads 8 SDF cells for the trilerp plus 6 for the central-difference gradient, vs ~24 bytes for the per-sample fixed data. SOA gives the hardware coalesced loads on the per-sample arrays and lets the SDF reads dominate profile.

Data model

The simulation core is built around four host-allocated, GPU-mirrored structures that every solver consumes via the Solver::step contract:

                ┌─────────────┐
                │   Model     │   immutable: bodies, shapes, joints,
                │  (Buffer<T>)│   particles, springs, equality
                └─────┬───────┘
                      │
  ┌──────────┐ step  ┌─▼──────────┐  ┌─────────┐  ┌──────────┐
  │  State   │──────▶│   Solver   │◀─│ Control │  │ Contacts │
  │ (q, qd, f│       │  (XPBD/Aba │  │ (drives,│  │ (broad+  │
  │  body, …)│◀──────│   VBD/MPM) │  │ wrenches│  │  narrow) │
  └──────────┘       └────────────┘  └─────────┘  └──────────┘

All four types are defined in crates/molla/src/sim/ and re-exported from molla::sim.

Model — static, immutable scene description

Model is built once via a ModelBuilder and then never mutated by solvers. Every field is a Buffer<T> — a host Vec<T> paired with a lazily-allocated GPU mirror (wgpu::Buffer). The host slab is always authoritative; Model::upload_to_device(device, queue) ensures the GPU mirror matches.

Bodies, particles, shapes

pub struct Model {
    // Particles
    pub particle_count: usize,
    pub particle_mass:     Buffer<Real>,
    pub particle_inv_mass: Buffer<Real>,
    pub particle_radius:   Buffer<Real>,
    pub particle_flags:    Buffer<u32>,
    pub particle_world:    Buffer<i32>,
    pub initial_particle_q: Buffer<Vec3>,

    // Rigid bodies
    pub body_count: usize,
    pub body_mass:        Buffer<Real>,
    pub body_inv_mass:    Buffer<Real>,
    pub body_inertia:     Buffer<Mat3>,
    pub body_inv_inertia: Buffer<Mat3>,
    pub body_com:         Buffer<Vec3>,
    pub body_flags:       Buffer<u32>,
    pub body_world:       Buffer<i32>,
    pub initial_body_q:   Buffer<Transform>,

    // Collision shapes
    pub shape_count: usize,
    pub shape_body:        Buffer<i32>,   // owning body, -1 = world
    pub shape_geom_kind:   Buffer<u32>,   // GPU discriminant
    pub shape_geom_data:   Buffer<Vec3>,  // packed scalar params
    pub shape_transform:   Buffer<Transform>,
    pub shape_friction:    Buffer<Real>,
    pub shape_restitution: Buffer<Real>,
    // (…rolling/torsional friction, collision groups, PBR colours)
    pub meshes:        Vec<TriMesh>,       // host-side
    pub hulls:         Vec<Vec<Vec3>>,
    pub heightfields:  Vec<Heightfield>,
    pub sdfs:          Vec<SdfShape>,
    // …
}

Every per-entity property is a flat parallel array: a body i is the i-th entry of body_mass, body_inertia, body_com, … and so on. This Newton/Warp-style “Struct of Arrays” layout maps directly onto WGSL storage buffers — kernels index by thread id.

The GPU shape representation flattens the ShapeGeometry enum into shape_geom_kind (u32 discriminant: 0=Sphere, 1=Plane, 2=Box, 3=Capsule, 4=Cylinder, 5=Cone, 6=Ellipsoid, 0xff=host-only) and shape_geom_data (Vec3 of packed scalars). Mesh / hull / heightfield / SDF backing storage remains host-side via the meshes / hulls / heightfields / sdfs vectors, indexed by a mesh_id / hull_id / … u32 stored in shape_geom_data.

Constraints

// Distance constraints (cloth edges, ropes, springs)
pub spring_count: usize,
pub spring_a:              Buffer<u32>,
pub spring_b:              Buffer<u32>,
pub spring_rest_length:    Buffer<Real>,
pub spring_compliance:     Buffer<Real>,   // XPBD α = 1/k
pub spring_max_stretch:    Buffer<Real>,
pub spring_color_count:    usize,

pub spring_indices_by_color: Buffer<u32>,

// Equality constraints (CONNECT / WELD / JointMimic)

pub equality_body_b:   Buffer<i32>,
pub equality_anchor_a: Buffer<Vec3>,
pub equality_anchor_b: Buffer<Vec3>,
// …

// Mimic constraints: q_a = c0 + c1·q_b
pub mimic_count: usize,

pub mimic_c1:      Buffer<Real>,

Spring constraints carry a graph colouring (greedy, computed at build time) so the XPBD GPU kernel can solve a colour class in parallel without write-races. The same colouring is exposed at the vertex level (vertex_adjacent_springs_* + particle_indices_by_color) for VBD’s per-vertex Gauss-Seidel sweeps. See XPBD and VBD for how the CSR layout is consumed.

Joints & articulations

pub joint_count: usize,
pub joint_type:   Buffer<u32>,    // JointType discriminant
pub joint_parent: Buffer<i32>,
pub joint_child:  Buffer<i32>,
pub joint_x_p:    Buffer<Transform>,
pub joint_x_c:    Buffer<Transform>,
pub joint_axis:   Buffer<Vec3>,
pub joint_coord_offset: Buffer<u32>,  // CSR into joint_q
pub joint_dof_offset:   Buffer<u32>,  // CSR into joint_qd
pub joint_coord_total: usize,
pub joint_dof_total:   usize,

pub joint_limit_lower:    Buffer<Real>,
pub joint_limit_upper:    Buffer<Real>,
pub joint_friction:       Buffer<Real>,
pub joint_effort_limit:   Buffer<Real>,
pub joint_velocity_limit: Buffer<Real>,
pub joint_target_ke:      Buffer<Real>,  // joint-drive stiffness

// Articulations (kinematic trees) — Featherstone dispatches one
// workgroup per articulation.
pub articulation_count: usize,
pub articulation_start: Buffer<u32>,  // CSR over joints

Per-DoF arrays (limits, friction, effort cap, drive stiffness) are indexed by joint_dof_offset[j] + k for joint j’s k-th DoF. See Joints for the DoF accounting.

Tetrahedra, cables, muscles, soft surfaces

Tetrahedral soft bodies (tet_count, tet_indices, tet_dm_inv, Lamé constants, plasticity state), cables (cable_count, cable_particles, bending stiffness CSR), muscles (muscle_count, Hill parameters, CSR joint_muscle_*), and cross-mesh soft surfaces (soft_surfaces, soft_surface_tris, EE/VT adjacency) all live on Model with the same “flat SoA” discipline.

Multi-world support

Every per-entity slab carries a *_world: Buffer<i32> companion: bodies, particles, joints, articulations, equality constraints, and mimics each remember which world they belong to. Model.world_count and Model.gravity: Buffer<Vec3> (length world_count) parameterise per-world gravity. Solvers honour world ownership by routing each body/particle into its world’s gravity slot during integration.

This lets a single Model describe N parallel RL environments that the GPU dispatches as one workgroup grid — world_count is the outermost dimension. Newton’s “worlds” concept maps directly.

Global solver knobs

pub angular_damping: Real,        // applied per step
pub linear_damping:  Real,
pub particle_velocity_max: Real,  // stability cap
pub contact_margin: Real,         // broad-phase AABB slack
pub default_friction:    Real,
pub default_restitution: Real,

These are scalars (not buffers) — every solver reads them once per step. Per-shape overrides (shape_friction, etc.) take precedence where set (sentinel NaN = “use default”).

State — time-varying simulation data

pub struct State {
    pub particle_q:  Buffer<Vec3>,
    pub particle_qd: Buffer<Vec3>,
    pub particle_f:  Buffer<Vec3>,

    pub body_q:  Buffer<Transform>,      // pose (body-frame origin in world)
    pub body_qd: Buffer<SpatialVector>,  // (v_lin, ω) at COM, world frame
    pub body_f:  Buffer<SpatialVector>,  // applied wrench at COM, world

    pub joint_q:  Buffer<Real>,
    pub joint_qd: Buffer<Real>,

    // VBD plasticity (Stage 20.3/20.4)
    pub tet_f_plastic:      Buffer<Mat3>,
    pub tet_plastic_strain: Buffer<Real>,
    pub tet_back_stress:    Buffer<Mat3>,
}

State holds everything the solver mutates. The integrator contract is double-buffered:

solver.step(&model, &state_in, &control, &contacts, dt, &mut state_out);

Solvers may ping-pong state_in and state_out internally across substeps (see Featherstone and XPBD), but to the caller it’s a simple A→B copy.

Allocate via model.state(). The factory copies initial_body_q, initial_particle_q, initial_joint_q, and (for tet meshes) initial F_p into the working state; velocities + forces start at zero. State::clone_host makes a host-side replica (used by substepping wrappers) and State::copy_host_from does in-place copies between same-shape states.

body_q.translation is the body-frame origin in world, not the COM (the COM offset is Model.body_com). The angular component of body_qd is the body angular velocity in world frame, not body frame — same convention as Newton / Warp.

Control — per-step user inputs

pub struct Control {
    pub joint_target_mode: Buffer<u32>,            // per-DoF
    pub joint_target_pos:  Buffer<Real>,           // (rad / m)
    pub joint_target_vel:  Buffer<Real>,
    pub joint_target_kp:   Buffer<Real>,           // PD gain
    pub joint_target_kd:   Buffer<Real>,
    pub joint_force:       Buffer<Real>,           // feed-forward
    pub body_external_f:   Buffer<SpatialVector>,  // per-body wrench
}

joint_target_mode selects the per-DoF drive policy from JointTargetMode (None, Position, Velocity, PositionVelocity, Effort). The Featherstone backward pass folds drive torque + feed-forward joint_force + joint friction into each DoF’s u_k, then clamps by joint_effort_limit. See Featherstone.

Per-body external wrenches (body_external_f) are added at the COM in world frame — typical use is RL-style pushers, hand-of-god dragging, or aerodynamic forces from a wing model.

Allocate via model.control(); everything starts zero (drive mode = None = passive).

Contacts — collision pipeline output

pub struct Contacts {
    pub count: u32,
    pub capacity: usize,
    pub a_index: Buffer<u32>,        // first body / shape index
    pub b_index: Buffer<u32>,
    pub point:   Buffer<Vec3>,       // world-space
    pub normal:  Buffer<Vec3>,       // a → b
    pub depth:   Buffer<Real>,
    pub friction:           Buffer<Real>,
    pub rolling_friction:   Buffer<Real>,
    pub torsional_friction: Buffer<Real>,
    pub restitution:        Buffer<Real>,

    // CSR per-body indexing (built after each broad+narrow pass)
    pub body_contact_offsets: Buffer<u32>,    // length body_count + 1
    pub body_contact_indices: Buffer<u32>,    // length 2·count
}

count is the number of valid entries; the per-contact arrays are sized to capacity and only 0..count is meaningful.

The CSR body_contact_offsets + body_contact_indices is the per-body index built so the XPBD GPU kernel can dispatch one thread per body, processing only its own contacts (no cross-body write hazards). Every contact shows up under both endpoints, with the sign bit of the index marking which side the body is on:

  • top bit clear → body is the a side
  • top bit set (0x8000_0000) → body is the b side, real index = value & 0x7fff_ffff

Decode via Contacts::decode_index(packed) → (idx, is_b_side). Static-world peers (STATIC_BODY) are deliberately excluded — they have no body slot to update. This per-body Jacobi pattern is detailed in XPBD.

Pair friction / restitution follow Newton’s max(μ_a, μ_b) rule: the collision pipeline writes the per-contact value using shape_*_friction / shape_restitution with the NaN sentinel falling back to Model.default_friction / Model.default_restitution.

Buffer ownership recap

fieldownermutated by
Model.*built oncenothing (immutable at sim time)
State.*per-simsolver
Control.*per-stepuser code (between steps)
Contacts.*per-stepcollision pipeline (pipeline.collide)

All four upload to GPU via their respective upload_to_device(device, queue) helpers. The model uploads once before the first step; the state uploads on initial sim startup and is read back via download_from_device for the viewer / sensors; the control + contacts re-upload every step (the contact set turns over completely).

ModelBuilder

ModelBuilder is the ergonomic authoring surface for Model. It accumulates bodies, shapes, joints, particles, springs, cables, tetrahedra, equality constraints, mimics, and muscles in host-side Vec<T> buffers, then build() consumes the builder and emits a fully-baked Model with all CSR offsets, graph colourings, and BVHs computed.

use molla::sim::{ModelBuilder, BodyParams};

let mut b = ModelBuilder::new();
let body = b.add_body(BodyParams::new().with_position([0.0, 1.0, 0.0].into()));
b.add_shape_sphere(body, Default::default(), 0.5)?;
let model = b.build()?;
let mut state = model.state()?;

Bodies

pub fn add_body(&mut self, params: BodyParams) -> BodyId;

BodyParams is a builder-style struct:

pub struct BodyParams {
    pub mass: Real,           // kg; 0 = static / kinematic
    pub inertia: Mat3,        // at COM, body frame (kg·m²)
    pub com: Vec3,            // COM in body frame
    pub pose: Transform,      // initial world pose
    pub flags: u32,           // BodyFlags::DYNAMIC | KINEMATIC
    pub world: WorldId,
}

impl BodyParams {
    pub fn new() -> Self;                        // 1 kg cube-ish defaults
    pub fn with_mass(self, mass: Real) -> Self;
    pub fn with_inertia(self, inertia: Mat3) -> Self;
    pub fn with_spatial_inertia(self, si: SpatialInertia) -> Self;
    pub fn with_com(self, com: Vec3) -> Self;
    pub fn with_pose(self, pose: Transform) -> Self;
    pub fn with_position(self, p: Vec3) -> Self;
    pub fn with_world(self, world: WorldId) -> Self;
    pub fn with_flags(self, flags: u32) -> Self;
}

with_spatial_inertia is the recipe for shape-derived inertia: any ShapeGeometry computes a SpatialInertia given density via crate::math::inertia::*.

Each add_shape_* returns a ShapeId and is bound to a body (or BodyId::NONE for static-world shapes). The signatures share a common shape transform + per-shape material setup pattern.

ShapeGeometry

The full geometry tag enum (host-side, mirrored at build time into the GPU-friendly shape_geom_kind / shape_geom_data parallel arrays):

pub enum ShapeGeometry {
    Sphere      { radius: Real },
    Plane       { normal: Vec3 },                          // half-space
    Box         { half_extents: Vec3 },
    Capsule     { half_height: Real, radius: Real },       // local +Y axis
    Cylinder    { half_height: Real, radius: Real },
    Cone        { half_height: Real, radius: Real },       // apex at +Y
    Ellipsoid   { half_axes: Vec3 },
    Triangle    { v0: Vec3, v1: Vec3, v2: Vec3 },
    TriMesh     { mesh_id: u32 },
    ConvexHull  { hull_id: u32 },
    Heightfield { field_id: u32 },
    Sdf         { sdf_id: u32 },
}

Per-shape material:

pub fn set_shape_material(
    &mut self, shape: ShapeId,
    friction: Real, restitution: Real,
) -> Result<()>;

pub fn set_shape_friction_modes(
    &mut self, shape: ShapeId,

    &mut self, shape: ShapeId,

);

pub fn set_shape_collision_group(&mut self, shape: ShapeId, group: u32);
pub fn add_shape_collision_exclusion(&mut self, a: ShapeId, b: ShapeId);

Friction / restitution sentinels: NaN means “fall back to the model default”. Collision groups are 32-bit bitmasks (a.group & b.group != 0 to interact); explicit exclusions override.

    x_p: Transform, x_c: Transform, axis: Vec3) -> Result<JointId>;

begin_articulation is what splits joints into Featherstone’s “one workgroup per articulation” partitioning. The first add_joint_* opens articulation 0; further joints append until begin_articulation closes the chain.

Particles, springs, cables

pub fn add_particle(&mut self, position: Vec3, mass: Real, radius: Real,
    world: WorldId) -> u32;
pub fn pin_particle(&mut self, i: u32);              // mass → 0 = kinematic

pub fn add_distance_constraint(&mut self, a: u32, b: u32,
    rest_length: Real, compliance: Real, max_stretch: Real) -> usize;

// CABLE polyline = chain of distance constraints + bookkeeping

    max_stretch: Real) -> usize;

    particle_mass: Real, particle_radius: Real,

compliance is XPBD’s α = 1/stiffness in m/N; max_stretch is a hard cap on stretch ratio applied as a non-linear projection after the soft XPBD pass.

Cloth + tet meshes

Equality, mimic, muscle

    world: WorldId) -> usize;

    relative_rotation: Quat, world: WorldId) -> usize;

    poly: [Real; 5], world: WorldId) -> usize;

// Linear mimic (q_a = c0 + c1·q_b) — simpler API
pub fn add_mimic_constraint(&mut self, joint_a: JointId, joint_b: JointId,
    c0: Real, c1: Real, world: WorldId) -> usize;

// Hill-type muscle attached to a CABLE joint's linear DoF (Stage 42)
pub fn add_muscle(&mut self, joint: JointId,
    config: actuators::MuscleConfig) -> Result<usize>;

World + global knobs

pub fn set_world_gravity(&mut self, world: WorldId, gravity: Vec3);
pub fn set_angular_damping(&mut self, damping: Real);
