build() — finalise the model

pub fn build(self) -> Result<Model>;

build performs the heavy lifting that turns the host-side scratch into a sim-ready, GPU-uploadable Model:

  1. Closes the open articulation (begin_articulation semantics).
  2. Computes per-body inv_mass and inv_inertia (with the kinematic-body sentinel 0).
  3. Builds the spring graph colouring — greedy by particle adjacency, producing the spring_color_* CSR consumed by the XPBD GPU kernel.
  4. Builds the VBD per-vertex colouring + vertex_adjacent_springs CSR for VBD’s Jacobi sweeps.
  5. Builds per-vertex tet adjacency (vertex_adjacent_tets) + per-vertex cable-bending CSR.
  6. Computes per-tet Dm⁻¹ and rest_volume (pre-inverted at build so the VBD hot loop is branch-free).
  7. Computes joint coord / DoF CSR offsets (joint_coord_offset, joint_dof_offset).
  8. Registers soft surfaces (tet boundary tris + cloth tessellation tris) into the cross-mesh VT contact pipeline.
  9. Keeps registered triangle meshes as raw model data; geometry builds BVH/cache structures at collision or bake boundaries.
  10. Mirrors the host-side enum data into the GPU-friendly parallel arrays (shape_geom_kind / shape_geom_data).

After build, Model::upload_to_device(device, queue) is the one call that mirrors all the buffers into wgpu storage, ready for GPU-backed solvers and kernels.

Joints

A joint constrains the relative motion between two rigid bodies. molla inherits Newton’s joint taxonomy (xtra/newton/_src/sim/enums.py) and adds a single new entry — the Newton-style CABLE joint for stretchy ropes / muscle tendons (Stage 39E).

Joint-type taxonomy

JointTypeu32coordsDoFssemantics
Prismatic011translation along a fixed axis
Revolute111rotation about a fixed axis
Ball243spherical (3 angular DoF, quaternion coords)
Fixed300locks all 6 DoF
Free476unconstrained 6-DoF (xyz + quat)
Distance5766-DoF with anchor distance limit
D66766-DoF with per-axis lock / limit
Cable722linear stretch + isotropic bend

coord_count() is the number of entries the joint writes into State.joint_q; dof_count() is the matching length in State.joint_qd. They differ for joints whose orientation is parameterised by a quaternion (Ball, Free, Distance, D6) — joint_qd carries angular velocity in 3 components, not 4.

pub enum JointType { Prismatic, Revolute, Ball, Fixed, Free, Distance, D6, Cable }

impl JointType {
    pub fn coord_dof(self) -> (usize, usize);  // (coord_count, dof_count)
    pub fn coord_count(self) -> usize;
    pub fn dof_count(self)   -> usize;
}

The full taxonomy is laid out across four chapters:

  • Revolute / Prismatic / Fixed / Free
  • Ball / D6 / Distance
  • CABLE joint
  • Joint mimic

How DoFs map to joint_q / joint_qd

Model stores two CSR offset arrays that index into the flat State.joint_q / State.joint_qd slabs:

pub joint_coord_offset: Buffer<u32>,    // length joint_count + 1
pub joint_dof_offset:   Buffer<u32>,    // length joint_count + 1
pub joint_coord_total:  usize;
pub joint_dof_total:    usize;

Joint j owns coords joint_q[coord_offset[j] .. coord_offset[j+1]] and velocities joint_qd[dof_offset[j] .. dof_offset[j+1]]. The totals are the last entries of the offset arrays.

For a model that mixes joint types — say [Free, Revolute, Ball] — the layout is:

joint   type        coords (size)        DoFs (size)
─────── ─────────── ──────────────────── ─────────────────
0       Free        [0..7]   (7)         [0..6]   (6)
1       Revolute    [7..8]   (1)         [6..7]   (1)
2       Ball        [8..12]  (4)         [7..10]  (3)
─────── ─────────── ──────────────────── ─────────────────
total                        12                   10

Solvers read (coord_offset, dof_offset) once per joint and use the local sub-slice. The asymmetry (coords ≠ DoFs) only matters for the integrator and for differentiable-physics tape recording.

Targets and drives

Per-DoF drive policy lives in Control via the JointTargetMode enum:

pub enum JointTargetMode {
    None             = 0,    // passive — no drive torque
    Position         = 1,    // τ = kp·(q_target − q) + kd·(0 − qd)
    Velocity         = 2,    // τ = kd·(qd_target − qd)
    PositionVelocity = 3,    // PD around both
    Effort           = 4,    // τ = q_target  (direct torque)
}

The Featherstone backward pass featherstone.md folds the drive torque into the per-DoF u_k along with joint_force (feed-forward), joint_friction (Coulomb damping), and any muscle contribution; the result is then clamped by joint_effort_limit.

Limits, friction, effort, velocity

// On the Model, each is length joint_dof_total. NaN = unlimited.
pub joint_limit_lower:    Buffer<Real>,
pub joint_limit_upper:    Buffer<Real>,
pub joint_friction:       Buffer<Real>,   // Coulomb damping
pub joint_effort_limit:   Buffer<Real>,   // torque clamp
pub joint_velocity_limit: Buffer<Real>,   // post-step qd clamp
pub joint_target_ke:      Buffer<Real>,   // static joint-drive stiffness

D6 joints encode per-axis locks by setting lower == upper == 0 for the locked axes (no extra “locked” flag needed); the motion subspace builder drops those DoFs and the integrator skips them.

Articulations

A connected group of joints (one kinematic tree) is an articulation. The builder opens an articulation at the first add_joint_* after begin_articulation(); further joints append until the next begin_articulation(). The CSR

pub articulation_count: usize,
pub articulation_start: Buffer<u32>,    // length articulation_count + 1

records joint-index ranges. The Featherstone solver dispatches one workgroup per articulation, so two independent robots in the same Model run in parallel on GPU.

Equality constraints vs joints

A FIXED joint locks two bodies into one — it adds 0 DoFs to the simulation. An EqualityType::Weld does the same thing but as a post-step projective constraint rather than a structural part of the kinematic tree. The two are interchangeable in steady-state but differ during failure modes: a FIXED joint is rock-solid; a WELD has some compliance and shows up as 6 algebraic constraints in the XPBD equality solve.

Choose Fixed for permanent welds; choose Weld for closed loops (impossible to express as a tree) and for runtime-toggleable rigid links. See Joints — mimic for the polynomial JointMimic equality that closes 4-bar linkages.

Revolute / Prismatic / Fixed / Free

The four “primary” joint types are the workhorses of every articulated scene. Together they cover ~95 % of robotics use cases.

Revolute

JointType::Revolute = 1   // (1 coord, 1 dof)
b.add_joint_revolute(parent, child, x_p, x_c, axis: Vec3) -> Result<JointId>;

1-DoF rotation about a fixed joint-local axis. axis is in the joint’s local frame (x_p) and is normalised at build time — Error::Build fires on a near-zero or non-finite axis.

Joint-local transform:

J(q) = R(axis, q)   (pure rotation)
X_w_c = X_w_p · X_p · J(q) · X_c⁻¹

The motion subspace S is a single spatial-vector column:

S = (0, 0, 0; axis_x, axis_y, axis_z)   — axis is the angular row

Featherstone reads S from joint_axis, transforms it into the joint-world frame, and assembles the per-joint dynamics from there.

Typical use: hinges, motor joints, finger knuckles. The standard “manipulator” robot is N stacked revolutes.

let mut b = ModelBuilder::new();
let link = b.add_body(BodyParams::new());
b.add_joint_revolute(
    BodyId::NONE, link,
    Transform::IDENTITY,                                       // x_p: world frame
    Transform::from_translation(Vec3::new(0.0, 0.5, 0.0)),     // x_c: top of link
    Vec3::Z,                                                   // rotation axis
)?;

At q = 0, the pendulum hangs along -Y. At q = π/2, the right-hand rule curls −Y → +X, so the link points along +X.

Prismatic

JointType::Prismatic = 0   // (1 coord, 1 dof)
b.add_joint_prismatic(parent, child, x_p, x_c, axis: Vec3) -> Result<JointId>;

1-DoF translation along a joint-local axis. Same axis-validation as revolute. Joint-local transform:

J(q) = T(axis · q)         (pure translation)
S    = (axis_x, axis_y, axis_z; 0, 0, 0)   — axis is the linear row

Typical use: linear actuators, gripper finger sliders, rail joints.

Fixed

JointType::Fixed = 3   // (0 coords, 0 dofs)
b.add_joint_fixed(parent, child, x_p, x_c) -> Result<JointId>;

Locks all 6 relative DoFs. Writes J(q) = Identity and contributes no entries to joint_q / joint_qd. The Featherstone solver passes the joint through with zero acceleration.

Use Fixed when the child should rigidly track the parent and you want the solver to eliminate the DoF entirely rather than enforce a high-stiffness constraint each step. Two common patterns:

  • End-effector mount: bolt a sensor / camera shape to a rigid parent. The mount doesn’t move relative to the host, so a Fixed joint is faster than two bodies + a WELD equality.
  • Sub-body aggregation: procedural builders that split one rigid assembly into multiple component bodies use Fixed joints to glue them back together while preserving the visual hierarchy.

Free

JointType::Free = 4   // (7 coords, 6 dofs)
b.add_joint_free(parent, child, x_p, x_c) -> Result<JointId>;

Unconstrained 6-DoF “root joint” between a body and the world (or between two bodies, if you want a loose floater attached to a parent). Adds 7 coords [tx, ty, tz, qx, qy, qz, qw] and 6 DoFs [v_x, v_y, v_z, ω_x, ω_y, ω_z].

J(q) = T(t) · R(quat)
S    = (I_3, 0; 0, I_3)     — full 6-DoF motion subspace

Free joints are how molla represents a floating-base robot (a humanoid’s pelvis, a quadrotor’s body). The Featherstone ABA solves the full 6×6 articulated inertia at the root. A floating-base scene is just Free for the pelvis followed by Revolute / Ball joints for each limb.

Free vs add_body + Semi-Implicit: a free-floating rigid body that you’d otherwise integrate with SemiImplicitSolver becomes a Free-rooted articulation when you want to add downstream joints. The Free joint adds 6 DoFs to joint_qd; the body’s body_qd follows automatically. The two paths agree to roundoff for single-body scenes.

Quaternion housekeeping: the 7th coord qw is the scalar; the Featherstone integrator updates the quaternion via the small-rotation recipe q_new = normalize(q + 0.5·dt · (0, ω) · q), and re-normalises each step.

Comparison

RevolutePrismaticFixedFree
coord count1107
DoF count1106
GPU support✓✓✓✓
Joint drive (Control)✓✓—✓
Limits via set_joint_limits✓✓—per-axis
Procedural builder✓✓✓✓ (root)

See Multi-DoF joints for Ball, Distance, and D6, and Cable joint for the rope/tendon variant.

Ball / D6 / Distance

The three multi-DoF joint types are full reduced-coordinate citizens of Featherstone ABA: the same forward dynamics that drives a chain of revolutes handles a 3-DoF ball or a 6-DoF D6, with the motion subspace S growing to 3 or 6 columns and the per- joint D = Sᵀ I^A S matrix becoming 3×3 or 6×6.

Stage 17 introduced multi-DoF Featherstone; Stage 17.1 added the rigorous dense Cholesky D-solve for non-diagonal inertia (Free joints with COM offsets) and the velocity-level Lagrange multiplier for the distance constraint. Both are toggleable per-solver:

let solver = FeatherstoneSolver::new_cpu()
    .with_rigorous_d_solve(true)         // dense Cholesky on D
    .with_rigorous_distance(true);       // multiplier (vs hard clamp)

Ball joint

JointType::Ball = 2   // (4 coords, 3 dofs)
b.add_joint_ball(parent, child, x_p, x_c) -> Result<JointId>;

3-DoF spherical joint — pure rotation, no translation. Coords are a unit quaternion (qx, qy, qz, qw); DoFs are body-frame angular velocity (ω_x, ω_y, ω_z). Joint-local transform:

J(q) = R(quat(qx, qy, qz, qw))

Motion subspace (3 columns):

        ┌ 0  0  0 ┐                ex, ey, ez = the world-axis frame
S_ang = │ ex ey ez│                  expressed in joint-world (one
        └         ┘                  column per angular DoF)

Featherstone integrates the quaternion via the same small-rotation update as Free joints. Per-step quaternion re-normalisation keeps drift bounded.

Limits: per-DoF lower / upper bounds in joint_limit_lower / upper mean per-axis angle limits in the joint-local frame, applied as projective clamps after the integration step. Set them via set_joint_limits(joint, [lo_x, lo_y, lo_z], [hi_x, hi_y, hi_z]).

Use case: humanoid shoulders, hips, wrists; closed-chain robotic fingers. The Stage-17 humanoid demo uses Ball joints throughout the spine and limbs and a single Free joint at the pelvis.

let humerus  = b.add_body(...);
let shoulder = b.add_joint_ball(torso, humerus, x_p, x_c)?;
b.set_joint_limits(shoulder,
    &[-PI/2.0, -PI/3.0, -PI/4.0],
    &[ PI/2.0,  PI/3.0,  PI/4.0])?;

Distance joint

JointType::Distance = 5   // (7 coords, 6 dofs)
b.add_joint_distance(parent, child, x_p, x_c) -> Result<JointId>;

A 6-DoF “soft” pin between two anchor points with a [min_distance, max_distance] constraint. Storage matches Free (7 coords, 6 dofs) so the kinematics is identical; the limit is what makes it a distance joint.

Limits live in the first per-DoF slot pair:

b.set_joint_limits(j, &[min_dist, ...], &[max_dist, ...])?;
//                     │                  │
//                     └──────────────────┴── first slot = anchor distance

The other 5 slots are normally unlimited (NaN).

The Stage-17.1 polish replaced the original “hard-clamp” projection (p ← p · L_target / ‖p‖ plus radial-velocity zeroing) with a velocity-level Lagrange multiplier that satisfies the constraint exactly to within solver tolerance. The hard clamp remains as a fallback when the multiplier is numerically degenerate (collinear anchors). The behaviour is toggleable via with_rigorous_distance(bool) for A/B parity testing.

Use case: rope-like rigid links (a ball on a string with a rigid-body ball), suspension bridge segments. For elastic ropes use CABLE joints or distance constraints between particles.

D6 joint

JointType::D6 = 6   // (7 coords, 6 dofs)
b.add_joint_d6(parent, child, x_p, x_c) -> Result<JointId>;

The “Swiss army knife” 6-DoF joint with per-axis lock / limit. Coord layout matches Free / Distance ([tx, ty, tz, qx, qy, qz, qw]). A locked DoF is encoded by setting lower == upper == 0 in the per-DoF limit arrays — no separate “lock” flag is needed.

                  lower  upper       state
                  ─────  ─────       ─────
locked       :     0      0          DoF disabled (S column = 0)
unlimited    :    NaN    NaN         free motion
soft-limited :   -π/4    π/4         clamp + spring restoring force

The motion-subspace builder reads the limit pair and produces an effective DoF count ≤ 6. Locked DoFs are not integrated and don’t contribute to the per-joint D matrix.

D6 covers every joint pattern you’d otherwise need a fixed library for:

locked axesunlocked axesequivalent
Revolute (Z)tx, ty, tz, ωx, ωyωzadd_joint_revolute
Prismatic (X)ty, tz, ωx, ωy, ωztxadd_joint_prismatic
Universaltx, ty, tz, ωzωx, ωy(no dedicated type)
Cylindricaltx, ty, ωy, ωztz, ωx(no dedicated type)
Planartz, ωx, ωytx, ty, ωz(no dedicated type)

The Stage-17 multi-DoF Featherstone runs the same Cholesky on the effective D matrix regardless of how many axes are locked. The dedicated Revolute / Prismatic types remain in the API for clarity, but mechanically D6 covers them.

Reduced-coordinate dynamics — what changed at Stage 17

In Stage 17 the Featherstone backward pass was generalised from a 1-DoF rank-1 deflation to a per-DoF column rank-1 deflation:

For each DoF column S_k of the joint:
    U_k  = I^A · S_k
    D_k  = S_kᵀ · U_k                  (scalar)
    I^A := I^A − U_k U_kᵀ / D_k       (deflation)

After processing all DoFs of a joint, I^A is propagated to the parent. The forward pass then solves per-DoF q̈_k = (u_k − U_kᵀ · a_p) / D_k.

This sequential rank-1 path is exact when D = Sᵀ I^A S is diagonal, which is the case for Ball, Revolute, decoupled Free (no COM offset), and D6 with axis-aligned locks. For asymmetric Free joints — where the COM offset couples linear and angular DoFs — the off-diagonal entries of D matter; the Stage 17.1 with_rigorous_d_solve(true) path builds the full D matrix and solves D · q̈ = u_τ via dense Cholesky.

The two paths agree to roundoff on diagonal-D joints (Ball, Revolute, Prismatic, Fixed, Distance with aligned anchors); they differ only when D is non-diagonal.

CABLE joint

JointType::Cable is molla’s 2-DoF Newton-style rope joint, introduced in Stage 39E. It models a short tendon / rope segment between two rigid bodies with a linear stretch DoF along one axis and an isotropic bend DoF about a perpendicular axis. The two combine into a spring + damper torque pair that the Featherstone solver integrates as a regular reduced-coordinate joint.

DoF layout

JointType::Cable = 7        // (2 coords, 2 dofs)

joint_q[coord_offset[j] + 0]  = q_l   (linear stretch, m)
joint_q[coord_offset[j] + 1]  = q_b   (bend angle, rad)

joint_qd[dof_offset[j] + 0]   = q̇_l  (stretch velocity, m/s)
joint_qd[dof_offset[j] + 1]   = q̇_b  (bend angular velocity, rad/s)

The cable’s local transform is translate-then-rotate along the joint-local frame:

J(q) = T(q_l · ẑ) · R(q_b, x̂)

Convention:

  • Cable axis = joint-local +z (the rope direction at rest).
  • Bend axis = joint-local +x (the perpendicular bend axis).

The bend is isotropic (the choice of +x is deterministic but arbitrary — any rotation about a fixed perpendicular axis captures the curvature DoF in 1D).

Motion subspace

Two columns:

S_l = (z_world_x, z_world_y, z_world_z; 0, 0, 0)         (linear)
S_b = (0, 0, 0; x_world_x, x_world_y, x_world_z)         (angular)

z_world and x_world are the joint-local +z / +x expressed in world axes, computed via the parent’s world pose + the joint’s parent-frame transform.

Spring + damper dynamics

The cable joint differs from the other joint types in that it carries built-in restoring forces via per-joint static parameters stored on the Model:

pub joint_cable_stiffness_linear: Buffer<Real>,   // k_l (N/m)
pub joint_cable_stiffness_bend:   Buffer<Real>,   // k_b (N·m/rad)
pub joint_cable_damping_linear:   Buffer<Real>,   // c_l (N·s/m)
pub joint_cable_damping_bend:     Buffer<Real>,   // c_b (N·m·s/rad)

The Featherstone backward pass folds an extra term into the per-DoF generalised force:

τ_l = − k_l · q_l   − c_l · q̇_l            (stretch)
τ_b = − k_b · q_b   − c_b · q̇_b            (bend)

Combined with the standard Featherstone PD drive (if a JointTargetMode is active), feed-forward joint_force, and Coulomb joint friction, the full effort vector at the DoF is

u_k = τ_drive_k + τ_ff_k + τ_friction_k + τ_cable_k − c_damping · qd_k

then clamped by joint_effort_limit.

API

pub fn add_joint_cable(
    &mut self,
    parent: BodyId, child: BodyId,
    x_p: Transform,
    x_c: Transform,
    stiffness_linear: Real,    // k_l (N/m)
    stiffness_bend:   Real,    // k_b (N·m/rad)
    damping_linear:   Real,    // c_l (N·s/m)
    damping_bend:     Real,    // c_b (N·m·s/rad)
) -> Result<JointId>;

All four parameters must be finite and ≥ 0 — Error::Build fires otherwise.

let tendon = b.add_joint_cable(
    bone_a, bone_b,
    x_p, x_c,
    /* k_l */ 1.0e4,     // stiff axial spring
    /* k_b */ 0.5,       // soft bend
    /* c_l */ 50.0,
    /* c_b */ 0.05,
)?;

Use cases

  • Tendons / muscles. The Hill-type muscle actuator (Stage 42) attaches to a CABLE joint’s linear stretch DoF via b.add_muscle(joint, MuscleConfig{ … }). The muscle’s active contractile force f = a · f_max · f_L · f_V is added as a torque on q_l, pulling the cable shorter. See muscle actuator.
  • Rope segments connecting rigid pulleys. Each CABLE joint is one pulley-to-pulley segment; the spring + damper handle rope elasticity.
  • Soft skeletal links (e.g. cervical spine articulation in a biomechanical model). Multiple CABLE joints chained between vertebrae produce a smooth elastic curve.

Comparison: CABLE joint vs cable polyline

molla ships two cable primitives that look superficially similar but live at different layers:

CABLE joint (JointType::Cable)Cable polyline (ModelBuilder::add_cable)
Backing storageFeatherstone joint (2 DoFs)Chain of XPBD distance constraints between particles
SolverFeatherstone ABAVBD or XPBD
GeometryOne rigid segment (parent ↔ child)Polyline of N particles
Elastic modelPer-segment k + damperPer-segment XPBD compliance + bending hinge energy
Use caseRobotics tendons, biomechanical musclesSoft ropes, hair, fishing lines
BendingIsotropic, 1-DoFDiscrete hinge energy E_b = ½·k_b·(2 sin θ/2)²
Muscle attachYes (add_muscle)No (muscles drive a joint DoF)

The CABLE joint is the rigid-body, reduced-coordinate primitive; the cable polyline is the particle-based, position-projection primitive. Pick the former for muscle-driven biomechanics; pick the latter for visually-rich rope simulation. Stage 39E originated as part of the muscle deliverable so the muscle force has a “joint DoF to drive”; the polyline primitive predates it (Stage 20.1) and remains the canonical path for soft ropes.

Joint mimic

A mimic constraint couples two joint coordinates so the driven joint follows a function of the driver joint. molla ships two flavours:

  • Linear mimic — q_a = c0 + c1·q_b. Stored on Model.mimic_*. Simple two-parameter API for the common case (gripper finger pair, geared joint, scissor mechanism).
  • Polynomial mimic (Stage 32) — q_a = poly[0] + poly[1]·q_b + poly[2]·q_b² + … + poly[4]·q_b⁴. Encoded as EqualityType::JointMimic. Covers Newton’s JOINT equality type and the closed-loop kinematics it enables.

Both implementations run as post-step projective updates: after the Featherstone (or XPBD-rigid) integrator finishes a step, the mimic pass overwrites joint_q[driven] to satisfy the coupling. The driver’s velocity propagates by a Jacobian product the next step.

Linear mimic API

pub fn add_mimic_constraint(
    &mut self,
    joint_a: JointId,   // the driven joint (q_a is overwritten)
    joint_b: JointId,   // the driver joint (q_b is read)
    c0: Real,           // constant offset
    c1: Real,           // linear coefficient
    world: WorldId,
) -> usize;

Storage on Model:

pub mimic_count: usize,
pub mimic_joint_a: Buffer<i32>,
pub mimic_joint_b: Buffer<i32>,
pub mimic_c0:      Buffer<Real>,
pub mimic_c1:      Buffer<Real>,
pub mimic_enabled: Buffer<u32>,
pub mimic_constraint_world: Buffer<i32>,

Use cases:

  • Gripper finger pair (Robotiq 2-finger): one motor drives both fingers symmetrically. q_finger_b = q_finger_a → c0 = 0, c1 = 1.
  • Antagonist coupling: q_b = −q_a for opposing axes.
  • Constant offset stage: q_b = q_a + π/4 for a fixed-phase scissor cut.

Polynomial joint-mimic (Stage 32)

The quartic mimic is the polynomial extension that closes kinematic loops — the canonical example being a 4-bar linkage, where the “return” link’s angle is a non-linear function of the input link’s angle.

pub fn add_equality_joint_mimic(
    &mut self,
    driver: JointId,
    driven: JointId,
    poly: [Real; 5],    // [a0, a1, a2, a3, a4]
    world: WorldId,
) -> usize;

The polynomial:

q_driven = poly[0] + poly[1]·q_driver + poly[2]·q_driver²
                   + poly[3]·q_driver³ + poly[4]·q_driver⁴

Storage piggy-backs on the equality-constraint arrays via the EqualityType::JointMimic variant:

pub equality_count: usize,
pub equality_type: Buffer<u32>,                         // == 2 (JointMimic)
pub equality_mimic_driver_joint: Buffer<i32>,           // (-1 if not mimic)
pub equality_mimic_driven_joint: Buffer<i32>,
pub equality_mimic_poly:        Buffer<Real>,           // length 5 · equality_count

The equality_type slot discriminates which entries are “real” positional equalities vs joint-mimic entries; the post-step pass reads equality_mimic_* only when equality_type == JointMimic.

Why 4th-order?

Newton’s JOINT equality defines mimic via a polynomial up to q⁴. molla keeps the same native polynomial form because it is compact, GPU-friendly, and covers common gear/linkage relationships. Anything beyond quartic typically signals a kinematic problem better expressed as two independent joints + a position equality.

Examples

Use casepoly coefficients
Linear mimic with bias c0 + c1·q[c0, c1, 0, 0, 0]
Pure linear q_b = q_a[0, 1, 0, 0, 0]
Negated q_b = -q_a + π[π, -1, 0, 0, 0]
4-bar linkage (quadratic approx)[0, 1.0, -0.05, 0, 0]
Gear ratio 2:1[0, 2.0, 0, 0, 0]

For the 4-bar specifically, the exact transmission is transcendental; the quartic least-squares fit over the working range is usually accurate to <1 % positional error and Featherstone’s stiff regime absorbs the residual.

Stage 32 algorithm

The mimic projection runs after the Featherstone (or XPBD-rigid) substep:

for each mimic equality e:
    if not equality_enabled[e]: continue
    if equality_type[e] != JointMimic: continue
    j_driver = equality_mimic_driver_joint[e]
    j_driven = equality_mimic_driven_joint[e]
    q_drv = joint_q[coord_offset[j_driver]]
    q_target = poly[0] + poly[1]·q_drv + poly[2]·q_drv²
             + poly[3]·q_drv³ + poly[4]·q_drv⁴
    joint_q[coord_offset[j_driven]] = q_target
    # Velocity is the polynomial derivative · q̇_driver
    dpoly = poly[1] + 2·poly[2]·q_drv + 3·poly[3]·q_drv²
          + 4·poly[4]·q_drv³
    joint_qd[dof_offset[j_driven]] = dpoly · joint_qd[dof_offset[j_driver]]

The velocity propagation matches the chain rule so kinetic energy inside the kinematic loop is conserved to first order.

When to choose mimic vs gear / equality

Linear mimicPolynomial mimicGear (effort)Equality (CONNECT)
Closed kinematic loop✓✓✓ (positional)
Non-linear relation✓
Native serialization✓✓✓
Hard constraint✓ (projection)✓ (projection)XPBD-soft
Driver chooses force✓

For a 4-bar linkage, add_equality_joint_mimic is the right answer. For a Robotiq 2-finger gripper, add_mimic_constraint is enough. For an under-actuated tendon-driven hand, use a CABLE joint or model the tendon explicitly as particles.

Articulation (Featherstone ABA)

FeatherstoneSolver is molla’s full Articulated Body Algorithm (ABA) per Featherstone (2008) ch. 7 — the reduced-coordinate forward dynamics solver of choice for serial chains and trees of revolute / prismatic / ball / free / D6 / distance / cable joints.

It is a direct port of the structure in Newton’s solvers/featherstone/kernels.py, with spatial-vector primitives borrowed from Warp’s _src/math.py / builtins.py. The CPU path is the reference oracle; the GPU path (WGSL kernel featherstone.wgsl) implements the identical three-pass algorithm one workgroup per articulation.

use molla::solvers::{FeatherstoneSolver, Solver};

let mut solver = FeatherstoneSolver::new_cpu()        // or new_gpu(engine, &model)
    .with_substeps(4)
    .with_damping(0.05)
    .with_rigorous_d_solve(true)                       // dense Chol on D
    .with_rigorous_distance(true);                     // multiplier on Distance

solver.step(&model, &state_in, &control, &contacts, dt, &mut state_out)?;

The three passes

Each substep walks the articulation three times. Notation: S_ik = the k-th column of joint i’s motion subspace (in world frame), v_i, a_i = body spatial velocity / acceleration, I^A_i = articulated body inertia, p^A_i = articulated bias force, c_i = Coriolis term, f_grav_i = gravity bias.

Pass 1 — forward kinematics + body kinematics (root → leaf)

For each joint in declaration order:

1. Compute child world pose from parent + joint's local transform.
2. Build the world-frame motion subspace S_i (1, 2, 3, or 6 columns).
3. Body spatial velocity:        v_i = v_p + Σ_k S_ik · q̇_ik
4. Coriolis term:                c_i = v_i × (Σ_k S_ik · q̇_ik)
5. Body spatial inertia (world): I_i (transform body-frame Mat3 + mass)
6. Bias force:                   p^A_i = v_i ×* (I_i · v_i) − f_grav_i

The × and ×* are Featherstone’s spatial cross-product operators (see Spatial algebra).

Pass 2 — articulated inertia accumulation (leaf → root)

For each joint, processed in reverse declaration order:

For each DoF column S_k of joint i:
    U_k  = I^A_i · S_k
    D_k  = S_kᵀ · U_k
    u_k  = τ_drive_k + τ_ff_k + τ_friction_k + τ_cable_k − d · q̇_k
                                                          [− muscle_k]
    u_k -= S_kᵀ · p^A_i

    # Sequential rank-1 deflation (default path):
    I^A_i := I^A_i − U_k U_kᵀ / D_k
    p^A_i := p^A_i + U_k · u_k / D_k

# Propagate to parent in parent frame:
I^A_p += transform(I^A_i)
p^A_p += transform(p^A_i)

The sequential rank-1 deflation is exact when the per-joint matrix D = Sᵀ I^A S is diagonal, which covers Revolute, Prismatic, Ball, decoupled Free (no COM offset), Distance, and D6 with axis-aligned locks. For asymmetric Free joints where the COM offset cross-couples linear and angular DoFs the off-diagonal entries of D matter — the Stage 17.1 polish path (with_rigorous_d_solve(true)) builds the full D matrix and D · q̈ = u_τ is solved via dense Cholesky.

Pass 3 — forward acceleration solve (root → leaf)

For each joint i:
    For each DoF column S_k:
        q̈_k = (u_k − U_kᵀ · a_p) / D_k
    a_i = a_p + Σ_k S_k · q̈_k + c_i

Pass 4 — symplectic integration

q̇_new = q̇_old + dt · q̈
q_new  = q_old + dt · q̇_new        (or quaternion update for Ball/Free)

Symplectic (not just plain forward) Euler — the velocity is updated before the position, so energy drift is bounded for a wide range of dt.

Pass 5 — refresh body poses

After integration, a final FK pass writes state_out.body_q from the new joint_q so downstream consumers (sensors, contact pipeline, viewer) see consistent body world transforms.

Multi-DoF joint support (Stage 17)

joint type   coords  dofs    motion subspace S
─────────── ──────  ────    ───────────────────────────────
Revolute      1      1       (0; axis_w)
Prismatic     1      1       (axis_w; 0)
Fixed         0      0       — (skipped)
Ball          4      3       (0; ex_w, ey_w, ez_w)
Free          7      6       (I_3, 0; 0, I_3)
Distance      7      6       same as Free (limit applied post-step)
D6            7      6       same as Free, locked columns zeroed
Cable         2      2       (z_w; 0), (0; x_w)

The Stage 17 work generalised the backward pass from a 1-DoF rank-1 update to a per-DoF column rank-1 deflation — the same algorithm sequence, just looped over dof_count(joint) columns. Stage 17.1 added the rigorous dense-D solve for the asymmetric Free case (with_rigorous_d_solve) and the velocity-level Lagrange multiplier for the Distance constraint (with_rigorous_distance).

Joint drives, limits, friction

Each per-DoF u_k (the right-hand side of the backward pass) is the sum of:

u_k = τ_drive_k + τ_ff_k + τ_friction_k + τ_cable_k + τ_muscle_k
                                                  − d · q̇_k
  • τ_drive_k — from Control.joint_target_mode:
    • Position → kp·(q_target − q) + kd·(0 − qd)
    • Velocity → kd·(qd_target − qd)
    • PositionVelocity → kp·(q_target − q) + kd·(qd_target − qd)
    • Effort → q_target (interpreted as direct torque)
  • τ_ff_k — Control.joint_force[k] (feed-forward).
  • τ_friction_k = −Model.joint_friction[k] · q̇_k — Coulomb damping.
  • τ_cable_k = −k_l q_l − c_l q̇_l / −k_b q_b − c_b q̇_b for cable joints.
  • τ_muscle_k — Hill-type muscle force on a CABLE linear DoF (Stage 42; pre-computed by the muscle kernel into a per-DoF accumulator).
  • d · q̇_k — uniform solver.joint_damping.

After u_k is assembled, effort clamping applies:

u_k := clamp(u_k, −effort_limit_k, +effort_limit_k)    (NaN limit = unlimited)

After integration, velocity clamping applies:

qd_k := clamp(qd_k, −velocity_limit_k, +velocity_limit_k)

Joint position limits are not enforced inside Featherstone; the caller is expected to either:

  1. Use XPBD for the rigid-body solve and let it project joint limits, or
  2. Use the post-step joint_limit_lower / upper clamp pass in the viewer / wrapper layer, or
  3. Rely on a high joint_target_ke joint-drive stiffness to act as a soft limit barrier.

Substepping

let solver = FeatherstoneSolver::new_cpu().with_substeps(4);

Each outer step(dt) advances n inner substeps of dt/n, with the contact set (rare in Featherstone — typically empty) reused. The implementation ping-pongs state_out with a host-side scratch state to avoid intermediate allocations.

For most articulation workloads substeps = 1 is fine — Featherstone is second-order accurate and stable at large dt. Increase substepping when:

  • A joint hits its effort limit and the limit clamp introduces high-frequency content.
  • A Distance-joint constraint produces stiff oscillation at the multiplier-update frequency.
  • Coupling with an XPBD contact pass that runs at higher rate.

GPU port

The WGSL kernel featherstone.wgsl implements all three passes inline per workgroup (one workgroup = one articulation). Spatial-vector and spatial-matrix operations live as inline helpers using vec4<f32> and mat3x3<f32>. The kernel reads:

  • Model.joint_*, Model.body_*, Model.gravity, Model.articulation_start
  • State.joint_q, State.joint_qd, State.body_q, State.body_qd
  • Control.joint_target_mode/pos/vel/kp/kd/force, Control.body_external_f
  • Optional muscle torque buffer (Stage 42 GPU port — see muscle)

and writes the next-step joint_q, joint_qd, body_q, body_qd into state_out. The CPU and GPU paths agree to roundoff on every joint type — verified by the parity tests in tests/featherstone_gpu_parity*.rs.

The Stage 42 v3 GPU path also runs a muscle kernel pre-pass (MuscleKernel::dispatch_torque_sum) that fills a per-DoF muscle torque buffer from current activations; Featherstone reads from it in pass 2.

Differentiable Featherstone

Stage 23.1 added a forward-mode tape recorder that captures each step’s (q, q̇, τ) inputs:

solver.step_with_tape(&model, &state_in, &control, &contacts, dt, &mut state_out,
    &mut tape, &chain, q_id, qd_id, tau_id)?;

The reverse pass walks the tape backwards via FeatherstoneRevoluteChain::reverse to compute dJ/dq, dJ/dq̇, dJ/dτ. v1 supports serial revolute chains only — multi-DoF joints are gated behind the differentiability follow-up. See Featherstone adjoint for the full adjoint chapter.

Forward kinematics shortcut

When you only need world poses (not forward dynamics) — IK targets, contact-pipeline setup, sensor placement — call crate::sim::eval_fk directly:

use molla::sim::eval_fk;
eval_fk(&model, &mut state)?;       // writes body_q from joint_q

eval_fk is the pose-only kinematics subset of Featherstone’s pass 1 — no velocities, no inertia, no dynamics. Multi-branch trees work as long as joints are listed in topological order (parent-before-child), which is what ModelBuilder produces by construction.

CRBA / RNEA / Jacobian

Three standalone spatial-algebra primitives complement Featherstone for analytical control + planning work. They share the same world-origin spatial-vector convention and the same joint / articulation indexing, so the three compose trivially.

primitiveoutputalgorithmCPUGPU
crba::mass_matrixM(q), N×N joint-space mass matrixcomposite-rigid-body, Featherstone (2008) §6.3✓Stage 16
rnea::inverse_dynamicsτ for given (q, q̇, q̈)recursive Newton-Euler, Featherstone §5✓Stage 16
jacobian::jacobianJ(q), 6 × N body-point Jacobianper-DoF spatial column✓(CPU-only)

CRBA — joint-space mass matrix M(q)

pub fn mass_matrix(model: &Model, state: &State, articulation: usize)
    -> Result<Vec<Real>>;

Returns a flat N² row-major array (M[i,j] = out[i*N + j]) where N is the articulation’s total joint DoFs (counted via joint_dof_offset). For the implicit “single articulation = all joints” case, pass articulation = 0 regardless of Model.articulation_count.

M(q) is symmetric positive definite and is the matrix that satisfies

τ = M(q) · q̈ + C(q, q̇) + G(q)

where C is the Coriolis / centrifugal vector and G is gravity. The two share a closed-form decomposition: RNEA(q, q̇, q̈=0) returns C + G, so M · q̈ = τ − RNEA(q, q̇, 0) is the inverse-dynamics recipe for forward dynamics — useful as a sanity check vs Featherstone.

Algorithm

Three passes over the articulation:

  1. FK + per-body world-frame spatial inertia. Same as Featherstone pass 1, minus the dynamics terms.
  2. Leaf-to-root composite inertia. I^c_i = I_i + Σ I^c_j over child joints j.
  3. Per-joint column build. For joint i:
    • F = I^c_i · S_i (spatial force = composite inertia · subspace)
    • M[i, i] = S_iᵀ · F
    • Walk parent chain: M[i, p] = M[p, i] = S_pᵀ · F

Single-articulation; multi-DoF joints (Ball / Free / D6) are TODO for CRBA in v1 — the per-DoF axis split mirrors RNEA’s and lands together with the multi-DoF RNEA port.

RNEA — recursive Newton-Euler inverse dynamics

pub fn inverse_dynamics(model: &Model, state: &State,
    articulation: usize, qdd: &[Real]) -> Result<Vec<Real>>;

Given (q, q̇, q̈) returns the joint forces τ that would produce the requested accelerations. Two passes per articulation:

  1. Forward (root → leaf):

    v_i = v_p + S_i · q̇_i
a_i = a_p + S_i · q̈_i + v_i × (S_i · q̇_i)
f_i = I_i · a_i + v_i ×* (I_i · v_i)

  2. Backward (leaf → root):

    τ_i = S_iᵀ · f_i
f_p += f_i           (transferred via parent-child cross terms)

Gravity is folded into the base acceleration: a_root = −g, so every gravity-affected body sees an effective acceleration of −g relative to free-fall. Matches Featherstone §5 and Newton’s eval_rigid_id kernel.

Single-articulation, single-DoF joints (Revolute / Prismatic / Fixed) in v1. Multi-DoF joints return Err(Build) so callers fall back to Featherstone for forward dynamics or do a DoF expansion themselves.

Jacobian — 6 × N body-point Jacobian

pub fn jacobian(model: &Model, state: &State,
    articulation: usize, target_body: usize, point_local: Vec3)
    -> Result<Vec<Real>>;

For a serial chain:

v_target = J(q) · q̇

where J is 6 × N and v_target = (v_linear; ω) is the spatial velocity at point_local (in the target body’s frame), expressed in world axes. Layout is row-major: row r ∈ [0, 5], column k ∈ [0, N) gives the spatial-velocity contribution from joint DoF k. Columns for non-ancestor joints are zero.

This is the primary input to IK, operational-space control, and impedance regulation. The implementation walks the parent-of-target chain to mark ancestor joints, then builds each ancestor’s spatial column via math::spatial_jacobian_column:

For each ancestor joint k:
    parent_w = body_q[parent_of(k)]
    joint_w  = parent_w · joint_x_p[k]
    axis_w   = joint_w · joint_axis[k]
    r_world  = target_world − joint_w.origin
    col[k]   = spatial_jacobian_column(jt, axis_w, r_world)

For revolute: (axis_w × r_world; axis_w). For prismatic: (axis_w; 0). Multi-DoF joints (Ball, D6, Free) write 3 / 6 columns following the joint’s motion-subspace layout.

The Jacobian stays on CPU in v1; no consumer needs the GPU port yet (IK runs on CPU, operational-space control hasn’t been profiled under GPU load).

CPU + GPU kernel split (Stage 16)

Stage 16 split CRBA + RNEA into matched CPU oracles and GPU kernels:

kernelshaderpurpose
CrbaKernelcrba.wgslper-articulation M(q) build
RneaKernelrnea.wgslper-articulation τ(q, q̇, q̈)
JacobianKerneljacobian.wgslper-(articulation, target) J(q) (planned)

The kernel layout mirrors Featherstone’s: one workgroup per articulation, parallel passes over joints within the articulation where the algorithm allows (composite-inertia and force-propagation passes are serial by data dependency, but the per-joint column build in CRBA is embarrassingly parallel).

Parity tests in tests/spatial_kernels_*.rs exercise CPU and GPU paths against analytically derived M, τ, J for a hand-rolled double-pendulum + a 7-DoF KUKA-style arm.

Composition example — forward dynamics from M and τ_bias

use molla::solvers::{mass_matrix, inverse_dynamics};
use molla::math::dense_solve::dense_chol_solve;

let q  = state.joint_q.host()?;
let qd = state.joint_qd.host()?;

// Coriolis + gravity bias: τ_bias = RNEA(q, q̇, q̈ = 0)
let qdd_zero = vec![0.0; n_dof];
let tau_bias = inverse_dynamics(&model, &state, 0, &qdd_zero)?;

// Mass matrix
let m = mass_matrix(&model, &state, 0)?;

// τ_applied - τ_bias = M · q̈   →   q̈ = M⁻¹ · (τ_applied − τ_bias)
let mut rhs: Vec<f64> = tau_applied.iter().zip(&tau_bias).map(|(a, b)| a - b).collect();
let qdd = dense_chol_solve(&mut m.clone(), &rhs, n_dof)?;

This is the analytical recipe Featherstone implements directly (and more efficiently — Featherstone’s three passes are O(n) while M is O(n²) to assemble and O(n³) to invert). The composition is useful when you need the explicit M for IK damping, projection, or impedance control.

Inverse kinematics

IkSolver is molla’s analytical IK — a damped least-squares Levenberg-Marquardt solver with a L-BFGS quasi-Newton fallback, multiple position / orientation / joint-limit objectives, robust-loss support (Stage 24b), and a multi-seed batched GPU path (Stage 24a).

It runs entirely on top of crate::solvers::jacobian and crate::sim::eval_fk — no Featherstone dynamics, no contact solve. The same routine that captures world poses for the dynamics also captures world poses for the IK gradient.

use molla::solvers::{IkSolver, IkConfig, IkObjective};
use molla::math::robust_loss::RobustLoss;

let objectives = vec![
    IkObjective::Position {
        body: ee_body, point_local: Vec3::ZERO,
        target_world: Vec3::new(0.5, 0.3, 0.2),
        weight: 1.0,
    },
];

let ik = IkSolver::new(objectives)
    .with_config(IkConfig {
        max_iter: 100,
        residual_tol: 1.0e-4,
        step_tol: 1.0e-9,
        damping_init: 1.0e-3,
        damping_grow: 4.0,
        damping_shrink: 4.0,
        articulation: 0,
        loss: RobustLoss::L2,
    });

let result = ik.solve(&model, &mut state, &seed_q)?;
println!("converged in {} iters, residual = {}", result.iters, result.residual);

Objectives

pub enum IkObjective {
    /// Drive `body`'s `point_local` to `target_world` (3 residual rows).
    Position {
        body: usize, point_local: Vec3,
        target_world: Vec3, weight: Real,
    },
    /// Drive a relative orientation residual `2 · sin(θ/2)` style
    /// (imaginary part of `q_target · q_current⁻¹`).
    Rotation {
        body: usize, target: Quat, weight: Real,
    },
    /// Soft penalty when `q[dof]` exceeds `[lo, hi]` (1 residual row).
    JointLimit { dof: usize, lo: Real, hi: Real, weight: Real },
}

Multiple objectives stack into a single residual vector e and a combined Jacobian J. The LM step solves

(JᵀJ + λI) · dq = − Jᵀ e

with λ adapted per iteration (doubled on rejected steps, halved on accepted). The orientation residual uses the imaginary part of the delta quaternion so the gradient is well-defined through the antipodal identity q ≡ −q.

Robust losses (Stage 24b)

The default RobustLoss::L2 is the standard L2 normal-equations solve. The other losses run iteratively re-weighted least squares (IRLS): at each iteration the per-residual weight w_i = ρ'(r_i)/r_i is folded in as (JᵀWJ + λI) · dq = −JᵀWe.

losscharacteruse case
L2quadratic everywhereclean targets
Huberquadratic near 0, linear past δmildly noisy targets
Cauchylog barrier, bounded influencestrong outliers (drag from sensor)
Tukeyre-descending, rejects outliers past thresholdaggressive outlier reject

Solver health: Cholesky vs PSD pseudo-inverse

The Stage 24a robustness pass added a PSD pseudo-inverse fallback to the normal-equations solver. The primary path is dense Cholesky on JᵀJ + λI; on rare numerical failure (the matrix has a non-SPD pivot due to underflow / near-singularity at the workspace boundary) the solver falls back to a damped pseudoinverse computed from the symmetric eigendecomposition of JᵀJ + λI. Two atomic counters track the rates:

pub static IK_CHOL_ATTEMPTS:  AtomicUsize;
pub static IK_PSD_FALLBACKS:  AtomicUsize;

pub fn ik_solver_health() -> (usize, usize);

In well-conditioned scenes the fallback rate stays below 0.1 % — the counters are observability for catching pathological JᵀJ configurations (e.g. a wrist-singularity where two axes align).

Multi-seed sampling

When the cost landscape has local minima (long chains, tight orientation, mixed position + rotation objectives), the user can sweep multiple seeds and take the best:

pub fn solve_with_seeds(
    &self, model: &Model, state: &mut State, seeds: &[Vec<Real>],
) -> Result<IkResult>;

Returns the lowest-residual seed (early exits on the first converged seed). 5–10 random seeds are typically enough to escape local minima on a 7-DoF arm.

GPU batched IK (Stage 24a)

For RL workloads that need to solve the same objective from many seeds in parallel, the GPU path batches one LM solve per seed in a single workgroup grid:

#[cfg(feature = "gpu")]
pub fn solve_gpu(
    &self, engine: &Engine, model: &Model, state: &mut State,
    q0: &[Real],
) -> Result<IkResult>;

#[cfg(feature = "gpu")]
pub fn solve_gpu_with_seeds(
    &self, engine: &Engine, model: &Model, state: &mut State,
    seeds: &[Vec<Real>],
) -> Result<IkResult>;

Each seed gets its own LM trajectory; the kernel runs FK, Jacobian assembly, residual evaluation, and the Cholesky solve per workgroup in lockstep. The Cholesky fallback to PSD-pinv lives inside the kernel — same fallback counter is incremented per failed seed.

Typical perf: ~ 4× speedup for 32 parallel seeds on a 7-DoF arm (dev laptop, RTX-class GPU). The fixed overhead of dispatching one workgroup makes the GPU path slower below ~ 8 parallel seeds.

L-BFGS fallback

When LM stalls (rejected steps fail to reduce residual past a threshold), the solver switches to a L-BFGS quasi-Newton inner loop on the same residual cost. L-BFGS doesn’t need the JᵀJ build, so it’s robust to rank-deficient Jacobians at singularities, at the cost of slower asymptotic convergence (linear vs LM’s superlinear).

The switch is automatic — IkResult.iters counts the combined LM + L-BFGS iterations, IkResult.converged reflects the residual tolerance from IkConfig.residual_tol.

When to choose IK vs RL / trajectory optimisation

IkSolverRLTrajectory opt
Single pose target✓✗✗
Whole-arm path✗✓✓
Closed-form fast✓✗✗
Handles contact / dynamics✗✓✓
Differentiable through trajectory✗✗✓

IK gives you a q for a target. To turn that q into a motor command for a real robot, feed it as a JointTargetMode::Position target to Featherstone with appropriate PD gains. To find a trajectory that threads a sequence of IK targets, use the differentiable Featherstone adjoint (Stage 23.1) — see Featherstone adjoint.

Solvers overview

molla ships seven time-integration solvers, all implementing the common Solver trait so callers can swap integrators without rewiring the host loop:

pub trait Solver: Send + Sync {
    fn step(
        &mut self,
        model: &Model,
        state_in: &State,
        control: &Control,
        contacts: &Contacts,
        dt: Real,
        state_out: &mut State,
    ) -> Result<()>;
}

The choice of solver is driven by the simulation regime (rigid / soft / granular / fluid) and the stiffness / contact pattern. The matrix below summarises coverage; chapters below dig into each.

Picking a solver

                    │

                    │

                                                        Featherstone CABLE
