The Nedelec basis attaches DoFs to mesh edges, not vertices, and the local → global scatter applies an orientation sign. assemble_global detects the FunctionSpace::NedelecEdge { order } variant up-front and routes to a dedicated helper:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
if let FunctionSpace::NedelecEdge { order } = space {
    let map = NedelecDofMap::build(mesh);
    return assemble_global_nedelec(mesh, &map, element_visitor);
}
}

That assembler is described in the magnetostatics chapter.

Matvec wrapper

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn matvec(a: &BsrMatrix, x: &[Real]) -> Vec<Real>;
}

is an allocating wrapper around a.mv(x, &mut y). The closure-driven cg_solve and gmres solvers want \( y \leftarrow A x \) as an Fn(&[Real]) -> Vec<Real>, so every solver in the FEM module uses |x| matvec(&k, x) as its operator closure. The intermediate Vec<Real> allocation per iteration is ~~heap pressure but turns out to be negligible compared to the matvec itself for the mesh sizes molla cares about.

Worked example — heat equation steady state

The “all-boundary Dirichlet = 5 ⇒ interior is 5” contract test fits in 15 lines:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let mesh = FemMesh::tri_grid_2d(4, 4, 1.0, 1.0);
let space = FunctionSpace::P1Nodal;
let k = assemble_stiffness(&mesh, space, 1.0)?;
let n = space.ndof(&mesh);
let f = vec![0.0; n];

let bcs: Vec<_> = mesh.vertices.iter().enumerate()
    .filter(|(_, p)| /* on boundary */ )
    .map(|(i, _)| BoundaryCondition::Dirichlet { vertex: i as u32, value: 5.0 })
    .collect();

let u = solve_steady_state(&k, &f, &bcs, 500, 1e-10);
assert!(u.iter().all(|&v| (v - 5.0).abs() < 1e-6));
}

The assemble_stiffness call invokes assemble_global(mesh, P1Nodal, |c, v| compute_element_stiffness(c, v, 1.0)), which walks all 32 triangles, calls the kernel on each (\( 3 \times 3 \) blocks), scatters into 100 triplets (5 × 5 = 25 vertex grid → at most 5²·3³ entries), dedupes, and returns a CSR matrix with ~85 nnz. The solver chapter picks up from there.

Cross-references

  • Element kernels — what each visitor computes.
  • Function space — what space parameter the assembler accepts.
  • Boundary conditions — the BC reducer runs on the assembled matrix to produce the SPD reduced system.
  • Solvers — where CG meets the assembled BsrMatrix.
  • P2 assembly — the P2 variant assemble_global_p2 uses a dedicated P2DofMap because corner + edge-midpoint DoFs share one address space.
  • AMR assembly — assemble_global_amr adds a Galerkin constraint reduction Kc = T^T K T for non-conforming refinement.

Boundary conditions

Every assembled matrix needs boundary data folded into the linear system before CG / GMRES will produce a meaningful answer. Molla’s BC machinery lives in crates/molla-fem/src/bc.rs and supports five variants under a single enum:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub enum BoundaryCondition {
    Dirichlet        { vertex: u32, value: Real },
    DirichletVector  { vertex: u32, values: Vec<Real> },
    Neumann          { face: [u32; 3], flux: Real },
    NeumannTraction  { face: [u32; 3], traction: [Real; 3] },
    WeakDirichletDG  { vertex: u32, value: Real, sigma: Real },
}
}

All BCs are addressed by global DoF index (for vector spaces: dof = vertex * dim + component). The caller decides which vertices get pinned given the mesh — there’s no automatic boundary-detection in the BC reducer itself.

Symmetric Dirichlet reduction — the canonical reducer

apply_dirichlet (scalar) and apply_bcs (vector-aware) are the workhorses. apply_dirichlet is a thin wrapper:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn apply_dirichlet(k: &mut BsrMatrix, f: &mut [Real], bcs: &[BoundaryCondition]) {
    apply_bcs(k, f, bcs, &[], 1);
}
}

apply_bcs runs four passes in order:

  1. Pass 1 — integrate NeumannTraction into f. For every NeumannTraction { face, traction }, compute the 3D triangle area 0.5 · |b - a × c - a| and add (area / 3) · traction[c] to the RHS at each face vertex’s component DoF. This is the consistent P1 surface-integral lumping of a uniform traction. Order matters — Dirichlet overwrites the RHS, so any traction silently assigned to a constrained DoF is dropped (textbook “Dirichlet wins”).

  2. Pass 2 — collect pinned DoFs into a flat Vec<Option<Real>>. We need the full pin set up-front so the column-elimination pass can shift the RHS in one sweep. DirichletVector expands to one pin per component DoF in interleaved layout.

  3. Pass 3 — symmetric column elimination. For every non-pinned row \( i \), look at every entry \( K_{ij} \) where \( j \) is pinned with value \( v_j \); shift \( f_i \mathrel{-}= K_{ij} v_j \) and zero \( K_{ij} \). This is what restores the symmetry that the textbook row-only “pin” breaks: without it, a non-zero Dirichlet value would leak its contribution asymmetrically.

  4. Pass 4 — pin each constrained row. Zero every off-diagonal entry of the row, set the diagonal to 1, set f[r] = value.

The end result is an SPD reduced matrix when the parent is SPD, and a RHS that produces the correct interior values for non-zero Dirichlet data without further bookkeeping. CG / PCG retains its convergence guarantee on the reduced system. The test dirichlet_symmetric_reduction_preserves_symmetry pins this down on a tridiagonal Laplacian-like fixture.

Why symmetric reduction matters

Some textbooks teach the simpler asymmetric reducer (“zero the row, set the diagonal to 1”). That works for zero Dirichlet values but not for non-zero ones — and it breaks symmetry, so CG drifts off its convergence guarantee. The molla reducer always does the column shift

  • matrix zero so the resulting system is symmetric, SPD if the parent was, and correct for arbitrary Dirichlet values.
Before pinning vertex 0 to v = 2:    After symmetric reduction:

  [ 3  -1   0   0 ] [u₀]   [1]        [ 1   0   0   0 ] [u₀]   [ 2 ]
  [-1   3  -1   0 ] [u₁]   [1]        [ 0   3  -1   0 ] [u₁]   [ 3 ]    ← shift +2
  [ 0  -1   3  -1 ] [u₂]   [1]        [ 0  -1   3  -1 ] [u₂]   [ 1 ]
  [ 0   0  -1   3 ] [u₃] = [1]        [ 0   0  -1   3 ] [u₃] = [ 1 ]

After CG, u₀ = 2 exactly (identity row pin) and the interior values are the correct response to the BC shift.

Neumann is currently a no-op

The scalar Neumann { face, flux } variant is recorded in the BC list but not integrated into the RHS — the v1 weak form already drops the boundary integral for the zero-flux case, which is the homogeneous default. The neumann_is_a_noop_in_v1 test pins this. For non-zero fluxes, callers should integrate the surface contribution themselves (or use NeumannTraction for the vector-valued elasticity case, which is fully wired).

NeumannTraction for elasticity

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
NeumannTraction { face: [u32; 3], traction: [Real; 3] }
}

is the workhorse for “push this face with that traction vector” in elasticity scenes. The reducer integrates the consistent P1 surface integral and folds the resulting nodal forces into f before Dirichlet pinning. The adjoint chapter shows how this entry shape makes the gradient ∂J/∂t a one-liner.

DG Nitsche weak-Dirichlet

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
WeakDirichletDG {
    vertex: u32,
    value: Real,
    sigma: Real,
}
}

is fundamentally different — it never overwrites a row. Instead it modifies the global DG matrix by adding the symmetric interior-penalty boundary block

\[ a_{\partial\Omega}(u, v) = -\alpha \int_{\partial\Omega} (\nabla u \cdot \mathbf{n}) v , dS - \alpha \int_{\partial\Omega} u (\nabla v \cdot \mathbf{n}) , dS + \frac{\sigma \alpha}{h_F} \int_{\partial\Omega} u , v , dS \]

and the matching RHS

\[ \ell_{\partial\Omega}(v) = -\alpha \int_{\partial\Omega} u_D (\nabla v \cdot \mathbf{n}) , dS + \frac{\sigma \alpha}{h_F} \int_{\partial\Omega} u_D v , dS, \]

where \( u_D \) is the prescribed Dirichlet trace (linearly interpolated between the per-vertex values on each boundary face).

Apply via apply_dg_bcs:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn apply_dg_bcs(
    k: &mut BsrMatrix,
    f: &mut [Real],
    bcs: &[BoundaryCondition],
    mesh: &FemMesh,
    degree: usize,
    alpha: Real,
) -> Result<()>;
}

Faces where not every vertex carries a WeakDirichletDG entry are skipped; per-face \( \sigma \) is the max of the constituent vertex sigmas. The default penalty \( \sigma_{\text{rec}} = \text{degree} \cdot (\text{degree} + 1) \cdot 10 \) is exposed by:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn default_nitsche_sigma(degree: usize) -> Real;
}

That value sits in the “large enough for coercivity, small enough to avoid conditioning blow-up” sweet spot from the literature (Arnold-Brezzi-Cockburn-Marini).

The regular apply_bcs silently drops WeakDirichletDG entries so the same Vec<BoundaryCondition> can carry both CG and DG-bound variants. Internally, apply_dg_bcs re-extracts triplets from the matrix via column-scans, merges in the boundary triplets, and rebuilds the BSR — a O(n²) operation for n rows. It’s only used at solver setup, not per-iteration, so the cost is acceptable.

When to use weak vs strong Dirichlet

PropertyStrong (Dirichlet)Weak (WeakDirichletDG)
Continuity preservedyes (DoF pinned exactly)only as σ → ∞
Works on DG fieldsonly on per-cell DoFsyes (face integral)
Affects matrix patternno (zeroes existing entries)yes (rebuilds BSR with new block)
Conditioningidentical to parentgrows linearly with σ

Strong Dirichlet is the right answer for CG fields. Weak Dirichlet is the right answer for DG, where strong pinning has no clean semantics because the DoFs are per cell — you’d have to pick which cell’s DoF gets pinned at a boundary vertex.

Cross-references

  • Solvers — every solver calls apply_bcs or apply_dirichlet before handing the reduced matrix to CG.
  • Adjoint — the adjoint solve inherits the same BC reduction; NeumannTraction entries are stripped before pinning so they don’t double-count into the adjoint RHS.
  • DG basis and DG BC — where the Nitsche path is used in anger.
  • Signorini — non-penetration constraints are an inequality version of Dirichlet; the Uzawa loop builds on top of the standard BC reducer.

Top-level solvers

crates/molla-fem/src/solver.rs strings the pieces together. Every top-level solver in this chapter follows the same pattern:

  1. Clone the assembled matrix.
  2. Call apply_bcs / apply_dirichlet to produce a BC-reduced (K_red, f_red) pair.
  3. Seed the initial guess with Dirichlet values so CG starts with zero residual on the pinned rows.
  4. Hand |x| matvec(&K_red, x) to cg_solve (or pcg_solve).
  5. Return the result.

Tolerances default to:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub const DEFAULT_TOL: Real = 1.0e-8;
pub const DEFAULT_MAX_ITERS: usize = 2000;
}

— sufficient for the v1 contract tests at 16³ resolution.

Steady-state Laplace / Poisson

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn solve_steady_state(
    k: &BsrMatrix,
    f: &[Real],
    bcs: &[BoundaryCondition],
    max_iters: usize,
    tol: Real,
) -> Vec<Real>;

pub fn solve_steady_state_with_initial(...) -> CgResult;
pub fn solve_steady_state_pcg(...) -> CgResult;
}

Solves \( K u = f \) with Dirichlet BCs reduced symmetrically. The PCG variant builds a JacobiPreconditioner from K_red.diagonal() — typically cuts CG iters by 25–40 % on Laplacian-like SPD systems for free.

There’s also a vector-aware sibling that knows about elasticity:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn solve_steady_state_vector(
    k: &BsrMatrix,
    f: &[Real],
    bcs: &[BoundaryCondition],
    vertices: &[Vec3],
    dim: usize,
    max_iters: usize,
    tol: Real,
) -> Vec<Real>;
}

— same recipe but routes through apply_bcs so DirichletVector / NeumannTraction are honoured. dim is the per-vertex DoF count (3 for tets, 2 for plane-strain tris).

Transient parabolic — backward Euler

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn solve_transient(
    m: &BsrMatrix,
    k: &BsrMatrix,
    f: &[Real],
    u_old: &[Real],
    dt: Real,
    bcs: &[BoundaryCondition],
) -> Vec<Real>;
}

The backward-Euler step solves

\[ \left(\frac{M}{\Delta t} + K \right) u^{n+1} = f + \frac{M}{\Delta t} u^n. \]

The LHS is materialised via the private add_csr_scaled helper that walks both triplet lists and reuses BsrMatrix::from_triplets to dedupe; the RHS is built with a single matvec of M against u_old. Dirichlet BCs are then applied in tandem on (A, b) before CG.

solve_transient_pcg is the Jacobi-preconditioned variant. For repeated steps with the same left-hand side, solve_transient_pcg_restarted adds a recycled-Krylov initial guess:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct KrylovRestartCache { /* bounded recent correction vectors */ }

pub fn solve_transient_pcg_restarted(
    m, k, f, u_old, dt, bcs, x0, cache, max_iters, tol,
) -> CgResult;
}

The cache stores recent PCG correction directions. Before each solve, the restarted path computes a tiny minimum-residual projection in x0 + span(cache) and uses that projected vector as the PCG initial guess, then stores the new correction for the next step. This is the CPU oracle for Krylov restart/recycling in transient FEM steppers.

Wave equation — Newmark-β

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn solve_wave_transient(
    m: &BsrMatrix,
    k: &BsrMatrix,
    u_old: &[Real],
    v_old: &[Real],
    a_old: &[Real],
    dt: Real,
    beta: Real,
    gamma: Real,
    bcs: &[BoundaryCondition],
) -> WaveStepResult;
}

The classical Newmark-β implicit step for \( M\ddot u + K u = 0 \):

  1. Predictor: \( u_{\text{pred}} = u_{\text{old}} + \Delta t v_{\text{old}}
    • (\frac{1}{2} - \beta) \Delta t^2 a_{\text{old}} \).
  2. Solve: \( \left(\frac{M}{\beta \Delta t^2} + K\right) u_{\text{new}} = \frac{M}{\beta \Delta t^2} u_{\text{pred}} \).
  3. Corrector: \( a_{\text{new}} = (u_{\text{new}} - u_{\text{pred}}) / (\beta \Delta t^2) \), \( v_{\text{new}} = v_{\text{old}} + \Delta t [(1-\gamma) a_{\text{old}} + \gamma a_{\text{new}}] \).

The defaults β = 1/4, γ = 1/2 give the “constant-average-acceleration” variant, which is unconditionally stable for linear undamped wave problems. The constants are exposed as:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub const NEWMARK_BETA_DEFAULT: Real = 0.25;
pub const NEWMARK_GAMMA_DEFAULT: Real = 0.5;
}

After the corrector, v_new and a_new are zeroed on every Dirichlet DoF. Without that, a non-zero v_old or a_old on a pinned DoF (e.g. seeded from a consistent initial-acceleration solve) gets carried into a_new through u_pred and integrates to spurious boundary motion across steps. For time-varying Dirichlet data the caller is expected to overwrite the pinned v_new / a_new entries after each call.

Returns a WaveStepResult { u_new, v_new, a_new, residual, iters }.

Nonlinear static — Newton-Raphson

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn solve_nonlinear_static<KAsm, RAsm>(
    tangent_assembler: KAsm,
    residual_assembler: RAsm,
    f_ext: &[Real],
    bcs: &[BoundaryCondition],
    vertices: &[Vec3],
    dim: usize,
    max_newton_iters: usize,
    tol: Real,
) -> Vec<Real>
where
    KAsm: Fn(&[Real]) -> BsrMatrix,
    RAsm: Fn(&[Real]) -> Vec<Real>;
}

Solves \( R(u) = K_{\text{int}}(u) - f_{\text{ext}} = 0 \) by classical Newton iteration:

  1. Assemble the tangent K(u) via tangent_assembler(u).
  2. Compute the residual via residual_assembler(u).
  3. Build rhs = f_ext - K_int(u).
  4. Apply Dirichlet BCs with zero values (the absolute Dirichlet value is already baked into the seeded u; the Newton increment must satisfy du = 0 on constrained rows).
  5. Solve \( K , du = -R \) via cg_solve.
  6. Update \( u \leftarrow u + du \).
  7. Terminate on \( |du|_\infty < \text{tol} \) or when the residual norm grows for two consecutive iterations (divergence bail-out — emits a tracing::warn!).

v1 has no line search; small problems only. The hyperelasticity contract tests in crates/molla-fem/tests/ use this driver against the SVK kernel from elements.

Newton on distortion energy

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn solve_distortion_minimization(
    rest_mesh: &FemMesh,
    init_deformed: &[Vec3],
    max_iter: usize,
    tol: Real,
) -> Vec<Vec3>;
}

Newton-Raphson minimisation of the per-cell symmetric-Dirichlet distortion energy (see compute_element_distortion_energy). Each iteration assembles the global gradient \( g \) and Hessian \( H \), regularises the diagonal with \( 10^{-8} I \) to keep \( H \) SPD on degenerate elements, then solves \( H , dx = -g \) via CG. Termination: \( |dx|_\infty < \text{tol} \).

This is the driver behind the WarpFemDistortion viewer scene and the canonical “snap perturbed positions back to a low-distortion map” use case.

GPU steppers — Slice H

The GPU port keeps the state resident on the device across timesteps so per-step host↔device traffic is zero. Two stepper objects expose this:

WaveStepperGpu

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let mut stepper = WaveStepperGpu::new(
    engine, mesh, &m, &k,
    dt, beta, gamma, &bcs, &u, &v, &a)?;
for _ in 0..n_steps {
    let stats = stepper.step()?;       // GPU dispatches only
}
let (u, v, a) = stepper.read_state()?;
}

Internals:

  • BC-reduced \( A = \frac{M}{\beta \Delta t^2} + K \) is uploaded once (FemGpuData); the per-step BC column-shift bc_shift is also pre-computed (so the GPU never re-runs apply_bcs).
  • Persistent storage buffers hold (u, v, a) in f32.
  • Scratch buffers (u_pred, m_upred, b) are allocated once.
  • A Jacobi preconditioner inv_diag = 1 / diag(A_red) is extracted at construction; the per-step CG runs as PCG (~30 % iter reduction).
  • Each step() dispatches: predictor → M · u_pred → RHS build → PCG solve → corrector → copy u_new into the resident u buffer.

TransientStepperGpu

Same pattern for the backward-Euler transient step. Persistent buffers: u, f (source term, defaults to zero — write_f to update), and scratch (m_uold, b). The per-step source is write_f-controlled so a time-varying forcing works without rebuilding the stepper.

Both steppers expose read_u(), read_state(), write_state() / write_u() for the viewer reset path. The contract is “render thread reads back once per frame, simulation thread steps many times per frame without ever touching the host”.

Russell direct solver

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[cfg(feature = "russell")]
pub fn solve_steady_state_direct(
    k: &BsrMatrix,
    f: &[Real],
    bcs: &[BoundaryCondition],
) -> Result<Vec<Real>>;
}

Routes through a pure-Rust dense LU with partial pivoting (DirectSolver::factorize + back_solve). The upstream russell_sparse crate was deemed unworkable in molla’s nix devShell (see the rationale in russell.rs), so this stage ships a fallback that exposes the same new / factorize / back_solve / solve API shape.

Use this when:

  • CG stalls (indefinite or stiff systems).
  • The problem is very small and one LU is cheaper than many CG iters.
  • You’re doing “factor once, back-solve many times” (e.g. adjoint sweeps over multiple loads).

A hard cap MAX_DIRECT_DIM = 12_000 keeps the dense factor below ~1 GB; above that, callers should keep iterating with cg_solve.

Cross-references

  • Assembly — builds the input matrices.
  • BC — the reducer every solver invokes.
  • Adjoint — the gradient solve reuses solve_adjoint_with which mirrors this driver shape.
  • Stokes — Uzawa-CG uses the same cg_solve core on the Schur complement.
  • Signorini — projected Uzawa nests inner-CG calls inside the dual update loop.
  • Multigrid — the V-cycle wraps a coarsest-level Cholesky solve plus per-level ω-Jacobi smoothing.

P2 nodal elements

Stage 36.3 of the FEM stack added piecewise-quadratic elements on top of the v1 piecewise-linear framework. A P2 triangle carries 6 nodes — 3 corners + 3 edge midpoints — and a P2 tetrahedron carries 10 nodes — 4 corners + 6 edge midpoints. The implementation lives in crates/molla-fem/src/p2_element.rs.

Reference shape functions

In barycentric coordinates the P2 Lagrange basis is:

  • Corners \( N_i^c = \lambda_i (2\lambda_i - 1) \) — value 1 at corner \( i \), 0 at every other reference point.
  • Edges \( N_{ij}^e = 4 \lambda_i \lambda_j \) — value 1 at the midpoint of edge \( (i, j) \), 0 elsewhere.
#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn p2_tri_shape_functions(bary: [Real; 3]) -> [Real; 6];
pub fn p2_tet_shape_functions(bary: [Real; 4]) -> [Real; 10];
}

Edge ordering is fixed for the rest of the pipeline so the assembly and P2DofMap agree:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub const TRI_EDGES: [[usize; 2]; 3] = [[0, 1], [1, 2], [2, 0]];
pub const TET_EDGES: [[usize; 2]; 6] = [[0,1],[0,2],[0,3],[1,2],[1,3],[2,3]];
}

Tri layout: [c0, c1, c2, e01, e12, e20]. Tet layout: [c0, c1, c2, c3, e01, e02, e03, e12, e13, e23].

The reference-element identities the v1 tests pin down:

  • Partition of unity: \( \sum_i N_i \equiv 1 \) at every barycentric point. Checked at the centroid in p2_tri_partition_of_unity_at_centroid.
  • Kronecker delta on nodes: \( N_i \) is 1 at its own node and 0 at every other reference node.

Physical-space gradients

The physical-space gradients follow from the chain rule \( \nabla N(\lambda) = \sum_k (\partial N / \partial \lambda_k) \nabla \lambda_k \), where \( \nabla \lambda_k \) are the P1 hat-function gradients (constant per element):

  • Corner: \( \nabla N_i^c = (4\lambda_i - 1) \nabla \lambda_i \).
  • Edge: \( \nabla N_{ij}^e = 4(\lambda_j \nabla \lambda_i + \lambda_i \nabla \lambda_j) \).
#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn p2_tri_shape_gradients(bary: [Real; 3], vertices: &[Vec3; 3]) -> [Vec3; 6];
pub fn p2_tet_shape_gradients(bary: [Real; 4], vertices: &[Vec3; 4]) -> [Vec3; 10];
}

The gradient routines also satisfy a “partition of zero” identity \( \sum_i \nabla N_i \equiv 0 \) — captured by p2_tri_grad_partition_of_zero_at_centroid and the tet analogue. This is what makes \( K \cdot \mathbf{1} = 0 \) on every cell, which the mass-conservation contract tests rely on.

P2DofMap — corner + edge addressing

The P2 global DoF vector is laid out as:

  1. The first vert_count entries are the corner DoFs (DoF index i ↔ vertex i).
  2. The next edge_count entries are the edge-midpoint DoFs, in the order returned by compute_edges.
#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct P2DofMap {
    pub vertex_count: usize,
    pub edge_id: HashMap<[u32; 2], u32>,
}

impl P2DofMap {
    pub fn build(mesh: &FemMesh) -> Self;
    pub fn ndof(&self) -> usize;                   // vertex_count + edge_count
    pub fn edge_dof(&self, a: u32, b: u32) -> usize;
    pub fn local_to_global(&self, cell: &FemCell, local_idx: usize) -> usize;
}
}

local_to_global handles both halves of the layout:

Local idx (Tri)  →  Global DoF
  0..3              vertex_count[i]           (corner)
  3..6              vertex_count + edge_id    (edge midpoint)

Local idx (Tet)  →  Global DoF
  0..4              vertex_count[i]           (corner)
  4..10             vertex_count + edge_id    (edge midpoint)

A 2 × 2 × 2 tet grid has 27 vertices and 98 unique edges, giving 125 P2 DoFs total — the p2_nodal_ndof_is_vertex_plus_edge_count test verifies this.

Element matrices

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn compute_element_p2_mass(cell: &FemCell, vertices: &[Vec3]) -> Vec<Vec<Real>>;
pub fn compute_element_p2_stiffness(cell: &FemCell, vertices: &[Vec3], coeff: Real) -> Vec<Vec<Real>>;
}

Both kernels return an N × N row-major dense matrix (N = 6 for Tri, N = 10 for Tet) by quadrature loop:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
for q in &qpts {
    let n = p2_tri_shape_functions(q.bary);
    let w = q.weight * area;
    for i in 0..6 { for j in 0..6 {
        m[i][j] += w * n[i] * n[j];
    }}
}
}

Quadrature choices:

IntegrandDegreeTri ruleTet rule
Nᵢ · Nⱼ (mass)46-pt Dunavant11-pt Keast
∇Nᵢ · ∇Nⱼ (stiffness)26-pt (overkill)11-pt (overkill)

The 11-pt rule on tets is overkill for P2 stiffness (the integrand is only quadratic in the barycentric coordinates) but reusing the same rule for both mass and stiffness keeps the kernel simple — one quadrature pass per cell shared with the mass. The 5-pt Keast rule would be sufficient and is exposed for callers who need to optimise.

Sanity tests in p2_element.rs::tests:

  • p2_tri_mass_total_equals_area — \( \sum_{ij} M_{ij} = \int_K 1 \cdot 1 = |K| \).
  • p2_tet_mass_total_equals_volume.
  • p2_tri_stiffness_kills_constant_field — \( \sum_j K_{ij} = 0 \) for each row (a constant field has zero gradient).
  • p2_tet_stiffness_kills_constant_field.

Global P2 assembly

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn assemble_global_p2<F>(
    mesh: &FemMesh,
    map: &P2DofMap,
    element_visitor: F,
) -> Result<BsrMatrix>
where
    F: Fn(&FemCell, &[Vec3]) -> Vec<Vec<Real>>;
}

Mirrors assemble_global but uses P2DofMap::local_to_global to translate local node indices → global DoF indices instead of the simpler vertex_idx * dim + comp formula used by P1. The scatter loop is otherwise identical: build a flat triplet vector, hand to BsrMatrix::from_scalar_triplets.

For the matching vector-valued case (Taylor-Hood velocity), the FunctionSpace::P2Vector { dim } space layers dim components per node on top of the same corner+edge address space — see the Stokes chapter for the assembler that uses it.

Why P2 matters

Three reasons:

  1. Higher convergence rate. Best-approximation error scales as \( O(h^2) \) for P1, \( O(h^3) \) for P2. For smooth solutions this means a 2× mesh refinement cuts error by 4× (P1) vs 8× (P2) — the cross-over where P2 is cheaper per unit error is small.
  2. LBB stability for Stokes. The Taylor-Hood pair (P2 velocity, P1 pressure) is inf-sup stable, where P1/P1 is not. This is what makes the Stokes solver in stokes actually converge.
  3. Curved geometry. P2 elements can capture quadratic boundary deformation; P1 cannot. The viewer scenes for the higher-order demos (curvy heat, jellyfish soft body) lean on this.

Cross-references

  • Quadrature — the higher-order Gauss rules used here.
  • Stokes / NS — Taylor-Hood mixed elements (P2Vector { dim } × P1Nodal).
  • DG basis — P2 DG (DGNodal { degree: 2 }) reuses these exact reference shape functions but with per-cell DoFs instead of edge-shared ones.

Discontinuous Galerkin (DG)

The DG cluster — crates/molla-fem/src/dg_element.rs (~2700 lines) and dg_time_integrator.rs (~200 lines) — is the second-largest chapter set in the FEM stack. DG generalises classical continuous Galerkin (CG) by dropping inter-element continuity: a vertex shared by k cells gets k · ndof_per_cell DoFs total, one set per owning cell, and coupling between cells happens via numerical flux integrals on each shared face.

The DG framework is split into six sub-chapters in this docset:

  • Basis and per-cell DoFs — DGNodal { degree }, P0 / P1 / P2 layouts, dg_ndof_per_cell, and the Lagrange-vs- Bernstein basis trade-off.
  • Numerical fluxes — the NumericalFlux enum: Central, Upwind, LaxFriedrichs, Roe, plus the SWE specials (HLL, HLLC, RoeSwe).
  • Slope limiters — Barth-Jespersen scalar limiter and Krivodonova characteristic-wise limiter.
  • Time integration — SSP-RK2 / SSP-RK3 in the low-storage Shu-Osher form.
  • Boundary conditions — Nitsche weak Dirichlet, periodic face pairs.
  • GPU port — Stage 43 v4 status note.

This page gives the high-level overview that ties them together.

Why DG?

Three properties make DG the canonical choice for hyperbolic PDEs (conservation laws, advection, shallow-water, Euler):

  1. Local conservation. Each cell’s DoFs satisfy a discrete conservation law independently — the face flux is what couples them, and the flux is consistent. No mass leaks between elements through numerical error.
  2. Sharp discontinuity capture. Per-cell DoFs let the solution jump at faces; combined with a slope limiter you can resolve shocks in one cell instead of smearing them over many.
  3. Embarrassingly parallel assembly. No DoF is shared, so the element loop has no atomic-add hazard — the per-face flux block is the only cross-cell coupling, and that’s a tightly scoped read of two cells’ DoFs.

DG also has costs — k× more DoFs per shared vertex than CG, more complex BCs (Nitsche / weak Dirichlet — see dg_bc), and limiters that need careful tuning — so molla uses CG for elliptic / parabolic problems (heat, elasticity, Stokes) and DG for the hyperbolic specials (Burgers shock, SWE dam-break).

Stage timeline

StageCapability
39B v1P0 / P1 DG, SIP Laplacian flux, mass/stiffness per cell
43 v1NumericalFlux::{Central, Upwind, LaxFriedrichs, Roe}
43 v2SSP-RK2 / RK3 time integration; Nitsche weak Dirichlet
43 v3P2 DG, SWE-specific HLL / HLLC / RoeSwe, Krivodonova limiter
43 v4GPU port of HLL / HLLC / RoeSwe (queued)
C22D compressible Euler physical / Rusanov / HLL flux helpers

The DG semi-discrete system

For a scalar conservation law \( u_t + \nabla \cdot F(u) = 0 \) the DG weak form per cell \( K \) reads

\[ \int_K \phi_i u_t , dx

  • \int_K \nabla \phi_i \cdot F(u) , dx
  • \int_{\partial K} \phi_i , \hat{F}(u^-, u^+, \mathbf{n}) , dS = 0, \]

where \( \hat{F} \) is the numerical flux that couples the two sides of each face. The DG-mass matrix is block-diagonal (no shared DoFs), so the inverse mass is cheap to apply — typically the RHS routine inverts it on-the-fly inside du/dt = M⁻¹ R(u) before handing to the time integrator.

The dg_element.rs API exposes the building blocks:

For compressible-flow follow-ons, the Euler helpers mirror the SWE pointwise flux API:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn euler_pressure_2d(u: [Real; 4], gamma: Real) -> Real;
pub fn euler_flux_dot_n_2d(u: [Real; 4], n: Vec3, gamma: Real) -> [Real; 4];
pub fn compute_euler_numerical_flux_rusanov_2d(... ) -> [Real; 4];
pub fn compute_euler_numerical_flux_hll_2d(... ) -> [Real; 4];
}

The state is conservative (ρ, ρu, ρv, E), with an ideal-gas EOS.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn compute_element_dg_mass(cell, vertices, degree) -> Vec<Vec<Real>>;
pub fn compute_element_dg_stiffness(cell, vertices, coeff, degree) -> Vec<Vec<Real>>;
pub fn compute_dg_numerical_flux_block(...) -> ...;
pub fn compute_dg_flux_jump_block(...) -> ...;            // SIP elliptic
pub fn compute_nitsche_boundary_block(...) -> (Vec<Vec<Real>>, Vec<Real>);
pub fn compute_swe_numerical_flux_hll(...) -> ...;
pub fn compute_swe_numerical_flux_hllc(...) -> ...;
pub fn compute_swe_numerical_flux_roe(...) -> ...;
pub fn limit_solution(...);                               // Barth-Jespersen
pub fn limit_solution_characteristic(...);                // Krivodonova
pub fn compute_interior_faces(mesh) -> Vec<InteriorFace>;
pub fn periodic_face_pairs(mesh, axis) -> Vec<PeriodicPair>;
pub fn dg_nodal_positions(cell, vertices, degree) -> Vec<Vec3>;
pub fn assemble_dg_global<C, F>(...);
}

assemble_dg_global is the DG analogue of assemble_global — it visits every cell + every interior face and scatters into a per-cell BSR with B = 1.

Per-cell DoF layout

For DGNodal { degree } the cell offsets are a running sum:

offset[c]     = Σ_{c' < c} dg_ndof_per_cell(cells[c'], degree)
offset[c + 1] = offset[c] + dg_ndof_per_cell(cells[c], degree)

— so cell c’s local DoF i lives at global index offset[c] + i. This is what adjustment-set rebuilding and the DG-AMR face match routines key off.

Worked example — DG-P1 on a 4-triangle mesh

A four-triangle mesh sharing one center vertex would have \( 4 \text{ cells} \times 3 \text{ DoFs/cell} = 12 \) total DG-P1 DoFs, vs only \( 5 \) shared CG-P1 DoFs:

CG-P1 (5 DoFs):       DG-P1 (12 DoFs):

      v1                   v1_0 ─── v1_1
     /  \                  / \     / \
   v2 ── v0 ── v3        v2_0 v0_0 v0_1 v3_1
     \  /                  \   ╳   /
      v4                  v2_2 v0_2 v0_3 v4_3
                            \ /     \ /
                             v4_2 ─── v4_3

Each “ghost” DoF (e.g. v0_0) belongs to its owning cell only — shared vertices each show up four times (once per cell) and the four copies are coupled only through the four edges meeting at the center.

This shape generalises directly to tets in 3D; numbers scale as 4 DoFs/cell (P1 tet), 10 DoFs/cell (P2 tet).

Glossary

  • Average \( {w} = \frac{1}{2}(w^- + w^+) \) — mean of the two-sided trace of a field on an interior face.
  • Jump \( [w] = w^- - w^+ \) — scalar jump across the face; vector form \( [w] , \mathbf{n} \) for normal-flux work.
  • Numerical flux \( \hat F(u^-, u^+, \mathbf{n}) \) — the single flux value used at every quadrature point on a face, built from the two one-sided traces and the outward normal.
  • SIP — Symmetric Interior Penalty; the standard symmetric DG formulation for elliptic operators. See compute_dg_flux_jump_block.

Read on for the deep dives.

Stokes and Navier-Stokes

Incompressible Stokes / Navier–Stokes lives in crates/molla-fem/src/stokes.rs (~1600 lines) and uses Taylor–Hood mixed elements — P2 vector velocity + P1 scalar pressure — solved with a SIMPLE-style projection iteration on the pressure-Schur complement. A FFT-based alternative for periodic 2D grids lives in fft_ns.rs. The GPU port stokes_gpu.rs keeps the matrices resident on the device.

The Taylor-Hood mixed space

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct MixedTaylorHood {
    pub dim: usize,           // 2 (plane-strain) or 3
    pub map: P2DofMap,        // velocity addressing
    pub n_velocity: usize,    // (vert + edge) · dim
    pub n_pressure: usize,    // vert_count
}
}
  • Velocity lives in P2Vector { dim } — corner DoFs + edge- midpoint DoFs, each carrying dim components, interleaved as [ux₀, uy₀, uz₀, ux₁, ...].
  • Pressure lives in P1Nodal — one scalar per mesh vertex.

The Taylor–Hood pair is LBB-stable (inf-sup stable) for incompressible Stokes — the canonical safe choice for mixed velocity-pressure formulations. Equal-order P1/P1 is not stable and would need extra stabilisation; Taylor–Hood doesn’t.

The Stokes saddle-point system

\[ \begin{pmatrix} A & B^T \ B & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} u \ p \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} f \ 0 \end{pmatrix} \]

with:

  • A = velocity block = component-decoupled μ · ∇u : ∇v Laplacian. Each component is a P2 stiffness matrix scaled by viscosity μ.
  • B = divergence block = −∫_Ω q · ∇·u dx evaluated against the P1 pressure test function q.

The system is indefinite (it has the saddle-point structure with zero in the (2,2) block), so the molla CG cannot solve it directly. Instead we use a SIMPLE-style projection that splits the velocity update from the pressure correction:

SIMPLE iteration

  1. Predictor: \( A \cdot u^* = f - B^T \cdot p_{\text{old}} \). Solve via CG on the velocity-block matrix (component-decoupled SPD).
  2. Pressure correction: \( (B A_{\text{diag}}^{-1} B^T) \cdot \delta p = -B \cdot u^* \). The Schur complement on the diagonal of A. A_diag is the lumped diagonal of A (cheap; gives a diagonal SPD operator). Solve via CG on the matrix-free closure \( q \mapsto B \cdot (A_{\text{diag}}^{-1} \cdot B^T \cdot q) \).
  3. Update: \( u = u^* - A_{\text{diag}}^{-1} B^T \cdot \delta p \), \( p = p_{\text{old}} + \alpha \delta p \).
  4. Repeat until \( |B u| < \text{tol} \) (incompressibility residual).

α is a relaxation factor (typical 0.7–1.0 for Stokes; lower for stiff Navier-Stokes). The whole inner loop is built from cg_solve

  • matvec closures — no specialised saddle-point solver needed.

Public API

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn solve_stokes_steady(
    mesh: &FemMesh,
    th: &MixedTaylorHood,
    config: &StokesSimpleConfig,
    bcs: &[StokesBc],
    viscosity: Real,
) -> Result<StokesResult>;

pub fn solve_stokes_with_matrices(...);
}

StokesBc is its own enum (separate from BoundaryCondition because velocity needs vector-valued pinning and pressure needs a single-vertex anchor):

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub enum StokesBc {
    VelocityDirichlet { node: P2NodeRef, values: Vec<Real> },
    PressureAnchor    { vertex: u32, value: Real },
    NeumannTraction   { face: [u32; 3], traction: [Real; 3] },
}
}

The pressure anchor breaks the constant-pressure nullspace (the system is otherwise rank-deficient by one). Without it, CG drifts along the nullspace direction and δp grows unboundedly.

Per-element kernels

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn compute_element_stokes_velocity_block(cell, vertices, dim, mu)
    -> Vec<Vec<Real>>;    // (P2-vector × P2-vector) — the A^e block

pub fn compute_element_stokes_div_block(cell, vertices, dim, vert_count, n_pressure)
    -> Vec<Vec<Real>>;    // (P1 × P2-vector) — the B^e block

pub fn compute_element_mass_p2_vector(cell, vertices, dim)
    -> Vec<Vec<Real>>;    // (P2-vector × P2-vector) — for the transient case
}

The velocity block is block-diagonal in components: with the Laplacian form \( \mu \int \nabla u : \nabla v \) (rather than the symmetric stress form), the per-component blocks decouple and the assembler builds dim copies of the same P2 scalar stiffness, scaled by μ. Approximating the symmetric stress with the Laplacian is exact for fully-Dirichlet boundaries (the boundary integral cancels), which is what the lid-driven cavity test uses.

The divergence block uses the gradient identities \( \int_K q \nabla \cdot v , dx = -\int_K \nabla q \cdot v , dx + \text{(boundary)} \) and integrates via the 6-pt Dunavant rule on triangles or the 11-pt Keast rule on tets.

Time-stepping (Navier-Stokes)

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct NavierStokesConfig {
    pub dt: Real,
    pub viscosity: Real,
    pub max_simple_iters: usize,
    pub simple_tol: Real,
    pub max_advection_iters: usize,  // outer Picard / Newton on (u·∇)u
    pub advection_tol: Real,
}

pub fn solve_navier_stokes_step(mesh, th, config, bcs, u_old, p_old) -> Result<StokesResult>;
pub fn solve_navier_stokes_transient(...);
}

The momentum update is IMEX: implicit for the viscous + pressure parts, explicit for the convection (u·∇)u term. This is the classic Chorin–Marchuk fractional-step recipe.

For high Reynolds numbers, the explicit convection becomes oscillatory; the kernel-level compute_element_supg_convection adds Hughes’ streamline-upwind stabilisation, exposed at the assembly level via:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn assemble_convection_block_with_supg(
    mesh: &FemMesh,
    th: &MixedTaylorHood,
    velocity_field: &[Real],
    alpha: Real,
    h_per_cell: &[Real],
) -> Result<BsrMatrix>;
}

Lid-driven cavity test

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn build_cavity_bcs_2d(mesh: &FemMesh, th: &MixedTaylorHood, lid_velocity: Real) -> Vec<StokesBc>;
}

builds the canonical Stokes / NS test: zero velocity on three walls, \( (u_{\text{lid}}, 0) \) on the top wall, pressure anchored at the bottom-left corner. The viewer scene StokesCavity2D runs this and the resulting streamlines match Ghia-Ghia-Shin’s 1982 reference at Re = 100.

FFT-Poisson fractional-step (fft_ns.rs)

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[cfg(feature = "gpu")]
pub fn solve_navier_stokes_fractional_step(
    device, queue, kernel,
    n_grid: usize,         // power of two
    num_steps: usize,
    dt: f32, nu: f32,
) -> Result<Vec<[f32; 2]>>;
}

A complementary path to the Taylor-Hood Stokes solver. Same pipeline (predictor → pressure-Poisson → corrector) but discretised on a uniform 2D grid with periodic boundaries, and the pressure-Poisson solve uses the GPU FFT kernel instead of CG on a Schur complement:

\[ \hat p(\mathbf{k}) = -\frac{1}{|\mathbf{k}|^2} \cdot \frac{1}{\Delta t} (i \mathbf{k} \cdot \hat u^*(\mathbf{k})), \quad \hat p(\mathbf{0}) = 0 \]

with the constant nullspace gauge-fixed at \( \mathbf{k} = 0 \). The PoissonStencil enum picks between the tight 5-point stencil (for staggered-grid gradients) and the wide stencil (for collocated central-difference gradients) — passing the wrong one produces checkerboard divergence on the odd-even mode.

This is the path the WarpNavierStokesFftDemo viewer scene uses because it gets to a working 2D NS in two screens of code.

GPU port — stokes_gpu.rs

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[cfg(feature = "gpu")]
pub fn solve_stokes_gpu(...) -> Result<StokesGpuResult>;

#[cfg(feature = "gpu")]
pub fn solve_navier_stokes_gpu(...) -> Result<NavierStokesGpuResult>;
}

Uploads A, B, the mass matrix, BC metadata once; runs the SIMPLE loop with GPU sparse-matvec + resident CG inside each predictor / corrector. Stage 41 v5 added async-dot fusion for the inner CG so each iteration is a single compute pass.

Stage 41 v7 adds a resident SSP-RK selector:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub enum NavierStokesGpuTimeIntegrator {
    ImexEuler,
    SspRk2,
    SspRk3,
}
}

SspRk2 and SspRk3 apply the existing GPU IMEX Euler stage multiple times and form the Shu-Osher convex combinations with the combine_states WGSL entry point. Velocity and pressure stage vectors stay in device buffers for the whole step; the solver reads back only the final NavierStokesGpuResult.

The shader pair is:

  • crates/molla-fem/shaders/fem_stokes_assemble.wgsl — per-cell assembly of the velocity and divergence blocks (one workgroup per cell).
  • crates/molla-fem/shaders/fem_ns_advect.wgsl / fem_ns_rhs_assemble.wgsl — Navier-Stokes per-step convection, RHS construction, zero-mask, and SSP-RK state-combination kernels.

Cross-references

  • P2 elements — the velocity basis and DoF map.
  • Element kernels — per-cell SUPG.
  • Solvers — cg_solve driving the SIMPLE inner loops.
  • APIC — the FEM-MPM hybrid uses the Stokes solver’s P2 velocity block as its mesh-side velocity update (planned for Stage 37.6.1; v1 ships viscous smoothing instead).

APIC FEM-MPM coupling

The APIC (Affine Particle-In-Cell) hybrid couples a Material-Point-Method (MPM) particle representation with an FEM mesh-side velocity update. It lives in crates/molla-fem/src/apic_coupling.rs (CPU, Stage 37.6) and apic_coupling_gpu.rs (GPU, Stage 41 v2). Particles transfer momentum to mesh nodes via APIC weights, the mesh solves the velocity-field step, and particles read the updated node velocities back to update their own velocity and affine matrix.

Why APIC?

Three transfer schemes coexist in the literature:

SchemeProsCons
PICSimple, robustLoses angular momentum (one pass)
FLIPCheap, preserves momentumNoise injection ⇒ jittery particles
APICPreserves angular momentum cleanlyOne extra Mat3 per particle

Molla picks APIC because (a) the angular-momentum loss in PIC kills rotational scenes, (b) the FLIP noise is hard to control, and (c) APIC’s extra storage is a single Mat3 per particle — cheap.

Data structures

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct ApicParticle {
    pub x: Vec3,        // position
    pub v: Vec3,        // velocity
    pub c: Mat3,        // affine velocity matrix
    pub mass: Real,
}

pub struct ApicHybrid {
    pub mesh: FemMesh,
    pub particles: Vec<ApicParticle>,
    pub gravity: Vec3,
}
}

The affine matrix c captures the local velocity gradient at the particle’s location. PIC sets c = 0; APIC carries it forward to restore angular momentum across the P2G / G2P round-trip.

The per-step pipeline

For each substep Δt:

  1. locate_particle_tet — brute-force barycentric scan: for each particle, find the tet that contains it and return (tet_verts, P1_weights, vertex_positions). v1 does an O(P · T) scan; the apic_locate_tet.wgsl shader does the same on GPU.

  2. P2G (particle → grid) — each particle deposits momentum at the four vertices of its enclosing tet:

    \[ \text{node_momentum}[i] \mathrel{+}= w_i , m_p , (v_p + C_p \cdot (x_i - x_p)) \]

    where \( w_i \) is the P1 barycentric weight of \( x_p \) at tet vertex \( i \). Mass is also scattered proportionally so the caller can recover \( v_{\text{node}} = \text{momentum} / \text{mass} \).

  3. Mesh solve — recover node_velocity, add dt · gravity, apply Dirichlet BCs (no-slip walls pin to zero), and run one viscous Laplacian smoothing pass \( v \leftarrow v - dt \cdot \nu \cdot L v \) to dissipate sub-grid energy. This is a v1 stand-in for a full P1 Stokes pressure-Poisson projection — molla’s Stokes solver lives on Taylor-Hood (P2 velocity), so plumbing the APIC P1 deposit through P2 needs either a P2 deposit (rebuilds the contract) or an L2 projection between spaces (Stage 37.6.1).

  4. G2P (grid → particle) — gather mesh velocities back:

    \[ v_p^{\text{new}} = \sum_i w_i v_i, \quad C_p^{\text{new}} = \sum_i w_i v_i , (x_i - x_p)^T \cdot D^{-1} \]

    where \( D = \sum_i w_i (x_i - x_p)(x_i - x_p)^T \) is the per-tet second-moment matrix. For P1 tets this has a clean closed form — apic_coupling.rs evaluates it inline.

  5. Advect: \( x_p \mathrel{+}= dt \cdot v_p^{\text{new}} \).

Contract tests

The CPU implementation ships round-trip tests in crates/molla-fem/tests/fem_apic.rs:

TestWhat it verifies
apic_zero_dt_momentum_roundtripΣ m v exact through P2G → G2P (dt = 0).
apic_uniform_motion_no_advectionUniform velocity field unchanged after one substep.
apic_falling_particles_settleParticles in a box with gravity settle to box floor; KE stays bounded.

The “uniform motion” check is what c = 0 particles would fail at — APIC keeps it exact because the affine matrix captures the (zero) velocity gradient.

GPU port — Stage 41 v2

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[cfg(feature = "gpu")]
pub struct ApicGpuState { /* persistent buffers + pipelines */ }

impl ApicHybrid {
    #[cfg(feature = "gpu")]
    pub fn step_gpu(&mut self, state: &mut ApicGpuState, dt: Real,
                    bcs: &[BoundaryCondition], viscosity: Real) -> Result<()>;
}
}

ApicGpuState::new(engine, hybrid) uploads:

  • Mesh: vertices, cell_offsets, cell_indices.
  • Particles: x, v, c, mass, plus a per-particle loc slot that the locate kernel writes into.
  • Node graph: a precomputed adjacency CSR for the viscous-smoothing Jacobi sweep, built once on CPU at construction.

Per step the pipeline dispatches seven WGSL kernels in order:

locate_tet  →  reset_grid  →  p2g  →  grid_update
                 ↓
            viscous_smoothing (one Jacobi sweep)
                 ↓
              apply_bcs  →  g2p

The locate kernel is the only one with O(P · T) cost; for the contract-test sizes (≤ 200 particles, ≤ 500 tets) it’s fine. A follow-up version with a tet-BVH (crates/molla/src/geometry/tet_bvh.rs) would drop locate to O(P · log T) without changing the public API.

The Stage 41 v2 sub-3 measurement on the falling-particles fixture showed a 14.5× speedup over CPU at 200 particles in a 16³ tet mesh — locate-dominated workload, so the speedup grows further as the particle count rises.

Caveats

  • No real Stokes projection in v1. The viscous-smoothing placeholder is incompressible only in the limit \( \nu \cdot dt \to \infty \). A true pressure-Poisson on the P1 mesh is Stage 37.6.1.
  • Particles can drift out of bounds. Explicit advection occasionally overshoots a wall; the contract test clamps to the bounding box AABB to keep the demo honest.
  • Brute-force locate. O(P · T) on CPU and GPU; not a problem at v1 sizes but doesn’t scale to 10⁴+ particles or 10⁴+ tets.

Cross-references

  • APIC compute (when documented) — the raw particle-grid transfer primitive that the FEM hybrid wraps.
  • MPM solvers (when documented) — the pure-MPM variant for the Stokes-free case.
  • Stokes / NS — the planned full pressure-Poisson replacement for the viscous-smoothing placeholder.
  • Mesh — FemMesh is what ApicHybrid owns.

Adjoint / differentiable FEM

crates/molla-fem/src/adjoint.rs implements reverse-mode differentiation through the linear elasticity assembly + solve. Given a forward solve \( K(p) u = f(p) \) with design parameters \( p \) (Young’s modulus, applied traction, …) and a scalar loss \( J(u, p) \), the adjoint method computes \( \partial J / \partial p \) with one extra linear solve of the same matrix — independent of the dimensionality of \( p \).

This is what gives molla a differentiable FEM, used by the Stage 38.2 fitting demo and any forward-design optimisation that wants to invert “observed deformation” → “material property”.

The variational identity

Differentiate the equilibrium \( K(p) u(p) = f(p) \) with respect to \( p \):

\[ \frac{\partial K}{\partial p} u + K \frac{\partial u}{\partial p} = \frac{\partial f}{\partial p}. \]

So

\[ \frac{\partial u}{\partial p} = K^{-1} \left( \frac{\partial f}{\partial p} - \frac{\partial K}{\partial p} u \right). \]

For a loss \( J(u, p) \):

\[ \frac{\partial J}{\partial p} = \frac{\partial J}{\partial p}\bigg|_{\text{expl}}

  • \frac{\partial J}{\partial u} \cdot \frac{\partial u}{\partial p} \]

Now define the adjoint variable \( \lambda \) by

\[ K^T \lambda = \frac{\partial J}{\partial u}. \]

Then

\[ \frac{\partial J}{\partial p} = \frac{\partial J}{\partial p}\bigg|_{\text{expl}}

  • \lambda^T \left( \frac{\partial f}{\partial p} - \frac{\partial K}{\partial p} u \right). \]

For SPD \( K \) (linear elasticity, Laplacian, …), \( K^T = K \) so the same matrix is used for the adjoint solve — no transpose, no new factorisation.

solve_adjoint

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn solve_adjoint(
    k: &BsrMatrix,
    dj_du: &[Real],
    bcs: &[BoundaryCondition],
    vertices: &[Vec3],
    dim: usize,
) -> Vec<Real>;

pub fn solve_adjoint_with(...) -> Vec<Real>;  // exposes tol / max_iters
}

Pass:

  • k — the un-reduced stiffness matrix. The routine clones it, applies BCs internally (zero Dirichlet values + dropped NeumannTraction entries — see below), and runs cg_solve against the seed ∂J/∂u.
  • dj_du — \( \partial J / \partial u \), length n_dof.
  • bcs — same BCs the forward solve used.
  • vertices + dim — passed through to apply_bcs for any vector-valued constraints.

BC handling

The adjoint inherits the same Dirichlet reduction as the forward solve (zero out the row, set the diagonal to 1, RHS = 0 on constrained rows). Two subtleties:

  1. NeumannTraction is dropped. The adjoint RHS is ∂J/∂u, not the physical load. Including NeumannTraction would double-count the load into the adjoint variable. The internal pin_only filter strips out Neumann and NeumannTraction entries before pinning rows.
  2. Dirichlet values are replaced with zero. The forward solve pinned u[r] = v at Dirichlet rows; the adjoint must pin \( \lambda[r] = 0 \) (otherwise \( \lambda \) would carry spurious sensitivity at the prescribed DoFs). The Dirichlet vertex survives so the row pinning happens; only the value is forced to zero.

Defaults:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub const DEFAULT_ADJOINT_TOL: Real = 1.0e-10;
pub const DEFAULT_ADJOINT_MAX_ITERS: usize = 50_000;
}

Tighter than the forward solve to keep λ clean — gradient noise propagates if λ has stale CG iterates left in it.

Gradient w.r.t. Young’s modulus

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn compute_grad_youngs(
    mesh: &FemMesh,
    vertices: &[Vec3],
    u: &[Real],
    lambda: &[Real],
    poisson: Real,
    youngs: Real,
) -> Real;
}

The linear-elasticity stiffness matrix is linear in \( E \): both Lamé parameters

\[ \lambda_l = \frac{E \nu}{(1+\nu)(1-2\nu)}, \quad \mu = \frac{E}{2(1+\nu)} \]

are proportional to \( E \), so

\[ \frac{\partial K}{\partial E} = \frac{K}{E}. \]

The variational identity collapses to

\[ \frac{\partial J}{\partial E} = -\frac{1}{E} , \lambda^T K u. \]

The implementation computes \( \lambda^T K u \) element-by-element — assembles each local stiffness, gathers local \( u \) and \( \lambda \) in interleaved layout, computes the local \( \lambda^T K_e u \), sums. \( O(n_{\text{cells}}) \) total, no global matvec, no global sparse matrix touched.

The routine assumes:

  • \( \dim = 2 \) (tri plane-strain) or \( \dim = 3 \) (tet).
  • The loss \( J \) has no explicit \( E \) dependence — compliance, tip deflection, target-displacement L2 norms all read u only.

Gradient w.r.t. surface traction

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn compute_grad_load(
    vertices: &[Vec3],
    lambda: &[Real],
    traction_face: [u32; 3],
    dim: usize,
) -> [Real; 3];
}

For a uniform traction \( t \) on a triangular face, the consistent P1 lumping puts \( (area / 3) \cdot t_c \) into the RHS at each vertex’s component DoF. So

\[ \frac{\partial f}{\partial t_c} = \frac{area}{3} , e_c \text{ (summed over face vertices)}, \]

and the adjoint identity gives

\[ \frac{\partial J}{\partial t_c} = \frac{area}{3} \sum_{v \in face} \lambda_{v \cdot \dim + c}. \]

Triangle face area is computed in 3D via \( \tfrac{1}{2} |, (\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a}) \times (\mathbf{c} - \mathbf{a}) ,| \). Components beyond dim (e.g. asking for [Real; 3] from a 2D plane-strain run) come back as 0.

Stage 38.2 — Young’s modulus fitting in log space

The first end-to-end consumer of the adjoint is the Stage 38.2 demo that fits Young’s modulus \( E \) from observed deformation. The recipe:

  1. Start with an initial guess \( E_0 \).
  2. Forward solve: \( K(E) u = f \).
  3. Evaluate loss \( J(u) = \tfrac{1}{2} |u - u_{\text{obs}}|^2 \).
  4. Adjoint solve: \( K \lambda = u - u_{\text{obs}} \).
  5. Gradient: \( \partial J / \partial E = -\lambda^T K u / E \) via compute_grad_youngs.
  6. Adam update in log space: \( \log E \leftarrow \log E - \alpha \cdot g \cdot E \) (chain rule from \( \partial J / \partial \log E = E , \partial J / \partial E \)).

Log-space optimisation is the right answer because \( E \) ranges across many orders of magnitude (rubber: 1e6 Pa; steel: 1e11 Pa); linear-space Adam either overshoots soft regions or undershoots stiff ones.

The demo converges in ~50 Adam steps and matches finite-difference gradients to ~1e-3 relative.

Caveats

  • Linear elasticity only. SVK / plasticity adjoints (Stage 36.4.2) need to differentiate through the Newton iteration; deferred.
  • No Stokes / Navier-Stokes adjoint. Stage 36.4.1 — pressure- velocity coupling makes the bookkeeping fiddly. Deferred.
  • CPU only. The GPU port would mirror the forward GPU CG with the adjoint RHS as the seed.

Cross-references

  • Solvers — the forward solve the adjoint mirrors.
  • BC — the same reducer used; the adjoint drops NeumannTraction entries and zeroes Dirichlet values.
  • Element kernels — the per-cell elasticity stiffness that compute_grad_youngs re-assembles per element.
  • Autograd (when documented) — the upper layer that wraps adjoint solves into a tape.

Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR)

crates/molla-fem/src/amr_mesh.rs (~1750 lines) is the second-largest single source file in the FEM stack. It builds a refinement-tree on top of a base FemMesh, manages hanging nodes, balances levels 2:1, and produces a Galerkin-reduced system Kc = TᵀKT that you can hand to the existing solvers. Stages 45 v1 through v4 cover uniform refine, non-uniform refine via a criterion, DG-AMR face matching, coarsening with Krylov restart.

Data model

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct AmrMesh {
    pub base_mesh: FemMesh,
    pub refined_cells: Vec<RefinedCell>,
    pub refinement_levels: Vec<u8>,

    // hidden:
    cells: Vec<FemCell>,                // flat pool — leaves + refined
    vertices: Vec<Vec3>,                // flat pool — base + midpoints
    is_refined: Vec<bool>,
    is_removed: Vec<bool>,              // v4 coarsening
    midpoint_cache: HashMap<(u32, u32), u32>,
    hanging_nodes: Vec<HangingNode>,
}
}

The “flat pool” model is what makes AMR efficient:

  • cells[0..base.cell_count()] are the base (level 0) cells. Indices beyond that are children added by refinement.
  • vertices[0..base.vert_count()] are the base vertices. Indices beyond that are edge midpoints inserted by refinement.
  • A cell is a leaf iff !is_refined[i] && !is_removed[i].
  • The midpoint_cache keys on the sorted edge endpoint pair so two neighbouring cells refining the same edge produce the same midpoint vertex — the mesh stays watertight on shared, fully-refined edges.

Refinement records

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct RefinedCell {
    pub parent: u32,                   // flat cell index of parent
    pub children: RefinedChildren,     // 4 (Tri) or 8 (Tet) indices
    pub level: u8,                     // parent.level + 1
}

pub enum RefinedChildren {
    Tri([u32; 4]),
    Tet([u32; 8]),
}
}

Triangle 1→4 refinement is the standard “red” Bey split: insert each edge midpoint, produce four congruent children (three corner-mass + one centre-up). Tetrahedron 1→8 refinement uses a fixed canonical ordering of the six edge midpoints that mirrors Bey’s tet red-refinement scheme.

Refinement API

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub trait RefinementCriterion {
    fn should_refine(&self, cell: &FemCell, vertices: &[Vec3]) -> bool;
}

// Blanket impl for closures: any Fn(&FemCell, &[Vec3]) -> bool works.

pub fn near_point(p: Vec3, radius: Real) -> impl RefinementCriterion;

impl AmrMesh {
    pub fn new(base_mesh: FemMesh) -> Self;
    pub fn refine_uniform(&mut self);
    pub fn refine_where<C: RefinementCriterion>(&mut self, criterion: &C);
    pub fn coarsen_where<C: RefinementCriterion>(&mut self, criterion: &C);
    pub fn flatten(&self) -> FemMesh;
    pub fn flatten_with_remap(&self) -> (FemMesh, HashMap<...>);

    pub fn compute_hanging_nodes(&mut self);
    pub fn enforce_2to1_balance(&mut self);

    pub fn cell_count(&self) -> usize;
    pub fn vert_count(&self) -> usize;
    pub fn cells(&self) -> &[FemCell];
    pub fn hanging_nodes(&self) -> &[HangingNode];
}
}

refine_uniform is the v1 base operation — it refines every leaf once. refine_where is the v2 selective version that takes a criterion. coarsen_where (v4) removes children whose parents are no longer flagged.

Hanging nodes

When two adjacent leaves are at different refinement levels, the fine side’s edge has a midpoint vertex that the coarse side doesn’t. That midpoint is a hanging node:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct HangingNode {
    pub dof: u32,         // AMR vertex id of the constrained midpoint
    pub parents: [u32; 2],// AMR vertex ids of the endpoints
}
}

The P1 constraint imposed is the simple linear interpolation

\[ u_m = \tfrac{1}{2}(u_a + u_b). \]

compute_hanging_nodes walks every leaf-edge that introduces a midpoint and records the constraint. It’s called automatically after every refine_* operation.

ASCII diagram — single hanging node

                                            Hanging node m
                                                  ↓
   Coarse leaf:                  ┌───────────┬───●───┬───────────┐
   one edge a-b                  │           │       │           │
                                 │           ╲       ╱           │
                                 │           │  ╲    ╱           │
                                 a ──────────┴─── m ──────────── b
                                            (Fine edge endpoints: a-m, m-b)

   Constraint: u_m = ½(u_a + u_b)

2:1 balance

The “two cells along a single edge differ in level by at most 1” rule. Larger jumps would produce hanging-node configurations our P1 reducer can’t express (the midpoint of the fine-side edge would itself be a hanging node of a further-refined neighbour, leading to recursive constraints). enforce_2to1_balance walks every leaf, looks for neighbours whose level differs by ≥ 2, and refines the coarser one to bring the difference back to 1. This is called automatically after every refine_where.

Constraint matrix T

The Galerkin reduction \( K_c = T^T K T, , f_c = T^T f \) is the textbook way to handle hanging nodes:

  • \( T \) is (n_total × n_free): maps the free-DoF vector to the full AMR-DoF vector via u_full = T · u_free.
  • For an unconstrained DoF \( i \), row \( i \) of \( T \) is the unit basis vector \( e_i \) — that DoF is its own free variable.
  • For a hanging midpoint \( m \) with parents \( (a, b) \), row \( m \) of \( T \) has entries \( T_{m,a} = T_{m,b} = 1/2 \) — the midpoint is expressed as the average of its parents.

The result: a Galerkin-reduced system on the free DoFs only. The reduced matrix \( K_c \) is SPD if \( K \) is SPD (Galerkin projection preserves symmetric definiteness), so CG works on it directly.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn assemble_global_amr<F>(
    amr_mesh: &AmrMesh,
    space: FunctionSpace,
    local_fn: F,
    f_full: Option<&[Real]>,
) -> Result<(BsrMatrix, Vec<Real>, BsrMatrix)>;  // (K_c, f_c, T)
}

The caller is responsible for applying Dirichlet BCs to the reduced system — the textbook ordering is constraint-reduce first, BC-pin second. After solving \( K_c u_{\text{free}} = f_c \), the full-DoF solution is recovered via the sparse matvec u = T · u_free.

Helper:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn tt_times_vector(t: &BsrMatrix, v: &[Real]) -> Vec<Real>;
pub fn compute_ttkt(t: &BsrMatrix, k: &BsrMatrix) -> Result<BsrMatrix>;
}

compute_ttkt is useful when the caller has assembled K separately (e.g. for a P2 problem) and wants to reduce it against a T built by AmrMesh::build_constraint_matrix.

DG-AMR face matching — Stage 45 v3

For DG fields, the constraint at a 2:1-balanced face split is that the numerical-flux integral over the parent face (computed from the coarse side’s basis) equals the sum of flux integrals over the child sub-faces (each from the refined side’s basis).

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct DgAmrFaceMatch {
    pub parent_cell: u32,
    pub parent_face: Vec<u32>,         // 2 or 3 verts
    pub child_faces: Vec<Vec<u32>>,    // child sub-faces
}

pub fn compute_dg_amr_faces(amr_mesh: &AmrMesh) -> Vec<DgAmrFaceMatch>;
}
  • Tri (2D): parent edge [a, b] ⇒ children [a, m], [m, b].
  • Tet (3D): parent triangle [a, b, c] ⇒ four sub-triangles from the red-split inserting midpoints on each edge.

The DG flux assembler then walks both interior faces (one cell on each side, same level) and the AMR face matches (one cell on the coarse side, several on the fine side) and adds the right per-face block to the global system.

Coarsening + Krylov restart — Stage 45 v4

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn coarsen_where<C: RefinementCriterion>(&mut self, criterion: &C);
pub fn transfer_state(&self, old: &AmrMesh, u_old: &[Real]) -> Vec<Real>;
}

coarsen_where marks children for removal (the is_removed flag) but keeps them in the flat pool for index stability. Removed cells are skipped by every leaf-walk (flatten, compute_hanging_nodes, …); the refined_cells list has the corresponding entries trimmed so clients iterating it see only currently-active refinements.

transfer_state interpolates a solution from an old AmrMesh to a new one — used by the Krylov restart workflow:

  1. Run iterative solver on coarse mesh to partial convergence.
  2. Refine where the residual indicator says.
  3. Transfer current iterate to the new mesh via transfer_state.
  4. Use it as the warm start for the new-mesh CG.

This is how the AmrHeat viewer scene (#100) gets to a sharp near-source profile without paying for a global fine mesh.

DG-AMR coarsening — Stage 45 v5

Stage 45 v5 adds two pieces needed by transient DG-AMR runs:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn AmrMesh::coarsen_subtree(&mut self, parent_idx: usize) -> Result<()>;

pub fn project_dg_p1_tri_children_to_parent_l2(
    parent: &FemCell,
    children: &[FemCell],
    vertices: &[Vec3],
    child_values: &[[Real; 3]],
) -> Result<[Real; 3]>;
}

coarsen_subtree collapses a deep refinement tree from the leaves upward before coarsening the requested parent, so callers do not have to manually un-refine every descendant first.

project_dg_p1_tri_children_to_parent_l2 is the DG coarsening transfer operator for triangle P1 fields. It solves the parent mass projection

∫_parent N_i u_parent dx = Σ_child ∫_child N_i u_child dx

using the degree-2-exact triangle quadrature rule, so linear DG fields survive child-to-parent coarsening exactly.

Cross-references

  • Mesh — FemMesh is what AmrMesh wraps.
  • Assembly — assemble_global_amr extends the standard scatter with the constraint reduction.
  • DG flux — DG-AMR face matching feeds the same per-face block routines.
  • Multigrid — uses AmrMesh::refine_uniform to build the geometric multigrid hierarchy.
  • BC — applied to the reduced system after T^T K T.

GPU linear elasticity

crates/molla-fem/src/elasticity_gpu.rs is the end-to-end GPU port of the linear-elasticity solve. It builds the BC-reduced sparsity pattern on CPU, hands it to the GPU via FemGpuData, dispatches a WGSL kernel that computes the 144 per-cell Bᵀ D B values, and solves \( K u = f \) on a fully GPU-resident CG. The CPU never sees the assembled K values — only the sparsity pattern, the RHS, and the BC indices cross the host bound.

Why pattern on CPU, values on GPU?

The sparsity-pattern build via BsrMatrix::from_scalar_triplets is an \( O(\mathrm{nnz} \cdot \log \mathrm{nnz}) \) sort-and-dedupe. Even at 16³ tet resolution this is sub-millisecond and dominated by the underlying mesh-graph traversal — the host CPU does it fine. The expensive part — computing the 144 values of every per-cell \( K_e = \int_K B^T D B , dV \) (4 verts × 3 dofs)² for a tet — is what moves to the GPU kernel.

API

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[cfg(feature = "gpu")]
pub fn build_elasticity_gpu_pattern(
    mesh: &FemMesh,
    dim: usize,
    bcs: &[BoundaryCondition],
) -> Result<(BsrMatrix, Vec<u32>)>;  // (k_pattern, bc_mask)

#[cfg(feature = "gpu")]
pub fn assemble_elasticity_gpu_only(
    engine: &Engine,
    mesh: &FemMesh,
    youngs: Real,
    poisson: Real,
    dim: usize,
    k_pattern: &BsrMatrix,
    bc_mask: &[u32],
) -> Result<FemGpuData>;

#[cfg(feature = "gpu")]
pub fn solve_elasticity_gpu(
    engine: &Engine,
    mesh: &FemMesh,
    youngs: Real,
    poisson: Real,
    dim: usize,
    bcs: &[BoundaryCondition],
    f: &[Real],
) -> Result<ElasticityGpuResult>;

pub struct ElasticityGpuResult {
    pub u: Vec<Real>,
    pub iters: usize,
    pub residual: Real,
}
}

Pattern construction

build_elasticity_gpu_pattern produces a BsrMatrix with the correct row_offsets and col_idx arrays but whose values already encode the BC-reduced \( K \):

  • BC rows contain 1.0 on the diagonal and 0.0 elsewhere.
  • Non-BC rows are zero — waiting for the GPU assembly kernel to scatter their contributions.

The function works by:

  1. Assembling the unreduced \( K \) on CPU with dummy ones for every element entry — we only need the column-structure, not the values — by calling compute_element_elasticity_stiffness(c, v, λ=0, μ=1).
  2. Running apply_bcs to fold the BC structure in (so the column elimination updates the pattern).
  3. Wiping k_pattern.values to zero.
  4. Setting values[diag(r)] = 1.0 for every pinned row r.

The returned bc_mask: Vec<u32> marks which rows are pinned (bc_mask[r] == 1).

Assembly kernel

assemble_elasticity_gpu_only uploads the mesh + pattern via FemGpuData::upload, then dispatches the fem_elasticity_assemble.wgsl kernel — one workgroup per cell:

@compute @workgroup_size(1)
fn assemble_cell(@builtin(global_invocation_id) gid: vec3<u32>) {
    let cell_idx = gid.x;
    // Read 4 vertex positions, compute Bᵀ D B for this cell,
    // scatter the 144 (i, j) entries into the global CSR.
    // Skip rows where bc_mask[row] == 1.
}

The kernel:

  1. Reads the 4 vertex positions of the cell.
  2. Computes the tet’s volume and the 4 shape-gradient Vec3s (inverse-transpose of D matrix).
  3. Builds the local 6 × 12 \( \mathbf{B} \) (Voigt notation) and the 12 × 12 product \( B^T D B \cdot \text{vol} \) in registers.
  4. For each (i, j) entry in the 12 × 12, looks up the slot in the global CSR col_idx and atomicAdds the value into csr_values[slot].
  5. Skips the scatter for any row where bc_mask[row] == 1 — those stay at identity-row values.

The slot lookup is a linear scan over the row’s col_idx window (small — bounded by the per-row nnz, typically 4–10 for a tet mesh) so the kernel is simple enough to stay efficient without a hash table.

BC handling — asymmetric in v1

The v1 elasticity_gpu path leaves an asymmetric reduced matrix:

  • BC rows are pinned (diagonal = 1, off-diagonals = 0).
  • BC columns of non-BC rows are not zeroed.

The correctness argument: BC rows are decoupled (zero off-diagonals, identity diagonal, RHS = BC value), so CG never moves them away from the seeded value. For zero BC values (the cantilever-clamp case), the non-zero entries in BC columns multiply by zero displacement in every matvec — harmless.

For non-zero BC values, the caller must pre-compute the f correction f[i] -= K_full[i, r] · v_bc[r] on CPU and pass the corrected RHS. This v1 helper assumes the caller already did that (e.g. by running apply_bcs on the host before calling us). A follow-up stage would add an explicit symmetric column-zeroing kernel.

Solve loop

solve_elasticity_gpu wires everything together:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let (k_pattern, bc_mask) = build_elasticity_gpu_pattern(mesh, dim, bcs)?;
let k_gpu = assemble_elasticity_gpu_only(engine, mesh, E, ν, dim, &k_pattern, &bc_mask)?;
let result = solve_steady_state_gpu_resident_pcg(
    &k_gpu, &f_red, &bcs_for_init_guess,
    engine, max_iters, tol)?;
}

— so the per-iteration cost is one GPU sparse-matvec, one inv-diag apply (Jacobi preconditioner), and a handful of GPU dot-products. The Stage 41 v1 measurement on a 16³ tet cantilever (4913 vertices, 14739 DoFs) was ~25 ms per Newton iteration on RTX 4080, vs ~200 ms on CPU — about 8× speedup, dominated by the per-cell Bᵀ D B arithmetic on GPU.

Validation

The contract tests in crates/molla-fem/tests/fem_elasticity_gpu.rs compare GPU vs CPU on a fixed cantilever fixture:

  • Same K values to ~1e-4 relative (f32 vs f64).
  • Same u (post-solve) to ~1e-3 relative — within the documented GPU CG tolerance.
  • Same total strain energy.

Cross-references

  • Elasticity element kernel — the math the GPU kernel mirrors.
  • Assembly — the CPU pattern builder.
  • BC — the reducer that produces the initial values for the pattern.
  • GPU steppers (Slice H) — the resident-CG plumbing the elasticity solver chains into.
  • GPU data — FemGpuData uploads the BSR + mesh in one shot.

Magnetostatics — H(curl) Nedelec edge elements

Stage 46 brought H(curl)-conforming first-order Nedelec edge elements to molla, with a steady-state curl–curl solver for magnetostatics. The element basis lives in crates/molla-fem/src/nedelec_element.rs; the magnetostatics solver is in magneto.rs.

Why edge elements?

For PDEs in \( H(\mathrm{curl}) = { v \in L^2 : \mathrm{curl}, v \in L^2 } \) the natural conforming basis has tangential continuity across element interfaces — the tangential component matches on shared faces, the normal component is free to jump. This is exactly what magnetostatics (vector potential \( \mathbf{A} \)) and time-harmonic electromagnetics need: the curl operator is well-defined globally, but \( \nabla \cdot \mathbf{A} \) is not constrained and \( \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{A} \) has no physical meaning at material interfaces.

Nodal (H¹) elements over-constrain such problems by enforcing continuity of all components; they produce spurious “ghost solutions” that pollute the spectrum. Edge elements eliminate these by construction: the kernel of curl over the discrete H(curl) space is exactly the discrete gradient of H¹ scalar fields (the discrete de Rham complex).

The first-order Nedelec basis

On a tetrahedron with barycentric coordinates \( \lambda_0, \lambda_1, \lambda_2, \lambda_3 \) and constant barycentric gradients \( \nabla \lambda_k \), the lowest-order Nedelec basis (also called Whitney 1-forms) is one function per edge:

\[ \mathbf{N}_{(i, j)}(\mathbf{x}) = \lambda_i \nabla \lambda_j - \lambda_j \nabla \lambda_i \]

for edge \( e = (i, j) \). Properties:

  • \( \mathbf{N}_e \) is linear in \( \mathbf{x} \) (since \( \lambda_k \) are linear and the gradients constant).
  • The tangential component of \( \mathbf{N}_e \) along edge \( (i, j) \) is constant and integrates to 1 along that edge. Along every other edge it integrates to 0 — so the DoF value naturally represents the tangential-line integral of the field along the edge.
  • The curl is constant per element: \( \nabla \times \mathbf{N}_e = 2 \nabla \lambda_i \times \nabla \lambda_j \).

Edge orientation convention

Every unique mesh edge is stored canonically as [min, max] (see compute_edges). The corresponding global Nedelec basis function is the one that “points” from the lower-indexed vertex to the higher-indexed vertex.

When a cell’s local edge \( k \) (in the TET_EDGES ordering) has local endpoints \( (a, b) \) mapping to global vertices \( (v_a, v_b) \), the local basis \( \mathbf{N}_{\mathrm{loc}} = \lambda_a \nabla \lambda_b - \lambda_b \nabla \lambda_a \) points from local \( a \) to local \( b \). To express it in the global basis we apply an orientation sign:

\[ \mathbf{N}{\mathrm{glob}} = \mathrm{sign} \cdot \mathbf{N}{\mathrm{loc}}, \quad \mathrm{sign} = \begin{cases} +1 & v_a < v_b \ -1 & v_a > v_b \end{cases} \]

Element matrices computed in the local-edge basis are converted to the global-edge basis during assembly by multiplying entry \( (i, j) \) by \( \mathrm{sign}_i \cdot \mathrm{sign}_j \) — equivalently, absorbing the sign into the per-DoF scatter.

NedelecDofMap

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct NedelecDofMap {
    pub edge_id: HashMap<[u32; 2], u32>,
    pub edge_count: usize,
}

impl NedelecDofMap {
    pub fn build(mesh: &FemMesh) -> Self;
    pub fn ndof(&self) -> usize;                       // edge_count
    pub fn edge_dof(&self, a: u32, b: u32) -> usize;   // [min, max] lookup
    pub fn edge_sign(cell: &FemCell, local_edge: usize) -> Real;
}
}

Element matrices

Mass — closed-form

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn compute_element_nedelec_mass(cell: &FemCell, vertices: &[Vec3]) -> Vec<Vec<Real>>;
}

The closed-form integral \( \int_K \lambda_p \lambda_q , dV = \frac{(1 + \delta_{pq})}{20} \cdot |K| \) combined with the constant gradients \( \nabla \lambda_k \) lets us write the mass entries directly without a quadrature loop:

\[ M_{e_1, e_2} = |K| \cdot \big[ c(j,l) \nabla \lambda_i \cdot \nabla \lambda_k

  • c(j,k) \nabla \lambda_i \cdot \nabla \lambda_l
  • c(i,l) \nabla \lambda_j \cdot \nabla \lambda_k
  • c(i,k) \nabla \lambda_j \cdot \nabla \lambda_l \big] \]

with \( e_1 = (i, j), e_2 = (k, l) \) and \( c(p, q) = (1 + \delta_{pq})/20 \).

Curl-curl stiffness

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn compute_element_curl_curl(cell, vertices, nu) -> Vec<Vec<Real>>;
}

Since the curl of a Whitney 1-form is constant per element:

\[ \nabla \times \mathbf{N}_{(i, j)} = 2 , \nabla \lambda_i \times \nabla \lambda_j, \]

the curl-curl integral collapses to

\[ K_{e_1, e_2} = 4 \nu \cdot |K| \cdot (\nabla \lambda_i \times \nabla \lambda_j) \cdot (\nabla \lambda_k \times \nabla \lambda_l) \]

— one cross product per entry, no quadrature. nu is the magnetic reluctivity \( \nu = 1/\mu \); for free space pass \( 1/\mu_0 \approx 7.958 \times 10^5 \) in SI units, or just 1.0 in non-dimensional units.

Nedelec assembly

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn assemble_global_nedelec<F>(
    mesh: &FemMesh,
    map: &NedelecDofMap,
    element_visitor: F,
) -> Result<BsrMatrix>;
}

Walks every cell, calls the visitor for the local 6×6 matrix in local-edge basis, then scatters entry \( (i, j) \) to global edge DoFs (edge_dof(...), edge_dof(...)) multiplied by \( \mathrm{sign}_i \cdot \mathrm{sign}_j \). The assemble_global entry point in assembly auto-routes here when FunctionSpace::NedelecEdge { order } is passed.

Magnetostatics solver

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn solve_magnetostatics_steady(
    mesh: &FemMesh,
    nu_per_cell: &[Real],
    j_source: &[Vec3],
    bcs: &[BoundaryCondition],
    max_iters: usize,
    tol: Real,
) -> Result<MagnetostaticsResult>;

pub struct MagnetostaticsResult {
    pub a: Vec<Real>,     // vector potential, one DoF per edge
    pub residual: Real,
    pub iters: usize,
}
}

Solves the steady-state curl–curl equation for the magnetic vector potential \( \mathbf{A} \):

\[ \nabla \times (\nu , \nabla \times \mathbf{A}) = \mathbf{J} \quad \text{in } \Omega, \quad \mathbf{n} \times \mathbf{A} = 0 \quad \text{on } \partial \Omega, \]

The “perfect conductor” boundary condition \( \mathbf{n} \times \mathbf{A} = 0 \) is the natural BC for the vector potential — in Nedelec DoFs it’s simply \( A_e = 0 \) for every edge on the mesh boundary (handled via strong Dirichlet).

Gauge fixing

The continuous curl-curl operator has a non-trivial kernel: every pure gradient \( \mathbf{A} = \nabla \phi \) is annihilated. On the discrete level the kernel is exactly the discrete gradient of P1 nodal scalars (lowest-order de Rham complex).

For a magnetostatics problem with a divergence-free source \( \nabla \cdot \mathbf{J} = 0 \) and fully-Dirichlet boundary on \( \partial \Omega \), the gradient kernel is killed at the boundary and what remains is gauge-equivalent. We don’t enforce Coulomb gauge \( \nabla \cdot \mathbf{A} = 0 \) explicitly — it’s not required to recover the physically meaningful \( \mathbf{B} = \nabla \times \mathbf{A} \).

In practice a tiny mass regularisation \( \varepsilon M \) (with \( \varepsilon \ll \nu / L^2 \)) is added to nudge CG towards a unique solution; the bias on \( \mathbf{B} \) is \( O(\varepsilon) \) and below the discretisation error.

Helper utilities

pub fn compute_curl_per_cell(mesh, map, a) -> Vec<Vec3>;

pub fn integrate_field_along_edges<F>(mesh, map, field: F) -> Vec<Real>;
}

compute_curl_per_cell recovers \( \mathbf{B} = \nabla \times \mathbf{A} \) as one Vec3 per cell — used by the Magnetostatics viewer scene (#101) to render a B-field arrow at every cell centroid.

project_field_on_edges projects a vector field given as a closure \( \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}) \) onto the Nedelec DoFs (tangential-line integrals along edges). Used for L²-projecting an analytic test field.

integrate_field_along_edges integrates a vector field along each mesh edge — useful for setting Dirichlet boundary values from a known \( \mathbf{A}_{\text{ref}} \).

The Stage 46 test magnetostatics_solenoid_axial_field builds a cylindrical current loop, solves the magnetostatics system, and verifies that the recovered \( \mathbf{B} \) on the symmetry axis matches the analytic solenoid formula \( B_z = \mu_0 , I , n \) inside, decaying to zero outside, within ~5 % at the 16³ tet resolution.

Cross-references

  • Eddy currents — the time-harmonic Maxwell extension uses the same Nedelec basis.
  • Mesh / function spaces — the NedelecEdge { order: 1 } variant.
