Eddy currents — time-harmonic Maxwell

Stage 48 added a time-harmonic eddy-current solver on top of the H(curl) Nedelec basis from magnetostatics. It lives in crates/molla-fem/src/eddy_current.rs (~1450 lines, including the AMS preconditioner) and solves the complex curl–curl–mass system that arises from the Fourier transform of Maxwell’s equations.

Problem statement

Solve the time-harmonic vector-potential equation

\[ \nabla \times (\nu , \nabla \times \mathbf{A}) + i \omega \sigma \mathbf{A} - \omega^2 \varepsilon \mathbf{A} = \mathbf{J} \quad \text{in } \Omega \]

with \( \mathbf{n} \times \mathbf{A} = 0 \) on \( \partial \Omega \), where:

  • \( \mathbf{A} = \mathbf{A}{\text{re}} + i \mathbf{A}{\text{im}} \) is the complex magnetic vector potential (one tangential DoF per mesh edge in each of the real and imaginary parts).
  • \( \nu = 1/\mu \) is the magnetic reluctivity (real, per cell).
  • \( \sigma \) is the electric conductivity (real, per cell — only the conductor cells have non-zero values).
  • \( \omega = 2\pi f \) is the angular frequency (a single global scalar).
  • \( \mathbf{J} = \mathbf{J}{\text{re}} + i \mathbf{J}{\text{im}} \) is the source current density (one complex Vec3 per cell).
  • \( \varepsilon \) is electric permittivity (typically negligible at the frequencies of interest; included for completeness).

The off-diagonal \( i \omega \sigma \mathbf{A} \) term couples real and imaginary parts — this is the skin-effect mechanism that causes high-frequency fields to decay exponentially into a conductor.

Block-real reformulation

The complex unknown is split into \( (\mathbf{a}{\text{re}}, \mathbf{a}{\text{im}}) \in \mathbb{R}^{2N} \) (where \( N \) is the number of edges). Writing the curl–curl block as \( K_{\text{curl}} \) and the Nedelec mass scaled by conductivity as \( M_\sigma \), the discrete weak form becomes

\[ \begin{cases} K_{\text{curl}} \mathbf{a}{\text{re}} - \omega M\sigma \mathbf{a}{\text{im}} = \mathbf{f}{\text{re}} \ \omega M_\sigma \mathbf{a}{\text{re}} + K{\text{curl}} \mathbf{a}{\text{im}} = \mathbf{f}{\text{im}} \end{cases} \]

i.e. in block form:

\[ \begin{pmatrix} K_{\text{main}} & K_{\text{off}} \ -K_{\text{off}} & K_{\text{main}} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{a}{\text{re}} \ \mathbf{a}{\text{im}} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{f}{\text{re}} \ \mathbf{f}{\text{im}} \end{pmatrix} \]

with \( K_{\text{main}} = K_{\text{curl}} + \varepsilon M_N \) (tiny mass regularisation for the gradient gauge — same trick as magnetostatics) and \( K_{\text{off}} = -\omega M_\sigma \).

The full \( 2N \times 2N \) system is non-symmetric when \( M_\sigma \ne 0 \), so we use restartable GMRES instead of CG.

Solvers — three paths

solve_eddy_current_steady (v1) — Jacobi-preconditioned GMRES

The simplest path: build the block-real 2N × 2N system, extract its diagonal as the Jacobi preconditioner, and run restartable GMRES. This works on any system and is the right starting point for correctness validation. For the v1 skin-depth contract test, it converges in ~50 GMRES iterations.

solve_eddy_current_steady_ams (v2) — Auxiliary-Maxwell Solver

For larger systems the Jacobi preconditioner stalls because the curl-null space (gradients of P1 scalars) is left unaddressed. The Auxiliary Maxwell Solver (Hiptmair–Xu 2007) decomposes the preconditioning into:

  1. A “scalar auxiliary” Poisson solve in the H¹ space (handled by the multigrid hierarchy) — corrects the gradient component.
  2. A “vector auxiliary” Poisson solve in the P1 vector space — corrects the divergence-free component.
  3. A Jacobi smoother on the edge DoFs themselves.

The combination is provably mesh-independent under the discrete Helmholtz decomposition — iteration count stays bounded as h → 0.

build_discrete_gradient, build_p1_vector_interpolation, and build_p1_vector_laplacian are the ingredients:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn build_discrete_gradient(mesh: &FemMesh) -> Result<BsrMatrix>;
pub fn build_p1_vector_interpolation(mesh: &FemMesh) -> Result<BsrMatrix>;
pub fn build_p1_vector_laplacian(mesh: &FemMesh, dim: usize) -> Result<BsrMatrix>;
}

The first returns the discrete gradient \( G : \mathbb{R}^{n_{\text{verts}}} \to \mathbb{R}^{n_{\text{edges}}} \) that maps a nodal scalar to its tangential edge-integral (entries \( \pm 1 \) only — orientation-dependent). The second returns the Π interpolation \( \Pi : (P1)^3 \to \text{Nedelec} \) whose edge row integrates the average endpoint vector field along the canonical edge: \( (\Pi u)_e = \frac{1}{2}(u_a + u_b) \cdot (x_b - x_a) \). The third assembles the \( \mu \int \nabla u : \nabla v \) Laplacian on P1 vector space.

Stage 48 v5 enables the Π branch in AmsPreconditioner::apply by default. The preconditioner now combines edge Jacobi smoothing, the scalar gradient branch, and the vector-nodal Π branch. The latter uses a fixed-iteration CG solve on the pinned vector-P1 Laplacian so the overall preconditioner remains linear for GMRES. For compatibility experiments, AmsPreconditioner::with_pi_projection(false) restores the old gradient-only action.

solve_eddy_current_steady_ams_mg (v3) — AMS + Multigrid V-cycle

The v3 path replaces the auxiliary-block scalar solver with a geometric multigrid V-cycle on a uniformly refined mesh hierarchy. See multigrid for the V-cycle structure. Empirically this cuts the iteration count on the larger eddy fixtures (32³ tets) by 4–5× over the v2 fixed-iter CG.

solve_eddy_current_steady_ams_block (v6) — block-coupled AMS

The v6 path targets high ωσ, where the off-diagonal ±ω M_σ block dominates and a purely block-diagonal preconditioner stalls. It keeps the AMS action as the approximate inverse for K_main, but applies a fixed number of stationary refinement sweeps against the full block-real operator:

z0    = D^-1 r
z{i+1}= z{i} + D^-1 (r - A z{i})

where D^-1 means “apply AMS independently to the real and imaginary halves”. Because EddyCurrentConfig::block_precond_sweeps is fixed for the whole solve, this is still a linear preconditioner and remains safe inside GMRES. block_precond_sweeps = 1 recovers the old decoupled action; the default is 2.

Frequency sweeps and Coulomb-gauge projection

solve_eddy_current_frequency_sweep runs the same problem over a list of angular frequencies, using one of:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub enum EddyCurrentSolveMode {
    Jacobi,
    Ams,
    AmsBlock,
}
}

Each returned EddyFrequencySweepSample records the sampled omega, the EddyCurrentResult, and the remaining discrete gauge residual. When gauge enforcement is requested, both real and imaginary edge potentials are projected by solving

(G^T G) φ = G^T a
a_gauge = a - Gφ

where G is the discrete P1-to-Nedelec gradient. Pinned edge values are restored after projection, so boundary Dirichlet conditions are preserved. This removes the report-facing gradient ambiguity without changing the curl field used by the physical validation tests.

AmsPreconditioner

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct AmsPreconditioner {
    g: BsrMatrix,                 // discrete gradient
    k_aux_scalar: BsrMatrix,      // H¹ Laplacian
    pi: BsrMatrix,                // vector-P1 -> Nedelec interpolation
    k_aux_vector: BsrMatrix,      // P1 vector Laplacian
    diag_smoother: Vec<Real>,     // Jacobi smoother diagonal
    aux_solver: AuxSolver,        // CG or V-cycle
    mg_hierarchy: Option<MeshHierarchy>,
    mg_cycles_per_apply: usize,
}

impl AmsPreconditioner {
    pub fn build(mesh, map, k_main, n_aux_iters, ...) -> Result<Self>;
    pub fn apply(&self, r: &[Real]) -> Vec<Real>;
}
}

apply(r) computes \( M^{-1} r \) where \( M^{-1} \) is the AMS preconditioner action — three sub-steps fused into one call. The mg_hierarchy slot is None for the v2 path and Some(...) for v3.

EddyBlockOp — block-real GMRES operator

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct EddyBlockOp<'a> {
    k_main: &'a BsrMatrix,
    k_off: &'a BsrMatrix,
    n: usize,
}
}

implements the LinearOperator trait expected by gmres — exposes mv(x, y) over the block layout x = [a_re ; a_im], y = [...]. This is the way to avoid actually assembling the full \( 2N \times 2N \) matrix (which would double the memory cost) — instead we just dispatch two scalar matvecs per block-matvec.

Skin-depth contract test

The Stage 48 test eddy_current_skin_depth_decay solves the eddy-current problem in a conducting half-space with a tangential boundary current at the free surface. The analytic solution decays exponentially with depth at the skin depth

\[ \delta = \sqrt{\frac{2}{\omega \mu \sigma}}. \]

At the test frequency (\( f = 60 \) Hz, copper-like \( \sigma = 5.96 \times 10^7 \) S/m, \( \mu = \mu_0 \)), \( \delta \approx 8.5 \) mm. The solver matches the analytic decay profile to ~3 % at 16³ tet resolution and within a few percent of the phase shift between real and imaginary parts.

gmres_with_precond

pub fn gmres_with_precond<P>(

    config: IterConfig,
) -> CgResult
where
    P: Fn(&[Real]) -> Vec<Real>;

A generic restartable GMRES driver that takes any LinearOperator + any preconditioner closure. Used internally by the eddy-current solver but exposed publicly so callers with their own non-symmetric systems can reuse it.

  • Magnetostatics — the curl-curl machinery that this builds on (steady, real case).
  • Nedelec basis — the edge-element basis.

Multigrid and AMG

crates/molla-fem/src/multigrid.rs ships geometric multigrid (Stage 48 v3) on a uniformly refined mesh hierarchy. The AMS preconditioner uses one V-cycle in place of its inner CG solve. Algebraic multigrid (AMG, Ruge–Stüben — Stage 48 v4) is queued; the module docs lay out exactly what it needs.

MeshHierarchy

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct MeshHierarchy {
    pub meshes: Vec<FemMesh>,           // coarsest first
    pub laplacians: Vec<BsrMatrix>,     // per-level scalar Laplacian
    pub prolongations: Vec<BsrMatrix>,  // level i → i+1
    pub pinned_per_level: Vec<Vec<u32>>,
    pub jacobi_omega: Real,             // ω = 2/3 default
    pub pre_smooth: usize,              // 3 by default
    pub post_smooth: usize,              // 3 by default
    /* hidden: coarsest_chol, coarsest_n */
}
}

All matrices are sized for scalar P1 (one DoF per vertex). The AMS auxiliary problem is scalar P1, so we don’t need the vector form here.

Hierarchy construction

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn build(
    base_mesh: &FemMesh,
    n_refines: usize,
    pinned_vertices_finest: &[u32],
) -> Result<Self>;
}

Procedure:

  1. Build the AmrMesh via repeated refine_uniform — n_refines times. Each level has 8^n_refines times more tet cells than the base.
  2. Identify the pinned positions on the finest mesh. At coarser levels, a vertex is pinned iff its physical position matches (within pin_tol = 1e-9) at least one pinned position on the finest mesh. This is exact for uniform refinement (every coarse vertex survives in every finer mesh).
  3. If pinned_vertices_finest is empty, pin vertex 0 of every level to break the constant-vector nullspace (so Laplacians become SPD and dense Cholesky on the coarsest level succeeds).
  4. Build prolongation operators \( P_i : V_i \to V_{i+1} \) via P1 barycentric interpolation — for each fine vertex, find the coarse tet containing it, write (1, 4) entries with the barycentric weights of that tet’s vertices.
  5. Build per-level Laplacians. Level 0 is assembled directly; each coarser level above 0 is built via Galerkin coarsening \( K_{i-1} = P^T K_i P \) using compute_ttkt.
  6. Apply per-level pinning (symmetric row + column elimination — same trick as apply_bcs).
  7. Pre-factorise the coarsest Laplacian via dense Cholesky and cache the lower-triangle. Each V-cycle’s coarsest solve is then two triangular sweeps.

V-cycle

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl MeshHierarchy {
    pub fn v_cycle(&self, r: &[Real]) -> Vec<Real>;
    pub fn solve_to(&self, b: &[Real], tol: Real, max_cycles: usize) -> Vec<Real>;
}
}

Standard geometric V-cycle on level \( \ell \):

v_cycle(level, b):
    if level == 0:
        return cholesky_solve(b)
    u ← 0
    for _ in 0..pre_smooth:
        u ← jacobi_step(u, b, ω)
    r ← b − K[level] · u
    r_coarse ← Pᵀ · r
    e_coarse ← v_cycle(level − 1, r_coarse)
    u += P · e_coarse
    for _ in 0..post_smooth:
        u ← jacobi_step(u, b, ω)
    return u

jacobi_step is the damped Jacobi sweep \( u \leftarrow u + \omega D^{-1}(b - K u) \) with default \( \omega = 2/3 \) — optimal-ish for the P1 Laplacian spectrum.

The pre-smooth + restrict + recurse + prolong + post-smooth pattern is symmetric in the symmetric-smoother sense, so the resulting preconditioner action is symmetric — required for the AMS path to preserve coercivity.

Integration with AMS

In AmsPreconditioner::apply(r), when the optional mg_hierarchy: Option<MeshHierarchy> is set, the inner K_aux · w = r_aux solve uses one V-cycle instead of the v2 fixed-iter CG. Linearity is preserved (each call applies exactly mg_cycles_per_apply V-cycles, defaulting to 1), so the AMS-MG preconditioner is still linear and CG / GMRES converge.

AMG — Ruge-Stüben (Stage 48 v4, queued)

The module docstring lays out exactly what an algebraic-multigrid extension needs:

1. C/F splitting

Classify rows as C (coarse) or F (fine) using the Ruge-Stüben strong-connection criterion:

\[ |A_{ij}| \ge \theta \cdot \max_{k \ne i} |A_{ik}| \]

with typical \( \theta = 0.25 \). Greedily promote C candidates by independent-set heuristic on the strong-connection graph.

2. Interpolation operator

For each F row, build the interpolation row as a weighted sum of strong-C neighbours. Standard formula:

\[ P_{F, C} = -\frac{A_{F, C}}{\sum_{C’} -A_{F, C’}} \]

with off-diagonal F → F contributions distributed onto the C neighbours (the “classical” interpolation).

3. Galerkin product

Same \( P^T A P \) as the geometric path, but with the algebraic P from step 2 instead of geometric P1 interpolation. Reuses compute_ttkt from amr_mesh.

4. Smoother choice

Gauss-Seidel typically beats Jacobi for algebraic problems where the matrix has stronger off-diagonal structure than the geometric Laplacian. A red-black ordering (or symmetric forward + backward GS) is needed for V-cycle symmetry.

5. Coarsening termination

Stop coarsening when the coarse matrix has ≤ 100–1000 rows (dense direct-solve cutoff).

Wiring

The AMS-MG path in AmsPreconditioner does not need to change for v4 — it already accepts an arbitrary MeshHierarchy, so swapping geometric → algebraic coarsening is a self-contained MeshHierarchy::build_from_matrix(K, ...) constructor.

Cost / scaling

For the AMS-MG path on a 32³ tet eddy-current problem (~125 k edges):

SolverGMRES itersTime/iterTotal
Jacobi-PCG~5002 ms1.0 s
AMS (v2, fixed-iter CG aux)~308 ms240 ms
AMS-MG (v3, V-cycle aux)~254 ms100 ms

The V-cycle per-iter cost is lower than CG because the cheaper Jacobi smoother + direct coarse solve replaces an inner CG loop of ~30 iterations. Algebraic MG (v4) is expected to bring further wins on the 64³ test, especially in the presence of jumps in \( \nu \) / \( \sigma \) coefficients that geometric MG handles poorly.

Cross-references

  • Eddy currents — the consumer of MeshHierarchy.
  • Magnetostatics — same scalar Laplacian feeds both.
  • AMR — compute_ttkt and the uniform-refinement primitives MeshHierarchy::build calls.
  • Solvers — cg_solve is the iterative driver that uses the V-cycle as a preconditioner.

Non-conforming meshes — L² projection and contact

Two FEM meshes that share no DoFs need a transfer operator to move a scalar field from one to the other. The textbook recipe is L² projection mediated by a cross-mesh mass matrix, which lives in crates/molla-fem/src/nonconforming.rs. Stages 47 v1–v4 cover scalar projection, vector projection, surface-only (contact) variant, and a penalty-contact force that integrates against it.

The math

For source mesh \( S \) (carrying \( u_S \)) and target mesh \( T \) (where we want \( u_T \)):

\[ M_{ts}^{st} = \int_T \phi_t^T(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \phi_s^S(\mathbf{x}) , d\mathbf{x}, \quad M_{tt} = \int_T \phi_t^T \cdot \phi_t^T , d\mathbf{x}, \quad u_T = M_{tt}^{-1} , M_{st} , u_S. \]

  • \( M_{st} \) is rectangular (n_target × n_source). It’s the “cross-mesh mass” — couples a target scalar DoF to a source scalar DoF.
  • \( M_{tt} \) is the target mesh’s own consistent mass matrix (SPD, square, CG-solvable).
  • The integral that defines \( M_{st} \) is computed on the target cells — that way \( \phi_t^T \) is a simple polynomial in each integration sub-domain, and we only need to evaluate \( \phi_s^S \) at each quadrature point via barycentric tet-location in the source mesh.

Properties (P1 nodal, target-side quadrature)

  • Constant reproduction. \( u_S \equiv 1 \Rightarrow u_T \equiv 1 \) exactly (modulo CG tolerance). The reason: \( M_{st} \cdot \mathbf{1}S \) reproduces the target lumped row sums \( \int \phi_t^T \cdot \sum_j \phi_j^S , dx = \int \phi_t^T , dx \), which is also \( M{tt} \cdot \mathbf{1}_T \).
  • Linear reproduction. With degree ≥ 2 quadrature, the projection is exact on affine source fields up to floating-point round-off (P1 contains all affine functions exactly, and the L² projector onto a space that includes the source field is the identity).
  • Quadratic loss. A quadratic source field is not in P1, so the projection introduces an \( O(h^2) \) error; halving \( h \) cuts the error by ~4× — the standard P1 best-approximation rate.

NonconformingField

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct NonconformingField<'a> {
    pub source: &'a FemMesh,
    pub target: &'a FemMesh,
    coupling_matrix: BsrMatrix,   // M_st  (n_target × n_source)
    target_mass: BsrMatrix,       // M_tt  (n_target × n_target)
    domain: IntegrationDomain,    // Volume or Surface
}

impl<'a> NonconformingField<'a> {
    pub fn new(source: &'a FemMesh, target: &'a FemMesh) -> Result<Self>;
    pub fn new_surface(source: &'a FemMesh, target: &'a FemMesh) -> Result<Self>;
    pub fn project(&self, u_source: &[Real]) -> Result<Vec<Real>>;
    pub fn project_vector(&self, u_source: &[Real], dim: usize) -> Result<Vec<Real>>;
    pub fn is_surface(&self) -> bool;
}
}

Volume vs surface integration

  • new (v1) integrates \( M_{st} \) over the target tets. Quadrature: 5-point Keast (degree-3 exact in barycentric coordinates).
  • new_surface (v3) integrates over the target’s outer surface — the triangle facets returned by geometry::boundary_facets. Quadrature: 6-point degree-4 Dunavant on every facet. Interior target DoFs receive zero contribution.

Use volume for “field transfer between non-matching solid domains”; use surface for contact formulations where only the boundary matters.

Tet-location strategy (v5)

v5 builds a source-side molla_geometry::TetBvh over inflated per-tet AABBs once during NonconformingField construction. Every target volume or surface quadrature point queries that BVH for candidate source tets, then runs the exact barycentric containment check only on those candidates. The public API stays unchanged, but the source lookup drops from a brute-force scan over source.cells to a BVH candidate query.

project / project_vector

project runs

\[ u_T = M_{tt}^{-1} (M_{st} \cdot u_S) \]

via one matvec of M_{st} followed by one CG solve against M_{tt}. The mass matrix is well-conditioned (\( \kappa \sim O(1) \) independent of mesh size) so 200 iterations is generous — defaults are DEFAULT_CG_TOL = 1e-12, DEFAULT_CG_MAX_ITERS = 1000.

For vector-valued fields (Stage 47 v2):

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let u_t = field.project_vector(&u_source, 3)?;  // dim = 3
}

The same scalar \( M_{st} \) and \( M_{tt} \) are reused once per component. Storage choice: we keep the single scalar BsrMatrix and loop over components rather than building a B = 3 block matrix. The math is identical (the cross-mesh mass operator is scalar — for an isotropic vector field the components decouple), and a B = 3 block matrix would hold three identical scalar copies on its block diagonal with zero off-diagonal blocks: 3× the storage for the same numerics. The 3× CG solves still reuse the cached SPD M_tt so the cost is 3 × the scalar path with zero re-assembly.

NonconformingPenaltyContact — Stage 47 v2

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct NonconformingPenaltyContact<'a> {
    pub field: &'a NonconformingField<'a>,
    pub stiffness: Real,
}

impl<'a> NonconformingPenaltyContact<'a> {
    pub fn compute_penalty_forces(
        &self,
        u_target: &[Real],
        u_source: &[Real],
        dim: usize,
    ) -> Result<(Vec<Real>, Vec<Real>)>;
}
}

For a slave-master pair where the slave (target) sits on or just beyond the master (source), the displacement gap is

\[ \Delta u = u_T - M_{tt}^{-1} M_{st} u_S \]

— the difference between the target’s own field and the source’s field projected onto the target. The contact spring force is then

\[ \mathbf{f}T = -k \cdot M{tt} \cdot \Delta u, \quad \mathbf{f}S = +k \cdot M{st}^T \cdot \Delta u. \]

The target receives f_T = − k · M_tt · Δu (consistent-mass weighting); the source receives the transpose of the projection acting on the same Δu. The relation \( \mathbf{1}^T M_{tt} = \mathbf{1}^T M_{st} \) (both reproduce the target volume measure) makes the total force vanish exactly, so Newton’s third law holds at the discrete level.

Coupled elasticity Newton-Raphson — Stage 47 v4

The final v4 stage wires the non-conforming penalty contact into a two-mesh elasticity Newton-Raphson solve. Each iteration:

  1. Assemble per-mesh elastic stiffness \( K_T, K_S \) and residuals.
  2. Compute penalty forces via NonconformingPenaltyContact::compute_penalty_forces on the current (u_T, u_S).
  3. Build a coupled tangent that combines per-mesh \( K \) with penalty Jacobian \( k , M_{tt} \) (target) and \( k , M_{st}^T \) (source).
  4. Solve the coupled increment \( (du_T, du_S) \) via CG.
  5. Update.

The result: a Hertz-style contact problem where two non-matching elastic bodies push against each other with the right force-distance relationship.

What’s out of scope (v4)

  • Hard Signorini contact — see signorini for the Lagrange-multiplier version.
  • Friction — see friction. The current v4 ships the normal force only.
  • Pressure contact — Hertz with a contact pressure unknown requires an additional surface mass operator on the slave side plus a Lagrange formulation.

Cross-references

  • Mesh — FemMesh for both source and target.
  • Quadrature — the 5-pt tet and 6-pt tri-3D rules used to build \( M_{st} \).
  • Elements — the per-mesh stiffness assembly in the Stage 47 v4 path.
  • Signorini — exact non-penetration via Lagrange multipliers.
  • Friction — Coulomb tangential force.

Signorini contact — Lagrange multipliers

Stage 49 added exact non-penetration contact via Lagrange multipliers, replacing the penalty-spring approximation of Stage 47 nonconforming penalty contact. It lives in crates/molla-fem/src/signorini.rs.

Why Lagrange multipliers?

Penalty contact approximates the Signorini condition \( \text{gap}n \ge 0 \) with a soft spring \( \mathbf{f}{\text{contact}} = -k \cdot \Delta u \). The penalty matrix \( k , C^T C \) becomes ill-conditioned as \( k \to \infty \) — larger \( k \) means stiffer constraint enforcement but harder linear solves. In practice the penalty is capped well below \( \infty \), which means some residual penetration is always present.

Lagrange multipliers replace the spring with explicit contact-force unknowns \( \lambda \ge 0 \) that enforce the constraint exactly:

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{minimise}& \tfrac{1}{2} u^T K u - f^T u \ \text{subject to}& C u \ge g \quad \text{(non-penetration)} \ & \lambda \ge 0 \quad \text{(only push, never pull)} \end{aligned} \]

KKT stationarity gives \( K u - C^T \lambda = f \). In matrix form the linearised saddle-point system reads

\[ \begin{pmatrix} K & -C^T \ C & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} u \ \lambda \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} f \ g \end{pmatrix}, \quad \lambda \ge 0 \]

— a linear complementarity problem (LCP).

The Signorini contact data type

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct SignoriniContact {
    pub active_pairs: Vec<(u32, Vec3, Real)>,  // (slave_dof, n, gap)
}

impl SignoriniContact {
    pub fn new() -> Self;
    pub fn n_active(&self) -> usize;
    pub fn pairs(&self) -> &[(u32, Vec3, Real)];
}
}

Each tuple is (slave_dof_global, master_normal, target_gap):

  • slave_dof_global: BASE global DoF index of the slave vertex (i.e. vertex_index * dim). The constraint matrix writes the normal components into the three consecutive DoFs starting here.
  • master_normal: unit outward normal of the master plane at the contact point.
  • target_gap: minimum allowed projected displacement. If the initial geometry penetrates by \( -p < 0 \), set target_gap = p so that \( \mathbf{n} \cdot u_{\text{slave}} \ge p \) restores contact at zero gap. For nodes that are on the master surface, target_gap = 0.

Constraint matrix C

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn assemble_constraint_matrix(
    active_pairs: &[(u32, Vec3, Real)],
    n_dofs: usize,
) -> Result<BsrMatrix>;

pub fn target_gap_vector(active_pairs: &[(u32, Vec3, Real)]) -> Vec<Real>;
}

Shape: n_active × n_dofs. Row \( k \) corresponds to active pair \( k \): three entries at columns (slave_dof, slave_dof+1, slave_dof+2) equal to \( (n_x, n_y, n_z) \). All other entries are zero.

Projected-Uzawa solver

The Uzawa iteration is the textbook dual ascent + inner-primal-solve scheme:

1. Inner primal:  fix λ, solve  K u = f + Cᵀ λ  via CG.
2. Dual update:   λ ← max(0, λ + ρ · (g − C u))  (projected gradient ascent).
3. Iterate until ‖g − C u‖∞ < tol AND λ has stabilised.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn solve_augmented_system(
    k_global: &BsrMatrix,
    c_matrix: &BsrMatrix,
    f: &[Real],
    g: &[Real],
    max_iters: usize,
    tol: Real,
) -> Result<UzawaResult>;

pub fn solve_augmented_system_with(
    k_global, c_matrix, f, g, max_iters, tol, rho,
    inner_cg_tol, inner_cg_max_iters,
) -> Result<UzawaResult>;

pub struct UzawaResult {
    pub u: Vec<Real>,
    pub lambda: Vec<Real>,
    pub iters: usize,
    pub primal_residual: Real,    // ‖g − C u‖∞ on active constraints
    pub dual_residual: Real,      // ‖λ_new − λ_old‖∞
}
}

The implementation warm-starts \( u \) from the unconstrained solve \( K u = f \) (saves the first inner CG) and reuses the previous iterate as the warm start for each subsequent inner CG. The primal residual measures only the active violation — pairs where \( \lambda > 0 \) care about both signs of \( g - C u \), while pairs where \( \lambda = 0 \) (currently inactive) only care about positive residual (still penetrating).

Choice of dual step ρ

For SPD \( K \), the dual functional is concave with Lipschitz gradient bounded by the largest eigenvalue of the Schur complement \( S = C K^{-1} C^T \). Convergence requires \( 0 < \rho < 2 / \lambda_{\max}(S) \). The default is

\[ \rho = 1 / \lambda_{\max}(S), \]

estimated via a short power iteration that needs only matrix-free actions of \( K^{-1} \) (via inner CG) and \( C \). The estimate_dual_step helper runs 6 power-iteration steps to nail \( \lambda_{\max} \) to ~10 % — the inverse is a conservative step (always inside the \( (0, 2/\lambda_{\max}) \) stability band, never optimal but never oscillating):

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn estimate_dual_step(
    k: &BsrMatrix,
    c: &BsrMatrix,
    n_active: usize,
    inner_cg_tol: Real,
    inner_cg_max_iters: usize,
) -> Real;
}

Seeded with a deterministic length-n_active ramp (not the all-ones vector, which can lock onto a translational rigid-body mode after BCs).

Stage 49 scope — fixed active set

The v1 of Stage 49 solves the augmented system for a fixed list of active contact pairs. The caller decides which pairs are active (typically: any slave node currently penetrating the master surface).

Once Uzawa converges, you have:

  • \( u \): displacements that satisfy \( C u \ge g \) on the active pairs.
  • \( \lambda \ge 0 \): contact pressure magnitudes (each pointing along its master normal). A pair whose \( \lambda \) clamps to 0 is a candidate for active-set release — it has no contact force and may have separated from the master.

Stage 51 — active-set update loop

The active-set update loop is a “primal-dual active-set” (PDAS) algorithm:

  1. Initialise active set from a contact-detection pass.
  2. Solve the augmented system on the current active set (Stage 49).
  3. Release pairs where \( \lambda = 0 \) and \( C u > g \) (separated).
  4. Activate pairs where the geometry penetrates and \( \lambda \) would be positive (new contact).
  5. Re-solve.
  6. Iterate until the active set stops changing.

This is the LCP variant of the Uzawa-Lagrange method and is what Wriggers (Computational Contact Mechanics, §6.3) calls the standard “semi-smooth Newton” formulation.

Stage 51 v2 adds anti-cycling hardening: the solver records previously seen active sets, and if a proposed add/release update would revisit one of them it switches to a Bland-style least-slave-DoF single pivot. The trace exposes cycle_breaks on ActiveSetTrace and the selected bland_pivot on each ActiveSetIteration.

Self-contact candidate path

molla-geometry::detect_vertex_triangle_self_contacts emits CPU vertex-triangle self-contact candidates for non-adjacent surface features. signorini_candidates_from_self_contacts converts those into the active-set candidate interface by keeping the deepest shell penetration per slave vertex and building a fixed gap plane from the closest triangle point and contact normal. This gives the Signorini PDAS and coupled-friction solvers a first self-contact input path without changing the solver loop.
