  • BC — strong Dirichlet on the parent \( K \) is applied before handing to the Uzawa loop; the routine assumes \( K \) is SPD after BCs.

Coulomb friction (Stage 50)

Stage 50 is the follow-up to Stage 49 Signorini contact: once the normal force \( \lambda_n \) is known via Lagrange multipliers, tangential friction follows a Coulomb law that constrains the friction force to lie inside a per-contact friction disc.

The FEM-side implementation extends crates/molla-fem/src/signorini.rs with solve_augmented_system_with_friction + ContactPair (carrying the slave DoF, master normal, and an orthonormal tangent basis). Stage 50 v2 also exposes FrictionState plus separate static/kinetic coefficients (μ_s, μ_k), while with_friction(μ) keeps the old μ_s == μ_k behaviour. The 3-component multiplier per pair (1 normal + 2 tangents) shares a single projected-Uzawa loop with the Stage 49 normal-only path. Particle/cloth- side Coulomb friction has separate implementations in crates/molla-solvers/src/vbd_soft_contact.rs and crates/molla-kernels/src/soft_vt_contact.rs (position-form analogue on different state types).

The Coulomb friction model

For each active contact pair with normal multiplier \( \lambda_n \ge 0 \), static friction coefficient \( \mu_s \ge 0 \), and kinetic friction coefficient \( \mu_k \ge 0 \):

  • Sticking (no slip): \( |\boldsymbol\lambda_t| \le \mu_s \lambda_n \) with the tangential velocity \( v_t = 0 \).
  • Sliding (kinetic): \( |\boldsymbol\lambda_t| = \mu_k \lambda_n \) and \( \boldsymbol\lambda_t = -\mu_k \lambda_n , \hat v_t \) (opposes motion).

The friction force lies inside the Coulomb friction cone of the contact:

                            λ_n
                            ↑
                            │
                            │   ─── static cone (μ_s slope)
                            │  /
                            │ /
                            │/_______________→
                                                |λ_t|
            (λ_t, λ_n) feasible iff
            |λ_t| ≤ μ_s · λ_n  (stick)
            |λ_t| = μ_k · λ_n  (slip)

For an FEM contact with 3D normal \( \mathbf{n} \) and two orthonormal in-plane tangents \( \mathbf{t}1, \mathbf{t}2 \), the constraint becomes: \( (\lambda{t_1}, \lambda{t_2}) \) lies inside the static disc of radius \( \mu_s \lambda_n \), or on the kinetic boundary \( \mu_k \lambda_n \) once it slips.

Algorithmic plan

The textbook semi-smooth Newton recipe (Wriggers, §6.5):

1. Tangent constraint matrix

In addition to the normal-direction constraint matrix \( C_n \) (one row per active pair), build the tangent constraint matrix \( C_t \) with two rows per active pair — one for each tangent direction:

C_t[2k    , slave_dof+0..+2] = (t1.x, t1.y, t1.z)
C_t[2k + 1, slave_dof+0..+2] = (t2.x, t2.y, t2.z)

The tangents \( (\mathbf{t}_1, \mathbf{t}_2) \) are picked deterministically: \( \mathbf{t}_1 \) is a fixed projection of \( \mathbf{e}_x \) onto the plane orthogonal to \( \mathbf{n} \) (or \( \mathbf{e}_y \) if \( \mathbf{n} \approx \pm \mathbf{e}_x \)), and \( \mathbf{t}_2 = \mathbf{n} \times \mathbf{t}_1 \).

2. Augmented system

\[ \begin{pmatrix} K & -C_n^T & -C_t^T \ C_n & 0 & 0 \ C_t & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} u \ \boldsymbol\lambda_n \ \boldsymbol\lambda_t \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} f \ g_n \ g_t \end{pmatrix} \]

with \( g_t = 0 \) for the sticking case (zero tangential slip).

3. Augmented Uzawa with friction-cone projection

Each Uzawa outer iteration:

  1. Inner primal: \( K u = f + C_n^T \boldsymbol\lambda_n + C_t^T \boldsymbol\lambda_t \) via CG.

  2. Normal dual update: \( \lambda_n \leftarrow \max(0, \lambda_n + \rho_n (g_n - C_n u)) \) — same as Signorini.

  3. Tangent dual update: \( \boldsymbol\lambda_t \leftarrow \boldsymbol\lambda_t + \rho_t (g_t - C_t u) \), then project onto the friction disc using the static/kinetic rule:

    \[ \boldsymbol\lambda_t \leftarrow \begin{cases} \boldsymbol\lambda_t & \text{if } |\boldsymbol\lambda_t| \le \mu_s \lambda_n \ \mu_k \lambda_n \cdot \dfrac{\boldsymbol\lambda_t}{|\boldsymbol\lambda_t|} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \]

  4. Loop until both primal and dual residuals are below tolerance.

The friction-disc projection is what makes the scheme semi-smooth — it’s continuous but not differentiable on the disc boundary, which is why classical Newton fails but Uzawa’s projected gradient works.

4. Static vs kinetic friction

Static and kinetic friction coefficients differ in practice (\( \mu_s > \mu_k \) — it takes more force to start slipping than to sustain it). The textbook model treats this as two regimes:

  • Stick (no slip): \( |\boldsymbol\lambda_t| \le \mu_s \lambda_n \), any value inside the disc is admissible. The projection step uses \( \mu_s \).
  • Slip (kinetic): \( |\boldsymbol\lambda_t| = \mu_k \lambda_n \), opposing the slip velocity. The projection step uses \( \mu_k \).

A per-contact FrictionState records the final projection regime (Inactive, Stick, or Slip). The current implementation classifies directly from the projected dual update; it does not yet add a velocity-threshold hysteresis loop.

Expected API

When the module lands, the signatures will look like:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct ContactPair {
    pub slave_dof: u32,
    pub normal: Vec3,
    pub tangent_u: Vec3,
    pub tangent_v: Vec3,
    pub target_gap: Real,
}

pub struct SignoriniContact {
    pub active_pairs: Vec<ContactPair>,
    pub friction_static_coeff: Real,
    pub friction_kinetic_coeff: Real,
}

pub fn solve_augmented_system_with_friction(
    k_global: &BsrMatrix,
    contact: &SignoriniContact,
    f: &[Real],
    max_iters: usize,
    tol: Real,
) -> Result<FrictionUzawaResult>;

pub fn solve_active_set_signorini_with_friction(
    k_global: &BsrMatrix,
    candidates: &SignoriniContactCandidates,
    f: &[Real],
    friction_static_coeff: Real,
    friction_kinetic_coeff: Real,
    max_outer_iters: usize,
    gap_tol: Real,
    inner_max_iters: usize,
    inner_tol: Real,
) -> Result<ActiveSetFrictionResult>;
}

The result returns both \( u \), \( \boldsymbol\lambda_n \), and \( \boldsymbol\lambda_t \) (the projected tangential forces), plus the per-pair stick/slip flag for diagnostics.

The active-set variant is the coupled Stage 49/50 path: the PDAS loop discovers the current normal active set, and each inner solve uses the stacked normal+tangent Coulomb system. Released contacts zero their normal multiplier, tangent multipliers, and FrictionState in one outer iteration, so friction is no longer a post-pass over a preselected contact set.

Rate-and-state friction

For advanced tribology / geology workloads, the FEM crate also exposes the Dieterich-Ruina aging law as reusable per-contact helpers:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct RateStateFrictionParams {
    pub mu0: Real,
    pub a: Real,
    pub b: Real,
    pub v0: Real,
    pub dc: Real,
}

pub struct RateStateFrictionState {
    pub theta: Real,
}

pub fn rate_state_friction_coeff(
    params: RateStateFrictionParams,
    state: RateStateFrictionState,
    slip_rate: Real,
) -> Real;

pub fn advance_rate_state_friction(
    params: RateStateFrictionParams,
    state: RateStateFrictionState,
    slip_rate: Real,
    dt: Real,
) -> (RateStateFrictionState, Real);
}

The coefficient is μ = μ0 + a ln(v/v0) + b ln(θ v0 / dc), and the state evolves with the aging law dθ/dt = 1 - vθ/dc. The helpers are intentionally solver-agnostic: Signorini, VBD, or particle contact pipelines can own the state vector and feed the updated coefficient into their existing friction-cone projection.

What’s already in the codebase

Friction is implemented (and tested) for these non-FEM paths:

ModuleFriction model
solvers/vbd_soft_contact.rsPosition-form Coulomb friction inside VBD substep
kernels/soft_vt_contact.rsPosition-form Coulomb friction for soft-vs-tri contact
geometry/hydroelastic.rsDefault μ per hydroelastic patch
sim/model.rs, sim/builder.rsPer-shape μ storage + builders
compute/implicit_mpm.rsCoulomb friction for MPM particles

These all live at the rigid / particle / cloth layer; the FEM-multiplier version is the missing piece that will unify the contact-friction story across all body types.

Why this is non-trivial

Three reasons it isn’t a simple copy-paste from particles:

  1. Direction-dependent tangent basis. Picking \( \mathbf{t}_1, \mathbf{t}_2 \) consistently across active pairs matters when neighbouring contacts share slave nodes — a stick-to-slip transition shouldn’t flip basis on you.
  2. The friction-disc projection is non-smooth. Classical Newton needs semi-smooth or smoothed variants; Uzawa’s projected gradient handles it natively but converges sub-linearly near the disc boundary.
  3. Coupling with normal dual update. The friction limit \( \mu \lambda_n \) moves every time \( \lambda_n \) updates, so the tangent projection sees a moving target — the convergence analysis needs both updates to descend in lockstep.

The reference implementation in xtra/newton/newton/solvers/ (particle-side friction) and the textbook chapter in Wriggers cover these details; the FEM-side port is a self-contained extension that slots into the existing Signorini machinery.

Cross-references

  • Signorini — the normal-only contact this layers on top of.
  • Nonconforming — penalty-contact precursor for small-displacement bodies.
  • Solvers — the augmented-system solver framework the friction extension will plug into.

Phase-field fracture

molla-fem::phase_field contains the first CPU oracle for brittle phase-field fracture. The current model is the standard frozen-history AT2 scalar damage update on the same P1 triangle/tetrahedron meshes used by the rest of FEM.

The degradation law is:

\[ g(d) = (1-d)^2 + k,\qquad 0 \le d \le 1 \]

with history updated irreversibly as:

\[ H_{n+1} = \max(H_n, \psi^+). \]

For a frozen tensile-energy history H, the assembled weak form is:

\[ \int_\Omega G_c \ell \nabla d \cdot \nabla \eta

  • (G_c/\ell + 2H) d\eta,dx = \int_\Omega 2H\eta,dx. \]

Public API

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct PhaseFieldFractureParams {
    pub critical_energy_release_rate: Real,
    pub length_scale: Real,
    pub residual_stiffness: Real,
}

pub fn phase_field_degradation(damage, residual_stiffness) -> Real;
pub fn update_phase_field_history(previous, tensile_energy_density) -> Real;
pub fn phase_field_fracture_energy_density(d, grad_d_norm_sq, history, params) -> Real;

pub fn assemble_phase_field_fracture_system(mesh, history, params) -> Result<(BsrMatrix, Vec<Real>)>;
pub fn solve_phase_field_fracture_jacobi(mesh, damage_old, history, params, max_iters, tol)
    -> Result<PhaseFieldFractureSolveResult>;
}

assemble_phase_field_fracture_system reuses the existing element mass and stiffness kernels, averaging nodal history per element. The Jacobi solver is deliberately conservative: every iterate is clamped to damage_old <= damage <= 1, making it a simple CPU correctness oracle for later Newton/AMG/GPU paths.

Raycaster

Raycaster is molla’s batched closest-hit ray sensor. It mirrors Newton’s SensorRayCaster one-for-one and is the primitive that LIDAR-style point-cloud sensors, proximity probes, and pixel visibility queries all build on top of.

The implementation lives in crates/molla/src/sensors/raycast.rs with the heavy math (per-primitive ray intersection + outward-normal computation) in crates/molla-kernels/shaders/raycast.wgsl. Following molla’s GPU-first rule, the Rust orchestrator owns the per-batch ray / hit buffers and the dispatch wrapper; the CPU oracle path is only used inside parity tests.

What it computes

For each ray (origin, direction) and a max_distance budget, the kernel returns the closest hit:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct RayHit {
    pub shape_id: Option<u32>,   // index into Model::shape_geometry
    pub body_id: BodyId,          // owner body, BodyId::NONE for static
    pub t: Real,                  // hit distance along the ray (f64::INFINITY = miss)
    pub point: Vec3,              // world-space hit point
    pub normal: Vec3,             // world-space outward surface normal
}
}

The direction is not required to be unit-length. t is measured in whatever units direction carries — pass a unit direction to read distance in metres, or a non-unit direction to read the parametric t that lands the hit at origin + t · direction.

Supported primitives

The GPU kernel walks every shape on every ray (no BVH culling in v1; that lands when the GPU mesh BVH integration ships, tracked in the module-level doc comment). It handles five primitives:

KindMath
SphereClosed-form quadratic
BoxSlab intersection in local frame, 6 faces
CapsuleCylinder + 2 hemisphere caps in local frame
CylinderInfinite cylinder + 2 disc caps
PlaneSingle half-space (+Y outward normal in local)

Each primitive transforms the ray into the shape’s local frame using the inverse of the body world pose × shape local pose, intersects in local coordinates, then transforms the closest hit point + normal back into world space.

Triangle / TriMesh shapes carry a 0xff “skip” sentinel in Model::shape_geom_kind so the GPU walks past them without aborting. The mesh BVH already ships (Stage 15, see geometry/bvh) but the integration with raycast.wgsl is still TODO. The raycast_adjoint CPU module provides a finite-difference fallback for inverse-rendering experiments that need triangles in the loop.

API

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use molla::compute::Engine;
use molla::sensors::Raycaster;
use molla::math::Vec3;

let engine = Engine::new_gpu()?;
let mut sensor = Raycaster::new(&engine, /* max_rays = */ 64)?;

let origins    = vec![Vec3::new(0.0, 5.0, 0.0); 1];
let directions = vec![Vec3::new(0.0, -1.0, 0.0); 1];
let hits = sensor.cast(&engine, &model, &state, &origins, &directions, 100.0)?;

if let Some(shape) = hits[0].shape_id {
    println!("hit shape {shape} at t={:.3}, n={:?}",
             hits[0].t, hits[0].normal);
}
}

Raycaster::new(engine, max_rays) allocates the per-batch GPU buffers up-front and is cheap thereafter: every cast call reuses the same device storage, so spinning up a new sensor per frame is unnecessary (and wasteful). The max_rays parameter is the capacity ceiling; calls with fewer rays simply dispatch a smaller threadgroup count.

The orchestrator validates input slices on every call:

  • origins.len() == directions.len().
  • origins.len() <= max_rays (set at construction).

Failures surface as Error::Solver.

Ray bundle generation

For LIDAR-style scans, the caller usually generates a fan of rays around a single origin. The convenience pattern is to precompute the direction list once (the rays sweep a polar grid in body frame) and multiply by the body pose each frame, then call cast once per sensor sweep. The TiledCamera chapter covers the more specialised case of pinhole-camera bundles where direction generation itself runs as a GPU kernel.

State requirements

Model and State must have their device mirrors uploaded before cast runs — call Model::upload_to_device(engine) once after building, and ensure State::body_q is current on the device (the solvers already keep it there). The kernel reads state.body_q through its device buffer and accepts the shapes via the static Model::shape_* slabs.

Cross-references

  • Sensors / TiledCamera — the multi-channel pinhole-camera sensor built on the same intersection routines but with on-device ray generation + multi-camera batching.
  • Sensors / Raycast adjoint — Stage 37.7 CPU finite-difference adjoint used for inverse-rendering demos while the analytic ∂t/∂param adjoint is on the backlog.
  • Geometry / Shape primitives — defines Model::shape_geom_kind + the per-primitive parameter layout the WGSL kernel reads from.

TiledCamera

TiledCamera is molla’s batched, multi-channel pinhole camera sensor. It mirrors Newton’s SensorTiledCamera: a single dispatch() runs a two-pass kernel for every camera in the batch and writes per-pixel (depth, color, normal, albedo, shape_index) into device buffers of shape (num_cameras, height, width).

It’s the workhorse for pixel-observation RL environments, where you typically have one camera per parallel world and want all of them rendered in lock-step so the policy sees a tensor of shape (num_envs, H, W, channels) each step.

Source: crates/molla/src/sensors/tiled_camera.rs. Shaders: crates/molla-kernels/shaders/camera_rays.wgsl (ray generation) and crates/molla-kernels/shaders/camera_trace.wgsl (closest-hit + shading).

Pipeline

Each dispatch() runs two kernels back-to-back:

  1. Ray generation (CameraRaysKernel). Per-pixel (camera, x, y) triples are turned into world-space (ray_origin, ray_direction) pairs using the per-camera world pose + shared intrinsics (vertical FOV, aspect ratio). One thread per pixel.

  2. Closest-hit trace (CameraTraceKernel). One thread per pixel walks every primitive shape, keeps the nearest hit within max_distance, and writes whichever channels the caller asked for via CameraChannels. Hits beyond max_distance are reported as miss.

Both kernels share Model + body-pose buffers with the rest of the engine — no data round-trips to the host between passes, no per-frame uploads beyond the per-camera pose array.

Configuration

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct TiledCameraConfig {
    pub width: u32,
    pub height: u32,
    pub fov_y_radians: f32,
    pub channels: CameraChannels,
    pub ambient: Vec3,           // ambient RGB added to every shaded pixel
    pub light_dir: Vec3,         // world-space directional light vector
    pub light_color: Vec3,       // directional-light colour (× n·-L)
    pub max_distance: f32,
    pub near: f32,               // informational, not enforced in v1
}
}

Default produces a 128×96 pinhole at 60° vertical FOV with a warm-white directional light and a soft blue ambient — useful for a viewer thumbnail without wiring custom lighting.

Width / height / camera count are fixed at construction time because the output buffers are sized then. Everything else can be flipped at any frame via set_config() — including the channels mask, so you can render only depth on most frames and turn on the full RGBA + normal stack only for the frames you log.

Channels

CameraChannels is a bitmask of which output buffers to write:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl CameraChannels {
    pub const COLOR: Self        = Self(1 << 0);
    pub const DEPTH: Self        = Self(1 << 1);
    pub const NORMAL: Self       = Self(1 << 2);
    pub const ALBEDO: Self       = Self(1 << 3);
    pub const SHAPE_INDEX: Self  = Self(1 << 4);
    pub const ALL: Self          = ...; // all five OR'd together
    pub const NONE: Self         = Self(0);
}
}

The semantics:

  • COLOR — Lambert-shaded RGB packed into a u32 (8 bits per channel). Cheap, suitable for visualisation thumbnails.
  • DEPTH — Real (f64) ray-parametric t per pixel. -1.0 marks a miss. This is the channel the depth-loss / pose-recovery loops consume.
  • NORMAL — world-space outward normal per pixel as Vec3. Zero vector on miss. Useful for inverse-rendering or as a feature channel for the policy.
  • ALBEDO — unshaded per-shape colour (no lighting). Useful for rendering pipelines that want to apply post-process lighting themselves.
  • SHAPE_INDEX — Model::shape_geometry index of the hit shape (u32::MAX for miss). This is the instance-segmentation channel: every pixel tells you exactly which body-owned shape lit it up.

Bits are combined with |:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let cfg = TiledCameraConfig {
    channels: CameraChannels::DEPTH | CameraChannels::SHAPE_INDEX,
    ..Default::default()
};
}

Channels not in the mask are skipped at write time inside the kernel (the backing buffers are always allocated, so the mask can be flipped per-frame without reallocation).

API

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use molla::compute::Engine;
use molla::sensors::{TiledCamera, TiledCameraConfig, CameraChannels};
use molla::math::Vec3;

let engine = Engine::new_gpu()?;
let cfg = TiledCameraConfig {
    width: 256,
    height: 192,
    channels: CameraChannels::COLOR | CameraChannels::DEPTH,
    ..Default::default()
};
let mut cam = TiledCamera::new(&engine, cfg, /* num_cameras = */ 16)?;

// Aim the cameras. The convenience helper builds a lookAt pose.
for i in 0..16 {
    let eye = Vec3::new(0.0, 1.5, 4.0);
    let tgt = Vec3::ZERO;
    cam.set_camera_look_at(i, eye, tgt, Vec3::Y)?;
}

cam.dispatch(&engine, &model, &state)?;
let depth = cam.download_depth(&engine)?;
let color = cam.download_color(&engine)?;
}

Per-camera poses use molla’s Transform (position + rotation), where rotation maps the canonical camera axes (+X right, +Y up, -Z forward) into world. set_camera_look_at(idx, eye, target, up_hint) builds the same pose without the caller having to compose a quaternion by hand — it’s the same matrix as the classical OpenGL lookAt, just expressed via a rotation quaternion.

Output buffers are laid out image-major, row-major within an image. The linear pixel index for (cam, x, y) is exposed via:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let idx = cam.pixel_index(cam_id, x, y);
let d   = depth[idx];
}

The download_* helpers wrap Buffer::download + Buffer::host into a single call that returns a borrow on the per-pixel slice — useful when the policy code wants to view the depth tensor without copying.

Tiled multi-camera × multi-world layout

In Newton’s RL recipe, each parallel world owns its own camera and all of them render together. molla handles that the same way: the caller picks num_cameras = num_worlds at construction time, then either calls set_camera_pose(world_i, world_i_camera_pose) each frame, or — more often — pre-bakes the per-world camera offset into the pose buffer once and updates only the world-root body each step. The resulting depth / colour buffers are tensors of shape (num_worlds, H, W) ready to feed straight into the policy.

Scope (Stage 14)

Sphere · Plane · Box · Capsule · Cylinder · Cone are intersected on the GPU. TriMesh / ConvexHull / Heightfield / SDF carry the 0xff “skip” sentinel in Model::shape_geom_kind — they’re invisible to the camera until the GPU mesh BVH integration lands (same blocker as Raycaster).

Cross-references

  • Sensors / Raycaster — same intersection logic, but caller-supplied rays instead of on-device generation.
  • Geometry / Gaussian splats — the 3DGS family of differentiable renderers covered in Differentiable Physics / Gaussian splat renderer; unrelated raster path but the rays it consumes match camera_rays.wgsl’s output format.
  • Architecture / Design rules for the GPU-first contract these kernels follow.

IMU

ImuSensor produces six-DoF inertial readings for a batch of sensor mounts: linear acceleration (specific force) plus angular velocity, both expressed in the sensor’s local frame. It mirrors Newton’s SensorImu accelerometer + gyroscope combo and is the primitive that locomotion / balance policies build their proprioceptive observation vector on.

Source: crates/molla/src/sensors/imu.rs. Shader: crates/molla-kernels/shaders/imu.wgsl.

Reading + mount types

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct ImuMount {
    pub body: BodyId,
    pub local_pose: Transform,   // sensor pose in body frame
}

pub struct ImuReading {
    pub accelerometer: Vec3,     // specific force, sensor frame [m/s²]
    pub gyroscope: Vec3,         // angular velocity, sensor frame [rad/s]
}
}

The local_pose is the sensor’s pose in the body’s frame: position is the mount point, rotation rotates the sensor’s local axes (+X forward, +Y up, etc. — whatever convention your IMU chip uses) into the body’s frame. The kernel pushes both accelerations and angular velocities into the sensor frame before returning them, so the policy sees the same numbers the embedded controller would see on the real robot.

Specific force semantics

The accelerometer outputs specific force, not coordinate acceleration. At rest on the ground, the IMU reads +g along whichever local axis points upward through the sensor (gravity is the reaction force the table applies to keep the chip stationary, not the literal acceleration of the chip in the world frame). A body in free fall reads ≈ 0. This matches every real-world IMU datasheet and Newton’s convention.

Acceleration via finite difference

Newton reads body_qdd (linear + angular accelerations) directly from the solver. molla doesn’t carry that field as part of State, so ImuSensor::update finite-differences successive body_qd snapshots:

a_lin = (qd.linear  - qd_prev.linear ) / dt
a_ang = (qd.angular - qd_prev.angular) / dt

The sensor owns a per-body shadow prev_body_qd buffer that gets rolled forward after each successful dispatch. On the very first update() call the sensor is unprimed: it just snapshots the current body_qd into prev_body_qd and returns an empty Vec (the alternative would be a nonsense impulse from comparing against zeros). Discard the first frame’s reading on real captures, or call reset() after a teleport / scene reset to force re-priming on the next step.

The kernel then transforms the linear acceleration into the sensor frame, adds the centripetal + tangential terms that come from the IMU not sitting at the body’s COM (a = a_com + α × r + ω × (ω × r) in body frame, where r is the sensor offset), then subtracts gravity to produce the specific-force output.

API

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use molla::compute::Engine;
use molla::sensors::{ImuMount, ImuSensor};
use molla::math::{Transform, Vec3};

let engine = Engine::new_gpu()?;
let mounts = vec![
    ImuMount {
        body: chassis_id,
        local_pose: Transform::new(
            Vec3::new(0.0, 0.05, 0.0),  // 5 cm above the chassis origin
            Quat::IDENTITY,
        ),
    },
];
let mut imu = ImuSensor::new(&engine, &model, &mounts)?;

// First call returns Vec::new() (priming snapshot).
let _ = imu.update(&engine, &model, &state, dt)?;

// Subsequent calls return one reading per mount.
for step in 0..n_steps {
    integrator.step(&engine, &model, &mut state, &control, dt)?;
    let readings = imu.update(&engine, &model, &state, dt)?;
    for (i, r) in readings.iter().enumerate() {
        println!("imu[{i}] a={:?} ω={:?}", r.accelerometer, r.gyroscope);
    }
}
}

ImuSensor::new validates every mount’s body index against model.body_count and rejects empty mount lists. The number of sensors is fixed at construction time; if a scene needs more, build a separate ImuSensor (each owns its own GPU buffers and dispatch state).

Reset semantics

ImuSensor::reset() clears the primed flag. The next update() call will re-snapshot body_qd into prev_body_qd and return an empty vec, identical to the very first call. Use this after:

  • Scene re-initialisation / episode boundary.
  • Teleporting a body by writing directly into state.body_q.
  • Any operation that breaks the finite-difference assumption that the velocity changed smoothly between the previous and current step.

Cross-references

  • Sensors / Frame transform — pose tracking instead of inertial; complementary observation channel.
  • Sensors / Contact sensor — for the “robot is on the ground” signal that complements an IMU’s accelerometer reading.
  • Solvers / Semi-implicit integrator — supplies state.body_qd each step.

Contact sensor

ContactSensor reduces the per-frame Contacts buffer into one per-body summary: count, max depth, summed normals, mean point. It mirrors Newton’s SensorContact and is the primitive that “foot is on the ground”, “robot tipped over”, and proximity-shielding controllers consume.

Source: crates/molla/src/sensors/contact.rs. Shader: crates/molla-kernels/shaders/contact_aggregate.wgsl (one GPU thread per body, walks the contact CSR).

Reading

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct BodyContactReading {
    pub count: u32,            // number of contacts the body is in
    pub max_depth: Real,       // largest penetration depth (m)
    pub normal_sum: Vec3,      // Σ (sign · normal), points along net push
    pub centroid: Vec3,        // mean contact point, world frame
}
}

The sign in normal_sum is flipped when the body is the b-side of a contact, so the resulting vector always points along the direction the contact force is pushing this body. Zero count contacts ⇒ max_depth = 0, both vectors are zero.

What it does not measure

This sensor reports geometric / kinematic summaries only — it does not surface contact forces or λ impulses. Wiring the per-contact lambdas from the XPBD velocity-projection pass into a sensor channel is its own piece of solver work; for the v1 contract (“is body touching anything? where?”) the geometric summaries cover the common cases:

  • Foot in contact? — count > 0.
  • Foot pressed how hard? — max_depth is a proxy for normal force, since XPBD penetration depth scales linearly with reaction impulse via the compliance term α = 1/k·dt².
  • Which direction is the body being pushed? — normal_sum (un-normalised, so its magnitude reflects the spread + count).
  • Where, on the body, is the push concentrated? — centroid.

API

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use molla::compute::Engine;
use molla::sensors::ContactSensor;

let engine = Engine::new_gpu()?;
let mut sensor = ContactSensor::new(&engine, &model)?;

// After the solver has populated `contacts`:
let readings = sensor.update(&engine, &contacts)?;
for (body_idx, r) in readings.iter().enumerate() {
    if r.count > 0 {
        println!(
            "body {body_idx}: {} contacts, depth={:.4} m, push direction={:?}",
            r.count, r.max_depth, r.normal_sum,
        );
    }
}
}

ContactSensor::new(engine, model) allocates one slot per body in the model — i.e. the output vector always has length model.body_count. Bodies with no contacts this frame land at a zeroed reading; callers typically filter by count > 0.

The sensor is reusable across many steps. The output buffers stay on the device between calls and only get downloaded inside update(); if you want to consume the readings device-side, pull the buffers off ContactSensor (Stage 18.1 internal API) instead of paying the readback cost.

Performance

The kernel is launched with one thread per body. Each thread walks that body’s slice of the contact CSR (contacts.body_offsets[body]..body_offsets[body+1]) — typically very short (4–8 contacts for an articulation foot, often 0). The CSR layout matches the rest of the contact pipeline so no permutation step is needed.

Cross-references

  • Geometry / Narrow phase — where the per-contact tuples come from (GJK / EPA / MPR).
  • Geometry / Contact reduction — how the raw contacts are deduplicated before reaching the sensor.
  • Sensors / IMU — common partner: an accelerometer combined with a foot-contact flag is enough to close a basic ZMP-style balance loop.

Frame transform sensor

FrameTransformSensor tracks the world pose of an arbitrary set of frames (a frame = a body + a local pose) and — optionally — every frame’s pose expressed in a reference frame. It mirrors Newton’s SensorFrameTransform and is the primitive for end-effector tracking, chase-cam targets, and trajectory recording.

Source: crates/molla/src/sensors/frame_transform.rs. Shader: crates/molla-kernels/shaders/frame_transform.wgsl (one thread per target).

Targets + reading

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct FrameTarget {
    pub body: BodyId,
    pub local_pose: Transform,
}

pub struct FrameReading {
    pub world: Transform,    // target's world pose
    pub relative: Transform, // target's pose expressed in reference frame
}
}

local_pose defines where on the body the frame sits and how it is oriented (the “tool tip”, “camera bracket”, or “left-foot heel” of the body). The world pose is the body’s state.body_q pose composed with local_pose; the relative pose is the world pose pre-multiplied by the inverse of the reference frame’s world pose.

If the sensor was built without a reference (reference = None at construction), relative == world for every target — i.e. the sensor degenerates to a pure forward-kinematics readout.

API

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use molla::compute::Engine;
use molla::sensors::{FrameTarget, FrameTransformSensor};
use molla::math::{Transform, Vec3, Quat};

let engine = Engine::new_gpu()?;

let base_ref = FrameTarget {
    body: base_id,
    local_pose: Transform::IDENTITY,
};
let tool_tip = FrameTarget {
    body: last_link_id,
    local_pose: Transform::new(Vec3::new(0.0, 0.0, 0.12), Quat::IDENTITY),
};

let mut sensor = FrameTransformSensor::new(
    &engine,
    &model,
    Some(base_ref),
    &[tool_tip],
)?;

let r = sensor.update(&engine, &state)?;
println!("tool world  = {:?}", r[0].world.position);
println!("tool in base= {:?}", r[0].relative.position);
}

When a reference is supplied, it occupies index 0 of the sensor’s internal target array — the kernel computes its world pose first so later threads can chain through its inverse. The returned Vec only contains the caller-supplied targets; the reference is an implementation slot.

If you want both an absolute readout and a chain-relative readout of the same frame, register it twice: once with None reference (or with a different reference), once with the chain root.

Use cases

  • End-effector tracking for IK / manipulation: register the tool tip with the robot base as reference. The relative.position is what an IK solver targets; the world.position is what the viewer draws.
  • Chase-camera targets: register the head bone with the world root as reference. The camera follows world.position.
  • Per-trajectory logging: register every relevant body with a fixed reference (e.g. the scene root) and snapshot the readings each step — directly produces the per-frame transform tensor a motion-capture replay or RL reward function consumes.

Cross-references

  • Sim / Joints — the body poses returned by this sensor are the composition of state.body_q (FK output) with the user-supplied local_pose.
  • Sim / Inverse kinematics — typical consumer of the relative channel.
  • Sensors / IMU — complementary observation channel.

Composable actuator pipeline

Stage 18.1 introduced molla’s composable actuator pipeline — a thin orchestrator that wires three pluggable stages in series:

Delay  →  Controller  →  Clamping

It mirrors Newton’s Actuator class (xtra/newton/_src/actuators/actuator.py) and is the structure that PD / PID, neural, and DC-motor clamping controllers all plug into. The orchestrator type is molla::actuators::Actuator.

Source: crates/molla/src/actuators/actuator.rs. Each stage lives in its own file (delay.rs, controller_*.rs, clamping/*.rs) and has its own WGSL kernel (shaders/actuator_*.wgsl, shaders/clamping_*.wgsl).

The three stages

1. Delay

Pushes the current command targets into a per-DOF circular buffer and reads the per-DOF lagged sample. Use to emulate the communication / actuation lag of real hardware. When constructed with delay_steps == 0 for every actuator, the kernel passes the current target through unchanged (zero-overhead passthrough). See Delay (used inside the pipeline) for configuration knobs.

2. Controller

Consumes the (possibly lagged) targets and writes raw effort into Control.joint_force[dof]. Concrete variants live behind the ControllerStage enum so the orchestrator can hold a non-Box controller without dynamic dispatch in the per-substep hot path:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub enum ControllerStage {
    Pd(ControllerPipelinePd),
    Pid(ControllerPipelinePid),
    NeuralMlp(ControllerNeuralMlp),
    Lstm(ControllerNeuralLstm),
}
}
  • Pd / Pid — closed-loop joint-space controllers; see PD / PID controllers.
  • NeuralMlp / Lstm — learned policies whose output writes directly into joint_force; see Neural controllers. The MLP / LSTM read their observation vector from a host-pushed buffer (set_inputs(...)) rather than from the delay-stage outputs, so the delay still ticks each step but produces nothing the policy consumes.

3. Clamping

Modifies Control.joint_force[dof] in place to enforce actuator-physics limits. Variants:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub enum ClampingStage {
    None,                              // no-op
    MaxEffort(ClampingMaxEffort),      // symmetric cap |τ| ≤ τ_max
    DcMotor(ClampingDcMotor),          // four-quadrant DC-motor envelope
    PositionBased(ClampingPositionBased), // shared (q → τ_max) lookup table
}
}

All clamps read the current effort plus whatever state they need (joint position for PositionBased, joint velocity for DcMotor) and write the clipped value back into the same joint_force slot. See DC motor clamping for the torque-vs-speed envelope details.

API

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use molla::actuators::*;

let delay = Delay::new(
    &engine,
    &[DelayConfig { dof: 0, delay_steps: 4 },
      DelayConfig { dof: 1, delay_steps: 4 }],
    /* max_delay = */ 8,
)?;

let pd = ControllerPipelinePd::new(&engine, &model, &[
    ControllerPipelinePdConfig { dof: 0, kp: 50.0, kd: 5.0 },
    ControllerPipelinePdConfig { dof: 1, kp: 50.0, kd: 5.0 },
])?;

let clamp = ClampingMaxEffort::new(&engine, &[
    ClampingMaxEffortConfig { dof: 0, max_effort: 20.0 },
    ClampingMaxEffortConfig { dof: 1, max_effort: 20.0 },
])?;

let mut actuator = Actuator::new(
    delay,
    ControllerStage::Pd(pd),
    ClampingStage::MaxEffort(clamp),
);

// Per-substep:
actuator.step(&engine, &state, &mut control, dt)?;
}

Actuator::step(engine, state, control, dt) runs all three stages in order on the GPU; dt is consumed only by the integral term of the PID controller (the PD / MLP / LSTM variants ignore it).

The orchestrator does not verify that the per-stage DOF lists match in arity or order — the caller is responsible for keeping the configs aligned. The motivation is composition flexibility: a neural policy that writes to 12 DOFs while a ClampingMaxEffort caps only the 4 most powerful actuators is a perfectly reasonable configuration, and forcing equal arity at the API layer would preclude it.

DOF aliasing

Each stage’s per-DOF config list is independent, but inside one stage every config slot must target a unique DOF. Two PD actuators driving the same DOF would race in Control.joint_force[dof]; the constructor in ControllerPd::new explicitly rejects duplicates with a Solver error.

If two pipelines drive disjoint DOF sets and run in parallel, that’s fine — the caller orchestrates the order. If two pipelines drive overlapping DOFs, the caller must zero joint_force between them or accept that the second write wins.

Equivalence with the standalone controllers

A pipeline configured as (delay_steps = 0, ctrl = PD, clamp = MaxEffort) is bit-exact equivalent to the standalone ControllerPd with the same gains — same kernel, same write-once-into-joint_force semantics. The pipeline form gives you the option to swap in delay or different clamping without touching the controller code, at the cost of one extra passthrough kernel dispatch per step.

Cross-references

  • PD / PID controllers — controller-stage details.
  • Neural controllers — MLP / LSTM controllers inside ControllerStage::NeuralMlp / Lstm.
  • DC motor clamping — back-EMF clamp variant.
  • Muscle (Hill-type + SEE) — alternative actuator family that runs through solvers::featherstone rather than this pipeline (no pipeline integration yet — Stage 42 deliberate).

PD / PID controllers

The ControllerPd and ControllerPid types are molla’s canonical joint-space closed-loop controllers, mirroring Newton’s ControllerPD and ControllerPID minus the feed-forward / const-effort plumbing. They come in two flavours:

  • Standalone — ControllerPd and ControllerPid read directly from Control.joint_target_* and write to Control.joint_force, one kernel dispatch per step.
  • Pipeline — ControllerPipelinePd and ControllerPipelinePid read from upstream Delay output buffers and otherwise behave identically; they’re the controllers the composable pipeline plugs into.

Source: crates/molla/src/actuators/controller_pd.rs, controller_pid.rs, controller_pipeline_*.rs. Shaders: shaders/actuator_pd.wgsl, shaders/actuator_pid.wgsl, shaders/actuator_pipeline_*.wgsl. Per molla’s GPU-first rule, all effort math runs in WGSL — the Rust orchestrators only own the per-actuator parameter buffers and the dispatch wrapper.

PD: effort law

effort = kp · (target_pos − q) + kd · (target_vel − qd)
effort = clamp(effort, −max_effort, +max_effort)   if max_effort > 0

Stateless. The cap is symmetric and disabled when max_effort == 0. For asymmetric caps or position-dependent caps, drop the in-kernel cap (set max_effort = 0 in the controller and bolt a ClampingMaxEffort / ClampingPositionBased on top via the pipeline).

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct ControllerPdConfig {
    pub dof: u32,            // index into joint_q / joint_qd / joint_force
    pub kp: Real,            // N/m or N·m/rad
    pub kd: Real,            // N·s/m or N·m·s/rad
    pub max_effort: Real,    // 0 disables the cap
}
}
#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let pd = ControllerPd::new(&engine, &model, &[
    ControllerPdConfig { dof: 0, kp: 100.0, kd: 10.0, max_effort: 50.0 },
    ControllerPdConfig { dof: 1, kp: 100.0, kd: 10.0, max_effort: 50.0 },
])?;

// Per-step:
pd.step(&engine, &state, &mut control)?;
}

PID: effort law + anti-windup

err   = target_pos − q
err_d = target_vel − qd
i_t   = clamp(i_{t-1} + err · dt, −integral_max, +integral_max)
effort = kp · err + ki · i_t + kd · err_d
effort = clamp(effort, −max_effort, +max_effort)   if max_effort > 0

Stateful: each step updates the per-actuator integral accumulator from the previous step’s value. The kernel writes the new integral into a ping-pong buffer that the orchestrator swaps after every dispatch, avoiding a host round-trip.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct ControllerPidConfig {
    pub dof: u32,
    pub kp: Real,
    pub ki: Real,
    pub kd: Real,
    pub integral_max: Real, // 0 disables the integral cap (anti-windup)
    pub max_effort: Real,   // 0 disables the effort cap
}
}

Anti-windup

integral_max is the symmetric clamp on the integral accumulator itself — applied before multiplication by ki. This is the simplest form of anti-windup: it prevents the integrator from running away during prolonged saturation (when the plant can’t respond fast enough to the requested effort). The alternative — back-calculation or conditional integration — would buy slightly faster recovery from saturation at the cost of extra plumbing; the symmetric clamp is sufficient for the trajectory-tracking use cases that drive most RL / teleop demos.

ControllerPid::reset() zeros both ping-pong sides of the integral buffer — useful at episode boundaries.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let pid = ControllerPid::new(&engine, &model, &[
    ControllerPidConfig { dof: 0, kp: 100.0, ki: 5.0, kd: 10.0,
                          integral_max: 2.0, max_effort: 50.0 },
])?;

for _ in 0..n_steps {
    pid.step(&engine, &state, &mut control, dt)?;
    integrator.step(&engine, &model, &mut state, &control, dt)?;
}
}

Single-DOF assumption

Both controllers read state.joint_q[dof] / state.joint_qd[dof] and write control.joint_force[dof] directly — they assume q and qd use the same index. This is true for revolute / prismatic joints; not true for ball / free joints whose q carries quaternion components while qd carries angular velocity (the two arrays diverge in length).

Position-tracking PD on a quaternion isn’t well-defined anyway, so this is a soft restriction in practice — multi-DoF orientations should be driven by an external orientation-error controller that writes effort to the corresponding qd slots after computing the torque from the quaternion error.

Validation + DOF uniqueness

The constructors validate:

  • dof is in range against model.joint_dof_total.
  • No two entries share the same dof (would race in joint_force[dof]).

A failure surfaces as Error::Solver at construction; the per-step kernel cannot fail because the validation already ran.

Pipeline variants

ControllerPipelinePd and ControllerPipelinePid have the same config types, the same effort math, and the same anti-windup semantics. The only difference is the source of the target: they read from upstream Delay::out_pos() / out_vel() buffers instead of from control.joint_target_*. That makes them the natural drop- in for the composable pipeline; use the standalone variants when there’s no delay stage.

Cross-references

  • Composable actuator pipeline — the Delay → Controller → Clamping orchestrator that hosts the pipeline-flavoured variants.
  • DC motor clamping — replace the in-kernel symmetric cap with a four-quadrant DC-motor envelope.
  • Neural controllers — MLP / LSTM controllers that share the per-step contract (write into joint_force via DOF indices, optional clamping bolt-on).

Neural controllers

molla ships two on-device neural-controller flavours that drop a pre-trained policy into the actuator pipeline without ever round-tripping the network outputs through the host:

  • ControllerNeuralMlp (Stage 18.1) — fixed-architecture 3-layer feed-forward MLP with tanh non-linearities.
  • ControllerNeuralLstm (Stage 31) — single-cell LSTM forward pass + linear output projection, hidden + cell state carried on the device across substeps.

Both write directly into Control.joint_force[dof] and plug into the composable actuator pipeline via the ControllerStage::NeuralMlp / ControllerStage::Lstm variants, so downstream clamping (effort cap, DC-motor envelope, etc.) sees the policy’s output just like any other controller’s.

Source: crates/molla/src/actuators/controller_neural_mlp.rs, controller_neural_lstm.rs. Shaders: shaders/actuator_neural_mlp.wgsl + actuator_neural_mlp_scatter.wgsl, shaders/actuator_neural_lstm.wgsl.

MLP — ControllerNeuralMlp

Architecture (hard-coded in WGSL):

y = W3 · tanh(W2 · tanh(W1 · x + b1) + b2) + b3

Configurable sizes via ControllerNeuralMlpConfig (input_dim, hidden_dim ≤ 256, output_dim). All three dims are bumped to a shared MAX_HIDDEN constant in the WGSL kernel; recompilation isn’t needed to switch dimensions, only hidden_dim ≤ 256 is enforced.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct ControllerNeuralMlpConfig {
    pub input_dim: u32,
    pub hidden_dim: u32,   // <= 256
    pub output_dim: u32,
}

pub struct MlpWeights<'a> {
    pub w1: &'a [Real], pub b1: &'a [Real],
    pub w2: &'a [Real], pub b2: &'a [Real],
    pub w3: &'a [Real], pub b3: &'a [Real],
}
}

Row-major layout:

SlabShapeLength
w1[hidden_dim × input_dim]H · I elements
b1[hidden_dim]H elements
w2[hidden_dim × hidden_dim]H · H elements
b2[hidden_dim]H elements
w3[output_dim × hidden_dim]O · H elements
b3[output_dim]O elements

controller.expected_weight_dims() returns the exact tuple so callers can size their tensors without re-deriving the math.

Per-step contract

The MLP forward pass runs as a single WGSL dispatch; the outputs are scattered into Control.joint_force[dof_indices[i]] by a second dispatch (actuator_neural_mlp_scatter.wgsl). The controller owns:

  • The inputs buffer (input_dim floats). Pushed each step by the caller via set_inputs(queue, values) — typical sources are proprioceptive sensors (joint angles, IMU readings) and task observations.
  • The outputs buffer (output_dim floats). Downloadable via download_outputs(...) for diagnostic UIs; otherwise stays on the device and feeds the scatter pass directly.
  • The six weight slabs (immutable after set_weights).
  • The dof_indices map (output[i] → joint_force[dof_indices[i]]). Duplicate DOFs are rejected at construction to avoid scatter races.
#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let cfg = ControllerNeuralMlpConfig {
    input_dim: 24, hidden_dim: 128, output_dim: 12,
};
let dof_indices: Vec<u32> = (0..12).collect();
let mut mlp = ControllerNeuralMlp::new(&engine, cfg, &dof_indices)?;
mlp.set_weights(&device, &queue, &MlpWeights { w1, b1, w2, b2, w3, b3 })?;

for _ in 0..n_steps {
    let obs = build_observation(&state, &sensors);
    mlp.set_inputs(&queue, &obs)?;
    actuator.step(&engine, &state, &mut control, dt)?;   // runs forward + scatter
}
}

LSTM — ControllerNeuralLstm

Single-cell recurrence with a linear output projection. The hidden state h_t and cell state c_t live on the device across substeps, so the controller can express stateful policies without any host round-trip per step.

i_t = σ(W_i · x_t + U_i · h_{t-1} + b_i)
f_t = σ(W_f · x_t + U_f · h_{t-1} + b_f)
g_t = tanh(W_g · x_t + U_g · h_{t-1} + b_g)
o_t = σ(W_o · x_t + U_o · h_{t-1} + b_o)
c_t = f_t ⊙ c_{t-1} + i_t ⊙ g_t
h_t = o_t ⊙ tanh(c_t)
y_t = W_y · h_t + b_y

LstmWeights lays out all 14 slabs (per gate: w_g input-projection H × I, u_g recurrent-projection H × H, b_g bias H × four gates, plus the output linear w_y O × H and b_y O). controller.expected_weight_dims() returns the same shape as a LstmWeightDims struct so callers can iterate / zip with named fields.

Hidden-state reset

reset_hidden_state(...) zeros both h and c on the device. Call at episode boundaries — without it the policy effectively “remembers” context from the previous trajectory, which is exactly the wrong inductive bias for an off-policy RL replay buffer.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let cfg = ControllerNeuralLstmConfig {
    input_dim: 24, hidden_dim: 64, output_dim: 12,
};
let mut lstm = ControllerNeuralLstm::new(&engine, cfg, &dof_indices)?;
lstm.set_weights(&device, &queue, &LstmWeights { ..weights })?;

for episode in 0..n_episodes {
    lstm.reset_hidden_state(&engine)?;
    for _ in 0..n_steps {
        let obs = build_observation(&state, &sensors);
        lstm.set_inputs(&queue, &obs)?;
        actuator.step(&engine, &state, &mut control, dt)?;
    }
}
}

Weight loading

Both controllers expect row-major weight slabs and validate the total length at set_weights time. The mismatch error includes both the expected and actual lengths so a bad weight slab shows up at load rather than at the first frame of inference.

Weight slabs are row-major:

  • Dense layer weights use [out, in] order and flatten row-major.
  • Recurrent matrices use the gate order documented on LstmWeights.
  • Recurrent state should always be initialised by the controller itself (new zeros h_state and c_state); don’t try to load it from a checkpoint.

Single-DoF + uniqueness

Same restriction as PD / PID: each dof_indices[i] must be unique inside one controller (else the scatter writes race). The constructor checks both bounds (dof_indices[i] < model.joint_dof_total) and uniqueness; a duplicate produces a Solver error.

Cross-references

  • Composable actuator pipeline — wires neural controllers into the Delay → Controller → Clamping chain.
  • PD / PID controllers — same per-step contract, hand-tuned gains instead of learned weights.
  • Differentiable physics / Tape-based autograd — train or tune policies inside molla using the autograd tape.

DC motor clamping

The Clamping* family enforces actuator-physics limits after the controller has written raw effort into Control.joint_force[dof]. Three variants ship today, all configurable via the composable pipeline’s ClampingStage:

  • ClampingMaxEffort — symmetric per-actuator cap |τ| ≤ τ_max.
  • ClampingDcMotor — four-quadrant DC-motor torque-vs-speed envelope (back-EMF + current limit).
  • ClampingPositionBased — shared (position → τ_max) lookup table, useful for joints whose available effort drops near hard limits.

Source: crates/molla/src/actuators/clamping/. Shaders: shaders/clamping_*.wgsl. Every clamp reads its inputs, computes the clipped effort, and writes it back into the same joint_force[dof] slot — no auxiliary buffers, no host round-trip.

ClampingDcMotor — four-quadrant envelope

Models a brushed DC motor with current-limited torque ceiling. Parameters mirror what’s on a real motor datasheet:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct ClampingDcMotorConfig {
    pub dof: u32,
    pub stall_torque: Real,       // τ_stall : peak torque at zero velocity
    pub no_load_speed: Real,      // ω_nl    : velocity at zero torque
    pub max_motor_effort: Real,   // τ_cap   : current-limited torque ceiling
}
}

The physical model is:

back-EMF envelope:    τ_line(ω) = τ_stall · (1 − ω / ω_nl)
current cap:          τ_cap
applied:              τ_avail(ω) = min(τ_line(ω), τ_cap)

In the four-quadrant case (positive and negative ω, motoring and regenerating), the envelope is mirrored across the origin to form a trapezoid, and the kernel clamps the requested effort to lie inside it.

The corner velocity

The linear envelope τ_stall · (1 − ω/ω_nl) and the current cap τ_cap intersect at a corner velocity

ω_corner = ω_nl · (1 + τ_cap / τ_stall)

stored per-actuator in corner_velocity and recomputed every time set_params(...) runs. Beyond ω_corner the linear envelope is already below the cap and the cap doesn’t bite — and worse, the linear envelope would flip sign without the clamp, sending the torque limit into the wrong quadrant. The kernel clamps ω to ±ω_corner before evaluating the line, which keeps the envelope well-defined for arbitrarily high velocities.

If τ_cap ≥ τ_stall the corner is ω_nl itself (the cap is inactive — the linear envelope is the binding constraint everywhere).

Validation

The constructor rejects:

  • no_load_speed <= 0 — would divide by zero in the envelope.
  • stall_torque < 0 — physically meaningless.
  • max_motor_effort < 0 — physically meaningless.

set_params(...) accepts in-place updates of all three parameters plus the implicit corner_velocity recompute, making it cheap to sweep motor sizes during tuning without rebuilding the GPU resources.

API

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use molla::actuators::{ClampingDcMotor, ClampingDcMotorConfig};

let dc = ClampingDcMotor::new(&engine, &[
    ClampingDcMotorConfig {
        dof: 0,
        stall_torque: 12.0,     // N·m
        no_load_speed: 30.0,    // rad/s
        max_motor_effort: 8.0,  // N·m current-limited ceiling
    },
])?;

// Wire into the actuator pipeline:
let mut actuator = Actuator::new(delay, ctrl, ClampingStage::DcMotor(dc));
}

ClampingMaxEffort — symmetric cap

The simplest clamp:

τ_clipped = clamp(τ, −τ_max, +τ_max)   if τ_max > 0
τ_clipped = τ                          if τ_max == 0  (disabled)

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct ClampingMaxEffortConfig {
    pub dof: u32,
    pub max_effort: Real,  // 0 disables (passthrough)
}
}

Equivalent to the in-kernel symmetric cap on ControllerPd, exposed as a standalone clamping stage so the controller can be replaced (e.g. with a neural policy) without losing the safety net. set_max_effort(...) updates the caps in-place from host data.

ClampingPositionBased — shared lookup table

All actuators in one stage share the same (position → max_effort) table; the table is interpolated linearly per-DOF using the current state.joint_q[dof]. Models joints whose available torque drops as they approach their hard limits (e.g. real servos that current-limit near end-stops).

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let pb = ClampingPositionBased::new(
    &engine,
    /* dof_indices = */ &[0, 1, 2],
    /* positions   = */ &[-1.57, -0.5, 0.0, 0.5, 1.57],
    /* efforts     = */ &[ 0.0,   5.0, 20.0, 5.0, 0.0 ],
)?;
}

The constructor validates that positions is monotonically non-decreasing (else the linear-interp dispatch’s binary-search behaviour is undefined) and that every effort is non-negative.

Why a clamp instead of a tighter controller?

Real motors saturate. A PD controller doesn’t know it’s commanding a torque the motor cannot deliver — feeding the raw effort into the integrator would cause overshoot, oscillation, or integrator wind-up. The clamping stage models the actuator (whose envelope is physics, not control), and the controller is free to ignore it. Pairing ControllerPid with ClampingDcMotor is the canonical recipe for an RL environment that wants the policy to learn the motor’s natural envelope.

Cross-references

  • Composable actuator pipeline — defines ClampingStage and wires the clamp after the controller.
  • PD / PID controllers — typical upstream controller stages.
  • Neural controllers — same upstream slot, learned weights instead of hand-tuned gains.

Muscle (Hill-type + SEE)

Stage 42 added a biomechanical Hill-type muscle actuator that drives CABLE joints — the joint type molla provides for 1-DoF linear-stretch DOFs like tendons or muscle-tendon units (MTUs). Together they let molla simulate musculoskeletal models in the OpenSim / MyoSuite tradition without leaving the GPU-first pipeline.

The muscle ships in five progressive cuts (v1 → v5):

  • v1 — Single muscle per joint, instantaneous activation, rigid tendon. Hill three-element model only.
  • v2 — Adds Thelen-style series-elastic tendon (SEE), first-order excitation → activation filter, and per-joint co-contraction via a CSR (multiple muscles summed at the solver level).
  • v3 — GPU kernel (shaders/muscle.wgsl) for the per-step torque computation on host-allocated parallel buffers.
  • v4 — SEE Newton solve runs on the GPU with full host parity.
  • v5 — Per-muscle tendon stiffness ratio is stored in model buffers and consumed by both CPU and GPU SEE paths; pennation remains per-muscle on both paths.

Source: crates/molla-actuators/src/muscle.rs. Shader: crates/molla-kernels/shaders/muscle.wgsl. The host-side Hill model is always compiled (no GPU feature gate) so unit tests and the CPU solver can use it directly.

Three-element Hill model

Total path length of the MTU splits between the contractile fibre (at pennation angle α) and the series-elastic tendon:

l_total = l_m · cos(α) + l_t

In cable coordinates, q_l = 0 means the MTU is at rest (fibre at l_opt, tendon at slack). The active fibre force comes from the Hill model:

f_fibre = a · f_max · f_L(l_m / l_opt) · f_V(v_m / v_max)

with the tendon-side balance

f_tendon(ε) = f_fibre · cos(α),    ε = (l_t − l_t_slack) / l_t_slack

Force–length curve

Gaussian centred at l_norm = 1.0:

f_L(l_norm) = exp( − ((l_norm − 1) / σ)² ),   σ = 0.45

Peaks at 1.0, falls to 0 outside [0.4, 1.6]. Implementation in force_length(l_norm); the choice of a Gaussian (rather than the piecewise-polynomial Thelen curve) is for cheap GPU evaluation and analytical differentiability — within the operating range it’s within a few percent of Thelen.

Force–velocity curve (Hill hyperbola)

            ⎧ 0,                              v_norm ≤ −1
f_V(v_norm) ⎨ (1 + v_norm) / (1 − v_norm/A_F), −1 < v_norm < 0
            ⎩ F_V_max − (F_V_max − 1) · e^{−K_V · v_norm}, v_norm ≥ 0

with A_F = 0.25, F_V_max = 1.5, K_V = 5. Returns 1.0 at v_norm = 0 (isometric), 0 at v_norm = −1 (full shortening), and asymptotes to ≈ 1.5 for large positive v_norm (eccentric lengthening). The exponential lengthening branch is a smooth saturating ramp instead of Thelen’s two-piece formulation — same reasoning as the force-length curve.

Tendon force–strain curve

Quadratic past slack so the slope vanishes at ε = 0 (C¹ continuous); zero below slack (tendons don’t push):

f_t(ε) = f_max · k · ε²,    ε > 0
f_t(ε) = 0,                 ε ≤ 0

k = (stiffness_ratio / 2)². With Thelen’s default stiffness_ratio = 30, k = 225, the tendon reaches f_max at ε ≈ 6.7 % — mid-range for real tendons. Matching the linear tendon’s E·A = stiffness_ratio · f_max slope at the f_t = f_max strain pins the constant.

Activation lag

The Hill curves take the filtered activation a, not the raw excitation u. molla models the lag with a first-order ODE:

da/dt = (u − a) / τ_act

update_muscle_activation(model, dt) integrates one step with implicit Euler:

a_{n+1} = (a_n + (dt / τ) · u) / (1 + dt / τ)

Implicit Euler is unconditionally stable for any dt > 0 — there is no CFL condition. τ_act defaults to 20 ms (DEFAULT_TAU_ACTIVATION, matching Thelen 2003). Muscles with τ_act ≤ 0 get an instantaneous a := clamp(u, 0, 1) (v1 behaviour, useful for unit tests).

Activations are clamped to [0, 1] after each update. Call this before the dynamics solver every step:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use molla::actuators::update_muscle_activation;
// 1. user writes new neural drives:
model.muscle_excitation.host_mut()?[i] = 0.6;
// 2. low-pass filter into activation:
update_muscle_activation(&mut model, dt)?;
// 3. step the solver — Featherstone reads model.muscle_activation
solver.step(...)?;
}

SEE Newton solve

When l_tendon_slack > 0, Muscle::torque(q_l, qd_l) runs a damped Newton solver on the tendon strain ε to balance the fibre–tendon force equation:

f_fibre(l_m(ε), v_m(ε)) · cos(α) − f_t(ε) = 0

The seed ε₀ picks between the geometric strain (when the MTU is stretched past rest) and the analytic-root strain √(a · cos α / k) (when the MTU is at rest but the fibre is active). Up to 8 iterations; damped step size ≤ 0.5 · |ε| prevents overshoot near l_m = l_opt where df_L/dε vanishes. Convergence criterion |residual| < 1e-4 · f_max. Typical step count: 2–3 inside the operating envelope.

The rigid-tendon fast path (when l_tendon_slack == 0) skips the Newton solve entirely and matches the v1 behaviour bit-for-bit — useful as a regression oracle.

Co-contraction (CSR)

Multiple muscles per joint are summed at the solver level via a CSR laid out as parallel buffers on Model:

  • model.joint_muscle_offsets[j..j+1] — start / end indices into the per-joint slice.
  • model.joint_muscle_indices[k] — flat list of muscle ids attached to each joint.
  • Per-muscle data lives in parallel model.muscle_config, model.muscle_activation, model.muscle_excitation, model.muscle_tau_activation etc.

Antagonist pairs are modelled with a per-muscle polarity ∈ {+1, −1} flag that flips the fibre kinematics so the Hill curves see the muscle’s own coordinate frame. The torque returned at the joint level is the sum of m.torque(q_l, qd_l) across the muscles in the CSR slice; flexor + extensor pairs on the same joint cancel naturally.

GPU kernel (v3, v4)

shaders/muscle.wgsl runs the per-step torque computation in parallel across all muscles. The kernel reads the Model::muscle_* parallel buffers and writes per-muscle torque contributions into a joint_force scatter buffer; the Featherstone solver’s torque-injection pass then sums them into the joint-space tau vector.

v4 ships the SEE Newton solve on the GPU too, with full host parity (verified by parity tests in crates/molla-solvers/tests/joint_muscle_gpu.rs). The same damped Newton kernel runs across all muscles in lockstep — no per-muscle control divergence inside the 8 iterations, because every muscle that converges early simply repeats its converged solution for the remaining iterations.

Configuration

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct MuscleConfig {
    pub f_max: Real,            // peak isometric force (N)
    pub l_opt: Real,            // optimal fibre length (m)
    pub v_max: Real,            // peak shortening velocity (m/s)
    pub activation: Real,       // a ∈ [0, 1] (initial filtered state)
    pub excitation: Real,       // u ∈ [0, 1] (initial neural drive)
    pub tau_activation: Real,   // τ_act (s), default 0.020
    pub l_tendon_slack: Real,   // 0 ⇒ rigid tendon, > 0 enables SEE
    pub tendon_stiffness_ratio: Real, // E·A / f_max, default 30
    pub pennation_angle: Real,  // α₀ at l_opt (rad), default 0
    pub polarity: Real,         // +1 / −1 (antagonist flag)
}
}

Default::default() gives a “medium” mammalian limb muscle: 100 N peak isometric, 5 cm optimal fibre length, 0.5 m/s peak contraction, rigid tendon (v1 compatibility).

Cross-references

  • Sim / Featherstone ABA — torque- injection consumer of the per-muscle force.
  • Composable actuator pipeline — currently separate from the muscle path (Stage 42 deliberate); muscles feed Featherstone directly without going through the Delay → Controller → Clamping chain.
  • References: Zajac 1989 (“Muscle and Tendon: Properties, Models, Scaling…”), Thelen 2003 (“Adjustment of Muscle Mechanics Model Parameters to Simulate Dynamic Contractions in Older Adults”).

molla-vehicle overview

crates/molla-vehicle is the wheeled-vehicle simulation crate: terrain, tires, suspension, driveline, a lightweight chassis, and the differentiable system-identification demo. It is deliberately dependency-free (no other workspace crates), and is re-exported through the facade as molla::vehicle::*. It is also the home of the real_tire/ tree — the deformable tetra-FEM tire that the tire viewer scenes (119–123) and the 40-wheel GPU scaling effort build on (PLAN_REALTIRE.md / PROGRESS.md at the repo root track that work).

Subsystems

ModuleWhat it provides

The crate itself is host-side; its GPU twins live in molla-kernels (tire_brush.wgsl, tire_fem*.wgsl, bekker/DEM/thermal/transient tire kernels) and are validated by the tire_* hardware lanes:

make test-gpu P=molla-kernels T=tire_fem_gpu
make test-gpu P=molla-kernels T=tire_brush_gpu

The CPU↔GPU status of each tire lane is recorded in real_tire/parity_ledger.rs and the TireFemTorqueGpuStatus / TireFemMatrixFreeNewtonGpuStatus contracts in molla-kernels.
