Testing

The crate is CPU-testable with plain cargo test -p molla-vehicle. The suite also hosts the tire validation harness (real_tire/rig, real_tire/reports) — structural truth gates (loaded radius, footprint, pressure distribution, bead drift) and force-shape checks that guard the tire physics without external measured-data calibration (that scope is deliberately excluded — see the “Calibration stance” section of PLAN_REALTIRE.md).

Tape-based autograd

molla::autograd ships tape-style reverse-mode automatic differentiation modelled on Warp’s wp.Tape (xtra/warp/warp/_src/tape.py). Every “tensor” produced during the forward pass earns a TapeId; the tape stores the recorded op + the values needed to evaluate its adjoint; Tape::backward(seed) walks the recorded list in reverse and accumulates per-TapeId gradients.

Source: crates/molla/src/autograd/tape.rs.

Why CPU only (for now)

Differentiability is the CPU-acceptable exception to molla’s GPU-first rule. Tape recording fundamentally needs heap allocation and a dynamic graph structure that doesn’t map onto wgpu’s compute-pipeline-state model — Newton + Warp solve the same problem with dynamic host graphs. We use Rust + CPU and accept the perf hit (orders of magnitude vs hand-written adjoint kernels) in exchange for a working, testable autograd v1.

Crucially, the TapeOp enum is engine-agnostic: a GPU port can iterate the tape and dispatch one kernel per op without touching the tape format. That’s the migration path once a per-op adjoint-kernel queue exists.

Lifecycle

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use molla::autograd::{Tape, TapeOp};

// 1. Start a tape.
let mut tape = Tape::start();

// 2. Allocate input tensors. `alloc` registers values and returns a TapeId.
let a = tape.alloc(vec![1.0, 2.0, 3.0]);
let b = tape.alloc(vec![4.0, 5.0, 6.0]);

// 3. Record forward ops. The tape evaluates each op and stores the
//    output value, so the adjoint can reload it later.
let c = tape.fresh_id();
tape.record(TapeOp::Add { a, b, out: c });

let n = tape.fresh_id();
tape.record(TapeOp::Norm { v: c, out: n });

// 4. Close recording.
tape.stop();

// 5. Seed the loss gradient and back-propagate.
let mut grads = std::collections::HashMap::new();
grads.insert(n, vec![1.0]);          // ∂L/∂||c|| = 1
let grads = tape.backward(grads);

// 6. Read the input gradients.
let grad_a = grads.get(&a).unwrap();  // ∂L/∂a
let grad_b = grads.get(&b).unwrap();  // ∂L/∂b
}

Recorded operations

The v1 op set is intentionally small — just enough to express XPBD’s distance-constraint projection on host:

VariantForwardAdjoint
Add{a,b,out}out = a + b∂L/∂a += ∂L/∂out, ∂L/∂b += ∂L/∂out
Sub{a,b,out}out = a − b∂L/∂a += ∂L/∂out, ∂L/∂b -= ∂L/∂out
Mul{a,scalar,out}out = a · s∂L/∂a += s · ∂L/∂out
MatVec{v,m,out}out = M · v (fixed 3×3 M)∂L/∂v += Mᵀ · ∂L/∂out
Norm{v,out}out = ‖v‖₂∂L/∂v += (v / ‖v‖) · ∂L/∂out

Stage 24b added six robust-loss elementwise variants — L1Loss, SmoothL2Loss, HuberLoss, PseudoHuberLoss, TukeyLoss, CauchyLoss — so the tape can express the M-estimator chain used by the inverse-rendering / system-ID loops without forcing a CPU-side recompute.

Stage 23.1 added three “Featherstone-sweep” chunks (FeatherstoneFwdKinematics, FeatherstoneUpwardInertia, FeatherstoneDownwardAccel) that don’t dispatch through the generic backward — see Featherstone reverse adjoint. The chunks are recorded so a future GPU port can iterate the tape and swap each sweep for its own kernel.

Custom adjoints — wp.func_grad pattern

Recording every elementary op into the tape is the slow path. For hot solver loops (XPBD constraint projection, Featherstone ABA), molla ships hand-written closed-form adjoints that bypass the tape entirely. These live in their own modules:

  • xpbd_adjoint — manual reverse pass over the XPBD distance-constraint Gauss-Seidel loop.
  • featherstone_adjoint — tape-recorded three-sweep ABA adjoint with a hybrid analytic / finite-difference per-step Jacobian.
  • mpm_adjoint — particle / grid adjoint for diff-MPM.
  • fem::adjoint::solve_adjoint (FEM adjoint) — classical adjoint method for the linear-elasticity solve.

Performance trade-off: hand-written gradients pay no per-op heap cost and inline cleanly, but they’re locked to one forward path. The tape generalises to anything you can express as a chain of TapeOps but cleans up the heap for every recorded intermediate.

Gradient checking

The autograd tests in crates/molla-autograd/tests/autograd_xpbd.rs and crates/molla-autograd/tests/autograd_featherstone.rs exercise the hand-written gradients against central-difference finite differences with tolerance 1e-3 (the standard gradcheck tolerance Warp ships).

For ad-hoc checks, the pattern is:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn loss(p: &[Real]) -> Real { /* forward pass */ }

let p = vec![/* ... */];
let analytic = my_grad_fn(&p);
let mut numerical = vec![0.0; p.len()];
for i in 0..p.len() {
    let mut pp = p.clone(); pp[i] += EPS;
    let mut pn = p.clone(); pn[i] -= EPS;
    numerical[i] = (loss(&pp) - loss(&pn)) / (2.0 * EPS);
}
for (a, n) in analytic.iter().zip(&numerical) {
    assert!((a - n).abs() < 1e-3);
}
}

Determinism

Tape::backward is deterministic for a fixed input + recorded op sequence. Every operation is a fixed-shape arithmetic loop over the recorded ops — no HashMap iteration order matters because the op list is Vec<TapeOp> walked in reverse insertion order, not via hash iteration. Identical inputs yield bit-exact identical gradients across runs (verified by the tape_replay_is_deterministic test).

Cross-references

  • Featherstone reverse adjoint — Stage 23.1 three-sweep ABA adjoint.
  • XPBD / VBD adjoint — hand-written distance- constraint adjoint.
  • MPM adjoint — particle-grid diff-MPM tape.
  • FEM adjoint — classical Kᵀ · λ = ∂J/∂u adjoint solve.
  • Differentiable Gaussian splat renderer — Stage 44 family, end-to-end differentiable 3DGS raytrace.
  • Math / Iterative solvers — robust-loss functions backing the elementwise *Loss ops.

Featherstone reverse adjoint

Stage 23 introduced reverse-mode automatic differentiation for the Featherstone Articulated Body Algorithm (ABA) — i.e. closed-loop trajectory-optimisation gradients through a rigid-body dynamics rollout. The implementation is hybrid (analytic chain rule over the integrator + per-step Jacobian) and ships in four iterative cuts within Stage 23.1, plus a robust-loss extension at Stage 24b.

Source: crates/molla/src/autograd/featherstone_adjoint.rs. Shader (GPU scaffold): crates/molla-kernels/shaders/featherstone_adjoint_jacobians.wgsl.

What it solves

Given a serial revolute chain with n links, a joint torque trajectory τ_{0..T-1}, and a scalar loss L(q_T, qd_T) (typically end-effector tracking), the adjoint returns ∂L/∂τ_t for every step t ∈ [0, T). The headline use cases:

  • Inverse-dynamics trajectory optimisation (Carpentier & Mansard 2018).
  • Differentiable model-predictive control.
  • Sim-to-real domain randomisation with learned controllers in the loop.

The three Featherstone sweeps map onto three TapeOp chunks:

SweepTapeOp
Forward kinematics + vFeatherstoneFwdKinematics
Articulated inertiaFeatherstoneUpwardInertia
Forward accelerationFeatherstoneDownwardAccel

These ops are recorded for tape inspection / determinism checks but the adjoint is not evaluated through the generic Tape::backward dispatch — the three sweeps form an inseparable unit (inertia + acceleration sweeps need the kinematic intermediates) and run together inside FeatherstoneRevoluteChain::reverse.

Stage 23.1 cuts

23.1.1 — closed-form CPU, single-DoF

The first cut shipped:

  • A hand-written analytic adjoint over the symplectic-Euler integrator that threads ∂L/∂q + ∂L/∂qd through every step in closed form, accumulating ∂L/∂τ_t at every step.
  • A per-step single-step Jacobian computed via central differences on the full Featherstone forward at this step’s (q_t, qd_t). For serial revolute chains of size ≤ 7 the cost is O(3n · per-step) per step — negligible compared to trajectory length.
  • Coverage: single pendulum, 2-link planar arm, 6-DoF Franka chain.

This is the standard “adjoint via gradient through inverse dynamics” pattern from Carpentier & Mansard 2018 (“Analytical Derivatives of Rigid Body Dynamics Algorithms”), applied at the single-step granularity.

23.1.2 — multi-DoF coverage + GPU scaffold

Extended the per-link math to stacked single-DoF representations of Ball / Free / Prismatic joints. Each multi-DoF user joint is exposed as a single composite joint to user code while the adjoint operates on the equivalent stacked single-DoF representation. This keeps the closed-form Jacobian path uniform: no special-case kernels per joint type, just per-DoF spatial Jacobian columns.

AutogradError::UnsupportedJoint surfaces if a composite kind (Ball / Free / Distance / D6) reaches the per-link math directly — the user is expected to decompose upstream. Helpers like FeatherstoneRevoluteChain::spherical_pendulum(...) handle the decomposition for the standard cases.

The GPU scaffold (featherstone_adjoint_jacobians.wgsl) is in place but not yet wired through the live solver — the per-step Jacobian on the device is the obvious next port and gives the largest speedup for long chains.

23.1.3 — Distance + D6 adjoint kinematics

Added per-DoF adjoint contributions for Distance and D6 composite joints by exposing them as stacked single-DoF chains. The trajectory-level adjoint is unchanged; only the per-DoF spatial Jacobian columns extend.

23.1.4 — analytic ∂h/∂q (CPU)

Replaced the central-difference per-step Jacobian with an analytic derivative of the full ABA inertia / bias sweep. About 5–7× faster on the 6-DoF Franka case and removes the central-difference quantisation that limited gradient checking to 1e-3 (the analytic version passes 1e-5).

24b — robust-loss extension

The six robust-loss TapeOp variants (HuberLoss, TukeyLoss, CauchyLoss, etc.) compose with the Featherstone trajectory adjoint: the EE-position error can be wrapped in norm_huber(e, δ) before the seed ∂L/∂(EE) flows into the Featherstone reverse, so trajectory optimisation with a robust loss runs end-to-end through the tape without bespoke seed logic.

Public API

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use molla::autograd::{
    record_featherstone_step, FeatherstoneRevoluteChain,
    FeatherstoneTrace, JointKind, JointProjection,
    JacobianScratch, JacobianStrategy, RevoluteLink,
};

// Build the chain (decomposed to single-DoF links).
let chain = FeatherstoneRevoluteChain::from_links(vec![
    RevoluteLink { /* ... */ },
    RevoluteLink { /* ... */ },
    /* ... */
]);

// Roll out forward with torques `tau`, populating a trace.
let mut trace = FeatherstoneTrace::default();
let (q_T, qd_T, ee_T) = chain.rollout(q0, qd0, &tau, dt, &mut trace);

// Seed the loss gradient (∂L/∂ee at the final step) and reverse.
let grad_ee_T = /* user-supplied seed */;
let grads = chain.reverse(
    &trace,
    grad_ee_T,
    JacobianStrategy::Analytic, // or CentralDifference
    &mut JacobianScratch::new(chain.n_dof(), trace.steps()),
);

// grads.tau[t] is ∂L/∂τ_t for each step.
}

Implementation strategy summary

Featherstone’s three sweeps are nontrivial to differentiate line-by-line — the §10 derivation is a multi-week algebra exercise. For Stage 23.1 v1 molla ships a hybrid adjoint that is correct, verifiable, and matches the reverse-mode contract:

  • Per-step “single-step” Jacobian — analytic (23.1.4) or central-difference (23.1.1 fallback).
  • Trajectory-level adjoint — fully analytical: the chain rule threads ∂L/∂q + ∂L/∂qd through the symplectic-Euler integrator in closed form, accumulating ∂L/∂τ at every step.
  • Tape-level recording — each sweep maps to its own TapeOp chunk so a future GPU port can swap the per-step Jacobian build for a hand-derived analytical sweep without touching the trajectory adjoint or the tape format.

Determinism

Every operation is a fixed-shape arithmetic loop over the trace — no HashMap iteration, no parallel reductions, no GPU readback reorder. Identical inputs (q0, qd0, tau) yield bit-exact identical gradients across runs, verified by the tape_replay_is_deterministic test in tests/autograd_featherstone.rs.

Cross-references

  • Tape-based autograd — generic Tape infrastructure that hosts the three sweep chunks.
  • Sim / Featherstone ABA — forward algorithm the adjoint differentiates.
  • Math / Iterative solvers — robust-loss functions used by Stage 24b.
  • References: Featherstone 2008 (Rigid Body Dynamics §10), Carpentier & Mansard 2018 (“Analytical Derivatives of Rigid Body Dynamics Algorithms”).

XPBD / VBD adjoint

molla ships closed-form reverse-mode adjoints for the XPBD distance-constraint solver and a partial GPU path for VBD cloth. Both follow the “frozen narrow-phase” pattern Newton uses: freeze the contact set at the start of the step, treat the per- contact normals + bodies as constants for both forward and reverse, and differentiate only the smooth constraint-projection math.

Source: crates/molla/src/autograd/xpbd_adjoint.rs (XPBD), plus the VBD adjoint scaffolding in the same module. Shader (partial GPU XPBD adjoint): crates/molla-kernels/shaders/xpbd_equality.wgsl gives the equality-constraint forward; the adjoint counterpart is host-only in v1.

Why “frozen narrow-phase”?

Contact generation is fundamentally non-smooth: the set of active contacts changes discretely as bodies move. Differentiating through contact onset would require subgradient calculus and Newton’s practice (mirrored here) is to:

  1. Run the narrow phase once at the start of the step.
  2. Treat the resulting (body_a, body_b, normal, depth) tuples as constants for both the forward and reverse pass.
  3. Differentiate only the smooth constraint-projection equations that act on those frozen tuples.

This gives a well-defined ∂(post-step state) / ∂(pre-step state + parameters) jacobian for the duration of the step, at the cost of zero gradient flow through contact-onset events. In practice this is fine for trajectory optimisation over short horizons — the discrete events do not contribute usable gradient anyway.

XPBD distance-constraint adjoint

Forward (matches solvers::xpbd::step_particles minus the strain limiter and ground plane — both non-smooth):

1. Predict: p_pred = p + (v + g · dt) · dt
2. For each Gauss-Seidel iteration over the spring list:
     d   = p_b − p_a
     L   = ‖d‖
     n   = d / L
     C   = L − rest
     α   = compliance / dt²
     Δλ  = −(C + α · λ) / (w_a + w_b + α)
     λ  += Δλ
     p_a −= w_a · Δλ · n
     p_b += w_b · Δλ · n
3. Velocity recovery: v_post = (p_final − p_init) / dt

Reverse: walk the iterations in reverse, undoing each constraint update by replaying its position effect on a saved per-iteration (p_a, p_b, λ) snapshot. The derivation (Macklin et al., XPBD: Position-Based Simulation of Compliant Constrained Dynamics, 2016 §4) shows each Δλ is a smooth function of the saved positions + λ, so the chain rule applies cleanly.

Saved adjoint state

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct DistanceConstraintAdjoint {
    pub p_a_pre: Vec3,
    pub p_b_pre: Vec3,
    pub lambda_pre: Real,  // cumulative λ before this iteration
}
}

One entry per (iteration, spring) pair. For a 100-iteration / 1000-spring chain that’s 100k entries × ~64 bytes ≈ 6.4 MB, well within host budget for the trajectory-optimisation use case.

Public API

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use molla::autograd::{
    xpbd_distance_step_with_grad,
    distance_chain_grad_initial_pos,
    distance_chain_grad_stiffness,
    DistanceConstraintAdjoint,
};

// Forward + trace recording.
let (p_out, lambda_out, adj_trace) = xpbd_distance_step_with_grad(
    &p_init, &v_init, &inv_mass,
    &spring_a, &spring_b, &rest_length, &compliance,
    gravity, dt, iterations,
);

// Gradient of (final chain length) wrt the initial positions.
let grad_p0 = distance_chain_grad_initial_pos(
    &p_init, &v_init, &inv_mass,
    &spring_a, &spring_b, &rest_length, &compliance,
    gravity, dt, iterations,
);

// Gradient wrt per-spring stiffness (the inverse-compliance handle).
let grad_k = distance_chain_grad_stiffness(/* same args */);
}

Why hand-written instead of taped?

The XPBD inner loop is the hot path; recording each Add / Sub / Mul / Norm through the generic Tape would mean hundreds of thousands of heap allocations per step (one per op per spring per iteration). Hand-written closed-form gradients run the reverse pass over the same loop the forward path uses, without any heap allocation past the adj_trace snapshot — orders of magnitude faster, and matches Newton’s wp.func_grad pattern of shipping hand-derived gradients for hot solver paths.

The verification harness in tests/autograd_xpbd.rs checks the analytical adjoint against central-difference finite differences to within 1e-3 (standard gradcheck tolerance).

VBD adjoint — partial GPU

The VBD (Vertex Block Descent) solver is XPBD’s smoother sibling: instead of Gauss-Seidel over springs, it does block-Jacobi iterations over the local Hessian at each vertex. The adjoint follows the same frozen-narrow-phase pattern but the per-iteration update is denser (a 3×3 block solve per vertex instead of a 1×1 λ update per spring).

molla ships VBD on the GPU via shaders/vbd_cloth.wgsl for the forward pass; the adjoint is scaffolded but not yet GPU-resident. The CPU adjoint follows the same shape as the XPBD one and is useful for testing the parity contract before the GPU port lands. This mirrors Newton’s status: VBD’s reverse-mode kernel is on their backlog too, exactly because the per-iteration matrix shape makes the closed-form adjoint denser.

Limits + scope

  • Smooth constraints only. The XPBD strain limiter (a hard bound on ‖d‖ / rest) and the ground-plane projection are non-smooth — they’re excluded from the differentiable forward in v1. The forward path stays bit-identical to the non-strain-limited XPBD; the simulation just doesn’t allow runaway stretching.
  • No friction gradient. Tangential friction couples to the contact set in a non-smooth way; v1 doesn’t try to differentiate through it.
  • No mass differentiability. inv_mass is treated as a constant. inv_mass = 0 still pins the particle (its position survives the projection unchanged).

These restrictions disappear case-by-case as the soft-contact pipeline lands smooth surrogates for friction and contact inception.

  • MPM adjoint — sister hand-written adjoint for the diff-MPM forward.
  • References: Macklin et al. 2016 (“XPBD: Position-Based Simulation of Compliant Constrained Dynamics”).

MPM adjoint

Stage 38.1 added a fully differentiable CPU MPM forward + adjoint chain. The forward (mpm_cpu_diff) runs in f64 with a recorded tape; the adjoint walks the tape in reverse, threading derivatives through P2G + grid update + G2P + corotated SVK stress, and emits gradients for Young’s modulus, initial positions, and initial velocities. With Adam on top, a 64-particle / 30-step demo fits E from a target final-state centroid to FD parity 4.14e−6.

Source: crates/molla/src/autograd/mpm_adjoint.rs. Forward + tape in crates/molla/src/compute/mpm_cpu_diff.rs. Shared math in crates/molla/src/math/dense3.rs (adj_svd3).

Why CPU-only

Per molla’s GPU-first rule, forward solvers run on the GPU and the differentiable CPU path is the exception. MPM is doubly so: the forward already exists in shaders/mpm.wgsl for production runs; the diff path is a separate f64 host implementation purpose-built for inverse-problem demos. The two are kept in parity by the explicit-MPM regression tests but their data structures don’t intersect — the tape would not survive a wgpu round-trip.

Forward pipeline (single step)

P      = 2μ(F − R) + λ tr(S − I) R       # corotated PK1 (SVD: F = U Σ Vᵀ; R = U Vᵀ)
stress = −dt · vol · P · Fᵀ              # Cauchy stress contribution
P2G:   for each (p, node):
         mom_grid[node]  += w · m · (v + C · (xn − xp))
                          + (4w/dx²) · stress · (xn − xp)
         mass_grid[node] += w · m
grid:  v_grid = mom_grid / mass_grid + g · dt
       floor: v_grid.y = max(v_grid.y, 0)  if node below floor
              v_grid.x *= damp, v_grid.z *= damp
G2P:   for each p:
         v_new   = Σ_node w · v_grid
         C_new   = Σ_node (4w/dx²) · v_grid · (xn − xp)ᵀ      # APIC
         pos_new = pos + v_new · dt
         F_new   = (I + dt · C_new) · F

The Lamé constants (μ, λ) enter only through P. Everything else is geometric.

Adjoint chain

P     = 2μ(F − R) + λ tr(S − I) R
g_E   = g_μ · dμ/dE + g_λ · dλ/dE
        with  dμ/dE     = 1 / (2(1+ν))
              dλ/dE     = ν / ((1+ν)(1−2ν))

The PK1 derivative corotated_pk1_adjoint(...) returns (adj_F, adj_μ, adj_λ) given the upstream adj_P. The F chain in turn threads through the SVD adjoint adj_svd3 (so R and S are differentiated as smooth functions of F).

The B-spline weight w(pos) and the associated scatters mass_grid = Σ_p w · m_p and mom_grid are chained back into grad_pos_t so multi-particle / multi-step gradients are accurate — verified against finite differences to within 1e−2 relative error on the same 64-particle / 30-step / 16³-grid demo.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct StateAdjoint {
    pub grad_pos: Vec<Vec3>,
    pub grad_vel: Vec<Vec3>,
    pub grad_c: Vec<Mat3>,
    pub grad_f: Vec<Mat3>,
    pub grad_mu: Real,
    pub grad_lambda: Real,
}

impl StateAdjoint {
    pub fn grad_youngs(&self, poisson: Real) -> Real;  // composes dμ/dE + dλ/dE
}

pub fn backward(tape: &MpmTape, grad_pos_final: &[Vec3]) -> StateAdjoint;
}

Tape layout + cost

For T steps × N particles × G³ cells:

  • Particle tape ≈ T · N · 200 B.
  • Grid tape ≈ T · G³ · 56 B.
  • One full backward pass costs roughly 3× a forward pass (the SVD adjoint is the dominant cost, slightly more expensive than the forward SVD).

The 64-particle / 30-step / 16³-grid demo:

  • Tape ≈ 30 · (64 · 200 + 4096 · 56) ≈ 7 MB.
  • Backward ≈ 100 ms on a laptop CPU (debug build).

End-to-end example — fitting Young’s modulus

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use molla::compute::mpm_cpu_diff::{
    mpm_cpu_diff, MpmCpuConfig, MpmTape,
};
use molla::autograd::mpm_adjoint::{backward, forward_backward_e_centroid_loss};

let mut tape = MpmTape::default();
let cfg = MpmCpuConfig { /* dt, dx, gravity, floor, damp, ... */ };
let mut state = /* initial particles */;

// One forward step records into `tape` and updates `state`:
mpm_cpu_diff(&cfg, &mut state, &mut tape);

// Compute J = ‖centroid(state_T) − target‖² and ∂J/∂E in one call.
let (loss, grad_e) = forward_backward_e_centroid_loss(
    &cfg, &state0, target_centroid, n_steps,
);

// Adam step on E (in log space — see fem.md for the same trick).
e -= lr * grad_e;
}

FD parity for the demo’s gradient: 4.14e−6 relative error (grad_E_analytic vs central difference at ε = 1e−4). The same chain composes with robust losses — wrap the centroid residual in norm_huber before seeding ∂J/∂(centroid).

What’s not differentiable

  • Floor friction damping (v_grid.{x,z} *= damp) is differentiable, but the max(v_grid.y, 0) floor clamp is non-smooth at the contact surface. The current implementation keeps the max in both forward and reverse with the standard sub-gradient convention (dy/dx = 0 when clamped, 1 when passing through) — fine for trajectories that don’t sit exactly on the floor.
  • Implicit-Bingham + semi-implicit MPM variants ship a separate forward in shaders/implicit_mpm.wgsl. Their adjoint is on the backlog; only the explicit forward in mpm_cpu_diff is differentiable in v1.

FEM adjoint

Stage 38.2 ships the classical adjoint method for the linear- elasticity FEM solve: given a forward problem K(p) · u = f(p) and a scalar loss J(u, p), the adjoint computes ∂J/∂p with one extra linear solve of the same matrix — independent of the dimensionality of p. The implementation reuses molla’s existing sparse-matrix infrastructure (BSR + CG) and exposes a single solve_adjoint(...) entry-point.

Source: crates/molla-fem/src/adjoint.rs. Forward solver: crates/molla-fem/src/elasticity_gpu.rs / crates/molla-fem/src/solver.rs. Glue with optimisers: molla::math::optim::Adam.

Algorithm (textbook recap)

  1. Forward: solve u = K(p)⁻¹ · f(p).
  2. Adjoint: solve Kᵀ · λ = ∂J/∂u. For SPD K (linear elasticity always is), Kᵀ = K, so the same matrix is reused.
  3. Gradient: ∂J/∂p = ∂J/∂p|_explicit + λᵀ · (∂f/∂p − ∂K/∂p · u).

For linear elasticity the per-element stiffness scales linearly with Young’s modulus E:

  • μ = E / (2(1 + ν)), λ_Lamé = E · ν / ((1 + ν)(1 − 2ν))
  • Both are proportional to E, so ∂K/∂E = K / E globally.

The gradient collapses to

∂J/∂E = −λᵀ · K · u / E

for load-independent loss functions, and to a slightly longer form when f depends on E too.

Traction-load gradient

For an applied traction t on a face with area A, P1 consistent lumping gives f_v += (A / 3) · t per face vertex (component-by- component):

∂f/∂t_c = (A / 3) · e_c summed over the 3 face vertex DoFs

so

∂J/∂t_c = (A / 3) · Σ_{v ∈ face} λ_{v · dim + c}

For each face component the gradient is a one-pass sum over the face’s vertex DoFs — O(face_count) total, no extra solves.

Public API

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use molla::fem::adjoint::{
    solve_adjoint, solve_adjoint_with,
    compute_grad_youngs, compute_grad_load,
};

// 1. Forward (existing FEM solver).
let u = solve_elasticity(&mesh, &bcs, e, nu, traction)?;

// 2. Adjoint: one CG solve of K · λ = ∂J/∂u.
let lambda = solve_adjoint(&mesh, &bcs, e, nu, &grad_j_wrt_u)?;

// 3. Compose ∂J/∂E.
let grad_e = compute_grad_youngs(&mesh, &bcs, e, nu, &u, &lambda);

// 4. Compose ∂J/∂t (per face component).
let grad_t = compute_grad_load(&mesh, &bcs, &lambda, /* face_ids = */ &faces);
}

solve_adjoint_with(..., cg_solve) lets the caller pass a custom CG closure — handy when chaining with the same preconditioner used in the forward to keep iteration counts identical.

Adam in log space — fitting E from a target deflection

The Stage 38.2 demo recovers E from a target deflection measured at the free end of a beam. Two practical tricks:

  1. Optimise ξ = ln(E) instead of E directly. This guarantees E > 0 at every step without a projection, and the gradient dJ/dξ = dJ/dE · E naturally rescales — Adam learns at a sensible step size across orders of magnitude.

  2. Use Adam, not vanilla SGD. The J(E) landscape for an elasticity inverse problem is steep but smooth; Adam’s momentum + per-parameter learning-rate adaptation converges in ~50 iters where SGD would need 500.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use molla::math::optim::Adam;

let mut opt = Adam::new(/* lr = */ 0.05);
let mut xi = (e_initial.ln(),);   // single-parameter Adam state
for _ in 0..n_iters {
    let e = xi.0.exp();
    let u = solve_elasticity(&mesh, &bcs, e, nu, traction)?;
    let j = loss(&u);
    let dj_du = grad_loss_u(&u);
    let lambda = solve_adjoint(&mesh, &bcs, e, nu, &dj_du)?;
    let grad_e = compute_grad_youngs(&mesh, &bcs, e, nu, &u, &lambda);
    let grad_xi = grad_e * e;
    opt.step(&mut xi.0, grad_xi);
}
}

This produces an E estimate within 1 % of ground truth on the demo beam after ~50 Adam iterations.

Boundary-condition handling

Dirichlet BCs are eliminated by row-and-column elimination in both forward and adjoint solves, so the BC rows don’t pollute either linear system. The same elimination structure is reused (computed once at mesh build), so the adjoint solve costs roughly the same as the forward — a single matrix factorisation / preconditioner setup amortises across both.

Neumann (traction) BCs enter through the right-hand side and are differentiable per the formula above; the BC structure is otherwise unchanged.

Validation

The Stage 38.2 tests compare the analytic gradient against central-difference FD at ε = 1e−3 · E and pass to within 5e−3 relative error on the cantilever beam case (hex mesh of ~10k DoFs).

Raycast adjoint

Stage 37.7 ships a finite-difference adjoint for the raycast pipeline — closed-form analytic adjoints (∂t_hit / ∂param per primitive) are deferred to Stage 37.7.1. The FD path is enough to make inverse-rendering loops work (gradient-descent on a shape’s pose to match a target depth image, mirroring Warp’s example_diffray.py) and serves as the oracle for the future analytic version.

Source: crates/molla/src/sensors/raycast_adjoint.rs. Forward (GPU): crates/molla/src/sensors/raycast.rs (see Raycaster).

CPU-only by design

Even when the analytic adjoint lands, it’s likely to stay CPU-resident: the FD adjoint probes the forward pass O(P · N_rays) times (one ± perturbation per parameter), and every probe runs the same closest-hit math. Pushing that onto the GPU would not help — the bottleneck is per-probe latency, not per-probe throughput, and the dependency graph between probes is dense enough that they can’t be batched cleanly.

The CPU adjoint runs a compact (params, rays)-parameterised forward (forward_with_loss) so a single FD perturbation is one function call. The same forward routine is what Raycaster::cast runs on the GPU; the parity-test harness pins the two to within floating-point tolerance.

Forward + loss contract

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct Ray { pub origin: Vec3, pub direction: Vec3 }
pub struct RayScene { pub shapes: Vec<SdfShape> }

pub enum SdfShape {
    Sphere { param_offset: usize, radius: Real },
    PlaneY { height: Real },
    PlaneZ { depth: Real },
}
}

Parameters are unstructured: each Sphere consumes 3 slots (xyz); the flat layout is [s0.x, s0.y, s0.z, s1.x, s1.y, s1.z, ...]. The scene’s n_params() method returns the next safe offset for adding a sphere without overlap (overlapping ranges silently couple gradients between shapes and produce optimisation behaviour that’s almost impossible to debug — the constructor panics on overlap).

The image is a flat Vec<Real> of per-ray hit distances; misses carry Real::INFINITY. The default L2 loss skips any pixel where either side is ∞ so silhouette boundaries don’t blow up the residual.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn forward_with_loss(
    scene: &RayScene,
    params: &[Real],
    rays: &[Ray],
    target_image: &[Real],
    max_distance: Real,
) -> (Vec<Real>, Real);   // (image, loss)

pub fn compute_loss_l2(image: &[Real], target: &[Real]) -> Real;

pub fn compute_grad_raycast(
    scene: &RayScene,
    params: &[Real],
    rays: &[Ray],
    target_image: &[Real],
    max_distance: Real,
    eps: Real,
) -> Vec<Real>;   // dL/dparam, length = params.len()
}

compute_grad_raycast uses central differences: g_i = (L(p + ε e_i) − L(p − ε e_i)) / (2ε). The ε choice trades off quantisation noise (small ε is dominated by floating-point round- off) and truncation error (large ε violates the linear expansion); the standard recipe ε = 1e−4 works well across the demo scenes.

Use case — pose recovery from a depth image

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use molla::sensors::{Ray, RayScene, compute_grad_raycast, forward_with_loss};
use molla::math::optim::Adam;

let mut scene = RayScene::new();
let sphere_off = scene.n_params();
scene.add_sphere(sphere_off, /* radius = */ 0.5);

let rays = build_orthographic_ray_grid(64, 64);
let target_image: Vec<f64> = /* reference depth image */;

let mut params = vec![0.0, 0.0, 0.0];   // initial sphere centre
let mut opt = Adam::new(0.02);

for _ in 0..200 {
    let (_, loss) = forward_with_loss(&scene, &params, &rays, &target_image, 100.0);
    let grad = compute_grad_raycast(&scene, &params, &rays, &target_image, 100.0, 1e-4);
    opt.step_vec(&mut params, &grad);
    println!("loss = {loss:.6}");
}
}

200 Adam iterations on a 64×64 grid land the sphere centre to within 1 mm of the target across the demo scenes — same regime as Warp’s example_diffray.py.

Why not the analytic adjoint?

For a sphere at parameter offset p, the analytic derivative of t_hit with respect to centre is

∂t / ∂c = − ( o − c + t · d ) / ( d · (o − c + t · d) )

— easy enough for sphere + plane, less easy for capsule / cylinder boundary cases, and tedious for the triangle / mesh path. Stage 37.7’s pragmatic call was to ship FD now and analytic later when a specific use case (e.g. a learned 3DGS supervision pipeline) demands the speedup. The FD path runs in a few hundred ms for the 64×64-grid demo, which is fine for the contract test.

The Warp reference (example_diffray.py) uses wp.Tape over a triangle mesh; molla’s equivalent v1 trades triangle support for analytic sphere primitives + FD, which gives a cleaner contract test at the cost of expressiveness.

Differentiable Gaussian splat renderer

Stage 44 is molla’s differentiable 3D Gaussian Splat (3DGS) raytrace renderer — an end-to-end on-GPU rendering pipeline whose reverse pass scatters per-splat gradients (position, scale, rotation, colour, opacity, spherical-harmonic coefficients) from a pixel loss. It is the only fully GPU-resident differentiable path in molla today and the one that drove the per-splat atomic-CAS scatter idiom now reused by the FEM and contact pipelines.

Source: crates/molla/src/sensors/ (Rust orchestrators reuse the camera sensor scaffolding) and the WGSL shaders:

StageShaderPurpose
v1splat_raytrace.wgslForward α-composited raytrace
v2splat_raytrace_backward.wgslReverse adjoint (position/scale/rot/color/opacity)
v3splat_raytrace_sh.wgsl + *_sh_backward.wgslSH bands 0–2 (9 coeffs/channel)
v4splat_raytrace_sh_band3.wgsl + backwardSH band 3 (16 coeffs/channel)

The numbered commits are:

  • v1 forward (d4583a7) — top-K depth-sorted α-composite.
  • v2 reverse (237caa2) — pose-recovery Adam loop ships.
  • v3 SH (00d8083) — diffuse + ambient view-dependence, bands 0–2.
  • v4 band 3 (121c9d3) — directional specular highlights via the cubic basis, splitting diffuse + view-dependent terms (Kerbl 2023).

Forward — α-composited Gaussian raytrace

One thread per pixel. Each thread:

  1. Walks the full splat array.

  2. For each splat, transforms the ray into the splat’s canonical (unit-isotropic) frame using the inverse rotation + scale, then evaluates the response in that frame:

    m² = ‖d × o‖² / ‖d‖²        # closest-approach distance², canonical frame
ρ  = exp(−½ · m²)
α  = opacity · ρ

  3. Keeps a top-K mini-sort of the closest hits in front-to-back order (default MAX_HITS = 16, matching Newton’s gaussians_max_num_hits).

  4. α-composites them:

    T_0 = 1
for i in 0..K:
    C    += T_i · α_i · c_i
    T_{i+1} = T_i · (1 − α_i)
    if T_{i+1} < MIN_TRANSMITTANCE: break
alpha_out = 1 − T_K

MIN_TRANSMITTANCE = 0.003 (Newton’s gaussians_min_transmittance). Per-splat α below min_alpha = 1/255 is discarded — also matching Newton.

Reverse — gradient chain

The reverse kernel runs one thread per pixel and re-runs the exact same deterministic top-K insertion sort as the forward (the front-to-back order is uniquely determined by the splat array + ray, so no extra storage is needed). Then it walks the hit list back-to-front to accumulate per-splat gradients via the standard 3DGS α-composite recurrence.

α-composite adjoint

Let c_i be the (possibly view-dependent) RGB of hit i, α_i its alpha, T_i = ∏_{j<i}(1 − α_j) the front-prefix transmittance, and S_after = Σ_{j>i} c_j α_j T_j the RGB that piles up behind hit i. The reverse pass uses:

dL/dc_i = α_i · T_i · dL/dC_out
dL/dα_i = T_i · c_i · dL/dC_out  −  S_after · dL/dC_out / (1 − α_i)

The −S_after / (1 − α_i) term is the “what the splats behind me would have contributed if I hadn’t blocked them” correction — the recurrence is closed-form over the back-to-front walk because we can accumulate S_after in O(1) per step.

The forward writes alpha_out = 1 − T_final. v2 ignores dL/dalpha_out because the pose-recovery loss only uses RGB; extending to alpha-channel gradients is a one-line addition (an extra T_i · T_final / ((1 − α_i) · T_i) term in dL/dα_i).

α → opacity, ρ, m²

α = opacity · ρ,    ρ = exp(−½ m²)
dL/dopacity = ρ · dL/dα
dL/dρ       = opacity · dL/dα
dL/d(m²)    = −½ · ρ · dL/dρ

m² → canonical frame → (scale, rotation, position)

In the canonical frame, o_local = R⁻¹(o − c) ⊘ s and d_local = R⁻¹ d ⊘ s (where R⁻¹ = R* is the inverse quaternion, ⊘ is elementwise divide, s is the per-splat anisotropic scale, c is the centre).

crd = d_local × o_local
m²  = ‖crd‖² / ‖d_local‖²

The chain rule through crd, d_local, o_local lands gradients in (s, R, c). The full per-component chain is in the shader; the geometric form of each step is:

dL/dcrd      = (2 / ‖d_local‖²) · crd · dL/d(m²) − (2 · m² / ‖d_local‖²) · d_local · dL/d(m²)
dL/d(d_local) = (BAC-CAB: dL/d(d × o) = o × dL/d(d × o)ᵀ … see below)
dL/d(o_local) = symmetric counterpart

BAC-CAB quaternion derivative subtlety

The gradient of R⁻¹ v with respect to the rotation quaternion R needs care. Using the BAC-CAB identity (a × (b × c) = b (a · c) − c (a · b)) gives:

∂(R⁻¹ v) / ∂R = 2 (v × q̂ − q̂_w v − q̂ × (q̂ × v))

where q̂ is the vector part of R. The shader unrolls this using the explicit quaternion-rotate formula R⁻¹ v = v − 2 q̂ × (q̂ × v) + 2 q̂_w (v × q̂) (matches raycast.wgsl’s quat_rotate(quat_conj(q), v)) and differentiates it term-by-term. The key subtlety: each cross invocation contributes two non-commuting terms via BAC-CAB — one from the inner cross and one from the outer — and the signs must be tracked carefully. Newton’s gaussians.py derives the same expression with the same sign conventions.

Atomic-CAS f32 scatter

WGSL has no native atomic<f32>. Per-splat gradients are scattered via the standard atomicCompareExchangeWeak CAS loop on bit-cast u32 slots — the same idiom that shaders/fem_assembly.wgsl uses:

atomic_add(slot, v):
  old = atomicLoad(&buf[slot])
  loop:
    new_bits = bitcast<u32>(bitcast<f32>(old) + v)
    r = atomicCompareExchangeWeak(&buf[slot], old, new_bits)
    if r.exchanged: return
    old = r.old_value

One thread per pixel ⇒ contention is proportional to the number of pixels lit by any single splat. For the demo scenes this is typically < 100 ⇒ contention is mild and the CAS loops rarely spin more than 2–3 times.

v3 / v4 — Spherical harmonics

Bands 0–2 give 9 coefficients per channel × 3 channels = 27 SH coefficients per splat. Band 3 adds 7 cubic-basis coefficients per channel ⇒ 16 total × 3 = 48 SH coefficients per splat.

The view-dependent colour is evaluated against the unit view direction v̂ (camera → splat):

c(v̂) = Σ_l Σ_m c_{l,m} · Y_{l,m}(v̂)

with Y_{l,m} the real spherical-harmonic basis. The basis constants are the standard ones; v4 uses:

SH_C0  =  0.28209479177387814
SH_C1  =  0.4886025119029199
SH_C2A =  1.0925484305920792
SH_C2B = -1.0925484305920792
SH_C2C =  0.31539156525252005
SH_C2D = -1.0925484305920792
SH_C2E =  0.5462742152960396
SH_C3A = -0.5900435899266435
SH_C3B =  2.890611442640554
SH_C3C = -0.4570457994644658
SH_C3D =  0.3731763325901154
SH_C3E = -0.4570457994644658
SH_C3F =  1.445305721320277
SH_C3G = -0.5900435899266435

Per Kerbl 2023, v4 splits the diffuse band-0 coefficient from the view-dependent (bands 1+) coefficients so a static ambient + dynamic specular can be edited independently. The reverse kernel chain is identical to v2 for the geometric quantities; only the colour assembly changes (the per-band dL/dc_{l,m} now involves the SH basis terms evaluated at v̂).

Pose-recovery Adam loop

The v2 ship-test runs an Adam optimisation that recovers a 3-DoF translation of a Gaussian splat cloud from a target RGB image:

for step in 0..n_iters:
    forward: render(splats translated by p) → pred_rgb
    loss:    L = ‖pred_rgb − target‖²  (per-pixel L2)
    reverse: dL/dp = scatter splat gradients, average position gradient over splats
    update:  p ← Adam(p, dL/dp)

Converges in ~200 iterations for typical scenes. Gradient verification against finite differences passes at 1e−3 relative tolerance for all geometric channels; SH gradients tolerate 1e−2 because the basis-coefficient sums introduce more round-off.

Cross-references

  • Geometry / Gaussian splats — splat-data model + forward rendering details.
  • Sensors / TiledCamera — same ray- generation infrastructure feeds this kernel.
  • Tape-based autograd — not used here: the splat reverse is fully hand-written and GPU-resident, the canonical wp.func_grad-style example for molla.
  • Math / Optimizers — Adam shared with the rest of the autograd demos.
  • References: Kerbl et al. 2023 (“3D Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Radiance Field Rendering”), Newton gaussians.py.

Bevy adapter

molla_viewer is a Bevy 0.18 application. It is the only crate in the workspace that depends on Bevy — the engine crate has zero Bevy footprint. This chapter documents the Bevy integration patterns the viewer uses; they are the same patterns you would use to embed molla in your own Bevy app.

What the viewer pulls in

From bin/molla_viewer/Cargo.toml:

  • bevy = "0.18" with a curated feature list — ECS, render, PBR, scene, picking, gizmos, asset, scene, X11, Wayland.
  • bevy_egui = "0.39" for the immediate-mode UI.
  • bevy_frost — egui-themed glass UI kit.
  • bevy_glacial — orbit camera + grid + gizmos plugin.
  • mimalloc as the global allocator — egui’s tessellator thrashes the system allocator and mimalloc cuts frame time from ~120 ms to ~13 ms in the heavy demos.

The ECS model

molla state lives in Bevy resources, not components. Two top-level singletons:

  • Sim — owns the molla::Model, the current State, the Control, the Contacts, the active solver, and the compute::Engine. Created at startup; rebuilt every time the user picks a new scene from the dropdown.
  • SimStats — wall-clock frame timing, solver telemetry, contact counts. Updated each frame; consumed by the diagnostic pane.

Per-scene runtime state (target sliders, accumulated time, MPM particle counts, the IK solver instance, etc.) lives in per-scene resource types:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[derive(Resource, Default)] struct LidarState { ... }
#[derive(Resource, Default)] struct ImuExampleState { ... }
#[derive(Resource, Default)] struct ContactExampleState { ... }
// ... ~40 of these total
}

Each scene has at most two of these: one for the simulation update logic, one for the right-rail UI pane.

The SystemParam 16-tuple ceiling

Bevy’s SystemParam derive macro has a hard 16-element ceiling on tuple length. Both apply_scene_switch (the system that runs on scene change to reset per-scene state) and control_pane (the system that draws the right-rail UI) need access to ~40 resources at once.

The viewer’s solution is to bundle per-scene resources into named SystemParam structs:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[derive(bevy::ecs::system::SystemParam)]
struct SceneStates<'w> {
    lidar: ResMut<'w, LidarState>,
    imu: ResMut<'w, ImuExampleState>,
    contact: ResMut<'w, ContactExampleState>,
    arm: ResMut<'w, ArmExampleState>,
    actuator: ResMut<'w, ActuatorExampleState>,
    gpu_ik: ResMut<'w, GpuIkArmState>,
    camera: ResMut<'w, CameraExampleState>,
    stats: ResMut<'w, SimStats>,
    gpu_np: ResMut<'w, GpuNpExampleState>,
    gpu_bp: ResMut<'w, GpuBpExampleState>,
    quad: ResMut<'w, QuadrotorState>,
    reference_pendulum: ResMut<'w, ReferencePendulumState>,
    diff_arm: ResMut<'w, DiffArmExampleState>,
    diff_arm6: ResMut<'w, DiffArm6ExampleState>,
    mesh: ResMut<'w, MeshToolsExampleState>,
    neural: ResMut<'w, NeuralPolicyExampleState>,
    // ... ~30 more
}

fn apply_scene_switch(mut sim: ResMut<Sim>, mut scene_states: SceneStates) {
    // sim takes 1 slot, scene_states takes 1 slot — well under 16.
}
}

PaneSceneStates is a parallel bundle of the same resources but declared independently so control_pane can borrow them disjointly from apply_scene_switch.

The convention going forward: whenever you add a new scene with its own state struct, add the field to BOTH SceneStates and PaneSceneStates. This is the pattern documented in the PLAN.md Stage 22 “Bevy plumbing constraint” note.

The update / draw cycle

Each scene contributes one system that runs on Update. Conditional dispatch via current_scene == Scene::X:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn update_mpm_example(
    sim: Res<Sim>,
    mut mpm_state: ResMut<MpmExampleState>,
    pending: Res<PendingSceneSwitch>,
) {
    if pending.0 != Some(Scene::Mpm) { return; }
    // ... call mpm_state.simulation.step_n_with(...)
    // ... rewrite gizmo positions
}
}

The actual step happens through molla’s step_simulation system, which dispatches to the active Solver for most scenes. Scenes that have their own substep loop (MPM, FEM steppers, neural controllers) short-circuit step_simulation and run their own update system.

Egui control panes via bevy_frost

The right-rail UI is composed of one control_pane system that calls egui::Window::show() with bevy_frost styling. Each scene contributes a small block inside the match:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn control_pane(/* ... */ mut pane_states: PaneSceneStates) {
    egui::SidePanel::right("rail").show(ctx, |ui| {
        match scene {
            Scene::Mpm => {
                ui.add(egui::Slider::new(&mut pane_states.mpm.friction_angle, 5.0..=45.0));
                ui.label(format!("Particles: {}", pane_states.mpm.particle_count));
            }
            Scene::Camera => {
                pane_states.camera.draw_thumbnails(ui);
            }
            // ... ~100 more arms
        }
    });
}
}

The “input firewall” — preventing egui mouse clicks from also triggering camera orbit — is provided by bevy_glacial which reads pane rects from the egui frame state and clips its own input.

The full keybinding table is in bin/molla_viewer/src/main.rs in the handle_hotkeys system.

Embedding molla in your own Bevy app

If you want a molla simulation inside an existing Bevy app rather than the molla viewer:

  1. Add molla = { path = "...", default-features = true } to your Cargo.toml. Default-on gpu ensures the wgpu paths compile.
  2. Create the Engine at startup and store it in a resource:
#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[derive(Resource)]
struct MollaEngine(molla::compute::Engine);

fn setup(mut commands: Commands) {
    commands.insert_resource(MollaEngine(
        molla::compute::Engine::new(molla::compute::Backend::Gpu).unwrap()
    ));
}
}
  1. Build a procedural Model via ModelBuilder and store it in another resource.
  2. Step in a FixedUpdate system:
#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn step_physics(
    engine: Res<MollaEngine>,
    mut sim: ResMut<MyMollaSim>,
    time: Res<Time<Fixed>>,
) {
    sim.solver.step(&sim.model, &sim.state, &sim.control, &sim.contacts, time.delta_secs() as f64, &mut sim.next_state).unwrap();
    std::mem::swap(&mut sim.state, &mut sim.next_state);
}
}
  1. Copy sim.state.body_q into your Bevy Transforms each frame.

That’s the entire integration surface. molla doesn’t care that it’s inside Bevy; it doesn’t even know Bevy exists.

Viewer overview

molla_viewer is the Bevy 0.18 application that exercises every solver, kernel, sensor, and FEM stepper molla ships. It is the showroom and the integration test, all in one binary.

Architecture in one diagram

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                molla_viewer (single Bevy app)            │
│                                                          │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │  Sim resource                                    │    │
│  │    - molla::Model      (current scene's model)   │    │
│  │    - molla::State      (positions / velocities)  │    │
│  │    - molla::Control    (joint targets, wrenches) │    │
│  │    - molla::Contacts   (collision output)        │    │
│  │    - Box<dyn Solver>   (active solver)           │    │
│  │    - compute::Engine   (wgpu device + queue)     │    │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
│                                                          │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │  SceneStates SystemParam bundle                  │    │
│  │    - per-scene resources (~40 of them)           │    │
│  │  PaneSceneStates SystemParam bundle              │    │
│  │    - same resources, reborrowed for UI           │    │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
│                                                          │
│  Systems:                                                │
│    apply_scene_switch  - rebuild Sim on dropdown change  │
│    step_simulation     - dispatch to active Solver       │
│    update_<scene>      - per-scene custom update logic   │
│    sync_to_bevy        - copy molla state into bevy::Transform │
│    control_pane        - egui right-rail UI              │
│    diagnostic_pane     - bottom-left perf readout        │
│    handle_hotkeys      - keyboard shortcuts              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

How a scene works

Every scene in the viewer follows a four-part recipe:

  1. A variant in the Scene enum (Scene::Pile, Scene::Mpm, Scene::FemBeam, …). The enum currently has ~100 variants.
  2. A build_scene arm in Sim::build_scene(scene: Scene) that constructs the molla::Model via ModelBuilder and (if the scene has its own particle / mesh / actuator state) initialises the corresponding per-scene resource.
  3. A label in Scene::label() like "01 Pile" or "47 FEM heat (Stage 36 v1)". The number prefix doubles as the dropdown ordering and the historical reference for the scenes.md catalog.
  4. Optionally: an update_<scene> system if the scene has custom step logic that needs to run outside the standard step_simulation dispatch. MPM, FEM, and the differentiable scenes all have their own update systems.

The control flow

Each frame:

  1. Bevy’s runner calls handle_hotkeys — keyboard input may queue a scene switch into PendingSceneSwitch.
  2. apply_scene_switch checks PendingSceneSwitch, and if non-empty, calls Sim::build_scene(...) to rebuild the model, picks the right solver, resets every per-scene resource through SceneStates, and clears the bevy world of the previous scene’s gizmo entities.
  3. step_simulation runs the active Solver::step(...) if the scene uses the standard pipeline. Scenes with their own update loop (Scene::Mpm, Scene::FemHeat, etc.) short-circuit and call their own update_* system instead.
  4. sync_to_bevy copies sim.state.body_q into each tracked entity’s Transform. Cloth / soft body / MPM scenes copy per-particle / per-vertex positions into a deforming Bevy Mesh.
  5. control_pane renders the right-rail egui UI. Each scene’s pane is one match arm reading + writing the corresponding PaneSceneStates field.
  6. diagnostic_pane renders bottom-left perf data:
    • Active solver name + backend (CPU / GPU).
    • Frame time (ms).
    • Body count + contact count.
    • Optional Tracy frame markers when --features profile.

The CPU↔GPU toggle

The diagnostic pane has a [CPU] / [GPU] radio button. Clicking it sets Sim::backend and triggers an in-place solver rebuild:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
match (current_solver_kind, backend) {
    (SolverKind::Xpbd, Backend::Cpu)  => XpbdSolver::new_cpu(),
    (SolverKind::Xpbd, Backend::Gpu)  => XpbdSolver::new_gpu(&engine)?,
    (SolverKind::Featherstone, Backend::Cpu) => FeatherstoneSolver::new_cpu(),
    (SolverKind::Featherstone, Backend::Gpu) => FeatherstoneSolver::new_gpu(&engine)?,
    (SolverKind::Vbd, Backend::Cpu)   => VbdSolver::new_cpu(),
    (SolverKind::Vbd, Backend::Gpu)   => VbdSolver::new_gpu(&engine)?,
}
}

The simulation continues running while the toggle is flipped — no window restart, no recompile. This is the load-bearing demonstration of the CPU↔GPU design rule.

Visual conventions

  • Rigid bodies render via Bevy PbrBundle with palette-coloured materials. A toggle key T switches to Muli-style activity shading: sleeping bodies turn grey.
  • Cloth / soft body / FEM mesh renders as a single Bevy Mesh with per-frame vertex rewrites. Wireframe overlay is a toggle on most cloth / FEM panes.
  • Particles (MPM, sparse-grid, autograd-particle scenes) render as gizmo points — Bevy’s Gizmos::sphere(...) calls in the draw system.
  • Sensors render as gizmo lines + arrows: lidar rays, IMU axis triads, contact normals, camera-ray bundles.
  • Articulated bodies render with one bevy entity per body and one gizmo cylinder per joint axis.

Catalog summary

  • 101 scenes total, numbered #01–#101 in the dropdown.
  • 12 marquee scenes have single-letter hotkeys.
  • ~30 are direct ports of Warp examples (prefix Warp*).
  • ~25 are Newton-port scenes covering the Newton example tree.
  • ~12 are FEM steppers (Stages 36–46).
  • The remainder are original molla demos built around specific Stage deliverables.

Each scene’s source lives in bin/molla_viewer/src/main.rs. Search for the variant name (e.g. Scene::ImplicitMpmBingham) to find the build_scene arm, the per-scene state struct, the update system (if any), and the control_pane arm.

See viewer/overview.md for the architecture behind the catalog, and roadmap/stages.md for the chronological stage history that produced each scene.

Test strategy

molla treats tests as part of the engine, not as documentation. The quality bar from PLAN.md §1.3 is:

Every shipped feature must have:

  1. A trajectory or unit test against the Newton/Warp references (where applicable).
  2. A doctest or example demonstrating idiomatic use.
  3. A bench in criterion measuring cost per step.
  4. CPU-fallback parity: the same algorithm runs on CPU (single-threaded) for debugging, and produces bit-identical results modulo floating-point ordering nondeterminism on GPU.

Integration tests and Criterion benches live with the crate that owns the functionality under test: for example FEM tests in crates/molla-fem/tests/, solver and dynamics tests in crates/molla-solvers/tests/, kernel parity tests in crates/molla-kernels/tests/, and facade/product compatibility tests in crates/molla/tests/. Most GPU tests are #[ignore]-gated so the default cargo test lane runs CPU-only on machines that don’t have a wgpu adapter.

The testing pyramid

                  ┌──────────────────────────┐
                  │  reference-port tests    │   algorithm fixtures
                  │  (Newton + Warp parity)  │
                  ├──────────────────────────┤
                  │  CPU/GPU parity tests    │   #[ignore]'d, GPU-only
                  │  (same scene both paths) │
                  ├──────────────────────────┤
                  │  FD gradient tests       │   compare AD vs finite-diff
                  │  (adjoint correctness)   │
                  ├──────────────────────────┤
                  │  convergence rate tests  │   manufactured solutions
                  │  (FEM, h refinement)     │
                  ├──────────────────────────┤
                  │  smoke / scene tests     │   "does it build + step?"
                  ├──────────────────────────┤
                  │  unit tests              │   per-module algorithm checks
                  └──────────────────────────┘

Reference-port tests

The read-only xtra/newton/ and xtra/warp/ trees are treated as algorithm references, not as runtime dependencies. The pattern:

  1. Author a scene in molla using ModelBuilder.
  2. Port the upstream fixture or formula into Rust.
  3. Step molla for N substeps with the same dt and solver intent.
  4. Compare body poses, velocities, contacts, or scalar diagnostics to within a documented tolerance.

The facade-level ported assertions live at crates/molla/tests/oracle_newton.rs and do not shell out to external runtimes.

Conventions documented in the file header:

  • Newton’s narrow-phase returns a signed distance (positive = separated, negative = penetrating). molla returns Option<ContactManifold> where depth is positive penetration. The oracle adapter translates between the two.
  • Newton’s box “size” is the half-extent vector; molla calls it half_extents. Interchangeable.
  • Both follow “normal points from geom 0 toward geom 1” (a → b).

CPU/GPU parity (the everyday check)

The most-run test family. Every _gpu test follows the same recipe, regardless of whether it lives in crates/molla/tests/ or in an owning functionality crate:

  1. Build a Model with fixed-seed inputs.
  2. Step on CPU for N steps; collect trajectory.
  3. Reupload Model to the GPU, step on GPU for N steps; collect trajectory.
  4. Compare per-step: assert ‖pos_cpu - pos_gpu‖ < 1e-4 (the f32-narrowing tolerance), ‖quat_cpu - quat_gpu‖ < 1e-4, etc.

The CPU and GPU paths intentionally produce slightly different results because:

  • WGSL is f32 and the host is f64 — narrowing introduces ULPs of error per arithmetic op.
  • Floating-point reductions on GPU are order-dependent (atomic-add via CAS races); CPU reductions are sequential. Two GPU runs of the same kernel are not bit-identical to each other either.

The tolerance budget (1e-4 over hundreds of substeps) is what the parity tests assert.

Manufactured solutions for FEM

For FEM, the trajectory-oracle pattern doesn’t apply (PDE solvers don’t have analytic trajectories). Instead we use the method of manufactured solutions:

  1. Pick an exact solution u_ex(x, y, z, t) that’s smooth.
  2. Compute the residual r = ∂u_ex/∂t − α∇²u_ex symbolically.
  3. Use r as the RHS source term in the FEM solve.
  4. Run the solve. The numerical solution should approach u_ex at the documented convergence rate (O(h²) for P1, O(h³) for P2).
  5. Run on a mesh sequence (8³, 16³, 32³, …) and assert the error ratio matches the theoretical rate.

These tests live alongside the regular FEM tests in fem_*.rs. The ones that explicitly call out manufactured solutions:

  • fem_v1.rs — P1 heat equation, manufactured sin(πx)sin(πy).
  • fem_p2.rs — P2 heat, same manufactured solution, asserts the better convergence rate.
  • fem_stokes.rs — Taylor-Hood Stokes vs Ghia & Ghia reference.

Convergence rate tests

For iterative solvers (CG / PCG / BiCGStab / GMRES), tests assert that the iteration count grows as expected with problem size and shrinks with preconditioning:

  • fem_pcg_cpu.rs — CG vs PCG iteration sweep over 8³, 16³, 24³, 32³, 40³, 48³ meshes. PCG cuts iters by 25–31 %.
  • iterative.rs — CG on a 1D Laplacian, asserts iter count bounded by O(√n).

Performance gates

Some tests are perf gates rather than correctness checks. They assert that a measured ratio (CPU vs GPU, naive vs batched, …) beats a threshold:

  • mpm_perf.rs::mpm_step_n_beats_individual_steps — asserts step_n(60) is at least 2× faster than 60× step(). (Measured: 9.1×.)
  • fem_assembly_perf.rs — asserts GPU assembly beats CPU at 16³+.
  • mesh_bvh_perf.rs — asserts BVH query throughput at scale.

When a perf gate fails it’s the most actionable kind of failure — you have a measurement, a threshold, and a target to chase.

The vehicle crate’s embedded harness

molla-vehicle carries its own validation layer beyond plain unit tests: the real_tire/rig + real_tire/reports modules are a non-cfg(test) diagnostic harness (structural truth gates — loaded radius, footprint span, pressure distribution, bead drift — plus force-shape checks for slip curves, camber thrust, and aligning moment), exercised by the crate’s test suite (225 tests / 0 ignored as of 2026-07-02 — older docs citing 220/2, 221/1, or 222/0 are stale snapshots). The GPU twins of the tire physics are validated by the tire_* hardware lanes in molla-kernels, with per-lane status recorded in real_tire/parity_ledger.rs. See the molla-vehicle chapter.

What’s not covered by tests

Documenting honest gaps:

  • No fuzz testing. Tested inputs are deterministic; no randomized stress harness.
  • No long-running drift tests. Tests run hundreds of substeps, not millions. Long-term energy drift is observed but not asserted.
  • No multi-platform CI. The Makefile assumes nix + Vulkan; tests run only on Linux. Metal / DX12 paths compile but aren’t CI-exercised.
  • No external-runtime diff CI. Reference trees are not built or executed by molla; tests should port the relevant invariant into Rust.

These are roadmap items. Until they materialise, the everyday contract is “the test suite passes and the parity tolerances hold”.

  • Parity testing — the CPU/GPU parity pattern in detail.
  • FD gradient checks — central-difference vs analytic adjoint pattern.
  • Benchmarks — what each criterion bench measures.
  • GPU port status matrix — which solvers have GPU paths, which don’t, which have parity tests.

CPU/GPU parity testing

The CPU/GPU parity test is molla’s everyday correctness check. Every kernel has one. The pattern is the same regardless of what kernel is being tested.

The recipe

crates/molla-solvers/tests/cpu_gpu_parity.rs is the canonical example. Five steps:

  1. Gate the test. #![cfg(feature = "gpu")] at file top.
  2. Build the same scene twice. Once for CPU, once for GPU (or, more often, build once and use two state slots — the model is shared).
  3. Step the CPU path, collecting per-step trajectory.
  4. Step the GPU path, reading back state each step.
  5. Assert agreement within tolerance.

Skeleton:

#![allow(unused)]
#![cfg(feature = "gpu")]

fn main() {
use molla_compute::{Backend, Engine};
use molla_math::{SpatialInertia, Transform, Vec3};
use molla_sim::{BodyParams, Model, ModelBuilder};

fn build_scene(n: usize) -> Model {
    let mut b = ModelBuilder::new();
    for i in 0..n {
        let body = b.add_body(BodyParams::new()
            .with_spatial_inertia(SpatialInertia::sphere(1.0, 0.5))
            .with_position(Vec3::new(i as f64 * 1.5, 10.0, 0.0)));
        b.add_shape_sphere(body, 0.5, Transform::IDENTITY).unwrap();
    }
    b.build().unwrap()
}

#[test] #[ignore]
fn cpu_gpu_parity_semi_implicit() {
    let engine = Engine::new(Backend::Gpu).unwrap();
    let model = build_scene(8);
    let traj_cpu = run_cpu(&model, 60, 1.0 / 60.0);
    let traj_gpu = run_gpu(&engine, &model, 60, 1.0 / 60.0);
    for (i, (a, b)) in traj_cpu.iter().zip(traj_gpu.iter()).enumerate() {
        for (j, (xa, xb)) in a.iter().zip(b.iter()).enumerate() {
            let err = (xa.position - xb.position).length();
            assert!(err < 1e-4, "step {i} body {j}: pos err {err}");
        }
    }
}
}

Why #[ignore]

The default cargo test lane has to pass on CI runners without a GPU. wgpu::Adapter initialisation fails (or worse, picks a software adapter and runs glacially) when no real device is available. Gating the GPU lane behind #[ignore] lets the same test file:

  • Build successfully (the test is compiled, just not run).
  • Run on demand via cargo test -- --ignored when a real adapter is around.

The Makefile has one target per parity test family (make test-gpu, make test-gpu P=molla-solvers T=featherstone_gpu_parity, etc.) — each is just a cargo test --features gpu --test <name> -- --ignored invocation.

Fixed seeds, deterministic inputs

Parity tests use fixed-seed inputs to make failures reproducible. No rand::thread_rng(). The patterns are:

  • Hand-laid positions (Vec3::new(i as f64 * 1.5, 10.0, 0.0)).
  • Deterministic-hash inputs for “random” perturbations ((i * 0x9E3779B9) as f32 / u32::MAX as f32).
  • Reusable fixtures beside the owning crate’s tests, or in the facade test tree when the coverage is explicitly facade/product-level.

When a parity test fails, the developer can rerun it bit-for-bit identical to reproduce.

Tolerances

The tolerance budget depends on the operation count and the narrowing path:

OperationToleranceRationale
Single-step physics (per body)1e-4f32 narrowing introduces ~1e-6 per arithmetic op, accumulates over a step
Sensor readback (per ray)1e-4Same — single dispatch
60-substep trajectory1e-3Tolerance grows with step count
Adjoint vs FD (per gradient)1e-3 (rel)FD step size 1e-4–1e-6; finite-diff truncation is the wall
SH coefficient gradient1e-7Closed-form, no integrator state
FEM solve (per-DOF)dependsCG tol + f32 narrowing combine

The 1e-3 relative tolerance for adjoint-vs-FD is the standard molla budget. Tighter than that is the FD truncation wall; looser than that signals a real adjoint bug.

What if the CPU and GPU disagree

When a parity test fails:

  1. The CPU path is the oracle. Read it. Make sure the algorithm is what you think it is.
  2. Check the WGSL kernel. Compare the math op-by-op against the CPU code. The most common bugs are:
    • Index typos (v[i+1] vs v[i-1]).
    • Mat3 column-major vs row-major mix-up (glam is column-major; WGSL mat3x3 is column-major; the layout matches but it’s easy to flip while debugging).
    • Atomic-CAS misuse (forgetting to bitcast, forgetting the loop, forgetting to break on exchanged).
    • Single-precision overflow in cumulative reductions (manifests as one body’s position blowing up after thousands of substeps).
  3. Bisect the substep. If step 100 disagrees but step 1 agrees, write a smaller test that only steps once and inspects the divergence at the buffer level.

The WGSL has no printf. Debug by writing to a dedicated debug buffer and reading it back — the parity test framework can be extended to dump the contents of any buffer at the disagreement step.

Tests that don’t use the parity pattern

Some test families are intentionally CPU-only:

  • Unit tests in module #[cfg(test)] mod tests {} blocks. No #[ignore]. Run in the default lane.
  • Smoke tests (scene_smoke.rs, cpu_smoke.rs) — assert that a build + a few steps succeed without crashing. CPU-only.
  • Reference-port tests (oracle_newton.rs) — compare molla CPU output against Rust translations of Newton/Warp fixtures.

Some test families are intentionally GPU-only because the CPU path doesn’t exist or isn’t competitive:

  • Stage 24e sparse-grid mutable insert — only a GPU implementation ships.
  • LBVH build / refit — GPU-only.
  • Tile FFT — GPU-only.

These tests assert a GPU result against a CPU oracle hand-rolled in the test itself (e.g. a rustfft-based reference for FFT, a flat O(n²) reference for spatial-hash queries).

See also

  • GPU port status matrix — exhaustive list of what has parity tests and what doesn’t.
  • Test strategy — the higher-level testing philosophy.

Finite-difference gradient checks

molla’s differentiable paths (Featherstone reverse adjoint, XPBD / VBD adjoints, MPM adjoint, FEM adjoint, raycast adjoint, Gaussian splat adjoint) all ship with finite-difference gradient tests that cross-check the analytic gradient against central-difference numerical gradient.

This chapter documents the pattern, the tolerance budgets, and the common gotchas.

The central-difference oracle

Given a scalar loss L(x) and a parameter x[k], the central finite-difference gradient is:

∂L/∂x[k] ≈ (L(x + e_k h) - L(x - e_k h)) / (2 h)

where e_k is the k-th basis vector and h is the step size.

The standard pattern in molla tests:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn fd_grad<F>(x0: &[f64], h: f64, mut eval: F) -> Vec<f64>
where F: FnMut(&[f64]) -> f64
{
    let mut g = vec![0.0; x0.len()];
    let mut x = x0.to_vec();
    for k in 0..x0.len() {
        x[k] = x0[k] + h;
        let lp = eval(&x);
        x[k] = x0[k] - h;
        let lm = eval(&x);
        x[k] = x0[k];
        g[k] = (lp - lm) / (2.0 * h);
    }
    g
}
}

Then:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let g_analytic = my_adjoint(x0);
let g_fd       = fd_grad(&x0, 1e-5, |x| my_forward_loss(x));
for k in 0..x0.len() {
    let abs = (g_analytic[k] - g_fd[k]).abs();
    let rel = abs / g_analytic[k].abs().max(1e-12);
    assert!(rel < 1e-3, "grad[{k}]: analytic {} vs fd {} (rel err {rel})",
        g_analytic[k], g_fd[k]);
}
}

Tolerance budget

The standard tolerances in molla:

Test familyStep hToleranceNotes
Featherstone adjoint vs FD1e-51e-3 relMany integrator steps, accumulated error
XPBD adjoint vs FD1e-51e-3 relPosition-based projection, mild non-smoothness
MPM SVD-chain adjoint vs FD1e-51e-3 relHeavy nonlinear, narrow window for h
Raycast adjoint vs FDadaptive1e-3 relAdaptive FD step from add_sphere validate
Splat backward vs FD1e-51e-3 relPer-channel (pos / color / opacity / scale / quat)
SH coefficient gradientclosed-form1e-7 absNo integrator, closed-form derivatives
Spring rest-length grad1e-51e-3 relDiffSpring scene

The 1e-3 relative budget is the workhorse. Tighter than that, and finite-difference truncation error dominates — you’re measuring the wall, not the gradient. Looser than that signals a real bug.

For closed-form derivatives (no integrator state — like the spherical-harmonic basis coefficients), the budget tightens to 1e-7 absolute because there’s no accumulation site.

Choosing the step h

The step size has a Goldilocks zone:

  • Too small (e.g. 1e-12): the loss values L(x±h) are equal to machine precision. Numerator is round-off noise, gradient is meaningless.
  • Too large (e.g. 1e-2): higher-order Taylor terms become significant, central-difference is no longer a good approximation.
  • Just right: h ≈ 1e-5 for f64 evaluation. Round-off is below the truncation error, truncation error is below 1e-6.

For functions with kinks or discontinuities (XPBD constraint projection at the inequality boundary, MPM plasticity at the yield surface), the FD test side-steps the kink:

  • Pick a test point that’s strictly in the smooth interior.
  • For projection-onto-cone tests, perturb only in the tangent directions.
  • For yield-surface tests, perturb only within the elastic regime.

Tests that violate this pattern get false-positive FD disagreements and are eventually rewritten to use Moreau-envelope smoothing of the projection (Stage 23.1.3 D6 joint adjoint is the worked example).

Raycast adaptive FD

The raycast adjoint test (crates/molla-sensors/tests/raycast_adjoint.rs) uses adaptive FD because the residual is sensitive to the step size when rays graze the silhouette of a sphere:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// validate add_sphere offsets, then pick h that keeps the FD
// gradient away from the silhouette discontinuity.
let h = adaptive_fd_step(&x0, |x| residual(x));
}

The adaptive step picks the largest h such that |L(x+h) - L(x-h)| is still many ULPs above noise, then halves until the second-order finite-difference correction is small. This was added in commit 72dd668 to fix flaky tests that straddled the silhouette.

When the FD test fails

The triage:

  1. Print both gradients side by side. Look for sign flips or order-of-magnitude differences — these are bugs in the adjoint, not in the FD.
  2. Try a tighter h (1e-6) and a looser h (1e-4). If the FD disagrees with the analytic at both ends, the adjoint is wrong. If it disagrees at one and agrees at the other, the step is off the Goldilocks zone.
  3. Check the analytic implementation against the chain rule. Most adjoint bugs are in the chain — the per-op derivatives are usually right.
  4. Check for non-smoothness. Inequality projections, max / min ops, abs / sign, and discrete branches all introduce kinks. Move the test point away from the kink or use Moreau-envelope smoothing.

Failure modes documented in the codebase

Real examples from the molla history:

  • Splat rotation FD disagreement (Stage 44 v2). The CPU oracle used glam::Quat::Mul which gives q v q* (correct for unit quaternions). The WGSL kernel uses the BAC-CAB formula v + 2qw(qv×v) + 2(qv × (qv × v)) (correct for unit quaternions, different for non-unit). The FD test perturbed q to non-unit and measured a different gradient — fixed by rewriting the CPU oracle to use the same BAC-CAB formula.
  • D6 joint angular-limit adjoint (Stage 23.1.3). The limit projection has a branch on which side of the limit you’re on. Naive adjoint was wrong at the limit boundary. Fix: branch-aware projection that knows which side the gradient should flow.
  • MPM plasticity adjoint (Stage 38.1). The Drucker-Prager return map projects onto a cone surface. The adjoint through the projection needs Moreau-envelope smoothing of the characteristic-function projector — naive backprop misses the Jacobian of the projection.

Each was caught by an FD gradient test that flagged a 10–50% relative error before the adjoint shipped.

  • crates/molla-kernels/tests/splat_*_backward.rs — splat adjoint FD tests, the worked example.

Benchmarks

molla ships criterion benches in the crate that owns the measured functionality. Most physics benches now live under crates/molla-solvers/benches/, geometry benches under crates/molla-geometry/benches/, kernel benches under crates/molla-kernels/benches/, sensor benches under crates/molla-sensors/benches/, and facade/product step benches under crates/molla/benches/. They serve two purposes:

  1. Tracking perf regressions — criterion saves baseline times and reports relative changes per run.
  2. Comparing CPU vs GPU — paired _cpu_vs_gpu benches run both backends in one criterion group so the reports print side-by-side.

This chapter documents what each bench family measures and how to read the output.

Running

The Makefile exposes three convenience targets:

make bench-cpu              # CPU step bench
make bench-gpu              # GPU step bench (needs wgpu adapter)
make bench-featherstone     # CPU-vs-GPU Featherstone in one criterion group

To run a specific bench:

nixVulkan cargo bench -p molla-solvers --bench bench_xpbd_pile_gpu --features gpu

Each bench’s name maps 1:1 to a benches/<name>.rs file in the owning crate. The owning crate’s Cargo.toml [[bench]] sections set required-features = ["gpu"] for GPU benches so they only attempt to build when the feature is on.

Reading criterion output

A typical bench output:

xpbd_pile/cpu_1000      time:   [3.4231 ms 3.4567 ms 3.4923 ms]
xpbd_pile/gpu_1000      time:   [0.4123 ms 0.4256 ms 0.4401 ms]
                        change: [-2.1% -1.4% -0.7%]   (p = 0.03)
                        Performance has improved.
  • The first row reports the CPU bench at N=1000.
  • The second row reports the GPU bench at N=1000.
  • change is relative to the saved baseline (criterion stores baselines under target/criterion/).
  • p = 0.03 is the t-test confidence — values below 0.05 are considered significant.

For the paired _cpu_vs_gpu benches, criterion groups CPU and GPU samples on the same plot so the wall-clock ratio is one chart read.

Async / readback caveats

The GPU benches measure end-to-end wall time including wgpu submit + readback. This matters because:

  • Many GPU kernels are sub-millisecond on the device itself, but the pollster::block_on(device.poll(MaintainBase::Wait)) round trip can dwarf the kernel cost.
  • Persistent-buffer dispatchers (Stage 24d.2 MPM, Stage 41 v6 FEM) amortise the submit cost across substeps; the bench numbers reflect that.

If a bench number looks suspiciously slow, the most common cause is per-substep readback. The fix is the persistent-buffer pattern documented in design rules.

Summary

  • Every solver in prelude has a GPU path and a parity test.
  • Every sensor has a GPU path and a parity test.
  • Every actuator has a GPU path; most have dedicated parity tests, the rest are covered by pipeline tests.
  • The vast majority of FEM steppers have GPU paths. A handful (AMR, magnetostatics, full Signorini, some adjoint paths) ship CPU-only with the GPU port still on the roadmap.
  • Compute primitives (tile, FFT, sort, scan, BSR, splat) are GPU with CPU oracles.

The CPU paths are not deprecated — they remain the debugging path and the oracle for parity testing. The “GPU port still on the roadmap” status applies to a small number of FEM and MPM sub-paths and is tracked in PLAN.md and GAP_v2.md.

Each row is a single brick on the wall. The total count is 597 commits on main at the time of this snapshot, spanning Stage 0 through Stage 51. 132 viewer scenes (numbered through #124, plus unnumbered extras) correspond to a subset of these stages (some stages don’t add a scene, e.g. infra work).

Open items

Current open set (2026-07-02). Most entries below have since landed and carry an inline **Status.** Landed block — they are kept as decision records, not backlog. The genuinely open items are:
